records.title: Facial Flushing
records.intro: Facial flushing is a condition in which blood vessels become abnormally widened (dilated), causing the facial skin to redden easily and the redness to persist. Summer heat and strong ultraviolet (UV) light can worsen symptoms. If symptoms persist or worsen, please see a dermatologist.
records.tags_raw: Facial flushing, Flushing, Rosacea, UV exposure, Vasodilation, Face

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: This is a condition in which blood vessels become abnormally widened, causing the facial skin to redden easily and the redness to last for a long time. It is different from the temporary facial redness caused by embarrassment or emotion.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: Ultraviolet (UV) light damages collagen and elastic fibers, which help keep the skin firm, and causes blood vessels to widen. Collagen is a protein that supports and firms the skin. In particular, if a skin condition called rosacea is present, sun exposure in summer can cause flushing to worsen rapidly.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: When going outside, avoid direct sunlight by wearing a hat or using a parasol. It is important to thoroughly apply a sunscreen that is gentle on the skin to help prevent blood vessels from widening. If symptoms persist or worsen, please see a dermatologist.

records.title: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (“Hamburger Disease”)
records.intro: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a condition in which hemolytic anemia (anemia caused by the destruction of red blood cells), thrombocytopenia (a drop in platelets, the blood components that help stop bleeding), and acute kidney injury (a sudden decline in kidney function) occur together. It is also known as “hamburger disease,” a name that came from cases linked to eating undercooked hamburger patties. It occurs most often in children age 5 and younger. If these symptoms are suspected, please see a medical specialist right away.
records.tags_raw: Hemolytic uremic syndrome, Hamburger disease, HUS, E. coli, Acute kidney injury, Thrombocytopenia, Hemolytic anemia, Body swelling, Face swelling, Leg swelling, Swollen hands and feet, Loose stool, Watery diarrhea, Frequent bowel movements, Blood in stool, Bloody stool, Bright red stool

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a condition in which the following three problems occur together.
· Hemolytic anemia: Anemia caused by the destruction of red blood cells.
· Thrombocytopenia: A drop in platelets, the blood cells that help stop bleeding.
· Acute kidney injury: A sudden decline in kidney function.

HUS is broadly divided into two types: primary (atypical) HUS, which results from dysregulation of the complement system (a group of proteins that assist the immune response), and secondary HUS, which is caused by infection, medications, autoimmune disease, and similar factors.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
More than 70% of cases of HUS that develop after diarrhea are caused by infection with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (such as strain O157). Shiga toxin is a toxic substance produced by this bacteria.

■ Main Routes of Infection
· Eating undercooked meat (especially hamburger patties)
· Drinking insufficiently pasteurized milk or dairy products
· Consuming contaminated water, fruit, or vegetables
· Contact with someone who has diarrhea

HUS is known to occur more often in summer and in rural areas.
It can also occur due to Streptococcus pneumoniae infection or certain autoimmune diseases.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Diarrhea (sometimes bloody) usually appears first. Within the next few days, the following symptoms may also develop.
· Decreased urine output
· Pale skin from anemia
· Easy bruising from thrombocytopenia
· Swelling (edema)

In more than 50% of patients, kidney function declines enough that dialysis (a treatment that filters the blood using a machine) may be needed. Some patients have lasting kidney effects even after recovery, so long-term follow-up is needed. In severe cases, ongoing dialysis may be required.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Reducing the risk of infection is the most important form of prevention.
· Cook meat thoroughly all the way through.
· Wash your hands well before and after preparing food.
· Drink milk and dairy products that have been properly pasteurized.
· Always wash your hands after contact with someone who has diarrhea.
· Wash fruits and vegetables well under running water.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Because there is still no reliable way to stop the disease from progressing once it starts, prevention is especially important.

Please seek medical attention right away if any of the following occur.
· Decreased urine output along with diarrhea
· Pale skin or yellowing of the eyes
· Swelling or easy bruising
If a young child shows these symptoms after diarrhea, see a medical specialist without delay.

Even after recovery, please have kidney function checked at least once a year to monitor for lasting effects.

records.title: Gastric Submucosal Tumor
records.intro: A gastric submucosal tumor is a growth that forms beneath the inner lining (mucosa) of the stomach. It is found in about 1 to 2 out of every 100 people who undergo an upper endoscopy, and most are benign (not harmful to the body). However, some can become malignant, so regular follow-up is needed. If one is found during an endoscopy, please follow your doctor's guidance for management.
records.tags_raw: Gastric submucosal tumor, GIST, Myoma, Lipoma, Upper endoscopy, Endoscopic ultrasound, Biopsy

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
There are several types of gastric submucosal tumors.
· Leiomyoma (myoma): A growth in the muscle layer of the stomach wall, and the most common type.
· GIST (gastrointestinal stromal tumor): A growth arising from the wall of the digestive tract; some GISTs can later become malignant.
· Lipoma: A cluster of fat tissue that appears as a growth.

While ordinary stomach cancer arises from the stomach's inner surface (mucosa), a submucosal tumor develops in the layer beneath the mucosa. Because of this, it appears on endoscopy as a smooth, rounded bulge pushing inward from the stomach wall.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
A gastric submucosal tumor is usually discovered during an upper endoscopy as a smooth, balloon-like bulge in the stomach wall. It can be found through the upper endoscopy offered every two years as part of the national health screening program.

Additional tests may be done for a more precise diagnosis.
· Endoscopic ultrasound: Combines an ultrasound probe with the endoscope to examine the layers of the stomach wall in detail.
· Biopsy: A small sample of the growth is taken and examined under a microscope.

A newer technique has also been developed that allows a biopsy to be taken while viewing the area beneath the mucosa directly, using standard endoscopic equipment.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for a gastric submucosal tumor depends on its type, size, and likelihood of malignancy.

· Watchful waiting: For small, benign-appearing tumors, changes are monitored with regular endoscopic exams.
· Endoscopic or surgical removal: Performed when the tumor is large or malignancy is suspected.

Whether treatment is needed, and which method to use, should be decided after a thorough discussion with your doctor.

records.title: Stomach Cancer
records.intro: Stomach cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the stomach. A malignant tumor is an abnormal mass of cells that harms the body. It is common in Korea, with about 30,000 people diagnosed each year. In its early stages, it often causes no symptoms, which makes it hard to detect early. Regular upper endoscopy is very important for early detection. If you notice unusual symptoms or have concerns, please be sure to see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Stomach cancer, Upper endoscopy, Indigestion, Heartburn, Gastritis, Reflux esophagitis (GERD), Functional gastrointestinal disorder, Endoscopic resection, Regular checkup, Stomach pain, My stomach hurts, Stomachache, Abdominal pain, Food feels stuck, Bloating, Trouble digesting, Burning stomach, Stomach burning, Acid regurgitation

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Stomach cancer is a malignant tumor that arises from the stomach's mucosa (inner lining). It most commonly occurs in people in their 50s or older, but it can also appear in younger adults in their 20s and 30s.

Based on international classification, stomach cancer is broadly divided into two types.

· Intestinal-type stomach cancer: Grows as a distinct mass and is relatively easy to detect by endoscopy. It occurs mainly in people age 50 and older.
· Diffuse-type stomach cancer: Spreads widely beneath the stomach's mucosa without forming a distinct mass. It is harder to detect by endoscopy, and by the time it is diagnosed it has often already progressed. This type is relatively more common in younger patients.

Diffuse-type stomach cancer tends to spread quickly and respond less well to treatment, so its prognosis is less favorable. Even younger patients should stay alert to this risk.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The main risk factors are as follows.
· Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection
· A diet high in spicy or salty food
· Eating processed meat
· Smoking
· A family history of stomach cancer

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Early stomach cancer often causes no symptoms, or symptoms that are hard to tell apart from ordinary gastritis.

Please see a medical specialist if any of the following symptoms persist.
· Indigestion or heartburn lasting more than 2 weeks
· Unexplained weight loss
· Abdominal pain or a feeling of fullness
· Loss of appetite

Even without symptoms, adults age 40 and older are advised to have an upper endoscopy every 2 years.

Bloating or a burning stomach are not considered characteristic symptoms of stomach cancer on their own. However, if you have these symptoms, they may signal a treatable condition such as acid reflux, gastritis, or a stomach ulcer, so an upper endoscopy is recommended. If H. pylori infection is also present, treatment may be needed, since H. pylori is one of the risk factors for stomach cancer.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Surgery for stomach cancer is broadly divided into two types.

■ Curative Resection — surgery aimed at completely removing the cancer
Before surgery, imaging such as abdominal/chest CT and PET-CT (a scan that checks for cancer spread throughout the body) is used to assess whether surgery is possible. The extent of surgery depends on the tumor's location and stage.
· Total gastrectomy (removal of the entire stomach)
· Proximal gastrectomy (removal of the upper part of the stomach)
· Distal gastrectomy (removal of the lower part of the stomach)
· Pylorus-preserving gastrectomy (removal that spares the stomach outlet)
Without complications, the typical hospital stay after surgery is about one week. If the pathology of the removed tissue shows stage 2 or higher, adjuvant chemotherapy for 6 months to 1 year may follow.

■ Palliative Surgery — surgery aimed at relieving complications
Performed when complications such as obstruction, perforation, or bleeding occur. Its main goal is to manage these complications rather than to remove the cancer completely; if the cancer has already spread to other areas, palliative chemotherapy may also be used depending on the patient's overall condition.

The choice of treatment is made by your doctor based on your condition and the cancer's stage. Please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prognosis
sections.content:
Treatment outcomes for stomach cancer vary depending on the stage (how far the cancer has progressed). Thanks to the national cancer screening program, more early-stage stomach cancers are being found, and 5-year survival rates have been improving.
However, some advanced stomach cancers can recur even more than 5 years after surgery. Regular follow-up testing is important, and you should discuss your specific prognosis with your doctor.
※ Survival rate statistics can vary depending on when they were published. The most current statistics are available from the National Cancer Information Center.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Korea's national cancer screening program provides an upper endoscopy or upper GI series (barium X-ray) every 2 years for adults age 40 and older.

Even under age 40, screening is recommended if any of the following apply.
· Persistent indigestion, heartburn, or abdominal pain
· A parent, sibling, or child with a history of stomach cancer

The following lifestyle changes are important for preventing stomach cancer.

■ Foods and Habits to Avoid
· Processed meat, salted fish, salty food, and charred food (especially charred meat or fish): the grilling/charring process can produce carcinogens.
· A diet low in protein and high in refined carbohydrates
· Smoking: as with most cancers, smoking is a major cause of stomach cancer. Quitting is essential, including before and after stomach cancer surgery.
· Heavy alcohol use: alcohol is a known risk factor for stomach cancer.

■ Regular Screening
H. pylori infection, atrophic gastritis (thinning of the stomach lining), gastric adenomatous polyps, and a history of prior stomach surgery can all raise the risk of developing stomach cancer. Detecting and treating these conditions early through periodic upper endoscopy helps prevent stomach cancer.

■ Frequently Asked Questions
■ Does pu-erh tea help before stomach cancer surgery?
A typical amount of pu-erh tea is generally fine to drink before surgery. However, drinking too much can affect liver function, and its caffeine content can disrupt sleep, both of which could actually be harmful to your health before surgery.

■ Is makgeolli good for stomach cancer?
Makgeolli is a type of alcoholic beverage. Since alcohol is a known risk factor for stomach cancer, it is not recommended.

■ Should stomach cancer patients avoid red ginseng and ginseng?
They are not recommended during the immediate recovery period after surgery. Once a patient has recovered without recurrence to a general level of health, they may be consumed, but because they can affect liver function, please consult your doctor before taking them.

■ Does eating charred food cause stomach cancer?
Charred food, especially charred meat or fish, can produce carcinogens during the grilling process. These substances may cause cell mutations that can lead to cancer. It is best to avoid charred food as much as possible.

records.title: Colon Polyps
records.intro: A colon polyp is a benign growth that forms in the colon. Most cause no symptoms and are found incidentally during a colonoscopy. Because some polyps can develop into colorectal cancer, the standard practice is to remove them when they are found. If you are age 40 or older, please have regular colonoscopy screenings.
records.tags_raw: Colon polyp, Adenoma, Colorectal cancer, Colonoscopy, Polypectomy, Bloody stool, Colorectal cancer prevention, Stomach pain, My stomach hurts, Stomachache, Abdominal pain, Low energy, Fatigue, Feeling tired all the time, Can't have a bowel movement, Difficulty passing stool, Hard stool, Blood in stool, Blood in bowel movements, Bright red stool

sections.heading: Definition and Types
sections.content:
A colon polyp is a general term for a benign growth that forms on the lining of the colon.

Polyps are broadly divided into two types.
· Neoplastic (adenomatous) polyps: These can develop into colorectal cancer. The larger the polyp, the higher the chance it contains malignant cells.
· Non-neoplastic polyps (such as hyperplastic or inflammatory polyps): These are very unlikely to develop into cancer.

Because it is often difficult to tell whether a polyp is malignant just by looking at it, any polyp that is found is removed for both diagnostic and treatment purposes.

sections.heading: Causes and Risk Factors
sections.content:
The main causes and risk factors for colon polyps include the following.

· Frequently eating red meat, processed meat, or fatty foods: this can lengthen the time stool stays in the intestine, which may damage the cells of the intestinal lining.
· Obesity
· Alcohol use and smoking
· Excessive intake of carbonated beverages
· A family history of colon polyps or colorectal cancer

Polyps are detected roughly twice as often in men as in women, and detection becomes more frequent from the 40s onward.

sections.heading: Symptoms and Tests
sections.content:
Colon polyps usually cause no symptoms. In rare cases, a large polyp or one that bleeds can cause the following.
· Bloody or mucus-streaked stool
· Anemia from chronic blood loss (dizziness, fatigue, etc.)
· Rarely, signs of bowel obstruction (nausea, vomiting, constipation)

Regular screening is important even without symptoms. Tests used to detect colon polyps include the following.
· Colonoscopy: the most accurate method, allowing polyps to be found and removed in the same procedure.
· Fecal occult blood test (FOBT): checks for hidden blood in the stool.

Korea's national cancer screening program recommends a fecal occult blood test and colonoscopy starting at age 50. Because colorectal cancer has increasingly been diagnosed at younger ages, there is a growing trend toward recommending screening starting at age 45.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Colon polyps are removed during a colonoscopy. The method used depends on the polyp's size and shape.

· Forceps polypectomy: removes small polyps using small forceps.
· Snare polypectomy: uses a wire loop (snare) to grasp and remove the polyp.
· Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR): fluid is injected beneath the polyp before it is removed with a snare.
· Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD): an endoscopic knife is used to dissect and remove the lesion; used for relatively large lesions.

Even after removal, if pathology shows cancer cells at the cut margin, or if the cancer has invaded deeply, additional surgery may be needed.

sections.heading: Post-Procedure Precautions
sections.content:
After polyp removal, temporary abdominal discomfort may occur from air introduced during the procedure. This improves once the gas is passed.

Seek immediate medical attention if any of the following occur.
· Severe abdominal pain
· A large amount of bloody stool
· Dizziness

For 1 to 2 weeks after the procedure, please observe the following.
· Avoid strenuous exercise.
· Avoid alcohol.

A small amount of blood in the stool can occur temporarily after the procedure, but if it persists or worsens, please contact your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The following lifestyle habits can help prevent colon polyps.

· Reduce intake of red meat and processed meat.
· Eat plenty of fiber-rich vegetables and drink water regularly.
· Avoid smoking and alcohol.
· Maintain a healthy weight through regular exercise.

Along with these lifestyle habits, regular colonoscopy screening is the single most important step for preventing colon polyps and colorectal cancer. Please get screened once you reach the recommended age, even without symptoms.

records.title: Sugar Intake and Health
records.intro: Simple sugars, such as table sugar, need little digestion and are absorbed into the bloodstream quickly, which can cause blood sugar to rise sharply. Excessive intake raises the risk of obesity and metabolic disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends limiting free sugars to less than 10% of daily energy intake and suggests a further reduction to less than 5% for additional health benefits. Free sugars include added sugars and sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, and fruit juices.
records.tags_raw: Sugar, Table sugar, Blood sugar, Obesity, Carbohydrates, Simple sugars, Diabetes prevention, Diet

sections.heading: Simple Sugars and Health
sections.content:
Carbohydrates are broken down into glucose through digestion before being absorbed into the bloodstream. Simple sugars, such as table sugar, are different: they need little digestion and are absorbed into the bloodstream quickly, causing blood sugar to rise sharply.

Eating a lot of simple sugar can lead to the following problems.
· Obesity: simple sugars are high in calories and are digested and absorbed quickly, contributing to weight gain.
· Diabetes, high blood pressure, and dyslipidemia: obesity is a major risk factor for these conditions.
· Increased risk of cardiovascular disease

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy intake and suggests a further reduction to below 5% for additional health benefits (about 25 g per day for a 2,000-calorie diet). Free sugars include added sugars and sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, and fruit juices.

sections.heading: How to Eat Sugar Healthily
sections.content:
The following steps can help reduce sugar intake.

· Cut back on foods high in simple sugar, such as soft drinks and snack foods.
· It is better to get glucose from carbohydrate foods like rice and whole grains rather than from added sugar.
· Growing children and teens should also limit simple sugar intake. Water or milk are better choices than sugary drinks.

If you have diabetes or need to manage your blood sugar, please discuss a dietary plan with a medical specialist or a registered dietitian.

sections.heading: Types of Sugar
sections.content:
· White, brown, and dark brown sugar: these differ in how they are processed, but their effect on blood sugar is not significantly different. All are simple sugars that are absorbed quickly.
· Black sugar (heukdang): made by boiling down sugarcane juice without refining it, so it retains small amounts of nutrients such as calcium and iron. However, because of its high sucrose content, eating large amounts can still affect health.
· Corn syrup / starch syrup: made from starch; it is less sweet than sugar but has a similar calorie content.
· Artificial sweeteners (such as saccharin and aspartame): these produce sweetness using far smaller amounts than sugar and are considered safe within the Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) set by recognized authorities such as Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.

Phosphorus (phosphoric acid): found in large amounts in drinks such as cola. Excessive phosphoric acid intake can disrupt the body's calcium balance and negatively affect bone health, as calcium may be pulled from the bones to help neutralize it. For bone health, it is best to limit intake of phosphoric-acid-containing beverages.

records.title: Health Signs Seen in Your Stool
records.intro: The color, shape, and frequency of your stool can reflect the health of your digestive system. It is important to pay attention when you notice a change from your usual pattern. If unusual symptoms persist, please see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Stool, Bloody stool, Black stool, Bowel movements, Stool color change, Gut health, Digestive system, Loose stool, Watery diarrhea, Frequent bowel movements, Blood in stool, Blood in bowel movements, Bright red stool

sections.heading: Why Stool Reflects Your Health
sections.content:
Stool forms as food passes through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and colon. The liver, gallbladder, and pancreas are also involved in this process. As a result, a problem in any of these organs can change the color, shape, or pattern of your stool.

The most important thing is to know your own normal pattern and pay attention when you notice a change from it.

sections.heading: What Stool Color Can Tell You
sections.content:
Stool color varies from person to person depending on diet and bowel function. Pay attention when the color is different from your usual pattern.

· Black stool (the color of black bean noodles/jajangmyeon): may suggest bleeding in the stomach or duodenum. Seek immediate medical attention.
· Bloody stool (red): may suggest bleeding in the colon. Seek immediate medical attention.
· White or gray stool: can occur when bile is not being released properly, which may suggest a liver or bile duct problem.
· Green stool: can occur when bile is not fully broken down in the intestine, and in most cases is not a serious problem.

Black stool or bloody stool always requires immediate evaluation by a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Stool Shape and Bowel Movement Frequency
sections.content:
Bowel movement frequency and stool shape vary widely between individuals. Having a bowel movement 2 to 3 times a day, or once every 2 to 3 days, can both be considered normal as long as there is no discomfort.

What matters most is a sudden change from your own usual pattern. The following changes call for attention.

· Thin, narrow, or ribbon-like stool: may suggest a growth in the colon or rectum.
· Stool that floats and shows oily droplets: may suggest a problem with the gallbladder or pancreas.
· Acute diarrhea: can result from viral or bacterial gastroenteritis and often improves with rest and fluids. However, if it is accompanied by bloody stool or severe dehydration, seek care immediately.
· Chronic diarrhea (lasting several weeks or more): requires further evaluation for conditions such as chronic enteritis or colorectal cancer.

Conditions beyond the digestive system, such as thyroid dysfunction or diabetes, can also affect bowel movements. If unusual symptoms persist, please see a medical specialist.

records.title: Diabetic Retinopathy
records.intro: Diabetic retinopathy is a condition in which prolonged high blood sugar damages the tiny blood vessels and nerve tissue of the retina, the light-sensing layer inside the eye. About 15 to 30% of diabetic patients in Korea have this condition, and it is important to have an annual eye exam even without symptoms. Diabetic retinopathy is one of the three leading causes of blindness in Korea, so early detection and appropriate treatment are essential to protecting your vision.
records.tags_raw: Diabetic retinopathy, Macular edema, Retina, Neovascularization, Vitreous hemorrhage, Retinal detachment, Diabetes complications, Fundus exam, OCT, Vision loss, Blindness, Body swelling, Face swelling, Leg swelling, Swollen hands and feet, Blurry eyes, Trouble seeing, Blurred vision

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The retina is the thin layer of nerve tissue inside the eye that receives light and sends visual information to the brain. When blood sugar remains high over a long period, it damages the retina's tiny blood vessels and nerve tissue. This is called diabetic retinopathy.

■ Stages
- Nonproliferative stage (early to intermediate): the retina's tiny capillaries are damaged, causing small areas of bleeding. If there is no swelling in the macula (the center of the retina responsible for central vision), patients often notice no particular symptoms.

- Proliferative stage (advanced): in response to a lack of oxygen, fragile new blood vessels form on the surface of the retina. If these vessels rupture, they can cause vitreous hemorrhage (bleeding inside the eye) or retinal detachment (the retina pulling away from the back of the eye).

■ Macular Edema
When swelling develops in the macula, the center of the retina, it can cause blurred vision, reduced visual acuity, and distortion of central vision. If a change in glasses or contact lenses does not improve your vision, you should see an ophthalmologist.

sections.heading: Screening and Diagnosis
sections.content:
■ When to Get Screened
- Type 1 diabetes: a retinal exam should be done within 5 years of diagnosis.
- Type 2 diabetes: a retinal exam should be done at the time of diagnosis.
- Afterward: an annual eye exam is needed even without symptoms.

■ Testing Methods
- Fundus photography: takes photographs to check the condition of the retina.
- Fluorescein angiography: checks the condition of blood vessels and whether they are leaking.
- Optical coherence tomography (OCT): examines the retina's structure in detail to check for macular edema.

These tests can detect small areas of bleeding, swelling, or new blood vessel growth at an early stage.

When one eye is relatively unaffected, it can be hard to notice vision loss in the other eye. At home, cover one eye at a time to compare your vision, and see an ophthalmologist right away if you notice a difference.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Treating Macular Edema
This is most often treated with an anti-VEGF injection given directly into the eye. Because recurrence is common, repeated injections are often needed.

■ Treating Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
- Laser photocoagulation: uses a laser on the retina to suppress the growth of new blood vessels.
- Injection therapy: medication that suppresses new blood vessel growth is injected into the eye.
- Surgery: needed if vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment occurs. Once the disease reaches this stage, recovering vision can be difficult, which is why early detection is so important.

sections.heading: Risk Factors and Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
■ Main Risk Factors
- High blood sugar: the most important risk factor.
- High blood pressure and dyslipidemia: these should be managed alongside blood sugar.
- Smoking: narrows blood vessels and increases oxidative stress, accelerating damage to the retina's blood vessels. Quitting smoking is essential.

■ Lifestyle Management
- Manage blood sugar, blood pressure, and lipid levels appropriately through regular exercise and diet.
- Just as regular visits to an internal medicine doctor are needed for blood sugar control, an annual eye exam should become a routine habit, even without symptoms.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Diabetes Complications and Management
records.intro: When blood sugar remains high over time, diabetes can lead to complications in several organs, including the eyes, kidneys, nerves, and cardiovascular system. Preventing these complications requires blood sugar control along with managing blood pressure and cholesterol/lipid levels, as well as regular complication screening. Please continue treatment consistently with your doctor.
records.tags_raw: Diabetes, Diabetes complications, Blood sugar control, HbA1c, Retinopathy, Nephropathy, Neuropathy, Cardiovascular disease

sections.heading: Key Complications and Screening Tests
sections.content:
The main complications of diabetes and the screening tests needed for each are as follows.

· Diabetic retinopathy (eyes): a common cause of blindness in adults. An annual fundus exam (a test that checks the condition of the retina) is needed.
· Diabetic nephropathy (kidneys): a common cause of end-stage renal disease (complete loss of kidney function). An annual urine albumin test and glomerular filtration rate (GFR, a measure of kidney function) test are needed.
· Diabetic neuropathy (nerves): can lead to foot ulcers and lower-limb amputation. An annual neuropathy screening test is needed.
· Cardiovascular disease: the leading cause of death among people with diabetes. An annual assessment of cardiovascular risk factors is needed.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
Medication alone is not enough to manage diabetes. Lifestyle changes need to go hand in hand with treatment.

· Regular exercise
· A balanced diet: moderate carbohydrate intake, with plenty of vegetables and an appropriate amount of protein.
· Not smoking
· Limiting alcohol
· Maintaining a healthy weight

Diabetes can be well controlled with consistent management. Please have regular follow-up visits with your doctor.

sections.heading: Blood Sugar Control
sections.content:
The primary goal of diabetes management is preventing complications. Good blood sugar control can reduce microvascular complications, particularly those affecting the eyes, kidneys, and nerves.

Blood sugar control is tracked using the following measures.
· HbA1c (glycated hemoglobin): reflects average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. The general target is below 6.5%, though this is adjusted individually based on the patient's age, presence of complications, and risk of low blood sugar.
· Self-monitoring of blood glucose: using a glucose meter to check fasting blood sugar (80–130 mg/dL) and blood sugar 2 hours after a meal (under 180 mg/dL).

Your target blood sugar range and how to reach it should be decided together with your doctor.

sections.heading: Managing Blood Pressure and Dyslipidemia
sections.content:
People with diabetes often also have high blood pressure and dyslipidemia. Managing these together is necessary to help prevent cardiovascular complications.

· Blood pressure: the general target is a systolic pressure under 130 mmHg and a diastolic pressure under 80 mmHg. (mmHg is the unit used to measure blood pressure.)
· LDL cholesterol (“bad” cholesterol): targets depend on cardiovascular risk. A level below 100 mg/dL is generally recommended for patients who have had diabetes for less than 10 years and have no major cardiovascular risk factors or target organ damage. The target is generally below 70 mg/dL when diabetes has lasted 10 years or longer, or when major cardiovascular risk factors or target organ damage are present. A target below 55 mg/dL, with at least a 50% reduction from baseline, is recommended for patients with cardiovascular disease. A target below 55 mg/dL may also be considered for selected patients with target organ damage or three or more major cardiovascular risk factors, even without established cardiovascular disease.

If medication is needed, please follow your doctor's prescription.

records.title: Colorectal Cancer
records.intro: Colorectal cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the colon or rectum. It often causes no symptoms in its early stages, which makes regular colonoscopy screening important. A balanced diet and healthy lifestyle habits can help with prevention.
records.tags_raw: Colorectal cancer, Colonoscopy, Bloody stool, Polyps, Rectal cancer, Colorectal cancer prevention, Hereditary colorectal cancer, Dietary fiber, Low energy, Fatigue, Feeling tired all the time, Can't have a bowel movement, Difficulty passing stool, Hard stool, Blood in stool, Blood in bowel movements, Bright red stool

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Colorectal cancer is cancer that develops in the colon, the organ through which digested food passes. The section closest to the anus is called the rectum, and the rest is called the colon; a cancerous growth in either of these is called colorectal cancer.

Colorectal cancer is one of the most common cancers among Koreans. Because it often causes no symptoms in its early stages, it can be hard to notice. Regular colonoscopy screening and evaluation by a colorectal surgeon are essential.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Colorectal cancer causes almost no symptoms in its early stages. When symptoms do appear, the cancer has often already progressed to some degree.

■ General Symptoms
Weight loss, fatigue, poor appetite, anemia

■ Symptoms by Location
· Right-sided colon cancer: black stool, anemia, and sometimes a palpable mass in the abdomen.
· Left-sided colon cancer: bowel obstruction, constipation, and bright red bloody stool are common.
· Rectal cancer: bloody stool, a feeling of incomplete emptying, and narrow, thin stool.

Having constipation or bloody stool does not automatically mean you have colorectal cancer. However, if these symptoms persist, please have a colonoscopy.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Colorectal cancer develops from a combination of genetic factors, diet, and lifestyle.

■ Hereditary Colorectal Cancer
Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) are the main hereditary forms and together account for about 5% of all colorectal cancers. You are in a higher-risk group if a family member has had colorectal cancer, colon polyps, endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, or stomach cancer. If a first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or child) has had colorectal cancer, your risk can increase 2 to 8 times, so proactive early screening is important.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: If found early, colorectal cancer can often be removed simply through an endoscope without surgery. However, once the disease has progressed further, it needs to be surgically removed, typically through laparoscopic surgery (using small incisions in the abdomen) or robotic surgery. The treatment approach should be discussed with your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· Eat a balanced amount of protein, carbohydrates, and fat
· Limit red meat and animal fat, and reduce high-calorie foods
· Eat plenty of fiber-rich foods such as fresh vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, and seaweed
· Limit processed meat, salty food, smoked food, and fast food
· Avoid smoking and alcohol
· Maintain a healthy weight through regular exercise
· Some reports suggest that taking probiotics after colorectal cancer surgery may help restore gut microbiota

Above all, regular colonoscopy screening is the most important step.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content:
■ Diagnosis
Colonoscopy is the single most important test for diagnosing and preventing colorectal cancer. Under the national cancer screening program, adults age 50 and older can receive an annual fecal occult blood test, followed by a colonoscopy if the result is abnormal.

■ Treatment
Treatment for colorectal cancer depends on its stage (stage 1 to 4).
· Stages 1–3: surgery is the primary treatment, combined with chemotherapy depending on the stage.
· Stage 4 (with metastasis): chemotherapy is the main treatment, and surgery may also be considered in some cases.

Please discuss the treatment approach thoroughly with your doctor.

records.title: Aortic Valve Stenosis
records.intro: Aortic valve stenosis is a condition in which the aortic valve — a one-way door between the heart and the aorta that keeps blood flowing in a single direction — no longer opens properly, restricting blood flow. It is a common condition of aging: more than 1 in 10 people age 80 and older have it. In patients with severe disease and symptoms, the condition can worsen quickly without appropriate treatment, so evaluation by a medical specialist is very important.
records.tags_raw: Aortic valve stenosis, Aortic valve, TAVI, Heart valve, Age-related disease, Chest ache, Chest pain, Tight chest, Chest tightness, Collapsing, Losing consciousness, Fainting

sections.heading: Definition and Causes
sections.content:
The aortic valve opens to let blood flow from the heart into the aorta, and closes to prevent blood from flowing backward. As this valve opens and closes tens of thousands of times a day, it can gradually age along with the rest of the body and stop opening fully. This is aortic valve stenosis.
It can also occur at a younger age in people born with a valve that has only two leaflets instead of three (a bicuspid aortic valve), or in people with rheumatic heart disease.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Most patients have no particular symptoms for years while the stenosis slowly progresses. As the disease advances and places strain on the heart, the following symptoms can appear.
· Syncope (sudden loss of consciousness)
· Shortness of breath
· Chest pain

If any of these symptoms occur, please see a medical specialist promptly. In patients with severe disease and symptoms, the condition can worsen quickly without appropriate treatment.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
As blood flows through the narrowed valve, it produces a characteristic heart murmur (an abnormal sound heard through a stethoscope), which allows a doctor to suspect the condition during a physical exam. If a murmur is heard, an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) is used to confirm the diagnosis and assess its severity.
When surgical treatment may be needed, cardiac catheterization (a test in which a thin tube is guided through a blood vessel to closely examine the heart) is used to evaluate severity more precisely.
Patients diagnosed with moderate or greater stenosis should have regular follow-up and avoid strenuous exercise.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Medication plays only a supportive role, easing symptoms when heart failure is also present. For severe, symptomatic patients, medication alone has limited benefit, and valve replacement is needed to improve survival.

There are two approaches to valve treatment.

① Surgical treatment (valve replacement surgery): the damaged valve is replaced with a new one through open-heart surgery. The heart is stopped during the operation and a heart-lung machine is used.

② Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI): a non-surgical treatment in which a guide wire is passed through a blood vessel in the thigh to place a new artificial valve inside the old one. Because the chest is not opened, recovery is faster. The procedure varies by patient but can often be completed within an hour.

Whether surgery or TAVI is the more appropriate option is decided jointly by a team of specialists — including cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, and radiology — based on the patient's age, underlying conditions, blood vessel condition, and valve anatomy.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Aortic valve stenosis often goes unnoticed for a long time before symptoms appear. If you are older, have a known heart murmur, or experience unexplained fainting, shortness of breath, or chest pain, please be sure to see a cardiologist.
Because treatment can vary from patient to patient, please discuss your options thoroughly with a medical specialist.

records.title: Aortic Dissection
records.intro: Aortic dissection is a medical emergency in which the wall of the aorta — the largest artery in the body — tears starting from its inner layer. It is marked by the sudden onset of severe, stabbing chest pain. Without prompt treatment, it can be life-threatening. If these symptoms occur, please call emergency services (119 in Korea) right away and go to the emergency room.
records.tags_raw: Aortic dissection, Chest pain, Aorta, Emergency, High blood pressure, Cardiothoracic surgery, Vascular graft, Stent, Acute aortic dissection, Chest ache, Tight chest, Chest tightness, Weakness in arms or legs, One-sided weakness

sections.heading: What Is Aortic Dissection?
sections.content:
The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It begins at the heart and runs through the chest (thoracic aorta) and abdomen (abdominal aorta) before dividing just above the legs. Like the trunk of a large tree, it is the central pathway that supplies blood to the entire body.

The aortic wall has three layers, from the inside out: the intima, the media, and the adventitia. Aortic dissection occurs when the innermost layer, the intima, tears, allowing blood to flow into the space within the media, peeling the layers of the aortic wall apart much like the skin of an apple. “Dissection” refers to this separation of the layers.

The condition is classified as acute for the first 2 weeks after onset, and chronic afterward. It occurs most often in men in their 40s to 60s, and is about twice as common in men as in women.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The hallmark symptom of aortic dissection is the sudden onset of extremely severe pain.

■ Characteristics of the Pain
· A sudden, sharp pain often described as stabbing or tearing
· So severe that it can be difficult to control even with opioid pain medication
· Eases only once blood pressure is brought under control

■ Location of the Pain
The location of the pain depends on where the dissection occurs.
· Dissection near the heart (ascending aorta): pain in the front of the chest
· Dissection toward the back (descending thoracic aorta): severe pain in the back or lower back
· Dissection of the abdominal aorta: abdominal pain

In addition to pain, sudden loss of consciousness or weakness/paralysis in the arms or legs can also occur. If these symptoms appear, please call emergency services (119) right away.

Because the chest pain can resemble that of a heart attack (a blockage in the heart's blood vessels), testing is used to distinguish between the two.

sections.heading: Causes and Risk Factors
sections.content:
The most important cause of aortic dissection is high blood pressure, which is present in about 80% of patients.

■ Main Risk Factors
· High blood pressure (the most important factor)
· Smoking
· Diabetes
· Dyslipidemia
· Obesity and older age

■ Congenital and Genetic Causes
· Bicuspid aortic valve (an aortic valve that develops with an atypical structure from birth)
· Marfan syndrome (a genetic disorder affecting connective tissue)
· Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

Because these genetic and congenital causes can lead to aortic dissection even at a young age, regular checkups are important for people with these conditions.

Managing blood pressure is the single most important step in prevention.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
When aortic dissection is suspected, the following tests are performed quickly.

· Blood tests: used to help rule out other conditions.
· Electrocardiogram (ECG): helps distinguish the condition from a heart attack and similar conditions.
· Chest CT scan: the most important test for confirming aortic dissection. It precisely locates the dissection and helps determine whether surgery is needed.

Because treatment differs greatly depending on where the dissection is located, a fast diagnosis is essential.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment is determined by the location and extent of the dissection.

■ Surgical Treatment
When the dissection involves the portion of the aorta leaving the heart (the ascending aorta), immediate surgery is the standard approach. The torn section of the aorta is replaced with a vascular graft.

■ Medical Treatment
For dissections that do not involve the ascending aorta (such as the descending thoracic aorta), blood pressure-lowering medication is used first.

■ Stent Placement
If a dissection of the descending thoracic aorta cuts off blood flow to the abdominal organs or legs, a stent (a graft placed inside the vessel) may be inserted.

■ Hybrid Surgery
In a hybrid operating room, where both surgery and catheter-based procedures can be performed, the team can switch immediately to open surgery if the procedure is difficult or unsuccessful, allowing a faster response in an emergency.

After treatment, it is important to continue managing your overall health, including blood pressure, and to attend regular follow-up visits. The specific treatment is decided by your doctor based on your condition.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Because aortic dissection can immediately become a life-threatening emergency, prevention is especially important.

■ Managing the Four Preventable Risk Factors
· High blood pressure: measure your blood pressure regularly and take your medication consistently.
· Smoking: quit smoking.
· Dyslipidemia: cut back on high-fat foods and get regular checkups.
· Diabetes: keep your blood sugar well controlled.

■ General Lifestyle Habits
· Maintain a healthy weight through regular exercise.
· Eat a balanced diet.
· If you have a related condition such as a bicuspid aortic valve or Marfan syndrome, please have regular checkups with a cardiovascular and thoracic surgery specialist.

records.title: Metabolic Syndrome
records.intro: Metabolic syndrome refers to having at least 3 of the following conditions together: high blood sugar, high blood pressure, dyslipidemia, and abdominal obesity. Having metabolic syndrome raises the risk of serious conditions such as heart attack, stroke, and type 2 diabetes. It can be effectively prevented and managed through early detection and lifestyle changes, so please check your own status through regular health checkups and evaluation by a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Metabolic syndrome, Insulin resistance, Abdominal obesity, Visceral fat, High blood sugar, High blood pressure, Dyslipidemia, Triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
Metabolic syndrome may improve significantly with lifestyle changes.

■ Exercise
Do at least 30 minutes of aerobic exercise, such as walking, regularly each day.

■ Diet
- Cut back on processed foods and sugar.
- Maintain a diet centered on fiber-rich vegetables and whole grains.
- Limit alcohol, since excessive drinking raises triglyceride levels.

■ Weight Management
Losing just 5–10% of your current body weight can improve blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels all at once.

■ Sleep
A regular sleep schedule can help improve insulin resistance.

If lifestyle changes alone are not enough, medication — such as blood pressure medication, blood sugar medication, or a lipid-lowering drug — may need to be added. Please be sure to discuss this with a medical specialist before deciding.

sections.heading: Diagnostic Criteria and Risks
sections.content:
■ Diagnostic Criteria
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when 3 or more of the following 5 criteria are present.
- Waist circumference: 90 cm or more for men, 85 cm or more for women (Korean standard)
- Triglycerides: 150 mg/dL or higher
- HDL cholesterol: under 40 mg/dL for men, under 50 mg/dL for women
- Blood pressure: 130/85 mmHg or higher, or currently taking blood pressure medication
- Fasting blood sugar: 100 mg/dL or higher, or currently taking blood sugar medication

■ Risks of Leaving It Untreated
If metabolic syndrome is left untreated, high blood pressure, diabetes, and dyslipidemia can worsen, raising the risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease and early death. The risk of heart attack or stroke becomes more than twice as high as in people without the syndrome.
The following habits increase the risk of metabolic syndrome.
· Irregular meals and overeating
· Excessive consumption of instant/processed foods
· Frequent alcohol use
· Lack of exercise
· Irregular sleep
· Smoking

Even without symptoms, check these values regularly through health checkups, and see a medical specialist if any are abnormal.

sections.heading: What Is Metabolic Syndrome?
sections.content:
Metabolic syndrome is a state in which 3 or more of the following occur together in one person: high blood sugar, high blood pressure, dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides and/or reduced HDL cholesterol), and abdominal obesity. Rather than being separate, unrelated conditions, these problems tend to arise together from a shared underlying cause.

■ The Core Cause: Insulin Resistance
Insulin is the hormone that lowers blood sugar. When the body no longer responds properly to insulin, this is called “insulin resistance.” Once insulin resistance develops, blood sugar becomes harder to control; the body compensates by releasing more insulin, which increases sodium retention and raises blood pressure, and increases fat production in the liver, which raises triglyceride levels. Insulin resistance alone can therefore lead to abnormalities in blood sugar, blood pressure, and lipids all at once.

■ The Danger of Visceral Fat
Abdominal obesity — especially visceral fat concentrated around the upper abdomen — is a key risk factor for metabolic syndrome. Visceral fat harms blood vessel health and interferes with how insulin works. If your waistband feels tighter than before, or you find yourself wanting to loosen your belt, this can be a sign that lifestyle changes are needed.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The key to preventing and managing metabolic syndrome is correcting lifestyle habits.

· Regular exercise: helps reduce abdominal fat.
· Dietary changes: avoid overeating, and cut back on instant/processed food and alcohol.
· Not smoking
· Getting enough sleep
· Managing stress

Managing your waist circumference is especially important. A reduction in waist circumference is a more meaningful indicator of improved health than weight loss alone.

If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, exercise and dietary changes can help prevent and manage both conditions together.

If lifestyle changes alone do not lead to improvement, medication for diabetes, high blood pressure, or dyslipidemia may be considered. Please discuss this with your doctor.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
Metabolic syndrome may improve significantly with lifestyle changes.

■ Exercise
Do at least 30 minutes of aerobic exercise, such as walking, regularly each day.

■ Diet
- Cut back on processed foods and sugar.
- Maintain a diet centered on fiber-rich vegetables and whole grains.
- Limit alcohol, since excessive drinking raises triglyceride levels.

■ Weight Management
Losing just 5–10% of your current body weight can improve blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels all at once.

■ Sleep
A regular sleep schedule can help improve insulin resistance.

If lifestyle changes alone are not enough, medication — such as blood pressure medication, blood sugar medication, or a lipid-lowering drug — may need to be added. Please be sure to discuss this with a medical specialist before deciding.

sections.heading: Importance of Regular Checkups
sections.content:
Metabolic syndrome often causes no clear symptoms in its early stages, so it is frequently discovered incidentally during a health checkup.

■ Recommended Regular Screening
Please have your waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting blood sugar, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol checked regularly. If several of these values come back abnormal together on a health checkup, it may not simply be several separate problems — it could be a sign of metabolic syndrome.

If your waist circumference has been increasing, review your lifestyle habits now and work with a medical specialist to build a management plan.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
records.intro: Herpes zoster (shingles) is an infectious disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus. It is marked by severe pain and a band-like skin rash. If symptoms appear, it is important to see a medical specialist as soon as possible.
records.tags_raw: Herpes zoster, Shingles, Chickenpox, Virus, Neuralgia, Rash, Vaccination, Immune system, Low energy, Fatigue, Feeling tired all the time

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Shingles is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox in childhood. Even after chickenpox has healed, this virus remains dormant in the nerve ganglia (clusters of nerve cells) and can reactivate when the immune system weakens, causing shingles.
· It occurs most often in older adults. The risk rises significantly from age 60 onward.
· It can appear when immunity is weakened by stress, fatigue, or other illnesses.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· The rash appears in a band-like pattern and, characteristically, never crosses the body's midline.
· It often begins with a stiff, achy, or itchy sensation, similar to a muscle strain, before red patches and blisters develop.
· The skin rash usually clears up within 3 to 4 weeks, but pain can persist for 1 to 3 months.
· Postherpetic neuralgia: pain that continues for 3 months or more after the skin lesions have healed. This is the most common and most painful complication of shingles, and the risk is higher in people age 60 and older.

sections.heading: Treatment and Prevention
sections.content:
· Starting treatment quickly is essential. Beginning antiviral treatment within 72 hours (3 days) of the rash appearing significantly lowers the risk of lasting pain.
· If you suspect these symptoms, please see a medical specialist right away.
· Vaccination: adults age 50 and older are advised to get the shingles vaccine, which offers strong protection.

records.title: Flu (Influenza)
records.intro: The flu (influenza) is a respiratory infection caused by the influenza virus, and its cause and symptoms differ from those of the common cold. Annual vaccination is recommended each fall (September to November). If you develop symptoms such as high fever or severe muscle aches, please see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Flu, Influenza, Flu vaccination, Common cold, Influenza vaccine, Quadrivalent vaccine, Pneumonia, Sore throat, Scratchy throat, Pain when swallowing, Dry cough, Lingering cough, Cough that won't stop, Stuffy nose, Clear runny nose, Yellow nasal discharge

sections.heading: Differences Between the Flu and a Common Cold
sections.content:
The flu and the common cold differ in both their cause and their symptoms.

· Common cold: caused by more than 200 different viruses, including rhinovirus. Symptoms mainly include cough, runny nose, and sore throat.
· Flu: caused by the influenza virus. It causes prominent whole-body symptoms, such as high fever, severe muscle aches, and body aches.

The flu can lead to complications such as pneumonia or middle ear infection. If you suspect you have the flu, please see a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Why Annual Vaccination Is Necessary
sections.content:
The flu vaccine needs to be given every year, for two reasons.
· The antibodies produced by the vaccine gradually decline after about 6 months.
· The strains of influenza virus circulating can change from year to year.

Even if you had the flu last year, you should still be vaccinated again this year. Rather than fully preventing the flu, vaccination mainly makes symptoms milder and lowers the risk of complications if you do get infected.

Because it takes about 2 weeks after vaccination for antibodies to fully develop, it is best to complete vaccination between September and November, before flu season begins.

sections.heading: Recommended Recipients and Vaccine Types
sections.content:
Flu vaccination is strongly recommended for the following groups.
· Children, adults age 65 and older, and pregnant women
· People with chronic conditions such as diabetes or cardiovascular disease
· People with a weakened immune system
· Healthcare workers and family members who are in frequent contact with high-risk individuals

There are two types of flu vaccine: trivalent and quadrivalent.
· Trivalent vaccine: protects against 2 strains of influenza A and 1 strain of influenza B.
· Quadrivalent vaccine: protects against 2 strains of influenza A and 2 strains of influenza B.

For children (age 6 months to 8 years) receiving the vaccine for the first time, 2 doses are needed, 4 weeks apart. For adults, a single dose is sufficient.

sections.heading: Vaccination Precautions
sections.content:
Please consult a medical specialist before vaccination in the following situations.
· A serious reaction to a flu vaccine in the past
· Currently being treated for an acute illness (a mild cold without fever is not a reason to delay vaccination)

After vaccination, please keep the following in mind.
· Stay at the medical facility for 20 to 30 minutes afterward to be monitored for any reaction.
· It is best to avoid showering on the day of vaccination, since bacteria could enter through the injection site.

Pregnant women can receive the flu vaccine regardless of the stage of pregnancy, and it has been confirmed to be safe for the fetus.

sections.heading: Preventive Lifestyle Habits
sections.content:
In addition to vaccination, the following habits can help prevent the flu.
· Wash your hands frequently.
· When coughing or sneezing, cover your mouth and nose with a tissue, handkerchief, or your sleeve rather than your bare hands.
· During flu season, try to limit visits to crowded places. Extra caution is especially important for children, older adults, pregnant women, and people with chronic conditions, who have weaker immunity.

records.title: Frostbite
records.intro: Frostbite occurs when body tissue exposed to severe cold freezes. It most often affects exposed areas such as the fingers, toes, nose, and ears. In severe cases, the tissue can undergo necrosis (tissue death), which may require amputation of the affected body part. If you suspect frostbite, protect the area from refreezing and seek medical care right away.
records.tags_raw: Frostbite, Cold-related illness, Chilblains, Cold wave, Necrosis, Fingers, Toes, Winter health

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
You can help prevent frostbite in the following ways.

· Wear several thin layers of clothing, and protect exposed areas with gloves, a scarf, and a hat.
· Wet gloves or shoes make frostbite more likely. Change into dry ones right away.
· In cold environments, check your hands and feet often for any change in sensation.
· Older adults, children, and people with chronic conditions need to be especially careful.
· Alcohol reduces your ability to feel the cold, which raises the risk of frostbite. Please be careful.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: Third- and fourth-degree frostbite can require surgical treatment, so evaluation by a medical specialist is essential.

sections.heading: First Aid
sections.content:
When frostbite occurs, the most important thing is to prevent the affected area from freezing again.

① Remove any clothing, socks, or gloves from the affected area and move to a warm environment.
② Soak the area in warm water at 40–42°C (104–108°F) for 20 to 30 minutes. Check whether the skin color is returning to normal.
③ Water that is too hot, or applying direct heat, can make the damage worse. Never warm the area directly with a hot stove or heating pad.
④ Rubbing or massaging the affected area can cause further cell damage. Please avoid doing this. If blisters form, do not pop them; leave them intact to help prevent infection.
⑤ After first aid, be sure to visit a medical facility and see a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Frostbite occurs when soft tissue (such as skin and muscle) freezes and its blood supply is cut off due to exposure to severe cold, roughly –2°C to –10°C (28°F to 14°F).
The following situations make frostbite more likely.
· Having a blood-vessel-related condition such as diabetes, Raynaud's syndrome (a condition in which cold causes the blood vessels in the hands and feet to narrow), ischemic heart disease, or stroke
· Having blood vessels that are more vulnerable to cold, as in children or older adults
· Having weakened blood vessel function from chronic alcohol use or smoking
· Having blood circulation restricted by tight shoes, gloves, belts, watches, or rings

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Frostbite is a condition in which body tissue freezes from exposure to extreme cold. As skin temperature drops, blood flow to the area decreases. If blood flow is cut off completely, the tissue can suffer irreversible damage — damage that cannot be undone. Once skin temperature drops below freezing, cells freeze and are damaged, blood vessels constrict, and blood clots can form inside them, which can lead to tissue necrosis (tissue death).

Frostbite most often affects exposed areas farthest from the heart, such as the fingers, toes, nose, and ears.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Frostbite is classified into 4 degrees based on severity.

· 1st degree: the skin becomes swollen and red. Tingling or numbness may occur.
· 2nd degree: blisters form, and the outer layer of skin (epidermis) undergoes necrosis.
· 3rd degree: necrosis extends deeper into the skin and the tissue beneath it (subcutaneous tissue).
· 4th degree: necrosis reaches the bone and the skin turns black. Amputation of the affected body part may be required.

A frostbitten area often feels numb or tingly at first. Numbness does not mean the area is safe. If these symptoms appear, please see a medical specialist right away.

records.title: Chilblains
records.intro: Chilblains are a skin inflammation that develops after prolonged exposure to low temperatures of around 5–10°C (41–50°F) or damp, cold conditions. They are a milder form of cold-related injury than frostbite, but if symptoms are severe or keep recurring, please see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Chilblains, Cold-related injury, Frostbite, Cold exposure, Blood vessels, Fingers and toes, Body swelling, Face swelling, Leg swelling, Swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Chilblains can develop even without freezing temperatures, from prolonged exposure to a damp, cold environment around 5°C (41°F). They are the mildest form of cold-related injury.
· They tend to occur on the fingers, toes, heels, nose, ears, and legs.
· They occur more easily in people whose blood vessels are especially sensitive to cold.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· There are usually no symptoms at first; over time, red or purplish swelling (an inflamed, swollen area) develops.
· This is often accompanied by itching, a stinging pain, or a burning sensation.
· In severe cases, blisters or skin ulcers can form.
· Symptoms usually develop over several hours and clear up on their own within 2 to 3 weeks.
· In chronic cases, the condition tends to recur every cold season and disappear once the weather warms up.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
· Keep the affected area warm and get adequate rest.
· Medication suited to your symptoms can be considered after consulting a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· For prevention, focus on staying warm and avoiding exposure to cold air and dampness.
· Regular exercise, not smoking, and taking vitamins can help.
· Soaking your hands and feet in warm water or massaging them regularly can help improve blood circulation.

records.title: Head and Neck Cancer
records.intro: Head and neck cancer is a general term for malignant tumors that develop in the head and neck region, including the larynx, oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, nasal cavity, and nasopharynx. Because this area is involved in essential everyday functions such as breathing, swallowing, and speaking, treatment can be challenging. If you have a voice change lasting more than 6 weeks, a mouth sore that doesn't heal after 3 weeks, or a lump in the neck, please see an ENT (ear, nose, and throat) specialist.
records.tags_raw: Head and neck cancer, Laryngeal cancer, Oral cancer, Oropharyngeal cancer, Pharyngeal cancer, Neck lump, Voice change, Difficulty swallowing, ENT (otolaryngology), Body swelling, Face swelling, Leg swelling, Swollen hands and feet, Weakness in arms or legs, One-sided weakness

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Head and neck cancer includes all cancers that arise in the head and neck region. This includes the larynx (the voice box), oral cavity (mouth), oropharynx (upper throat), hypopharynx (lower throat), nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses (spaces around the nose), nasopharynx (behind the nose), salivary glands, and thyroid gland.

The head and neck have a complex anatomical structure and are responsible for functions essential to survival and quality of life, such as breathing, swallowing, speaking, and articulation. Because of this, preserving these functions is just as important as removing the cancer when treating head and neck cancer.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
If any of the following symptoms persist, head and neck cancer should be considered, and you should see an ENT specialist.

· A voice change lasting more than 6 weeks
· A mouth ulcer that hasn't healed after 3 weeks
· Swelling inside the mouth lasting more than 3 weeks
· Red or white patches on the oral mucosa
· Difficulty swallowing lasting more than 3 weeks
· Persistent one-sided nasal blockage or unusual discharge
· Loose teeth unrelated to gum disease
· A neck lump lasting more than 3 weeks
· Cranial nerve symptoms such as facial paralysis
· One-sided ear fullness lasting more than 3 weeks

A sore or growth in the mouth that lasts a long time may bleed. You may also feel something stuck in your throat or have pain when swallowing. If you can feel a hard lump in the neck, the cancer may have already spread.

Even if a symptom has lasted less than the periods listed above, please see a medical specialist if it concerns you.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
There are three main treatments for head and neck cancer: surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. These may be used alone or in combination.

· For early-stage cancer, surgery or radiation therapy alone is often used.
· For more advanced cancer, surgery combined with radiation therapy, or radiation therapy combined with chemotherapy, is often used.

The treatment approach is decided by a multidisciplinary team centered on otolaryngology (ENT), in which specialists from several fields consult together, taking into account the tumor's location, stage, pathology, and the patient's overall condition.

Minimally invasive techniques — such as transoral surgery using the da Vinci robotic system and endoscopic surgery — have been advancing in recent years, helping to reduce functional damage to patients.

sections.heading: Radiation Therapy
sections.content:
Radiation therapy plays an important role in treating head and neck cancer.

· For early-stage lesions, it can sometimes be as effective as surgery.
· For advanced cancer, it is mainly used as an adjuvant treatment after surgery.

Radiation therapy can help treat microscopic residual cancer or lymph node metastasis. However, it can cause side effects such as reduced saliva production and skin fibrosis.

Techniques such as 3D conformal radiation therapy and intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) have been advancing in recent years, helping to minimize radiation damage to healthy tissue. Please discuss the choice of treatment with a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Reconstruction After Surgery
sections.content:
To repair the defect left after head and neck cancer surgery, tissue is transplanted from another part of the patient's own body.

A free flap procedure is a highly technical surgery in which skin, muscle, and their blood vessels are taken together and transplanted, with the blood vessels reconnected under a microscope. Because the patient's own tissue is used, immunosuppressant medication is not needed.

More recently, the perforator flap — which takes only a thin layer of skin and its blood vessels without muscle — has become widely used. Its thin, flexible tissue allows for more natural reconstruction, which is favorable for both function and appearance.

This is a specialized surgery performed at medical centers with an experienced reconstruction team. Please discuss the treatment approach thoroughly with your doctor.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Robotic surgery can help preserve eating and speaking function closer to normal, improving quality of life. However, depending on the location and size of the tumor, traditional open surgery may sometimes be the better option, so a thorough discussion with your doctor is needed.

records.title: Headache
records.intro: Headache is a common symptom that almost anyone can experience, but it can also be a sign of a brain condition or a nervous system problem. If you find yourself relying too heavily on pain relievers to get rid of headaches, or if headaches are interfering with daily life, please don't try to judge the cause yourself — see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Headache, Migraine, Tension-type headache, Cerebral hemorrhage, Stress, Sleep disorder, Caffeine, Neurology, Head pain, Splitting headache, Pain at the back of the head, Weakness in arms or legs, One-sided weakness, Seeing double, Overlapping vision, Trouble falling asleep, Waking up often, Not sleeping deeply
keywords: Pain at the back of the head

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A headache is a symptom rather than a disease in itself. The most common type is a “primary headache” (such as a migraine or tension-type headache), which occurs from stress or muscle tension even without any underlying disease. A headache that results from an actual disease in the head is called a “secondary headache.”

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The biggest cause of headaches is unhealthy daily habits.
· Poor posture: hunching your head forward or using a pillow that's too high can tighten the neck muscles and bring on a headache.
· Sleep and environment: both too little and too much sleep can cause headaches. In cold winter weather, constricted blood vessels and muscles can also trigger frequent headaches.
· Other causes: coffee, alcohol, and smoking can also be triggers, and inflammation around the head, such as sinusitis or a middle ear infection, can cause headaches as well.

sections.heading: Warning Signs
sections.content:
Nausea and dizziness are common symptoms that can accompany a headache. However, if any of the following occur together with a headache, it may signal a serious emergency such as a brain hemorrhage, and you should go to a major hospital immediately.

· Weakness or paralysis in one arm, leg, or side of the face, or slurred speech
· A sudden, extremely severe headache unlike any you've experienced before
· A headache along with a high fever and vomiting
· A headache that worsens every time you strain during a bowel movement (a sign of possible brain hemorrhage)
· Dizziness along with blurred or double vision (diplopia)
· Sudden difficulty with calculations or a sharp drop in memory
· A first-ever headache in a person over 50 who has high blood pressure or diabetes

sections.heading: Headaches in Children
sections.content:
Young children often cannot describe a headache clearly in words, so careful observation by parents is important.

It is a good idea to have your child evaluated at a hospital if you notice any of the following.
· A child who was playing normally suddenly becomes very fussy, or the opposite — unusually listless
· Fever along with vomiting
· Cold symptoms and discomfort that don't improve for a long time despite taking cold medicine

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Headache treatment depends on the type and cause of the headache. Appropriate pain relief may be helpful, while regular sleep, meals, hydration, and stress management may reduce recurrent headaches.

■ Helpful Habits
Drink enough water, especially in hot weather, and try to maintain a consistent sleep and meal schedule. Caffeine can relieve headaches for some people but may trigger or worsen headaches for others. If headaches are frequent, discuss caffeine intake with your doctor.

■ Possible Dietary Triggers
There is no single food that prevents all headaches. Alcohol and some foods may trigger migraine attacks in certain people, but triggers differ. Unsweetened carbonated water can contribute to hydration, whereas sugary drinks should be limited. Keep a headache diary to identify your own triggers rather than avoiding entire food groups unnecessarily.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Good posture and quality sleep are the most important ways to prevent headaches.

· Good posture: slouching your back or hunching your head forward while sitting can have a negative effect. When walking, keep your spine upright and walk with energy.
· Stretching: when working at a computer, get up at least once an hour to do some light stretching and release tension in the neck muscles.
· Sleep habits: getting an adequate amount of sleep is important. If you have a sleep disorder that lowers sleep quality, such as snoring or insomnia, it's a good idea to have it treated, since it can trigger headaches.

records.title: Digital Implants
records.intro: A digital implant is a technique that uses advanced equipment to place a dental implant precisely and safely. To reduce side effects and ensure long-term use, careful diagnosis and coordinated care from dental specialists (oral and maxillofacial surgery, prosthodontics) are essential.
records.tags_raw: Dental implant, Digital implant, Intraoral scanner, Same-day implant, Dentistry

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A digital implant is a treatment method that uses advanced technology, such as a 3D intraoral scanner and a 3D printer, to calculate the ideal implant position on a computer beforehand and then place the implant with precision.

sections.heading: Advantages
sections.content: There is no need to bite down on a clay-like rubber material for a long time to take an impression, as was required in the past, making the process more comfortable. Because the position of the bone and nerves is checked using a 3D X-ray (3D CT scan), the surgery can be performed safely and accurately.

sections.heading: Treatment Process
sections.content: It is possible to extract a tooth, place the implant, and fit a temporary tooth all on the same day. However, this does not mean the entire treatment is finished in a single day — you will typically need 3 to 4 more visits afterward so the implant can fully bond with the bone and the final tooth can be fitted.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: For a safe implant that lasts, it is important to have thorough testing and coordinated care that also considers systemic conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure. After surgery, brushing consistently and getting regular dental checkups are essential to using the implant for a long time, much like a natural tooth.

records.title: Herniated Disc and Back Pain
records.intro: The intervertebral disc acts as a cushion between the bones of the spine. When a disc is damaged or pushed out of place, it can press on nearby nerves and cause pain and numbness. Most cases improve with conservative treatment, but if symptoms are severe or there are signs of nerve damage, evaluation by a medical specialist is needed.
records.tags_raw: Herniated disc, Disc herniation, Lumbar disc herniation, Thoracic spine, Low back pain, Leg numbness, Cauda equina syndrome, Arthroscopy, Nerve block, Numbness in hands and feet, Arm numbness, Tingling in the leg

sections.heading: Causes and Symptoms
sections.content:
■ The Difference Between Ordinary Back Pain and Disc-Related Pain
Back pain can occur in the lumbar spine (lower back) or the thoracic spine (upper/mid back). Lumbar pain has many possible causes, including the muscles, joints, ligaments, and discs, while thoracic pain is less common because the ribs limit movement in that area.

Pain caused by a disc problem may have no clear tender point (a specific spot that hurts when pressed), and is often accompanied by nerve-related symptoms such as leg numbness. Pain unrelated to a disc more often has a clear tender point at a specific location. A precise diagnosis requires evaluation and imaging by a medical specialist.

■ Why Leg Numbness Occurs
