A disc is made up of the nucleus pulposus (the soft, gel-like center) and the annulus fibrosus (the tougher outer ring). When the annulus fibrosus weakens, the nucleus pulposus can push outward and press on the nerve roots that control leg function, causing numbness.

■ Symptoms by Degree of Herniation
· When the nucleus pulposus only pushes against the annulus fibrosus: mild leg numbness from nerve irritation
· When the nucleus pulposus breaks through the annulus fibrosus: severe pain, loss of sensation, and muscle weakness
· In severe cases: cauda equina syndrome (compression of the bundle of spinal nerves) can occur, along with bowel or bladder dysfunction

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Conservative Treatment (tried first)
· Taking anti-inflammatory pain relievers and muscle relaxants
· Relaxing the spinal muscles with physical therapy
· Once pain has eased somewhat, starting exercises to strengthen the back muscles and stretching
· If conservative treatment does not help, a nerve block (a treatment that injects medication near the affected nerve) may be considered

■ When Surgery Is Needed
Surgery to decompress the nerve root is performed in the following situations.
· Bowel or bladder dysfunction, or muscle weakness (emergency surgery may be needed)
· Pain that does not improve with a nerve block and is severe enough to interfere with daily life and sleep

The treatment approach should be decided after a thorough discussion with your doctor.

records.title: Smoking, Health, and Quitting Smoking
records.intro: Both regular cigarettes and e-cigarettes are harmful to health. Smoking raises the risk of many conditions, including lung cancer and other cancers, cardiovascular disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Quitting smoking is not easy, but getting help from a medical specialist makes success more likely. If you've decided to quit, please work with a healthcare team rather than trying on your own.
records.tags_raw: Smoking, Smoking cessation, E-cigarettes, Nicotine, Tar, Lung cancer, Cardiovascular disease, COPD, Smoking cessation medication, Nicotine addiction, Weakness in arms or legs, One-sided weakness, Chest anxiety, Restlessness, Unexplained worry, Feeling down, Lack of motivation, Not wanting to do anything

sections.heading: E-Cigarettes vs. Regular Cigarettes: Which Is Less Harmful?
sections.content:
There are two types of e-cigarettes.

· Heated tobacco products: heat tobacco leaf without burning it directly, and the vapor is inhaled
· Liquid e-cigarettes (vapes): heat a nicotine-containing liquid and the resulting vapor is inhaled

E-cigarettes have often been marketed on the basis that they contain fewer harmful substances than regular cigarettes. However, it cannot be concluded that e-cigarettes are less harmful to health.

Here is why.
· Because e-cigarette vapor is inhaled, it can reach deep into the lungs (the alveoli). Even with a smaller amount of harmful substances, the absorption rate may be higher.
· The additives used in liquid e-cigarettes and their effects on the body have not yet been sufficiently studied.
· A recent rise in severe respiratory illness among young men is believed to be linked to e-cigarette use.
· Some research has also reported that e-cigarettes may have a worse effect on cardiovascular disease than regular cigarettes.

In short, both e-cigarettes and regular cigarettes are harmful to health.

sections.heading: Health Effects of Smoking
sections.content:
Cigarette smoke contains more than 4,000 harmful substances. The most notable are nicotine (which causes addiction), tar (a carcinogen), and carbon monoxide.

■ Cancer
· Laryngeal and lung cancer: these tissues come into direct contact with smoke, and more than 70% of cases are linked to smoking.
· Bladder, esophageal, and pancreatic cancer, leukemia, and liver, colorectal, and breast cancer also occur more often in smokers.

■ Vascular Disease
· Smoking damages the inner lining of blood vessels and narrows them.
· It raises the risk of ischemic stroke, brain hemorrhage, and heart attack.
· It can cause Buerger's disease, a narrowing of the small blood vessels in the hands and feet that can sometimes require amputation of the fingers or toes.

■ Lung Damage
· Once the alveoli (the tiny air sacs in the lungs) are destroyed, they do not recover.
· This can lead to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and emphysema.
· In severe cases, breathing difficulty can become so pronounced during daily life that supplemental oxygen is needed.

Smoking is also linked to a range of other conditions, including blood clots, dementia, metabolic syndrome, infertility, erectile dysfunction, and depression.

sections.heading: Why Quitting Is Hard: Nicotine Addiction
sections.content:
The main reason quitting smoking is so difficult is nicotine addiction.

When nicotine is absorbed into the body, it stimulates the central nervous system, producing an elevated mood and sharper concentration. However, about 30 minutes after smoking, nicotine levels in the blood drop sharply, leading to reduced concentration, anxiety, low mood, and restlessness. These are nicotine withdrawal symptoms.

Withdrawal symptoms begin about 2 hours after the last cigarette and peak on day 2 or 3. This addiction is the main reason smokers often cannot quit even though they know the risks.

Many smokers believe they “could quit anytime” if they truly wanted to, but they discover just how difficult it is once they actually try.

sections.heading: How to Quit Smoking
sections.content:
Getting help from a healthcare team is more effective than trying to quit on willpower alone.

■ Nicotine Replacement Products
Gum or lozenges deliver a small amount of nicotine to ease withdrawal symptoms.

■ Prescription Medications
Medications containing varenicline (Champix) or bupropion reduce withdrawal symptoms and curb cravings. Success rates are higher than with nicotine replacement products alone. Dosage and duration should follow your doctor's prescription.

■ Ways to Improve Your Chances of Success
· Tell the people around you that you've decided to quit, and ask for their support.
· Quitting all at once tends to be more effective than gradually cutting back.
· Prepare coping strategies in advance (such as drinking water or taking a walk) for when cravings hit.
· Smoking cessation clinics or the smoking cessation counseling helpline (1544-9030 in Korea, no area code needed) can provide expert support.

Be sure to consult a medical specialist to choose the smoking cessation method that's right for you.

records.title: Low Back Pain
records.intro: Low back pain is pain in the lower back, and it is common enough that about 80% of adults experience it at least once in their lifetime. Most cases improve with adequate rest and medication, but if it is accompanied by leg numbness or weakness, please see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Low back pain, Back pain, Sprain, Muscle, Ligament, Winter back pain, Stretching, Aching lower back, Lower back pain, Throwing out your back, Having a fever, Body feels hot, High fever, Low-grade fever, Numbness in hands and feet, Arm numbness, Tingling in the leg, Weakness in arms or legs, One-sided weakness

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Low back pain is pain that occurs in the lumbar spine (lower back).

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
There are many possible causes of low back pain, including the intervertebral discs, joints, ligaments, and muscles.

Simple low back pain with no clear underlying cause is often the result of a brief muscle or ligament strain from a sudden movement or even a sneeze.

Low back pain becomes more common in winter for the following reasons.
· Cold weather causes the muscles, ligaments, and blood vessels around the spine to tighten and stiffen.
· Less physical activity and more time spent hunched over reduce flexibility.
· More time spent sitting indoors places greater strain on the back muscles.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Simple low back pain is generally treated in the following order.

· Adequate rest and warmth: lying down and resting often improves symptoms on its own. Applying warm compresses to the painful area can also help.
· Medication: anti-inflammatory pain relievers (medications that reduce inflammation and pain) are used. Because inadequately controlled acute pain can progress to chronic pain, taking medication as directed is recommended.
· Injection therapy: if there is no improvement after about 2 weeks of medication, an injection of medication directly into the painful area may be considered.

The most important part of treatment is the patient's own exercise therapy. Medication and injections are supportive measures that provide faster symptom relief.

sections.heading: Prevention and Lifestyle Habits
sections.content:
The following habits can help prevent low back pain.

· Maintain good posture.
· After every 50 minutes of work, stand up and stretch for about 10 minutes.
· Stretch forward, backward, side to side, and with rotation, enough to feel a slight pull in the muscles.
· Stretch right after waking up in the morning as well.
· Strengthen your back muscles and ligaments through regular walking.
· Avoid smoking.
· In winter, ventilate your space so your body can adjust somewhat to the cold, while still keeping adequately warm.

sections.heading: When to See a Doctor
sections.content:
Please see a medical specialist if you experience any of the following.

· Numbness or weakness in an arm or leg
· A change in bowel or bladder function
· Pain that continues even after adequate rest and medication
· Pain at night, or pain accompanied by fever

records.title: Gastritis
records.intro: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach's mucosa (lining). It is often found on endoscopy even without symptoms. If left unmanaged, it can progress through atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia toward stomach cancer, so regular screening and lifestyle management are important.
records.tags_raw: Gastritis, Acute gastritis, Chronic gastritis, Atrophic gastritis, Intestinal metaplasia, H. pylori, Stomach cancer prevention, Stomach pain, My stomach hurts, Stomachache, Abdominal pain, Food feels stuck, Bloating, Trouble digesting, Burning stomach, Stomach burning, Acid regurgitation

sections.heading: Prevention and Lifestyle Habits
sections.content:
The following habits can help prevent and manage gastritis.

· Eat meals on a regular schedule and avoid overeating.
· Cut back on irritating foods (spicy, salty, or charred food).
· Avoid eating right before bed.
· Don't smoke, and cut back on alcohol.
· Reduce caffeine intake.
· Eat slowly and chew food thoroughly.
· Exercise regularly in a relaxed, enjoyable way.
· Eat fresh vegetables and food, and avoid salted or overly aged foods.

If you have risk factors or symptoms, please see a medical specialist and have regular endoscopic checkups.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach's mucosa (lining), and is classified as acute or chronic.

Having gastritis does not mean it will progress to stomach cancer right away, but if it is not managed, it can worsen as follows.
· Atrophic gastritis (thinning of the stomach lining): raises the risk of stomach cancer by about 6 times.
· Intestinal metaplasia (a change in the stomach lining so that it resembles intestinal lining): raises the risk of stomach cancer by 10 to 20 times.

Gastritis is often found on endoscopy even without symptoms, which is why regular endoscopic checkups are important.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The main causes of gastritis include the following.

· Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection: triggers inflammation in the stomach lining, and cell damage builds up with repeated exposure.
· Excessive intake of salty food: sodium can damage the cells of the stomach lining, which can lead to atrophic gastritis and stomach cancer.
· Heavy drinking and overeating
· Irritating food (spicy or salty food)
· Certain medications (especially NSAID pain relievers): long-term use without a doctor's supervision can damage the stomach lining.
· Stress

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Not everyone with gastritis has symptoms. Only about half of people with gastritis are thought to notice any symptoms.

The main symptoms include the following.
· Heartburn
· Abdominal pain
· Indigestion
· Discomfort in the upper abdomen

Regular endoscopic checkups are still needed even without symptoms.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for gastritis depends on the cause and the degree of inflammation.

· Acid-suppressing medication and stomach-protecting medication are used.
· If H. pylori infection is confirmed, eradication treatment is given based on your doctor's judgment.
· The following should be avoided.
  - Heavy drinking and smoking
  - Spicy or salty food, and caffeine
  - Highly acidic food (fruit juice, vinegar, etc.)
  - Irritating medications (consult a medical specialist before taking NSAID pain relievers)

Please discuss the treatment approach with your doctor.

records.title: Gastrointestinal Stricture
records.intro: A gastrointestinal stricture is a narrowing of a passage in the digestive tract, such as the esophagus, stomach, or intestine. When the passage narrows, food cannot pass through smoothly, which can cause symptoms such as abdominal bloating, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Depending on the cause and location, it is managed with endoscopic treatment or surgery. If you have these symptoms, please be sure to see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Gastrointestinal stricture, Stricture, Balloon dilation, Stent, Digestive system, Abdominal pain, Vomiting, Abdominal bloating, Stomach pain, My stomach hurts, Stomachache, Belly pain, Bloated belly, Gas in the stomach, Feeling full/distended

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
A gastrointestinal stricture can result from a variety of causes. The main ones are as follows.

· Post-surgical stricture: the most common cause, in which the site where tissue was cut and rejoined after surgery for stomach cancer, colorectal cancer, or similar conditions gradually narrows over time. Scar tissue forming at the surgical site can cause this narrowing.
· Ingestion of a corrosive substance: swallowing a strong acid or alkali can cause the esophagus to narrow.
· Other causes: a stricture can also develop after radiation therapy or other procedures.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
When a passage in the digestive tract narrows, the following symptoms can occur.

· Abdominal bloating: an uncomfortable feeling as if the abdomen is filled with gas.
· Abdominal pain: pain in the abdomen.
· Vomiting or nausea: food that cannot pass through may come back up or be vomited.

If these symptoms persist or worsen, please see a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
When a stricture occurs in an area reachable by endoscope (such as the esophagus, stomach, or colon), it can be treated endoscopically.

· Balloon dilation: a balloon is guided through the endoscope to the narrowed area and inflated to widen the passage.
· Stent placement: a mesh-like tube (stent) is inserted into the narrowed area, where it expands on its own to widen the passage.

If the stricture keeps recurring or does not respond to endoscopic treatment, surgery may be considered. Because treatment depends on the location, cause, and severity of the stricture, please discuss it thoroughly with your doctor.

records.title: Breast Cancer
records.intro: Breast cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in breast tissue, and it is one of the more common cancers in women. Surgical and reconstruction techniques continue to advance, and outcomes are generally good when the cancer is found early. If a breast screening shows an abnormal result, or if you notice a lump or a change in the skin, please see a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: Breast cancer, Breast cancer surgery, Breast reconstruction, Robotic surgery, Lymph nodes, Breast cancer screening, Inconclusive result, Lymphedema, Body swelling, Face swelling, Leg swelling, Swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Breast cancer is a disease in which cancer cells grow in the breast. The size of the tumor and how far it has spread vary from patient to patient. The biological characteristics of the cancer cells also differ — for example, whether they have receptors for female hormones or a specific protein called HER2 — so even patients with the same stage of cancer may need different treatment approaches.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Common symptoms of breast cancer include a hard, palpable lump, changes in the skin, and nipple asymmetry. In more advanced breast cancer, discomfort in the armpit or arm swelling can also occur. If you notice these symptoms, please see a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Breast cancer surgery generally involves two parts. Surgery is the foundation of breast cancer treatment, but it does not always mean removing the entire breast — about 70% of patients undergo “breast-conserving surgery,” in which only the area around the tumor is removed, preserving the shape of the breast. If the cancer is large or has spread to multiple areas, the entire breast may need to be removed; in this case, reconstruction using the patient's own tissue or an implant can restore the breast if desired.

■ Breast Surgery
This is the surgery that directly removes the cancer. It may involve removing the entire breast or only the tumor while preserving the breast, depending on the tumor's location, size, and the patient's condition.

■ Axillary Lymph Node Surgery
Lymph nodes are part of the body's immune system and are examined to check whether the cancer has spread elsewhere. If metastasis (spread of the cancer to another area) is confirmed, the lymph nodes are removed. In recent years, the trend has been to limit the extent of axillary surgery as much as possible, because a larger extent of surgery increases the risk of lymphedema (swelling caused by impaired lymph fluid drainage). When breast-conserving surgery is performed, current practice increasingly avoids removing all the lymph nodes even if some spread to the armpit is found.

■ Robotic Surgery
Robotic breast cancer surgery leaves only a small scar near the armpit, giving it a strong cosmetic advantage. Conventional surgery typically leaves a visible scar around the nipple or in the fold beneath the breast, whereas robotic surgery places a small incision scar toward the side of the body, which can also maximize the results of reconstruction. It is used for early-stage breast cancer and for preventive surgery in high-risk patients.

■ Oncoplastic Surgery
This technique reshapes the breast for a better cosmetic result at the same time the tumor is removed, allowing breast conservation and cosmetic outcome to be considered together.

The surgical approach is decided by your doctor based on your condition and the characteristics of the cancer. Please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with a medical specialist.

After surgery, additional treatments such as radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy are used to eliminate any cancer cells that may remain. In particular, patients with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer need to take hormone therapy (endocrine therapy) consistently for 5 to as long as 10 years to help prevent recurrence.

sections.heading: Postoperative Precautions
sections.content:
Breast cancer surgery rarely causes major restrictions on daily life afterward. In most cases, pain is mild enough that patients can be discharged the day after surgery.

However, please keep the following in mind.
· After reconstructive surgery, activity is limited for about 1 to 2 weeks while the incision heals.
· Depending on the extent of axillary (underarm) surgery, arm use may be limited for a time.
· There are no major restrictions on food intake.

Specific precautions can vary depending on the type of surgery and the patient's condition, so please follow your doctor's guidance.

sections.heading: Breast Reconstruction
sections.content:
After a total mastectomy, the breast (mammary) tissue is removed, leaving only the skin and a portion of the underlying fat. Breast reconstruction is the surgery that fills this space to recreate the shape of the breast. It is performed by plastic surgeons and generally involves two approaches.

■ Autologous Tissue Reconstruction
The breast is reconstructed using the patient's own tissue from another part of the body, such as the abdomen, back, or thigh. The main drawback is a scar at the donor site where the tissue was taken.

■ Implant-Based Reconstruction
This method involves inserting an implant, such as a silicone implant. There is some possibility of implant rupture, and a thick capsule (a hardened layer of scar tissue) can form around the implant, which in rare cases can cause pain or contracture (tightening from hardened tissue). Multiple studies indicate that the implant itself does not cause breast cancer and does not interfere with breast cancer diagnosis.

■ Recovery After Reconstruction
· In general, the arm and shoulder on the surgical side can be used again about 3 weeks after surgery.
· With abdominal tissue reconstruction, patients can typically resume regular activity after about 2 months.
· Skin sensation gradually returns over 1 to 2 years or more, but may not fully recover.
· Reconstruction using abdominal tissue does not affect future pregnancy or childbirth.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Finishing treatment does not mean you can immediately stop being vigilant about breast cancer, which is why regular follow-up checkups are so important. Rather than relying on general information sources or folk remedies, please work closely with your doctor and follow through with the adjuvant treatment that fits your cancer's specific biological characteristics.

Both obesity/overweight and being significantly underweight can raise the risk of breast cancer recurrence and death. Rather than favoring specific foods, it is better to eat a varied diet without excessive calories and maintain a healthy weight. Avoiding alcohol and exercising consistently at a moderate intensity can also help.

■ Frequently Asked Questions
■ My screening result came back “inconclusive” — is that okay?
An “inconclusive” result does not mean there is nothing wrong. It means further testing, such as an ultrasound or magnification imaging, is needed. Some people mistakenly treat this result as unimportant, which can delay diagnosis. If you receive an inconclusive result, please be sure to see a medical specialist.

■ What supplements are safe to take after surgery?
Omega-3 and vitamin D are generally recommended. Some research has linked vitamin D to a reduced risk of early breast cancer and a lower risk of death. Vegetables and fruits containing beta-carotene, such as broccoli and carrots, have also been reported to have antioxidant effects. Research on red ginseng has produced mixed results, so please consult your doctor before taking it. Any decision to take a supplement should be made after discussing it with your doctor.

■ Does breast cancer change the shape of the breast?
A hard, palpable lump is the most common symptom. Changes in the skin or nipple asymmetry can also occur. If you notice these changes, please see a medical specialist.

records.title: Robotic Mastectomy for Breast Cancer
records.intro: Robotic mastectomy is a minimally invasive surgery in which a surgeon controls a robotic system to remove the breast. A “mastectomy” refers to surgery that removes the entire breast. Compared with conventional surgery, the incisions are smaller and placed differently, offering a cosmetic advantage. Breast reconstruction may also be performed at the same time if needed. Whether this approach is right for you should be decided after a thorough discussion with your doctor.
records.tags_raw: Breast cancer, Mastectomy, Robotic surgery, Nipple-sparing, Breast reconstruction, BRCA, Nipple necrosis, Minimally invasive surgery

sections.heading: Advantages and Limitations
sections.content:
■ Advantages
· The incision is small and placed below the armpit, so no scar is visible on the front of the breast — a clear cosmetic advantage.
· Pain is relatively less than with conventional surgery.
· Because the incision is made farther away from the nipple, some studies report fewer complications related to nipple tissue damage. However, this can vary by individual, so please discuss it with your doctor.

■ Oncologic Safety
Short-term follow-up studies have reported no major difference in cancer recurrence or survival compared with conventional surgery. Because breast cancer can still recur even more than 5 years after surgery, longer-term follow-up data continue to be needed.

■ Limitations
· Surgery time can be longer than with conventional surgery.
· It is not covered by Korea's National Health Insurance, so there is an added cost.

sections.heading: Surgical Procedure
sections.content:
Robotic mastectomy is not performed by the robot on its own. The surgeon sits at a console, views the surgical field through a camera, and remotely controls the robotic arms throughout the entire procedure.

A small incision is made below the armpit (inside the bra line), and the robotic arms and surgical instruments are inserted through this opening to remove the breast tissue. During surgery, the surgeon works together with a surgical nurse, an assistant, and other medical staff, who monitor the patient's condition and the progress of the operation.

The magnified camera view and the robotic arms' flexible range of motion allow for precise surgery even in a narrow space.

sections.heading: Indications and Contraindications
sections.content:
■ When It Can Be Used
This approach can be used for patients who need a nipple-sparing mastectomy, provided there is no cancer cell invasion of the skin.
Robotic surgery may also be considered when the cancer has spread to the axillary lymph nodes.
It may also be considered for preventive mastectomy in patients at high risk of breast cancer, such as those with a BRCA gene mutation. The “BRCA gene” is a gene known to increase the risk of breast and ovarian cancer.

■ When It Cannot Be Used
Robotic surgery is not possible if cancer cells have invaded the skin or the area around the nipple.

The surgical approach best suited to you is determined by your doctor, so this decision should be made after a medical evaluation.

sections.heading: Preoperative Preparation
sections.content:
Before surgery, your surgeon designs an incision plan tailored to you and marks it on the skin in advance.

If breast reconstruction (surgery to restore the removed breast) is planned at the same time, a consultation with a plastic surgeon is needed beforehand.

For other general pre-surgery preparations, please follow the guidance of your medical team.

sections.heading: Postoperative Care
sections.content:
Recovery of the surgical site usually takes about 1 to 2 weeks. Pain tends to be relatively mild compared with conventional surgery. By about 2 weeks after surgery, most patients are able to resume daily activities without difficulty.

However, recovery speed can vary from person to person. Please follow your medical team's guidance regarding the specific length of hospital stay, wound care, and follow-up schedule.

Even after surgery, it is important to continue regular checkups to monitor for recurrence of breast cancer.

records.title: Implantable Bone Conduction Hearing Aid
records.intro: An implantable bone conduction hearing aid is a surgical option that can restore hearing for people who have difficulty using a regular hearing aid. A detailed hearing evaluation by an ENT specialist is essential to determine whether this surgery is appropriate.
records.tags_raw: Hearing loss, Bone conduction hearing aid, Conductive hearing loss, Hearing aid, Auditory rehabilitation, Hand tremor, Body tremor, Can't hear, Trouble hearing sounds

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: This is a specialized hearing aid system that delivers sound directly to the inner ear (the cochlea) using tiny vibrations transmitted through the skull, bypassing the ear canal.

sections.heading: Candidates
sections.content: This option is suitable for patients with conductive hearing loss who have a blocked ear canal, or who have difficulty wearing a conventional hearing aid that plugs the ear canal because of recurrent, draining middle ear infections.

sections.heading: Treatment Process
sections.content: Surgery is performed to implant a small vibrating device beneath the thin skin behind the ear, which transmits sound through the bone. Once the incision has healed (about 3 to 4 weeks later), a small external sound processor is attached to the skin with a magnet for everyday use.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Because the external device is electronic, it must be removed before washing or swimming. After surgery, the device needs to be adjusted several times, and a period of rehabilitation is needed for the brain to adapt until sound is heard naturally.

records.title: Breast Reconstruction
records.intro: Breast reconstruction rebuilds the breast after breast cancer surgery, helping with emotional healing as well. Finding the safest approach for your body type and condition requires a thorough evaluation and discussion with a plastic surgeon.
records.tags_raw: Breast reconstruction, Breast cancer, Implant, Autologous tissue, Plastic surgery

sections.heading: Timing of Surgery
sections.content: Breast reconstruction is divided into “immediate reconstruction,” performed at the same time as breast cancer surgery, and “delayed reconstruction,” performed later after all cancer treatment is complete. Immediate reconstruction preserves the patient's own skin, which usually gives a more natural-looking result.

sections.heading: Myths and Facts
sections.content: You can be reassured that reconstruction surgery does not increase the risk of breast cancer recurrence and does not interfere with breast cancer screening. Postoperative pain can be well controlled with pain-management injections, and if the two breasts turn out different in shape, the other breast can also be reshaped to match the reconstructed side as closely as possible.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Breast reconstruction is surgery that restores a breast that has been removed or changed in shape due to breast cancer treatment, using tissue from another part of the patient's own body or a silicone implant to recreate a result as close as possible to the original appearance.

sections.heading: Surgical Methods
sections.content: “Implant-based reconstruction” creates the breast using a silicone implant. The surgery is shorter and leaves no scar elsewhere on the body, making it a good option for those who want a faster recovery. “Autologous tissue reconstruction” uses tissue taken from the patient's own abdomen or flank, so the result feels soft and natural, like the patient's own tissue, with permanent results.

records.title: Types of Breast Reconstruction
records.intro: Breast reconstruction is surgery that restores a breast affected by a congenital or acquired defect. After breast cancer surgery, it can help patients overcome feelings of loss and depression, restore a sense of womanhood, and improve quality of life. It can also help prevent lymphedema and support physical balance.
records.tags_raw: Breast reconstruction, Breast cancer, Immediate reconstruction, Delayed reconstruction, Implant, Autologous tissue, Plastic surgery, Body swelling, Face swelling, Leg swelling, Swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Immediate vs. Delayed Reconstruction
sections.content: Immediate reconstruction is performed on the same day as the breast cancer surgery, and because the patient's own skin is preserved, the result tends to look natural. Delayed reconstruction is performed after all treatment — such as chemotherapy or radiation — is complete; because it must compensate for a shortage of skin, the result can look somewhat less natural.

sections.heading: Reconstruction After Total vs. Partial Mastectomy
sections.content: Reconstruction can also be performed after a partial mastectomy to prevent asymmetry and deformity. However, the surgical options are more limited depending on the location of the defect, and because it is not covered by national health insurance, it is performed less often than reconstruction after a total mastectomy.

sections.heading: Implant-Based vs. Autologous Tissue Reconstruction
sections.content: Implant-based reconstruction uses a tissue expander to stretch the skin before it is replaced with a permanent implant; surgery and recovery are relatively quick. Autologous tissue reconstruction (using tissue from the lower abdomen, latissimus dorsi muscle, or similar sites) involves more complex surgery and a harder initial recovery, but the result feels and looks considerably more natural.

sections.heading: Choosing a Reconstruction Method
sections.content: There is no single, absolute standard — the best method depends on factors such as the patient's body type, plans for future pregnancy, and whether radiation therapy will be needed. In particular, if radiation therapy is likely, autologous tissue reconstruction is generally recommended to reduce the risk of implant capsular contracture and infection.

sections.heading: Nipple and Areola Reconstruction
sections.content: If the nipple was removed as part of cancer treatment, it can be reconstructed using techniques such as local flap surgery, cartilage grafting, or shading tattoo techniques. This can sometimes be done at the same time as autologous tissue reconstruction, but it is most often performed about 6 months later, once the reconstructed tissue has stabilized.

sections.heading: Postoperative Care and Cancer Recurrence
sections.content: Breast reconstruction does not affect the risk of breast cancer recurrence, and normal imaging follow-up remains possible after surgery. Avoiding strenuous exercise or excessive movement for about one month after surgery is usually enough to allow a full return to daily activities and rehabilitation afterward.

records.title: Epidemic Keratoconjunctivitis
records.intro: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is a highly contagious eye infection caused by adenovirus. It occurs most often in summer, and symptoms include eye redness, a foreign body sensation, and eyelid swelling. Personal hygiene is important, and if symptoms appear, please consult an ophthalmologist.
records.tags_raw: epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, eye infection, adenovirus, conjunctivitis, redness, eyelid swelling, contagious, fever, having a fever, high fever, low-grade fever, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling in hands and feet

sections.heading: Transmission
sections.content: The infection spreads through eye discharge. It is transmitted through direct contact with an infected person or by touching objects the person has used (such as towels or eye drops) and then rubbing your eyes. Simply looking at an infected person's eyes does not spread the infection.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is a highly contagious form of conjunctivitis caused by adenovirus. Inflammation occurs in both the conjunctiva (the membrane covering the inside of the eyelids and the white of the eye) and the cornea (the transparent membrane covering the iris and pupil). It occurs mainly in summer and is so contagious that entire families can become infected.

Pharyngoconjunctival fever, caused by the same adenovirus, mainly affects children and is characterized by eye redness along with cold-like symptoms such as fever and sore throat.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis usually appear 5 to 14 days after infection.

Early symptoms:
· Eye redness
· Itching or mild pain

Symptoms as the condition progresses:
· A gritty, sand-like foreign body sensation
· Excessive tearing and eye discharge
· Significant eyelid swelling

In severe cases, the cornea may be damaged, causing intense light sensitivity and pain. In this case, vision may decline due to secondary bacterial infection. Symptoms typically last about 3 to 4 weeks before gradually improving. In children, systemic symptoms such as fever and swelling of the lymph nodes near the ear may be more pronounced.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Because this is a viral illness, there is no medication that eliminates the virus itself. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and preventing secondary infection.
· Antibiotic eye drops may be used to help prevent secondary bacterial infection.
· Cold compresses can help reduce swelling and pain.
· Getting adequate rest is important.
· Alcohol should be avoided, as it may worsen complications.
· Use only your own eye drops, and always wash your hands before and after applying them.

If symptoms appear, please consult an ophthalmologist for diagnosis and treatment.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· Wash your hands often with soap.
· Avoid touching or rubbing your eyes with your hands.
· Do not share personal hygiene items such as towels with others.
· If you have the infection, avoid crowded places such as swimming pools and vacation spots during the contagious period (about 2 weeks).
· It is best not to wear an eye patch. Wearing a patch raises the temperature around the eye, which can help bacteria grow more easily. Wear sunglasses instead if needed.

records.title: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
records.intro: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) occurs when tiny particles called otoconia become dislodged from the balance organ of the inner ear (the vestibular system) and enter the semicircular canals. Otoconia are small crystals made of calcium carbonate, sometimes described as "ear stones." The main symptom is a spinning sensation that occurs with changes in head position. If you experience dizziness, please consult an ENT specialist.
records.tags_raw: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, BPPV, dizziness, vertigo, vestibular system, semicircular canals, canalith repositioning, ear, balance, feeling dizzy, spinning sensation, unsteadiness, feeling faint, nausea, feeling like vomiting, vomiting, ringing in the ear, tinnitus, hearing loss, difficulty hearing

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The inner ear contains the vestibular system, which helps maintain the body's balance. The vestibular system is largely made up of two parts: one that detects straight-line movement (up-down, forward-backward), and the semicircular canals, which detect rotational movement.

Otoconia are calcium carbonate crystals located in the part of the vestibular system that detects straight-line movement. With aging, injury, or other causes, these crystals can loosen or break apart and migrate into the semicircular canals. Since the semicircular canals normally detect rotational movement, the presence of otoconia sends a false signal to the brain that the body is spinning even when it is not moving. This is what causes BPPV.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: BPPV occurs when small crystals (otoconia) that were near the semicircular canals become dislodged from their normal position and move around inside the canals, stimulating the nerves and causing severe dizziness.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The hallmark symptom of BPPV is rotational vertigo that worsens with changes in position. Vertigo refers to a spinning sensation, as though your surroundings are whirling around you.

Symptoms tend to occur especially in the following situations:
· When lying down
· When getting up from a lying position
· When turning your head from side to side while lying down

Auditory symptoms such as tinnitus (ringing in the ear) or hearing loss do not occur with BPPV. If these auditory symptoms occur along with dizziness, a different condition may be responsible, so please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content: BPPV is diagnosed by observing eye movements known as nystagmus, an involuntary, rhythmic movement of the eyes. By analyzing the direction and characteristics of the nystagmus triggered by specific positions, a specialist can determine which semicircular canal the otoconia have entered. This assessment must be made by a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Canalith repositioning is a treatment that moves the head through a specific sequence of positions, tailored to which semicircular canal the otoconia have entered, in order to guide the particles back to their original location. A single session may not be enough, and repeat treatments are often needed. Medication to help reduce dizziness and nausea or vomiting may also be prescribed.

This is a form of physical therapy that returns the dislodged crystals (otoconia) to their original position.

The most commonly used technique is the Epley maneuver, in which the physician moves the patient's head through a series of positions while the patient lies down, guiding the otoconia back into place. This treatment has been reported to improve symptoms in about 70% to 90% of patients.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
BPPV commonly recurs. To help lower the risk of recurrence, keep the following in mind:

· Avoid activities or movements that involve a strong impact to the head.
· Some research suggests that vitamin D supplementation may help reduce the recurrence rate. Please consult a medical specialist before taking supplements.
· It may help to keep on hand medication prescribed in advance to relieve dizziness in case of recurrence.

In some cases, BPPV improves on its own over time. However, without treatment, dizziness can persist for a long time. Dizziness can also be a symptom of other serious conditions, such as stroke, so if you experience dizziness, please be sure to get an accurate diagnosis from a medical specialist.

records.title: Secondary Amenorrhea
records.intro: Secondary amenorrhea refers to the absence of menstruation for three months or longer in a woman who previously had normal menstrual cycles. It has various causes, and if left unaddressed for a long time, it can affect overall health. Because treatment differs depending on the cause, evaluation by a medical specialist is needed.
records.tags_raw: amenorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, polycystic ovary syndrome, premature ovarian insufficiency, irregular periods, hormone testing, gynecology, irregular menstrual cycle, missed period, late period

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Secondary amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation for three months or longer in a woman who previously had normal menstrual cycles.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
· Pregnancy (should always be ruled out first)
· Endocrine disorders: polycystic ovary syndrome, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia (excess prolactin secretion from the pituitary gland)
· Hypothalamic dysfunction: excessive stress, excessive exercise, being underweight
· Premature ovarian insufficiency: menopause before age 40
· Structural abnormalities of the uterus, among others

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The following tests may be performed to identify the cause:
· Hormone tests: follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estradiol, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), prolactin, and others
· Metabolic tests: to check for anemia, diabetes mellitus, and electrolyte imbalances
· Pelvic ultrasound: to check for structural abnormalities of the uterus or ovaries (e.g., polycystic ovary syndrome)
· Brain MRI: to check for a pituitary tumor or hypothalamic abnormality
· Hysteroscopy: to examine the uterine lining when needed

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment depends on the underlying cause.

■ Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
· Weight management and improving insulin resistance (metformin)
· Oral contraceptives to induce menstruation and manage symptoms of excess androgen
· Progesterone or an intrauterine device (e.g., a levonorgestrel-releasing IUD) may be used to protect the uterine lining
· Ovulation-inducing medication if pregnancy is desired

■ Thyroid Disease
Treatment of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism

■ Hyperprolactinemia
Treated with dopamine agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline)

■ Hypothalamic Dysfunction
Weight gain, stress management, and hormone therapy after menopause

■ Premature Ovarian Insufficiency
Estrogen plus progesterone hormone therapy is recommended until at least age 50. Hormone therapy is important because the risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease increases.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.content:
■ What if I only get my period while taking birth control pills?
Birth control pills are not an ovulation-inducing medication. Menstruation artificially induced by birth control pills does not mean your underlying condition has improved. Bleeding that occurs while taking birth control pills should not be mistaken for your own natural menstrual cycle.

Whether you can stop taking birth control pills depends on the underlying cause of amenorrhea and your individual condition. If the underlying cause has been resolved, you may be able to stop. However, if ongoing hormone supplementation is needed, as with polycystic ovary syndrome or premature ovarian insufficiency, continued use may be necessary. Please discuss this with your doctor.

records.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Infection
records.intro: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a very common virus transmitted through skin-to-skin contact. More than half of sexually active women and men are estimated to have been infected with genital HPV at some point. Most infections clear on their own, but some types can cause conditions such as cervical cancer. Vaccination and regular screening are important.
records.tags_raw: human papillomavirus, HPV, cervical cancer, genital warts, sexual contact, virus

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a virus transmitted through skin-to-skin contact. More than 100 types have been identified to date, broadly divided into high-risk and low-risk types.

· High-risk types (types 16, 18, and others): can cause abnormal cervical lesions and cervical cancer.
· Low-risk types (types 6, 11, and others): can cause genital warts (warts that appear around the genitals).

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Most people infected with high-risk HPV have no symptoms. Infection with low-risk HPV can cause warts to appear around the genitals.

In most cases, the immune system clears the virus naturally. According to research conducted in Korea, the virus resolves on its own in about half of infected individuals within roughly 7 to 8 months. However, in some cases the infection persists and can progress to abnormal cervical lesions or cervical cancer.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
HPV is directly linked to cervical cancer, being detected in more than 99% of cervical cancer cases. Vaccination can help prevent infection with the major high-risk HPV types.

The ideal time for vaccination is before exposure to the virus, meaning before the start of sexual activity. Eligibility and the number of doses can vary by age, so please consult a medical specialist.

Because vaccination does not completely prevent all HPV types, it is important for adult women to receive regular cervical cancer screening even after vaccination.

sections.heading: Transmission
sections.content:
HPV is transmitted through skin-to-skin contact. In addition to sexual intercourse, it can also be transmitted through genital-to-hand or genital-to-mouth contact.

The risk of infection increases with a greater number of sexual partners. Most infected individuals are unaware they are infected and may unknowingly transmit the virus to others.

Using condoms can reduce the risk but does not eliminate it completely.

records.title: Sunburn
records.intro: Sunburn is an inflammatory skin reaction caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays during outdoor activity. It can go beyond simple discomfort and lead to systemic symptoms. If symptoms are severe or persistent, please be sure to consult a dermatologist.
records.tags_raw: sunburn, ultraviolet rays, UV exposure, burn, skin, summer, cooling, sun protection, fever, having a fever, high fever, low-grade fever, body shaking, chills, feeling cold and shivering, hand tremor, body tremor

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Sunburn is an inflammatory skin reaction that occurs with excessive exposure to ultraviolet rays. The UV index is highest in July and August, so extra caution is needed during outdoor activities in this period.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: About 4 to 6 hours after sun exposure, the skin becomes red and swollen. In severe cases, blisters may form. Systemic symptoms such as chills, fever, and nausea may also occur.

sections.heading: What to Do
sections.content: For mild symptoms, cool the skin with cold compresses or cool showers (3 to 4 times a day for 20 minutes each). Applying calamine lotion or a topical steroid cream can also help. Calamine lotion is a product used to soothe itching and skin irritation.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If blisters form, or if the pain is severe enough that even light contact with clothing hurts, do not pop the blisters. See a dermatologist right away.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: On days with a high UV index, it is best to limit outdoor activity between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. When going outside, apply sunscreen thoroughly and wear long sleeves and a wide-brimmed hat. Use a water-resistant sunscreen for water activities, and remember that UV rays are also stronger at high altitudes, so sunscreen is essential when hiking in the mountains.

records.title: Dental Implant
records.intro: A dental implant is a treatment that restores tooth function by placing an artificial tooth root into the site of a missing tooth when a natural tooth can no longer be treated. It is widely used because it can address some of the drawbacks of conventional dentures or bridges. Whether implant treatment is appropriate depends on an individual's health status and jawbone condition, so please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with a dental specialist before making a decision.
records.tags_raw: dental implant, tooth, gums, dentures, bridge, dentistry, peri-implantitis, jawbone, osteoporosis

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Most people are able to undergo implant treatment, but caution is needed for those with certain conditions.
· If you are being treated for osteoporosis: taking osteoporosis medications (such as bisphosphonates) or receiving injections for this condition may carry a risk of jawbone necrosis. Please be sure to inform your dental specialist beforehand.
· If you are taking antiplatelet medication (medication that prevents blood clotting): there may be a risk of excessive bleeding, so consultation with an internal medicine specialist before the procedure may be needed.
· If you are taking any medication or have any medical condition, please inform your dental specialist and make a decision after consultation.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A dental implant is a treatment that restores chewing function by placing an artificial tooth root into the jawbone in place of a natural tooth root, and then attaching an artificial tooth on top. It may be considered when a tooth must be extracted due to severe tooth decay or periodontitis (inflammation of the gums and jawbone), or when a tooth cannot be saved after trauma. Bridge treatment has the drawback of requiring adjacent teeth to be filed down, and dentures can sometimes fit poorly and cause discomfort. An implant does not affect neighboring teeth and can function similarly to a natural tooth.

sections.heading: Procedure and Recovery Time
sections.content: The length of the implant procedure and the recovery period can vary depending on the condition of the jawbone. If there is sufficient jawbone and the gums are healthy, the procedure can sometimes be done without an incision, which shortens the treatment time. If there is insufficient jawbone, bone grafting (alveolar bone regeneration) may be needed, which lengthens the procedure. After the implant is placed, it typically takes about 3 to 4 months for it to fully integrate with the jawbone before the artificial tooth can be attached. If bone grafting is performed, this can take 6 months or longer. Please discuss the specific treatment plan with your doctor.

sections.heading: Post-Procedure Care
sections.content: After implant placement, ongoing care is still needed, just as with natural teeth. Gum disease around the implant (peri-implantitis) can also occur. If peri-implantitis develops, the surrounding jawbone can be lost, causing pain and discomfort, and in severe cases the implant may need to be removed. Please visit your dentist regularly after the procedure for professional care. It is also important for patients to keep the implant clean themselves.

records.title: Cervical Cancer
records.intro: Cervical cancer develops in the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It is a cancer with a clearly identified cause and is preventable; regular screening and the HPV (human papillomavirus) vaccine can help reduce its occurrence. If you have symptoms that raise concern, or have not been screened, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: cervical cancer, HPV, human papillomavirus, uterus, gynecologic cancer, HPV vaccine, cervical cancer screening, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling in hands and feet, numbness in hands and feet, arm numbness, tingling leg

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.content:
Cervical cancer was once common enough to rank third among cancers in women. However, since screening began through the National Cancer Screening Program in 2000, and the HPV vaccine became available starting in 2006, the incidence rate has been steadily declining. As of 2019, cervical cancer was reported to occur less frequently than endometrial cancer (cancer of the lining of the uterus).
The mortality rate has also been decreasing. It was 2.6 per 100,000 people in 1999, falling to 1.7 per 100,000 in 2017. The 5-year survival rate is 79.8%, higher than the average 5-year survival rate of 70.6% for all cancers combined.
※ The statistics above reflect data available at the time of publication (2019–2021). The most current figures can be found through the National Cancer Information Center.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
One of the most notable features of cervical cancer is that its cause is clearly identified. The main cause is HPV, or human papillomavirus. During sexual intercourse, HPV can enter through small breaks in the cervix, and after an incubation period, it can transform normal cells into cancer cells.
Factors that increase the risk of HPV infection include early sexual activity, having multiple sexual partners, and sexual contact with a high-risk partner.
Menopausal status is not related to risk. By age group, incidence is highest in the 40s (26.8%), followed by the 50s (23.1%) and 30s (15.8%). This is largely because HPV infection acquired during the sexually active years of the 30s and 40s often takes about 10 years to progress to cancer.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for cervical cancer depends on the stage, which reflects how far the cancer has spread.

■ Surgery
Surgery can generally be performed up through stage IIA1. The extent of surgery varies by stage.
· Stage IA1: simple hysterectomy (removal of the uterus only)
· Stage IA2: modified radical hysterectomy (removal of the uterus and some surrounding tissue)
· Stage IB1 and beyond: radical hysterectomy (removal of the uterus and a wider margin of surrounding tissue)
For patients who wish to preserve fertility, uterus-sparing surgery may be an option if certain criteria are met.
However, for stage IB3 (tumor 4 cm or larger), additional radiation therapy or chemoradiation is more likely to be needed after surgery, so other treatments may be recommended instead of surgery in some cases.

■ Radiation Therapy / Chemoradiation
This is used when surgery is difficult or when additional treatment is needed after surgery.

The treatment approach is determined by your doctor based on your condition and cancer stage. Please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Postoperative Side Effects
sections.content:
■ Leg Swelling
When pelvic lymph node dissection (removal of lymph nodes in the pelvis) is performed along with surgery, impaired lymph drainage afterward can cause leg swelling known as lymphedema. Lymph fluid is a fluid that carries waste products out of the body. Sentinel lymph node biopsy, a method that checks only the essential lymph nodes, is increasingly used to minimize the extent of lymph node removal and reduce this complication.

■ Numbness in the Hands and Feet
Numbness in the hands and feet caused directly by the surgery itself is uncommon. It can occur temporarily from nerve compression due to prolonged positioning during a long surgery. However, if chemotherapy is given, numbness in the hands and feet can occur as a side effect of the chemotherapy drugs. This is called chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. It usually resolves, but in some patients the symptoms can persist. If you experience these symptoms, please inform your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Cervical cancer is a preventable cancer. Two measures are key.

■ Regular Screening
Cervical cancer progresses from low-grade lesions (early cell changes) to high-grade lesions (more advanced cell changes) and then to invasive cancer, a process that takes about 10 years. Annual cervical cancer screening can detect these changes before they become cancer, allowing for treatment at an earlier stage. Through the National Cancer Screening Program, women age 20 and older can receive free screening every two years.

■ HPV Vaccine
The HPV vaccine reduces the occurrence of precancerous cervical lesions and helps prevent progression to cancer. However, vaccination does not completely prevent cervical cancer. Regular annual screening is still needed even after vaccination.

■ Lifestyle
Maintaining healthy sexual practices is important. Condom use helps prevent HPV infection and other sexually transmitted infections, and is one way to help reduce the risk of cervical cancer.

records.title: Uterine Fibroids
records.intro: Uterine fibroids are benign tumors that commonly occur in women. If severe menstrual pain or bleeding is interfering with daily life, evaluation by an OB/GYN specialist is essential.
records.tags_raw: uterine fibroids, menstrual pain, heavy menstrual bleeding, benign tumor, robotic surgery

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Before surgery, imaging tests such as MRI are needed to accurately distinguish fibroids from other conditions, such as adenomyosis. The surgical approach and whether the uterus is preserved can depend on your plans for future pregnancy, so please be sure to discuss this with your doctor.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Many people have no symptoms at all. However, if a fibroid is large or located inside the uterine cavity, it can cause more severe menstrual pain and heavy menstrual bleeding.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: When surgery is needed, laparoscopic or robotic surgery, which uses small incisions rather than a large abdominal opening, is commonly performed. Robotic surgery can involve less blood loss and more precise suturing, which may allow for faster recovery.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Uterine fibroids are firm growths that form in the muscular wall of the uterus, the organ where a baby develops during pregnancy. They are benign tumors, not cancer.

records.title: Endometrial Cancer
records.intro: Endometrial cancer develops in the endometrium, the tissue lining the inside of the uterus. It is a gynecologic cancer that is becoming increasingly common in Korea. In its early stages, it can cause symptoms such as abnormal vaginal bleeding, and when detected early, the outlook tends to be relatively favorable. If you have abnormal bleeding, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: endometrial cancer, uterine cancer, abnormal bleeding, menopause, obesity, endometrium, gynecologic cancer

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The most common symptom of endometrial cancer is abnormal vaginal bleeding.

· In postmenopausal women, any vaginal bleeding should always be evaluated for endometrial cancer. Among postmenopausal women with vaginal bleeding, 10% to 20% are diagnosed with endometrial cancer.
· In premenopausal women, bleeding between periods or recurrent irregular bleeding can also raise suspicion for endometrial cancer.

When symptoms occur, the cancer is often found at a relatively early stage, which is associated with better treatment outcomes. If you have abnormal vaginal bleeding, please see a medical specialist right away.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for endometrial cancer is determined by the stage of the cancer and the patient's overall condition.

· Surgery: Removal of the uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes is the primary treatment. When performed laparoscopically, recovery tends to be faster.
· Radiation therapy: Used after surgery to help prevent recurrence, or when surgery is not feasible.
· Chemotherapy: Used for advanced endometrial cancer or when the risk of recurrence is high.
· Hormone therapy: Used selectively in certain patients.

Your doctor will determine the treatment approach based on your individual condition. When detected early (stage 1 or 2), the 5-year survival rate is over 80%, reflecting a relatively favorable outlook. Regular follow-up after treatment remains important.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The following tests are used to diagnose endometrial cancer:

· Transvaginal ultrasound: measures the thickness of the endometrium. If the lining is thicker than normal, further testing is needed.
· Endometrial biopsy: a sample of endometrial tissue is taken to check for cancer cells. This is required to confirm a diagnosis of endometrial cancer.
· Hysteroscopy: allows direct visualization of the inside of the uterus and can be combined with a biopsy.
· Imaging studies such as MRI: help determine the extent of the cancer.

Women with abnormal vaginal bleeding, especially postmenopausal women, should always undergo a biopsy.

sections.heading: Risk Factors
sections.content:
Major risk factors include the following:
· Excess exposure to estrogen: early first menstruation, late menopause, never having given birth, polycystic ovary syndrome, and others
· Obesity: a substantial proportion of early-stage endometrial cancers are associated with obesity
· Diabetes mellitus and high blood pressure
· Use of the breast cancer medication tamoxifen
· A family history of endometrial cancer
· Hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes (such as Lynch syndrome)

If you have any of these risk factors, please see a medical specialist as soon as any abnormal symptoms occur.

sections.heading: Definition and Risk Factors
sections.content: Endometrial cancer is a malignant tumor (cancer) that develops in the endometrium, the tissue lining the inside of the uterus. It most often occurs after age 50, but it can also occur before menopause.

records.title: Gastroenteritis
records.intro: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the intestines that causes symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Most cases resolve on their own within 2 to 3 days. The most important part of treatment is adequate fluid replacement. If symptoms are severe or last a long time, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the intestines, most often caused by eating contaminated food or by viral or bacterial infection.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms include the following:
· Diarrhea
· Vomiting
· Abdominal pain
· Fever

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The most important part of treating gastroenteritis is replacing enough fluids and electrolytes. You should replace more fluid than is being lost through diarrhea.

Barley tea, water, and sports drinks can all be used for fluid replacement.

For food, keep the following in mind:
· Choose foods that are easy to digest and mild, such as rice porridge, mashed potatoes, and bananas.
· Milk and dairy products can be harder to digest during gastroenteritis and are best avoided.
· Caffeinated foods and drinks can worsen abdominal pain.
· If your appetite is poor due to severe symptoms, fluid replacement alone is acceptable.

If symptoms are mild, it is best not to use antidiarrheal medication without a doctor's guidance. Antidiarrheal medication should not be used if bloody stool is present.

sections.heading: Preventing Transmission
sections.content:
Gastroenteritis can spread to others if personal hygiene is not maintained.

· Wash your hands often so that hands contaminated from vomiting or diarrhea do not come into contact with others.
· Always wash your hands before and after preparing food and after using the bathroom.

sections.heading: When to See a Doctor
sections.content:
Please consult a medical specialist in the following situations:

· Symptoms last longer than 3 days
· Bloody stool occurs
· A high fever persists
· Signs of dehydration are present (very little urine, severe dizziness, or a very dry mouth)
· The affected person is an infant, young child, older adult, or has a weakened immune system

records.title: Hoarding Disorder
records.intro: Hoarding disorder is a mental health condition characterized by a compulsive inability to discard items regardless of their actual value or usefulness. Living spaces can become so filled with belongings that they are no longer usable, raising hygiene concerns and the risk of accidents. Depression or anxiety disorders often occur alongside hoarding disorder. If symptoms are suspected, please consult a psychiatrist.
records.tags_raw: hoarding disorder, compulsive collecting, compulsion, discarding items, psychiatry, co-occurring depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Hoarding disorder is a mental health condition marked by a compulsive need to collect and keep items that have lost their value or usefulness, and an inability to discard them.

The two core features are:
· Difficulty discarding possessions
· Significant distress at the thought of having to get rid of them

Simply accumulating a large number of items, having belongings increase for unavoidable reasons, or not feeling distressed when discarding items does not meet the definition of hoarding disorder. Characteristic features include intense anxiety about losing possessions and fear of losing the information those items are believed to hold.

Commonly kept items include newspapers, magazines, old clothing, bags, books, and mail or documents, but any type of item can be involved.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms can begin as early as the teenage years, start to interfere with daily life in the 20s, and become clinically significant by the 30s. Symptoms tend to worsen with age. As living spaces become filled with accumulated items, the following problems can arise:

· No space left to cook in the kitchen
· No space left to sleep in the bed
· Chairs that can no longer be used for sitting
· Unhygienic living conditions

Safety problems can also occur:
· Risk of injury from tripping over piled items
· Food contamination or infection due to poor hygiene
· Increased fire risk from malfunctioning appliances

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The exact cause of hoarding disorder is not yet fully understood. The following factors are thought to play a role:

· Genetic factors
· Brain injury (hoarding symptoms can appear in some individuals following brain injury)
· Personality traits: indecisiveness is a characteristic feature

The condition most commonly seen alongside hoarding disorder is depression, which occurs in about half of patients with hoarding disorder. Anxiety disorders also co-occur in about 25% of cases.

Because coexisting conditions can make treatment more complex, comprehensive evaluation and treatment by a medical specialist is important.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Hoarding disorder requires professional treatment. Because patients often do not recognize the problem themselves or may refuse help, support and cooperation from family and others close to the patient are important.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the primary treatment approach. Medication may be used alongside therapy if depression or anxiety disorder is also present. Please discuss a specific treatment plan with a psychiatrist.

records.title: Hypothermia
records.intro: Hypothermia refers to a drop in core body temperature to 35°C or below. The lower the body temperature falls, the more dangerous the condition becomes, and in severe cases it can lead to cardiac arrest. It can occur with prolonged exposure to extreme cold or cold environments, and extra caution is needed when alcohol has been consumed. If hypothermia is suspected, please call 119 immediately or go to a hospital.
records.tags_raw: hypothermia, cold-related illness, cold wave, body temperature, core temperature, frostbite, winter health, hand tremor, body tremor

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Hypothermia is a drop in core body temperature to 35°C or below. It is classified into three levels of severity.

· Mild (32–35°C): whole-body shivering, along with impaired memory and judgment
· Moderate (28–32°C): confusion; below 31°C, the body loses the ability to shiver to generate heat
· Severe (below 28°C): the pulse slows, and the risk of arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat) rises sharply, which can lead to life-threatening cardiac arrest

According to data from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, more than 30% of cold-related illness cases occurred while the person had been drinking alcohol. Alcohol can dull the sensation of cold and allow body temperature to drop, so caution is advised.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
As body temperature drops, the following symptoms may occur:

· Whole-body shivering
· Pale or bluish skin
· Impaired memory and judgment
· Slurred speech or clumsy movements
· Confusion
· A slowing pulse

When body temperature becomes very low, affected individuals are often unaware of their own condition. If someone nearby notices these symptoms, it is important to act immediately.

sections.heading: First Aid and Treatment
sections.content:
If you find someone with hypothermia, take the following steps:

① Remove wet clothing to prevent further heat loss.
② Move the person to a warm environment.
③ Cover them with blankets to help retain body heat.
④ Call 119 immediately or transport the person to a hospital.

For patients with moderate or severe hypothermia, hospitals provide rewarming treatment such as warmed intravenous fluids and forced-air warming blankets. If the situation is difficult to manage on your own or symptoms are severe, please seek medical care immediately.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The following measures can help prevent cold-related illness:

· Wear several thin layers of clothing to stay warm.
· Wear gloves, a scarf, and a hat.
· Change gloves or shoes immediately if they become wet.
· Avoid strenuous outdoor activity, and check the wind chill temperature before going out.
· Older adults, children, and people with chronic conditions should take extra care to stay warm.
· In particular, strenuous physical activity in cold weather can raise blood pressure and worsen cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease in older adults. It is best to limit outdoor activity in such conditions.
· Indoors, maintain a comfortable temperature (around 20°C), and get light exercise and adequate fluids.

records.title: Hypotension (Low Blood Pressure)
records.intro: Hypotension refers to blood pressure that is lower than normal. Some people have chronically low blood pressure, but when blood pressure that was normal or high suddenly drops, it can lead to serious consequences within a short time. If you experience a sudden drop in blood pressure, please seek prompt evaluation by a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, essential hypotension, dizziness, blood pressure, shock, headache, a splitting headache, migraine, back-of-head pain, feeling dizzy, spinning sensation, unsteadiness, feeling faint, lack of energy, fatigue, feeling tired all the time, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent trips to the bathroom

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines hypotension as a systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg in women and below 110 mmHg in men.

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
Hypotension is broadly divided into two types.

① Essential hypotension: low blood pressure with no identifiable underlying cause. This mainly occurs in young, active individuals.

② Chronic persistent hypotension: caused by conditions such as heart disease (including myocardial infarction or valvular heart disease), endocrine disorders, excessive use of diuretics, severe dieting, diarrhea, or bleeding.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Many people with low blood pressure have no symptoms at all. When symptoms do occur, they typically include:
· Fatigue and lack of energy
· Dizziness
· Cold hands and feet
· Sleep disturbances
· Headache

A sudden drop in blood pressure can be more dangerous.
· It can cause a sudden loss of energy and dizziness.
· A large drop in blood pressure can reduce blood flow to multiple organs, leading to shock. Shock is a medical emergency that can be life-threatening if not treated promptly.

If you experience a sudden drop in blood pressure, please call 119 immediately and go to the emergency room.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
For essential hypotension, the following lifestyle habits may help:
· Eating slightly saltier food (only if you do not have high blood pressure)
· Sleeping with your head slightly elevated on a pillow
· Reducing stress and getting adequate sleep
· A high-calorie, high-protein diet along with moderate exercise
· Wearing compression stockings, which can reduce blood pooling in the legs
· Being cautious with hot baths, saunas, and foot baths, as these can lower blood pressure further

If symptoms do not improve, medication to raise blood pressure may be considered. Please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
records.intro: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a very common condition in men in which the prostate enlarges with age, narrowing the urethra and causing urinary symptoms. The prevalence rises with age, affecting about 50% of men in their 50s and 60% of men in their 60s. Without treatment, it can lead to complications such as acute urinary retention or kidney failure, so if you have symptoms, please consult a urologist.

sections.heading: What Is Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia?
sections.content:
The prostate is a male reproductive organ that surrounds the urethra just below the bladder. Benign prostatic hyperplasia occurs when the prostate enlarges with age, narrowing the urethra and causing urinary symptoms.

■ Prevalence
Prevalence rises with age: about 50% in the 50s, 60% in the 60s, 70% in the 70s, and 80% in the 80s.

■ Winter Precautions
In winter, when temperatures drop suddenly, obstructive symptoms can worsen, and more patients visit the emergency room for acute urinary retention, a sudden inability to urinate. Acute urinary retention can lead to kidney failure, so caution is needed.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
■ Obstructive Symptoms (caused by the prostate narrowing the urethra)
- A weak urine stream
- Difficulty starting urination or needing to strain
- An interrupted urine stream
- A sense of incomplete emptying after urination

■ Irritative Symptoms (caused by an overactive bladder)
- Needing to urinate again within 2 hours of the last time
- Difficulty holding urine when the urge occurs
- Waking frequently at night to urinate

Without treatment, these symptoms can lead to acute urinary retention, blood in the urine, recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, or kidney failure.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content:
■ Diagnosis
Diagnosis involves a medical history review, the International Prostate Symptom Score questionnaire, digital rectal exam (examining the prostate through the rectum), urine tests, blood tests (creatinine, prostate-specific antigen [PSA]), transrectal ultrasound, and uroflowmetry, among others.

■ Medication
- Alpha-blockers: relax the muscles of the prostate and bladder neck to improve urine flow. They are effective in 60% to 75% of patients. Possible side effects include headache, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension (a drop in blood pressure upon standing).
- 5-alpha reductase inhibitors: reduce the size of the prostate, though it takes 3 to 6 months for the effect to appear. Possible side effects include decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. If PSA levels do not decrease sufficiently after 6 months or more of use, testing for prostate cancer may be needed.

■ Surgical Treatment
Surgery is considered when symptoms are not controlled with medication or when complications are present. Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), an endoscopic procedure that removes the enlarged tissue, is the most common approach.
