records.title: Prostate Disorders
records.intro: Prostate disorders include benign prostatic hyperplasia, which causes difficulty urinating, and prostate cancer, which is increasing rapidly among men. Both conditions tend to have few or mild symptoms in their early stages, making them easy to overlook, but if left unaddressed, they can lead to serious complications such as urinary retention or kidney failure. If you have any urinary symptoms, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostate cancer, PSA, difficulty urinating, sense of incomplete bladder emptying, nocturia, hematuria, acute urinary retention, kidney failure, men's health, urinating frequently, frequent trips to the bathroom, blood in urine, red urine, bloody urine

sections.heading: Types and Occurrence of Prostate Disorders
sections.content:
The prostate is an organ that surrounds the urethra at the base of the bladder and produces, stores, and releases seminal fluid. With age, two main disorders can develop.

■ Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
The prostate enlarges, narrowing the urethra and causing urinary symptoms. Cases rise sharply from the 60s onward, but the number of patients in their 30s and 40s is also increasing, influenced by a more Westernized diet, stress, and lack of exercise.

■ Prostate Cancer
There are typically no symptoms in the early stages, so it is often diagnosed only after the cancer has progressed significantly. Because it commonly spreads to bone, some cases are diagnosed after a patient seeks care for bone pain.

■ Relationship Between the Two Conditions
Leaving benign prostatic hyperplasia untreated does not cause it to become prostate cancer. Because the two conditions can be difficult to distinguish by symptoms alone, accurate testing is needed. Men with a first-degree relative who has had prostate cancer should consider starting screening in their 30s.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
■ Symptoms of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (gradual onset)
- Weakened urine stream
- Frequent urination
- Interrupted urine stream or needing to strain to urinate
- Waking frequently at night to urinate (nocturia)
- A sense of incomplete emptying after urination
- Urgency that is difficult to control
- In severe cases, sudden complete inability to urinate (acute urinary retention)

■ Symptoms of Prostate Cancer
There are no symptoms in the early stages. As the disease progresses, symptoms similar to benign prostatic hyperplasia can occur, including difficulty urinating, blood in the urine, and bone pain.

Because bladder dysfunction and other conditions, such as a herniated disc or diabetes mellitus, can cause similar symptoms, an evaluation of bladder function is also needed.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Treatment of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
- Medication: used to relieve symptoms or prevent further prostate growth.
- Surgery: an endoscopic procedure is performed if medication is not effective or complications develop.

■ Treatment of Prostate Cancer
- Early stage (localized prostate cancer): surgery or radiation therapy may offer a favorable outlook.
- Very low-risk cases: active surveillance (regular monitoring without treatment) may be chosen.
- Advanced cases: treatment to block male hormones (androgen deprivation therapy) along with chemotherapy is used.

■ Complications of Leaving These Conditions Untreated
Recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, declining bladder function, and kidney failure can occur. If infection becomes severe, it can progress to urosepsis, a life-threatening condition.

sections.heading: Prevention and Screening
sections.content:
■ Lifestyle
- Reduce intake of caffeine, carbonated drinks, and alcohol.
- Eat a low-fat, high-fiber diet with plenty of fruits and vegetables (tomatoes in particular).
- Maintain a healthy weight through appropriate exercise and diet.
- Avoid holding in urine for long periods.
- Sitz baths or warm baths may help improve blood circulation around the prostate.
- Reducing fluid intake after dinner can help prevent nocturia.

■ Prostate Cancer Screening
The prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test is effective for early detection. Regular screening is recommended starting at age 45, and men with a first-degree relative who has had prostate cancer should consider starting screening in their 30s.

records.title: Prostate Cancer
records.intro: Prostate cancer often has no symptoms in its early stages, so it is frequently discovered only after it has progressed significantly. Early detection is possible through the PSA (prostate-specific antigen) blood test, and when found early, surgery or radiation therapy can offer a favorable outlook. Regular screening is important for men age 45 and older, especially those with a family history.
records.tags_raw: prostate cancer, PSA, prostate-specific antigen, robotic surgery, radiation therapy, prostate biopsy, family history, androgen deprivation therapy, early screening

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: There are no symptoms in the early stages. Because symptoms such as difficulty urinating or pain typically appear only after the disease has progressed significantly, early screening before symptoms develop is the most important factor. Because symptoms resemble those of benign prostatic hyperplasia, the cancer is often found only after it has advanced. If it spreads to bone (especially the spine), it can cause bone pain or fractures.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
If the cancer has not spread beyond the prostate, surgery or radiation therapy is used. Robotic surgery, which allows highly precise movements, is now widely used and may help reduce complications such as urinary incontinence or erectile dysfunction after surgery. If the cancer has spread, hormone therapy or chemotherapy is used.

■ Localized Prostate Cancer (cancer confined to the prostate)
- Robot-assisted surgery: removes the prostate, which sits deep in the pelvis, with precision using a magnified, 10x three-dimensional view. This can help minimize unnecessary damage to surrounding tissue.
- Radiation therapy: can be given without anesthesia or an incision, making it an option even for older patients. The latest precision radiation techniques concentrate radiation on the tumor itself, reducing damage to surrounding healthy tissue and shortening treatment time.
- Active surveillance: for cases with very low risk, regular monitoring without treatment may be used instead.

■ Advanced Prostate Cancer
Androgen deprivation therapy (treatment that blocks male hormones) is used along with chemotherapy.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
■ PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen) Test
This simple blood test can help identify a person's risk of prostate cancer. A high PSA level does not necessarily mean prostate cancer is present, but it is an important factor in deciding whether a prostate biopsy is needed. A biopsy is also performed if a digital rectal exam (examining the prostate through the rectum) or ultrasound shows abnormal findings, even if PSA is not elevated.

■ Recommended Screening Guidelines
- Age 45 and older: begin PSA testing
- Before starting medication for benign prostatic hyperplasia: check for coexisting prostate cancer
- Family history of prostate cancer: begin testing in your 30s

■ Benefits of Early Detection
When found early, surgery or radiation therapy can offer a favorable outlook. Once the cancer has advanced, hormone therapy and chemotherapy become necessary, increasing the overall burden of treatment.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Prostate cancer becomes more common with age and is most frequently seen in men in their 60s and older. A Westernized diet and a family history of the disease can also contribute to risk.

■ Major Risk Factors
- Age: risk rises sharply starting in the 60s.
- Diet: linked to excessive intake of animal fat.
- Family history: having one first-degree relative with prostate cancer raises risk about 2.5-fold, two relatives about 5-fold, and three relatives about 11-fold. If you have a family history, it is advisable to begin screening in your 30s.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The prostate is an organ found only in men, responsible for producing and storing seminal fluid. Prostate cancer occurs when cancer cells develop in this gland.

Prostate cancer is one of the fastest-growing cancers among men in Korea. An aging population and a more Westernized diet are considered the main contributing factors.

records.intro: Prostatitis is inflammation of the prostate, and about 10% to 12% of all men experience symptoms of it at some point. It is the most common prostate condition in men under age 50. Because treatment differs depending on the type, an accurate diagnosis is important. If you have symptoms, please consult a urologist.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
- A burning sensation when urinating, difficulty urinating, or frequent urination (especially at night)
- Urinary urgency (a sudden, strong urge to urinate)
- Pain in the abdomen, groin, or lower back
- Pain between the scrotum and rectum, pain in the genitals or testicles, or pain with ejaculation
- Cloudy urine or blood in the urine
- Flu-like symptoms (in acute bacterial prostatitis)

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: A prior history of prostatitis, urethral or bladder infection, repeated pelvic irritation from cycling or horseback riding, urinary catheter placement, a weakened immune system, or following a prostate biopsy

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
Prostatitis is broadly classified into four types.

① Acute bacterial prostatitis: develops suddenly due to bacterial infection, with flu-like symptoms such as fever and chills.

② Chronic bacterial prostatitis: results from repeated bacterial infection. Symptoms may be mild or absent, which can make treatment more difficult.

③ Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: the most common form. It develops without a clear cause, and symptoms may come and go.

④ Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis: causes no symptoms and is often discovered incidentally during infertility or prostate cancer testing.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
- Acute bacterial prostatitis: treated with antibiotics for at least 14 days. Severe cases may require hospitalization for intravenous antibiotics.
- Chronic bacterial prostatitis: treated with antibiotics for 4 to 12 weeks.
- Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: in addition to antibiotics and anti-inflammatory medication, prostate massage (a physical therapy technique that relieves pressure on the prostate), warm baths or warm compresses, and a donut-shaped cushion may be used.
- Avoid spicy or acidic foods, caffeine, carbonated drinks, and alcohol, and increase intake of fresh food and fluids.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: Maintaining good hygiene, avoiding prolonged sitting, exercising regularly, drinking enough fluids, eating plenty of vegetables and fruit, managing weight, managing stress, and practicing safe sex

records.title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Tear
records.intro: An anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear is a rupture of the ACL, a ligament located inside the knee joint. It most often occurs during sports involving quick changes in direction. Complete tears usually require surgical treatment. If you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: anterior cruciate ligament, ACL tear, knee ligament, sports injury, ligament reconstruction, arthroscopy, knee injury, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is a ligament inside the knee that connects the femur (thigh bone) to the tibia (shin bone). Its main function is to prevent the tibia from sliding forward relative to the femur and to keep the knee joint stable.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
An ACL tear typically occurs in the following situations:
· When changing direction quickly with the foot planted, a strong valgus force (the knee buckling inward) is applied
· When landing on one leg after a jump and the knee is forced into excessive extension
It frequently occurs in sports that require quick changes in direction, such as soccer and basketball. Knee injuries are also common during skiing.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: At the moment of injury, a popping sound or a sensation of the knee giving way may occur. This is followed by significant swelling and pain in the knee. Even after initial recovery, a feeling of knee instability (a sensation that the knee is giving way) can persist during activities that involve changing direction or exercise.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content: A definitive diagnosis requires MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). Immediately after the injury, the RICE method (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) should be used, and you should see a medical specialist as soon as possible.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
For complete tears, surgery is generally recommended. However, surgery may not be performed in patients who are older, have significant arthritis, or do not plan to return to sports.
The surgery is called ACL reconstruction, in which the torn ligament is replaced. A new ligament is created using either the patient's own tendon (autograft) or a donor tendon (allograft). It is performed arthroscopically, without a large incision. For active patients in their teens through 20s, reconstruction using the patient's own tendon is generally recommended.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation and Return to Sports
sections.content:
The rehabilitation process after surgery generally proceeds as follows:
· Early phase: range-of-motion exercises
· Middle phase: starting with isometric exercises (static muscle contraction with the joint held still) and gradually progressing to strength training
· Late phase: functional exercises, and for athletes, sport-specific skill training
Return to sports is generally recommended about 6 to 9 months after surgery. Thorough warm-up and cool-down before and after exercise are important for preventing sports injuries.

records.title: Vestibular Neuritis
records.intro: Vestibular neuritis is a condition in which inflammation of the vestibular nerve, located in the inner ear, causes severe spinning vertigo. If severe dizziness and vomiting continue for several days without relief, please visit a hospital for evaluation and medication from a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The vestibular nerve is the nerve in the inner ear that transmits balance information to the brain.
Vestibular neuritis occurs when this nerve becomes inflamed, often due to invasion by a cold virus or similar pathogen.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Unlike benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), vertigo occurs even at rest, without needing to be in a specific position, and this can last anywhere from several hours to several days.

Even while at rest, the eyes may move involuntarily and rapidly (nystagmus), and the intense sensation that the surroundings are spinning can also cause vomiting.

records.title: Schizophrenia
records.intro: Schizophrenia is a major mental illness in which the ability to distinguish reality from one's own thoughts and perceptions is impaired. In Korean, the disorder was previously called jeongsinbunyeolbyeong (literally, "split-mind disease") but was renamed johyeonbyeong in 2011; the new term means "tuning the strings," reflecting the idea that mental confusion arises when the brain's neural signaling is not properly tuned. With appropriate treatment and management, people with schizophrenia can maintain daily functioning.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Schizophrenia is thought to result from a combination of factors, including biological vulnerability in the brain, an imbalance of neurotransmitters (including dopamine), and psychological and environmental factors.

It typically develops between ages 15 and 35. In men, onset is most common in the late teens to mid-20s, while in women it is most common in the early 20s. There is no difference in overall prevalence between men and women.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Positive symptoms (experiences added beyond typical functioning): auditory hallucinations (hearing sounds or voices that are not actually there) and delusions (fixed, false beliefs), among others
· Negative symptoms (a reduction in normal functioning): social withdrawal, reduced motivation, difficulty maintaining hygiene, and blunted emotional expression, among others
· Disorganized speech and behavior: speech or behavior that becomes jumbled or difficult to follow

Schizophrenia typically develops between ages 15 and 35. In men, onset is most common in the late teens to mid-20s, while in women it is most common in the early 20s. There is no difference in overall prevalence between men and women.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
A diagnosis of schizophrenia is made when at least two of the major symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms) are present for at least one month, and when symptoms — including prodromal symptoms present before the illness fully develops — have continued for six months or longer.

At the time of initial diagnosis, blood tests, urine tests, brain imaging, and EEG (electroencephalogram) may be performed. These help rule out other causes of the symptoms, such as a brain tumor or a metabolic disorder, rather than schizophrenia itself. Diagnosis is made through an evaluation by a psychiatrist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Medication
Medication is essential in the treatment of schizophrenia. Antipsychotic medications are the core treatment and are particularly effective for positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. There are dozens of these medications, generally grouped into typical and atypical antipsychotics. They work by regulating the activity of neurotransmitters, including dopamine.

Common side effects include tremor, muscle stiffness, and restlessness (extrapyramidal side effects), as well as dry mouth, constipation, and weight gain (anticholinergic side effects). Side effects can vary depending on the specific medication.

■ Psychosocial Rehabilitation
Negative symptoms such as reduced motivation and social withdrawal are often difficult to control with medication alone. Psychosocial rehabilitation, which combines daily living skills education with social skills training, is typically provided alongside medication.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
■ Preventing Relapse
· Early detection and prompt treatment are important.
· Continue taking medication as prescribed, and always consult your care team before making any changes.
· Accepting the illness and making full use of available support can help.

■ Physical Health Management
Reduced activity from negative symptoms, along with the effects of some medications, can raise the risk of metabolic syndrome (a cluster of conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia). Maintaining a balanced diet and regular exercise for weight management is important.

Many people with schizophrenia who receive appropriate treatment are able to live in the community. Negative cases portrayed in the media often involve situations in which treatment was not received. Schizophrenia is not a matter of personal willpower; it results from a disruption in the brain's neural regulation. Like other physical illnesses, it is a condition that requires treatment, and a social perspective that welcomes affected individuals as members of the community is needed.

records.title: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT)
records.intro: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a treatment that transplants hematopoietic stem cells, the cells that give rise to white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. It was previously known as bone marrow transplantation, but the name changed once it became possible to collect these cells from peripheral blood as well. It is mainly used to treat blood-related malignancies, and both the treatment process and follow-up care afterward are important.
records.tags_raw: hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, bone marrow transplant, autologous transplant, allogeneic transplant, graft-versus-host disease, blood cancer, leukemia, lymphoma, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent trips to the bathroom

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
■ Definition
Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is a treatment that transplants hematopoietic stem cells, the precursor cells that give rise to the various blood cells. It is divided into two types based on the source of the cells.
· Autologous transplantation: uses the patient's own hematopoietic stem cells.
· Allogeneic transplantation: uses hematopoietic stem cells from a donor whose human leukocyte antigen (HLA) type matches the patient's.

■ Indications
In adults, this treatment is used for blood-related conditions such as acute and chronic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and aplastic anemia.

sections.heading: Transplant Process
sections.content:
① Pre-transplant conditioning chemotherapy: aims to eliminate remaining cancer cells and creates space in the bone marrow for the new hematopoietic stem cells to take hold. Because immunity is extremely weakened during this period, treatment is carried out in a sterile isolation room.
② Infusion of hematopoietic stem cells: the cells are infused into the bloodstream in a manner similar to a standard blood transfusion.
③ Confirming engraftment: the infused stem cells settle in the bone marrow and begin producing blood cells again. Engraftment is confirmed once the neutrophil count (a type of white blood cell) recovers to at least 1,000 and the platelet count to at least 20,000.
④ Discharge: patients are discharged once blood cell counts stabilize and they have recovered from the side effects of conditioning treatment. The process from transplant to discharge typically takes 3 to 4 weeks.

For allogeneic transplants, immunosuppressive medication is taken for a period of time after engraftment to help prevent graft-versus-host disease, in which the donor's immune cells attack the patient's own tissue.

sections.heading: Stem Cell Collection Method
sections.content:
■ Finding a Donor
For autologous transplants, the cells are collected from the patient. For allogeneic transplants, a donor with a matching HLA (human leukocyte antigen) type must be found. Full-match probability between siblings with the same parents is 25%. If no sibling is a match, an unrelated donor is sought through a hematopoietic stem cell registry.

■ Collection Method
Cells are mainly collected from peripheral blood. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is injected to mobilize hematopoietic stem cells from the bone marrow into the bloodstream, and the cells are then collected using a machine similar to a dialysis machine.

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content:
· Acute phase: nausea, vomiting, mouth sores, diarrhea, low blood cell counts, and infection (including sepsis)
· Graft-versus-host disease (allogeneic transplant): skin rash, diarrhea, and abnormal liver function (acute); can potentially involve the skin, mouth, joints, lungs, and digestive system throughout the body (chronic)
· Opportunistic infections: weakened immunity raises the risk of uncommon infections such as cytomegalovirus and fungal pneumonia

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
■ Precautions After Transplant
· Avoid raw or undercooked food for a period of time.
· Take immunosuppressive medication exactly as prescribed, and do not stop it on your own.
· Rather than being overly cautious, staying as active as your care team advises can support faster recovery.

Returning to daily life typically takes about 3 to 6 months after autologous transplantation, and longer after allogeneic transplantation. Regular outpatient follow-up is important, so please stay in close contact with your hematologist or transplant specialist about any new symptoms or concerns.

records.title: Metatarsalgia
records.intro: Metatarsalgia is pain that occurs in the ball of the foot, specifically the sole beneath the base of the second, third, and fourth toes. The metatarsals are the long bones in the foot that lead into the toes. Because it can have various causes, please consult a medical specialist for an accurate diagnosis.
records.tags_raw: metatarsalgia, ball of foot pain, sole pain, calluses, high heels, transverse arch, foot

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The "ball of the foot" is the wide part of the front of the foot, the area described as "wide" or "narrow" when choosing shoes. Pain occurring in the sole beneath the base of the second, third, and fourth toes in this area is called metatarsalgia.
The area hurts when standing still or walking, and pain can also be felt when the sole and top of the foot are squeezed firmly. Calluses or corns can develop at the site of pain, and the toes may become deformed into a claw-toe or hammer-toe shape.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Suddenly performing intense toe-flexing exercises can actually worsen symptoms. It is important to begin exercise only within a pain-free range and under the guidance of a specialist or therapist.
Even if calluses or corns are present, please do not try to remove them yourself, and consult a medical specialist instead.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment depends on the underlying cause.
· When caused by muscle tightness: calf-muscle stretching exercises can help. If excess weight is a factor, weight loss is important for relieving symptoms.
· Orthotic treatment: metatarsal pads or custom insoles can help reduce pressure on the painful area. Shoes with a soft sole material can also provide a cushioning effect.
· Changing footwear: switching to shoes with a wider toe box and a wider sole can help. For patients with joint damage from conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, shoes with a rocker-bottom sole are recommended.
Please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions about treatment.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The following tests may be used to accurately diagnose metatarsalgia:
· Physical examination of the foot
· X-ray (taken while bearing weight)
· Blood tests
· Plantar pressure measurement
· Nuclear medicine bone scan
· Ultrasound, MRI, or electromyography (EMG), if needed
If symptoms persist, please consult a medical specialist to determine the exact cause.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The main causes of metatarsalgia include the following:
First, tightness in the calf muscles or a shortened Achilles tendon (the tendon at the back of the heel). This causes too much weight to be placed on the front of the foot while walking. It is common in people who frequently wear high heels or elevator shoes, or who run or jump often.
Second, collapse of the transverse arch (the arch running across the front of the foot). This can occur when ligaments or muscles weaken due to bunions, rheumatoid arthritis, or trauma.
Third, a high-arched foot (pes cavus), in which the longitudinal arch (the arch running from front to back along the inside of the foot) is higher than normal. This is usually due to a genetic cause.
It can also occur from prolonged walking on hard surfaces or wearing shoes with a hard sole.

records.title: Seborrheic Dermatitis
records.intro: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic skin condition in which dry or greasy yellowish scales form on top of areas of erythema (redness). If symptoms recur, please consult a dermatologist.
records.tags_raw: seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff, scalp, eyebrows, erythema, scaling, dermatitis, winter

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Most often appears on the face, particularly at the inner eyebrows, forehead, upper eyelids, nasolabial folds (the creases beside the nose), and the outer edges of the nostrils.
· Often appears symmetrically on both sides.
· Low humidity and cold weather in winter and early spring tend to worsen symptoms.
· When it occurs on the scalp, it can appear as dandruff.
Please see a medical specialist for an accurate diagnosis and treatment.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Seborrheic dermatitis is a common skin condition, affecting about 2% to 5% of the population.

records.title: Rectal Cancer
records.intro: Rectal cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the rectum, the final section of the large intestine. It often causes almost no symptoms in its early stages and is frequently found incidentally, which makes regular screening very important. If you suspect this condition, please do not try to judge it yourself — be sure to see a medical specialist for a proper evaluation and testing.
records.tags_raw: rectal cancer, colorectal cancer, blood in stool, hemorrhoids, bowel obstruction, laparoscopic surgery, colonoscopy, indigestion, bloating, poor digestion, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent trips to the bathroom, constipation, difficulty passing stool, hard stool, blood on stool, bloody stool, bright red stool

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Rectal cancer typically has almost no warning symptoms in its early stages. As the cancer progresses, the following symptoms may appear:

· Change in bowel habits: stool that is narrower than usual, or a change in how often you have bowel movements
· Blood in stool: bright red blood mixed with stool. With hemorrhoids, blood typically appears after the stool has passed, but with rectal cancer, blood is often mixed directly into the stool.
· Bowel obstruction and indigestion: as the tumor grows and narrows the intestine, this can cause constipation, or, conversely, watery diarrhea.

If you feel a hard mass inside the anus or have severe pain, please do not assume it is hemorrhoids on your own — be sure to get it evaluated.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
A more Westernized diet, along with frequent alcohol consumption and smoking, is considered a leading cause. As a result, the number of rectal cancer patients under age 50 has been on the rise.

Genetic factors, or family history, are also very important. If a first-degree relative has had colorectal cancer, the risk for the rest of the family can be 2 to 8 times higher.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for rectal cancer depends on how far the cancer has progressed (its stage).

· Stage 0 to 1: In early stages, removal of the tumor via colonoscopy can offer a favorable outlook.
· Stage 2 to 3: Radiation therapy and chemotherapy are typically given for about 6 to 8 weeks before surgery to shrink the tumor. Surgery to remove the cancer then follows.

Open surgery through a large abdominal incision was once common, but laparoscopic surgery and robotic surgery, which use only small incisions, are now the main approaches. In particular, significant advances in techniques that preserve anal function without removing the anus have improved patients' quality of life.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
For rectal and colorectal cancer, early detection through regular health checkups is the most reliable form of prevention.

· Adults age 50 and older should have an annual fecal occult blood test to check for blood in the stool, and a colonoscopy should follow if the result is abnormal.
· Because recent research shows an increasing number of younger patients, screening every two years starting at age 45 is considered advantageous in terms of both cost and health.

Even at a younger age, if blood in the stool or indigestion continues, please do not simply attribute it to stress or heavy drinking — consult a medical specialist. This content is intended as general health information and is not a substitute for individual diagnosis.

records.title: Sphincter-Preserving Surgery for Rectal Cancer
records.intro: Whether the anus can be preserved during rectal cancer surgery depends on the location of the tumor and whether it has invaded the anal sphincter. Because this directly affects quality of life, please consult an experienced colorectal surgeon for an accurate diagnosis and treatment.
records.tags_raw: rectal cancer, sphincter preservation, ostomy, low anterior resection, Kegel exercises

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The rectum is the final section of the large intestine, connecting to the anus. The anus contains the important sphincter muscles that allow voluntary control over bowel movements. Removing rectal cancer while preserving these sphincter muscles is called sphincter-preserving surgery, or anal preservation.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Even when the anus is preserved, discomfort such as loose stool or frequent urges to have a bowel movement can occur right after surgery. This typically improves over time, and Kegel exercises (tightening the sphincter muscles) can help with recovery. Regular follow-up testing to check for recurrence should continue for up to 5 years after surgery.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: If the tumor is located at least 1 cm from the anus and has not invaded the sphincter muscles, the anus can typically be preserved. Shrinking the tumor with chemoradiation before surgery can further improve the chance of preservation. The surgical approach depends on the tumor's location; if the sphincter has been invaded, the anus must be removed and a stoma (an opening in the abdomen for stool collection, or ostomy) must be created.

records.title: Vaginitis
records.intro: Vaginitis is inflammation of the vagina and is common among women. Depending on the cause, it is classified as bacterial vaginosis, candidal vaginitis, trichomonas vaginitis, or atrophic vaginitis, among others. If you have symptoms such as discharge, odor, or itching, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: vaginitis, bacterial vaginosis, candidal vaginitis, trichomoniasis, atrophic vaginitis, vaginal discharge, itching

sections.heading: Types and Symptoms
sections.content:
Vaginitis is classified by cause as follows:

· Bacterial vaginosis: the most common type of vaginitis. It occurs when the normal balance of bacteria in the vagina is disrupted. It is characterized by increased discharge with a fish-like odor.
· Candidal vaginitis (vulvovaginal candidiasis): caused by a fungus (Candida). It is characterized by itching along with a thick, white, cottage cheese–like discharge. It tends to occur with reduced immunity or in warm, moist conditions.
· Trichomonas vaginitis: an infection caused by the parasite Trichomonas, mainly transmitted through sexual contact. It can involve yellow discharge, odor, and itching.
· Atrophic vaginitis: occurs when estrogen levels decline after menopause. It can involve itching, discharge, and vaginal bleeding.

sections.heading: Risk Factors
sections.content:
The risk of vaginitis can increase in the following situations:

· Wearing non-breathable underwear or panty liners for long periods can trap heat and moisture, changing the vaginal environment and leading to bacterial vaginosis or candidal vaginitis.
· Wearing tight-fitting clothing, such as leggings or skinny jeans, for long periods can also be a contributing factor.
· Washing inside the vagina with cleansers or soap can disrupt the vagina's normal acidic environment and worsen bacterial vaginosis.
· Candidal vaginitis tends to occur more easily when immunity is reduced, such as in diabetes mellitus.
· Trichomonas vaginitis is transmitted through sexual contact.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The following habits can help prevent vaginitis:

· Choose 100% cotton, breathable underwear.
· Use panty liners only during times of temporarily increased discharge, such as just before or after your period or during ovulation, and change them often. It is best not to use them at other times.
· Shower and change underwear promptly after exercise or heavy sweating.
· Do not wash inside the vagina with cleansers or soap.
· Adequate rest and nutrition can help prevent candidal vaginitis. If you have diabetes mellitus, managing blood sugar is important.
· Use condoms during sexual intercourse to help prevent trichomonas vaginitis.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment depends on the type of vaginitis.

· Bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas vaginitis: treated with antibiotics. For trichomonas vaginitis, it is important for the sexual partner to be treated as well.
· Candidal vaginitis: treated with antifungal medication.
· Atrophic vaginitis: vaginal estrogen tablets or cream can help when symptoms are significant. However, when only vaginal symptoms are present with no other menopausal symptoms, whether to take oral hormone medication should be decided after consultation with a medical specialist.

If you have symptoms, please seek an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment from a medical specialist rather than self-treating.

records.title: Scrub Typhus
records.intro: Scrub typhus is an acute febrile infectious disease that occurs mainly in the fall. It is caused by the bite of a chigger mite larva carrying the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. Covering the skin well during outdoor activity and showering afterward are key to prevention. If flu-like symptoms develop after outdoor activity in the fall, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: scrub typhus, mites, fall febrile illness, fever, rash, grave visits, outdoor activity, headache, a splitting headache, migraine, back-of-head pain, feverish, having a fever, high fever, low-grade fever, body shaking, chills, feeling cold and shivering, hand tremor, body tremor

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Scrub typhus is an acute febrile infectious disease caused by the bite of a chigger mite larva carrying the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It occurs mainly in the fall (September to November).

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
A mite bite does not necessarily mean you will develop scrub typhus. The disease occurs only when bitten by a mite carrying the bacterium.

Outdoor activities in grassy areas or places where field mice live — such as visiting family graves, hiking, or farm work — carry a higher risk.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms typically appear about 8 to 11 days after the mite bite.

The main symptoms include:
· High fever, chills, headache, and muscle aches (similar to a cold with body aches)
· A black scab (eschar) at the site of the mite bite
· A red rash on the trunk and limbs

The black eschar and rash are characteristic findings of scrub typhus. If flu-like symptoms develop after outdoor activity in the fall, please consider scrub typhus and be sure to visit a hospital.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content:
Based on symptoms alone, it is often difficult to distinguish scrub typhus from a common cold with body aches. If flu-like symptoms appear after outdoor activity in the fall, be sure to tell your doctor about your outdoor activity history.

Early treatment with the appropriate antibiotic can lead to rapid improvement in symptoms. If treatment is delayed, complications can occur in rare cases, so please seek immediate medical attention when symptoms appear.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Avoiding mite bites is the most important form of prevention.

Precautions for outdoor activity include the following:
· Wear long sleeves and long pants to minimize exposed skin.
· Apply insect repellent.
· Avoid lying down on grass or using the bathroom in grassy areas.
· Change clothes and shower promptly after outdoor activity.

There is currently no vaccine for scrub typhus. If symptoms develop after outdoor activity, seeking prompt medical care is important.

records.title: Vertebral Compression Fracture
records.intro: A vertebral compression fracture occurs when the impact of a fall onto the buttocks is transmitted to the spine, although in severe osteoporosis a vertebra can also collapse gradually without a significant impact. Severe back pain, including pain with coughing, is a main symptom. In older adults, prolonged bed rest during recovery can lead to complications such as pneumonia or pressure sores, so caution is needed. If you have back pain after a fall, please consult an orthopedic specialist.
records.tags_raw: vertebral fracture, compression fracture, spine, back pain, osteoporosis, fall, fracture in older adults, bone cement, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: What Is a Vertebral Compression Fracture?
sections.content:
A vertebral compression fracture occurs when the impact from a fall, transmitted from the buttocks to the spine, causes a vertebra to become crushed and collapse. It typically happens when falling into a sitting position.

If osteoporosis is severe, a vertebra can gradually collapse even without a significant impact. When fractures occur repeatedly in multiple vertebrae, the spine can curve forward, a deformity known as kyphosis. This is commonly seen in older adults with a forward-stooped posture.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of a vertebral compression fracture include:

· Severe back pain
· Pain not only with movement but also with something as simple as a light cough
· Difficulty standing or walking for long periods
· If multiple fractures occur or the condition is left untreated for a long time, the spine can develop a forward-curving deformity

When severe pain keeps a person from being active and confined to bed for a long period, the risk of serious complications such as pneumonia or pressure sores increases. If you have back pain after a fall, please do not leave it unaddressed — seek prompt medical evaluation.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
At the hospital, a physical examination is performed along with the following imaging tests:

· X-ray: can identify most fractures.
· CT (computed tomography): provides an accurate view of the fracture's detailed shape and severity.
· MRI: performed when the fracture is unclear on other imaging or to check for damage to surrounding soft tissue, such as muscles and ligaments.

In older patients, a bone density scan is often also performed to check for underlying osteoporosis.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The treatment approach depends on the severity of the fracture and the level of pain.

■ Nonsurgical Treatment
Pain relievers are used to reduce pain, and a brace (a support device for the spine) is worn to help prevent further collapse of the vertebra.

■ Surgical Treatment
When pain is severe or the risk of further vertebral collapse is high, a procedure that injects bone cement into the vertebra can be performed to stabilize it and reduce pain. This can now often be done under local anesthesia, which has reduced the surgical burden for older patients.

The treatment approach is determined by a specialist based on the patient's condition. Please be sure to consult an orthopedic specialist.

records.title: Asthma
records.intro: Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition in which the airways (the passages through which air moves in and out of the lungs) become hypersensitive, often due to allergic reactions, and narrow, causing recurring coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath. It is sometimes mistaken for a severe cough or cold, which can delay proper treatment. Symptoms can worsen with exposure to yellow dust, fine particulate matter, or pollen. If you have recurring coughing or shortness of breath, please consult a pulmonologist or allergist.
records.tags_raw: asthma, bronchi, allergy, cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, inhaler, bronchodilator, yellow dust, fine particulate matter, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, labored breathing, feeling of suffocation, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Asthma is a chronic condition in which the airways become overly sensitive (hyperresponsive) to external triggers and narrow as a result. When the airways narrow, air has difficulty moving in and out, causing a range of respiratory symptoms. A key feature of asthma is that symptoms tend to improve and worsen in cycles.

Asthma can occur at any age and is especially common in children and older adults. As yellow dust and air pollution have worsened, the number of asthma patients has tended to increase.

If asthma is suspected, taking only over-the-counter cold medication is not advisable, since certain cold medication ingredients can trigger an asthma attack — please be sure to see a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Asthma is a type of allergic condition. Its causes and aggravating factors include the following:

■ Major Allergy Triggers
· Dust mites
· Pollen
· Pet hair and dander
· Mold and cockroaches

■ Other Aggravating Factors
· Air pollution (fine particulate matter, yellow dust)
· Smoking and secondhand smoke: cause airway damage and inflammation, increasing the risk of developing asthma
· Respiratory infections (colds, influenza, etc.)
· Cold, dry air
· Exercise (particularly sudden exercise in cold weather without warming up)
· Stress

Having a family member with asthma or allergic rhinitis increases the likelihood of developing the condition.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of asthma include:

· Recurring cough: often worse at night or in the early morning.
· Wheezing: a whistling or high-pitched sound while breathing.
· Shortness of breath: a sensation of breathlessness and chest tightness.
· A feeling of chest tightness

Symptoms tend to cycle between flare-ups (asthma attacks) and periods of improvement. Improvement in symptoms does not mean the condition has fully resolved. If you have a severe, persistent cough or recurring difficulty breathing, consider the possibility of asthma.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Asthma is diagnosed based on symptoms, a physical examination, and lung function testing.

· Lung function test (spirometry): measures how narrowed the airways are. Asthma is diagnosed by checking whether lung function improves after inhaling a bronchodilator.
· Allergy testing: skin allergy testing or blood tests are used to identify the allergens involved.
· Airway hyperresponsiveness testing: measures how sensitively the airways react to a stimulus.

It is important to distinguish asthma from other conditions with similar symptoms, such as COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), heart failure, and bronchiectasis.

sections.heading: Treatment and Management
sections.content:
Because asthma is a chronic condition, ongoing treatment and management are essential.

■ Inhaled Medications
· Inhaled steroids (anti-inflammatory medication): the foundation of treatment, reducing airway inflammation. Consistent use can help prevent flare-ups.
· Bronchodilators: widen the narrowed airways to make breathing easier. These include fast-acting medications used immediately when symptoms occur, and long-acting medications used daily for prevention.
· Inhalers are only effective when used with the correct technique. Be sure to have your care team teach you the proper technique when you first receive a prescription.

■ Taking and Stopping Medication
· Do not suddenly stop your medication just because symptoms have improved, without first discussing it with your doctor. Asthma can worsen again.
· If asthma has been well controlled for several months to years, you may discuss with your specialist whether to gradually reduce medication.

■ Exercise
· When asthma is well controlled, any type of exercise is generally possible.
· Sudden exercise in cold, dry weather without warming up can trigger a flare-up.
· Warm up thoroughly before exercise, and if needed, use a bronchodilator beforehand.

■ Environmental Management
· Reduce exposure to your known allergens.
· When fine particulate matter levels are high, limit time outdoors and wear a mask.
· Quit smoking and avoid secondhand smoke.
· Wash your hands and get vaccinated to help prevent colds and influenza.

records.title: Osteoporosis in Patients with Asthma
records.intro: Long-term use of steroid medications used to treat severe or chronic asthma can lead to osteoporosis. When osteoporosis becomes severe, a vertebral compression fracture can occur even with minor impact, so caution is needed. Please have regular bone density testing and follow up with a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: asthma, osteoporosis, steroids, vertebral compression fracture, bone density, calcium, vitamin D, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: The Relationship Between Steroid Treatment and Osteoporosis
sections.content:
Steroid medications, in inhaled or oral form, are commonly used to treat asthma. However, long-term steroid use can suppress bone formation and lead to osteoporosis.
· The higher the dose, the greater the suppression of bone formation.
· Oral steroids have a more pronounced effect on reducing bone density than inhaled steroids.
· High-dose inhaled steroids can also contribute to osteoporosis, so caution is needed.
· Steroids can interfere with calcium absorption and vitamin D metabolism, which can further worsen bone loss.

sections.heading: Risk Factors for Osteoporosis
sections.content:
The following risk factors can further worsen osteoporosis in patients with asthma:
· Risk increases with higher steroid doses and longer duration of use.
· Postmenopausal women: already at increased risk of bone loss due to declining estrogen levels.
· Older patients: osteoporosis is often accompanied by muscle loss (sarcopenia).
· Insufficient calcium and vitamin D intake, low physical activity, smoking, and alcohol use also increase the risk of bone loss.
· Frequent asthma flare-ups requiring high-dose steroids further increase the risk of bone loss.

sections.heading: Symptoms and Diagnosis
sections.content:
Osteoporosis itself is usually painless, so many people are unaware they have it. However, once bones have weakened, a fracture can occur even with minor impact.
In patients with asthma, a compression fracture of the thoracic spine (upper back) can occur from coughing alone. If new pain develops in the back or side after coughing, a vertebral compression fracture should be considered.
Diagnosis is made using a bone density scan (DXA scan), which measures bone density at the spine and femur (thigh bone). A T-score of -2.5 or lower is diagnostic of osteoporosis.

sections.heading: Treatment and Prevention
sections.content:
The following measures can help prevent and manage osteoporosis in patients with asthma:
· Monitor bone health with regular bone density testing.
· Get adequate calcium (1,000–1,200 mg per day) and vitamin D (800–1,000 IU per day).
· Strengthen bone and muscle with weight-bearing exercise, such as walking and strength training.
· If diagnosed with osteoporosis, follow your specialist's prescribed medication regimen.
· Discuss with your doctor whether steroid use can be minimized where possible.
Preventing falls is also important for avoiding fractures. Creating a safer home environment — for example, reducing slip hazards and ensuring adequate lighting — can help.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Once a fracture occurs, the spine can develop a deformity (kyphosis, a forward-curving of the back), which is difficult to reverse. A back that has curved forward can lead to ongoing pain and reduced quality of life in daily activities.
The following groups are at especially high risk of osteoporotic fracture. In these cases, it is important to discuss more active treatment, such as bone-forming medications, with a specialist.
· A fracture within the past 12 months
· A fracture that occurred while already on osteoporosis medication
· Long-term steroid use that cannot be avoided
· A T-score of -3.0 or lower

records.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia
records.intro: Iron deficiency anemia is a condition in which a lack of iron in the body leads to a shortage of red blood cells. Common symptoms include pallor, fatigue, dizziness, and shortness of breath during exercise. It occurs especially frequently in women of childbearing age. If anemia persists for a long time, it can place strain on the heart, so identifying the cause and receiving appropriate treatment is important. If you suspect these symptoms, please consult a hematology-oncology specialist.
records.tags_raw: anemia, iron deficiency anemia, iron, hemoglobin, iron supplement, fatigue, pallor, dizziness, women of childbearing age, fainting, loss of consciousness, syncope, low energy, lethargy, persistent tiredness, indigestion, bloating, upset stomach, loose stools, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements, constipation, difficulty passing stool, hard stool, double vision, overlapping vision

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Anemia is a condition in which the blood contains too few red blood cells. Red blood cells carry oxygen to every part of the body. Hemoglobin, a protein within red blood cells, is responsible for carrying this oxygen.

Iron is an essential component in making hemoglobin. When iron is lacking, hemoglobin is not produced adequately, red blood cells decrease, and this results in iron deficiency anemia.

Dizziness does not always mean anemia. Dizziness can result from various causes, including nervous system disorders and inner ear (vestibular) problems. Dizziness caused by anemia typically occurs when standing up from a sitting position or suddenly changing posture.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Iron deficiency anemia can develop under the following circumstances.

· Inadequate iron intake: A diet lacking in iron. A predominantly vegetarian diet has a lower iron absorption rate than a diet that includes meat and can lead to anemia.
· Increased iron requirements: Growing children and adolescents, and women who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
· Chronic bleeding (blood loss): This is the most common cause in adults.
  - Women of childbearing age: Monthly menstrual bleeding, or increased menstrual flow due to uterine fibroids.
  - In men or postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anemia requires evaluation for chronic gastrointestinal (stomach, intestinal) bleeding.
· Impaired iron absorption: Prior intestinal surgery, malabsorption conditions, or long-term use of antacids (acid-reducing medications).

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of iron deficiency anemia include the following.

· Pale or yellowish appearance of the skin and the whites of the eyes (conjunctiva)
· Easy fatigue and low energy
· Dizziness when standing up from sitting, or a feeling of the vision going dark; brief fainting may occur in severe cases
· Shortness of breath during exercise (needing to rest due to breathlessness on stairs or inclines)
· Rapid heartbeat, and chest tightness or discomfort during exercise

If anemia is severe and persists for a long time, the heart may have to work harder to compensate, which can lead to heart failure (reduced heart function).

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Once iron deficiency anemia is diagnosed, identifying the underlying cause and taking iron supplements form the basic treatment.

■ How to take iron supplements, and precautions
· Oral iron supplements are the first-line treatment. Taking them on an empty stomach improves absorption when possible. However, if indigestion is severe, they may be taken right after a meal instead.
· Taking iron supplements together with vitamin C can help absorption.
· Taking them together with antacids (acid-reducing medications) reduces iron absorption. Avoid taking them together.
· Indigestion, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and dark-colored stools may occur after taking iron supplements. Dark stools simply reflect unabsorbed iron passing through and are not a cause for concern. However, if your stool is black, tarry, and sticky, it can be a sign of bleeding, so please see a doctor promptly. Digestive symptoms usually improve after an adjustment period.
· Stopping iron treatment as soon as hemoglobin returns to normal may leave iron stores depleted. Oral iron is commonly continued for about 3 months after hemoglobin normalization, although a longer or shorter course may be needed depending on the cause of iron deficiency, blood tests, and your doctor's advice.
· If symptoms are severe or oral supplements are difficult to take, injectable iron may be used instead.

Please discuss the method and duration of iron supplementation with your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The following lifestyle habits can help prevent iron deficiency anemia.

■ Iron-rich foods
· Meat: beef, pork, chicken
· Seafood: fish, shellfish
· Vegetables: leafy greens such as spinach, legumes

However, the iron in vegetables is absorbed less readily than the iron in meat. People who follow a predominantly vegetarian diet should pay particular attention to this.

■ Other precautions
· Avoid taking antacids frequently over a long period. Weakened stomach acid reduces iron absorption.
· Women of childbearing age should monitor their menstrual pattern and consult a medical specialist if menstrual flow is excessive.
· If men or postmenopausal women develop anemia of unknown cause, please undergo upper endoscopy and colonoscopy to check for possible gastrointestinal bleeding.

records.title: Early-Onset Dementia (Young-Onset Dementia)
records.intro: Dementia is not a disease that affects only older adults. Dementia that develops at a relatively young age, between 45 and 65, is called early-onset (presenile) dementia. Because it tends to progress faster than dementia in older adults, please consult a medical specialist without delay if symptoms occur.
records.tags_raw: early-onset dementia, young-onset dementia, alcohol-related dementia, lifestyle diseases, vascular dementia

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Even when a diagnosis of dementia is made in the late 60s, the disease process in the brain has often already been progressing slowly since the 40s or 50s. Frequent memory blackouts from heavy drinking at a young age should therefore not be dismissed lightly, and careful management is needed.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: This is a condition in which toxic substances accumulate in the brain or blood vessel problems develop at a young age, leading to declining memory and judgment. The number of dementia cases among adults in their 40s and 50s has recently increased sharply, nearly tripling compared with previous levels.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: The condition often begins with what appears to be severe forgetfulness, with memory and calculation ability gradually declining. Because outward appearance, such as social behavior and grooming, can remain largely intact, those around the person may not notice the illness until later.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
No single definitive cause has been identified, but the following factors are known to contribute to earlier onset.

· Severe stress and exposure to harmful environments
· Excessive dependence on smartphones or other digital devices
· Alcohol use: Alcohol-related dementia, caused by brain cell damage from excessive drinking, accounts for a significant proportion of cases.
· Lifestyle diseases: High blood pressure, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity make vascular dementia — caused by gradual damage to small blood vessels in the brain — more likely to develop. High blood pressure is considered the single greatest risk factor.

records.title: Spring Fatigue Syndrome
records.intro: Spring fatigue syndrome is a condition marked by a combination of fatigue, sleepiness, reduced appetite, and difficulty concentrating during the spring season. It occurs as the body temporarily adjusts to the increasing daylight hours of the season. It usually improves on its own within a few weeks and can be managed with exercise, a regular routine, and a balanced diet. However, fatigue that persists regardless of season may have a different cause, so please consult a medical specialist in that case.
records.tags_raw: spring fatigue syndrome, chronic fatigue, fatigue, spring fatigue, sleep disorder, fatigue recovery, vitamins, protein, lifestyle habits, low energy, lethargy, persistent tiredness

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Spring fatigue syndrome is a condition marked by a combination of unexplained tiredness, reduced appetite, and daytime sleepiness and lethargy during the spring. It is understood to occur as the body adjusts to the environmental change of lengthening daylight hours in spring.

■ Symptoms suggestive of spring fatigue syndrome
- Feeling tired for no apparent reason
- Reduced appetite and motivation
- Difficulty getting up in the morning
- Sleepiness and lethargy in the afternoon
- Wanting to rest even without having done strenuous activity
- The above symptoms recur each spring and resolve on their own within a few weeks

■ When spring fatigue syndrome is more likely
An irregular or sedentary winter routine, low intake of fresh vegetables and fruit, sleep disturbances or excessive morning sleepiness, and high stress levels

sections.heading: Distinguishing from Chronic Fatigue and Sleep Disorders
sections.content:
Spring fatigue syndrome can be distinguished from chronic fatigue and sleep disorders by the following features.

■ Spring fatigue syndrome vs. chronic fatigue
- Spring fatigue syndrome: Lasts a few weeks, recurs each spring, improves with rest, daily functioning largely maintained
- Chronic fatigue: Persists 3 months or longer, unrelated to season, does not improve with rest, functioning is impaired

■ Spring fatigue syndrome vs. sleep disorders
- Spring fatigue syndrome: Falling asleep and sleeping soundly are not difficult; naps are refreshing
- Sleep disorders: Difficulty falling asleep and shortened sound sleep; naps provide little benefit

If fatigue persists regardless of season or does not improve with rest, it may have another cause, such as thyroid dysfunction, anemia, depression, or hepatitis. In this case, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: How to Relieve Spring Fatigue Syndrome
sections.content:
■ 1. Regular exercise
Engage in activities such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, jump rope, or ball sports 3 to 5 times a week, for at least 30 minutes each session. Start with slow walking and gradually increase speed and duration every 1 to 2 weeks.

■ 2. A regular daily rhythm
Keep a consistent wake-up time each morning. If sleep is insufficient, a short nap after lunch is more effective than extending nighttime sleep.

■ 3. A balanced diet
- Supplement vitamins with fresh vegetables and fruit.
- Eating protein-rich foods at breakfast and lunch can aid alertness.
- A carbohydrate-heavy diet can promote sleepiness, so it is best to reduce it.
- Make use of seasonal spring foods (spring greens, young shoots, fresh fruit).

■ 4. Other measures
- Maintain smoking cessation and limit alcohol intake.
- Ventilate indoor spaces every 1 to 2 hours.
- Limit coffee to one or two cups a day (excessive intake can disturb sleep).
- Fatigue-relief supplements are only a temporary measure and do not address the underlying cause.

records.title: Pancreatic Cancer
records.intro: Pancreatic cancer is cancer that develops in the pancreas, an organ located deep within the body. Because it produces few early symptoms, it is often found at a later stage. Please do not attempt to self-diagnose using an online encyclopedia; if you notice any concerning symptoms, be sure to see a gastroenterology or hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery specialist.
records.tags_raw: pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy, abdominal CT, jaundice, chronic pancreatitis

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Because the pancreas is located deep within the abdomen, it is difficult to visualize clearly with standard ultrasound. Therefore, when pancreatic cancer is suspected, an abdominal CT (computed tomography) scan is typically performed first, followed by more detailed imaging such as MRI if needed.

The pancreas sits deep in the body, and gas in the stomach and intestines makes it difficult to view the entire organ on abdominal ultrasound. In addition, symptoms are often minimal until a tumor has grown large enough to affect nearby organs. For these reasons, early detection is very difficult. In some cases, pancreatic cancer is found incidentally during an abdominal CT performed as part of a routine health checkup.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms that may raise suspicion of pancreatic cancer include the following.
· Abdominal pain: Pain in the upper central abdomen (epigastric area) is particularly common.
· Jaundice: The skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow. Urine may also become dark brown or reddish in color.
· Weight loss: Unexplained weight loss occurring over several months.
· Digestive problems: Persistent indigestion without a clear cause.
· Changes in diabetes: Diabetes may suddenly develop, or existing diabetes may suddenly become difficult to control.

If symptoms are unclear or persistent, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for pancreatic cancer is determined by how far the cancer has progressed and the patient's overall condition. Treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and endoscopic or interventional procedures.

■ Surgery

Surgery is the most important treatment for pancreatic cancer. However, it is not an option for every patient; resectability is determined by comprehensively evaluating the tumor's location, involvement of major blood vessels, and whether distant metastasis is present. For resectable pancreatic cancer, adjuvant chemotherapy is given after surgery to lower the risk of recurrence.

■ Chemotherapy

Chemotherapy is used to help prevent recurrence after surgery, or to control disease progression when surgery is not feasible at the time of diagnosis. For borderline resectable pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy is often given before surgery to improve the chance of successful resection. In some cases of locally advanced pancreatic cancer, the possibility of surgery may be reassessed based on the response to chemotherapy.

■ Radiation therapy and supportive care

Radiation therapy may be considered together with chemotherapy in some patients, such as those with locally advanced pancreatic cancer. When jaundice, pain, vomiting, or nutritional problems are present, endoscopic procedures, biliary drainage, pain management, and nutritional support can help relieve symptoms and allow treatment to continue.

The treatment plan for pancreatic cancer is determined by comprehensively considering the cancer stage, imaging results, overall health status, and the patient's treatment goals. It is therefore important to discuss options thoroughly with a medical specialist to determine the most appropriate treatment approach for the individual.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The following factors are known to increase the risk of developing pancreatic cancer.
· Smoking: Smokers have a higher risk than non-smokers.
· Diabetes: If diabetes develops suddenly, particularly without a family history, please consult a medical specialist.
· Chronic pancreatitis: A condition involving persistent inflammation of the pancreas. Heavy alcohol use is a major cause.
· Obesity: Maintaining an appropriate body weight is important.
· Family history: If several immediate family members have had pancreatic cancer, please consult a medical specialist.
· Age: Most cases occur in people age 55 or older.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: Quitting smoking entirely is essential for pancreatic health. Reducing alcohol intake and managing weight through appropriate exercise are also important. If a family member has had pancreatic cancer, please be sure to undergo regular medical checkups.

sections.heading: Precautions When a Pancreatic Cyst Is Found
sections.content: A pancreatic cyst is a fluid-filled sac that forms within the pancreas. With the increasing use of health checkups, pancreatic cysts are now often found incidentally. Certain types of pancreatic cysts can progress to pancreatic cancer. If a pancreatic cyst is found, please consult a medical specialist to determine an appropriate follow-up schedule and method based on its size and characteristics. Regular follow-up monitoring is important.

records.title: Dementia Prevention
records.intro: Dementia does not appear suddenly; it results from harmful changes that accumulate in the brain over a long period of time. Building good habits in daily life from a young age is the best way to help prevent it. Making an ongoing effort to protect one's own health is especially important. If you or a loved one notices signs of memory loss or other cognitive changes, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: dementia prevention, three do's and three don'ts, depression, stress, aerobic exercise

sections.heading: Managing Your Mind
sections.content:
When under stress, forcibly telling yourself, 'don't think bad thoughts,' can actually make those thoughts stick more firmly in your mind. It is often better to trust that things will improve with time and to wait calmly.

Dwelling only in your thoughts on painful memories from the past that cannot be changed (trauma) can worsen depression. In these situations, stopping the rumination and moving your body — such as going outside for a walk in the sunlight — is one of the most reliable ways to support brain health.

sections.heading: The Three Don'ts: Things to Avoid
sections.content:
To protect your brain's blood vessels, avoid the following three things.

1. Do not neglect lifestyle diseases: High blood pressure, diabetes, and obesity age the brain's blood vessels and can raise dementia risk by up to 2.5 times. Careful diet management and exercise are needed.
2. Avoid heavy drinking and smoking: Heavy alcohol use directly damages brain cells, so if moderation is difficult, stopping altogether is advisable.
3. Watch for late-life depression: Depression can impair memory and concentration, producing symptoms that resemble dementia. Depression should be treated promptly when it occurs.

sections.heading: The Three Do's: Habits Worth Practicing Often
sections.content:
To help keep your brain young, practice the following three habits often.

1. Read and write often: Reading books or newspapers and writing by hand for about an hour a day supports mental sharpness.
2. Chew food thoroughly: The act of chewing stimulates brain nerves and promotes blood flow to the brain. Keep your teeth healthy and chew food well.
3. Walk often: Staying physically active helps prevent the buildup of toxic substances in the brain. Starting regular exercise, such as walking 30 minutes a day, from a young age is recommended.

records.title: Periodontal Disease (Gum Disease)
records.intro: Gum disease (periodontal disease), marked by bleeding and swollen gums, is not limited to the mouth — it can worsen systemic conditions such as dementia, heart disease, and diabetes. Regular visits to a periodontal specialist and routine dental scaling are essential.
records.tags_raw: periodontal disease, gum disease, dental scaling, dementia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, tooth sensitivity, sensitive teeth, gum pain, toothache

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Periodontal disease is inflammation of the gums caused by dental plaque (a buildup of bacteria). It begins as gingivitis, in which only the gums are swollen, and can progress to periodontitis, in which the bone that supports the teeth is gradually destroyed.

sections.heading: Relationship to Systemic Disease
sections.content: When gum inflammation is severe, bacteria and harmful substances can spread throughout the body through the bloodstream. These bacteria may raise blood sugar and worsen diabetes, contribute to blood clot formation and increase the risk of heart disease, and may even reach the brain and contribute to dementia. In pregnant women, it can also increase the risk of preterm birth.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: Thorough toothbrushing three times a day and dental scaling at least once a year are the most reliable ways to protect both gum health and overall systemic health.

records.title: Hemorrhoids
records.intro: Hemorrhoids are swollen vascular tissue inside the anus that may bulge or protrude outside the anus. Most of what is commonly referred to as 'piles' is, in fact, hemorrhoids. If you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: hemorrhoids, piles, anal fistula, anal fissure, rectal bleeding, anal pain, sitz bath, rubber band ligation, hemorrhoid surgery, constipation, difficulty passing stool, hard stool, blood on stool, bloody stool, bright red blood in stool

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Anal conditions commonly referred to as 'piles' are broadly divided into three types.
· Hemorrhoids: Swollen vascular tissue inside the anus that bulges or protrudes outside the anus. This is the most common type.
· Anal fissure: A tear in the lining of the anal canal or at the border between the anus and skin.
· Anal fistula: A condition in which pus forms in the tissue around the anus and spreads to form a tunnel-like tract.

These three conditions are collectively referred to as 'piles,' but the term 'piles' does not specifically mean hemorrhoids.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Hemorrhoids are mainly caused by postures and lifestyle habits that dilate the blood vessels in the anal area.
· Excessive straining during bowel movements due to constipation or diarrhea
· Prolonged sitting on the toilet (including using a smartphone or reading)
· Squatting or standing for long periods
· Insufficient fiber intake
· Heavy alcohol use (alcohol dilates blood vessels)
· Lifting heavy objects, or strenuous hiking
· Pregnancy and childbirth (increased abdominal pressure and tissue changes can worsen hemorrhoids)

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Bright red bleeding: Bleeding during bowel movements is the most common symptom, often occurring without pain.
· Prolapse: A sensation of something protruding from inside the anus during or after a bowel movement.
· Pain: Thrombosed hemorrhoids (in which blood clots and hardens within the vessel) are usually accompanied by severe pain.

Not all cases of bloody stool or anal pain are due to hemorrhoids. These symptoms can also indicate colorectal cancer or other conditions, so please consult a medical specialist if symptoms occur, and undergo a colonoscopy or other tests if needed.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment depends on the grade of the hemorrhoids (grade 1 to 4) and the symptoms present.

【Conservative treatment】
· Sitz baths: Soaking the anal area in warm water for 5 minutes, 3 to 4 times a day. This improves blood circulation and relaxes the anal sphincter, reducing pain and supporting healing. After a sitz bath, dry the area thoroughly and keep it dry.
· Stool softeners
· Dietary changes: Eating fiber-rich foods
· Improving bowel habits

【Surgical treatment】
Surgery is considered for grade 3 or higher hemorrhoids, in which the tissue protrudes and must be pushed back in by hand, or when frequent bleeding has caused anemia, or when a blood clot is causing severe pain.

Options include minor procedures (such as rubber band ligation or hemorrhoidal artery ligation) and more definitive surgery (such as hemorrhoidectomy or stapled hemorrhoidopexy). The treatment approach should be decided after consulting a medical specialist.

Hemorrhoids do not progress to colorectal cancer. However, because other conditions can cause similar symptoms, an accurate diagnosis by a medical specialist is important.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· Avoid spending long periods on the toilet using a smartphone or reading; aim to finish bowel movements within about 5 minutes.
· Avoid squatting or sitting cross-legged on the floor.
· Eat plenty of fiber-rich foods such as fruits and vegetables.
· Avoid heavy alcohol use.
· If you have hemorrhoids, avoid suddenly lifting heavy objects or engaging in strenuous hiking.

records.title: Kennedy Disease (Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy)
records.intro: Kennedy disease is a genetic condition that causes progressive weakness of the nerves and muscles. Because it progresses slowly over time, ongoing management by a neurology specialist is essential to help prevent complications.
records.tags_raw: hereditary disease, neurological disorder, Kennedy disease, muscle weakness, genetic testing, hand tremor, body tremor

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Kennedy disease is a hereditary condition, caused by an abnormality in genetic information inherited from a parent, that damages the nerves and muscles. A distinctive feature is that symptoms appear only in men.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: The condition results from an abnormally excessive repeat of a specific sequence within a gene — the body's genetic blueprint (DNA) — which leads to the production of an abnormal protein.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Weakness in the legs usually begins in adulthood, typically in the 40s. Hand tremor or muscle twitching may occur, and as the condition progresses, weakness in the facial muscles can make chewing and swallowing difficult.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: There is currently no treatment that cures the condition entirely. Management focuses on medications to reduce muscle cramping or tremor, along with therapies that help maintain mobility and breathing function.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: A daughter who inherits the gene will not develop the disease herself but may become a carrier (a person who carries the gene). If a family member has the condition, genetic testing is recommended.

records.title: Croup
records.intro: Croup is an emergency condition in which a child suddenly has difficulty breathing. Symptoms typically worsen at night and can become life-threatening, so prompt evaluation by a pediatric specialist or emergency care is needed.
records.tags_raw: croup, barking cough, difficulty breathing, common cold, airway swelling, breath holding, difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, choking sensation, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of the hands and feet
keywords: swelling of the hands and feet

sections.heading: Definition
