sections.content: Croup is a respiratory condition in which the upper airway narrows due to inflammatory swelling. It most commonly affects young children between 6 months and 3 years of age.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: Croup occurs when infection with a cold-causing virus, such as parainfluenza virus, leads to inflammation and swelling of the airway lining. Because children's airways are narrower than those of adults, they swell more easily.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: A distinctive barking cough, resembling the sound of a dog or seal, is characteristic. As the condition worsens, a wheezing sound may occur when breathing in, along with visible chest retractions and difficulty breathing.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: Treatment may include supplemental oxygen to ease breathing, along with inhaled or injected medications to reduce airway swelling. If breathing difficulty is severe, immediate hospitalization is necessary.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: A child may seem fine during the day but suddenly develop airway obstruction and breathing difficulty at night or in the early morning. Because this can be difficult to predict, if a child becomes very irritable or shows signs of breathlessness, go to the emergency room right away.

records.title: Snoring
records.intro: Snoring is a sound produced when the airway in the throat narrows during sleep. Although it may seem like a simple sleep habit, it can progress to sleep apnea. Sleep apnea is associated with various systemic conditions, including high blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke. If snoring is severe or accompanied by apnea, please consult an otolaryngology (ear, nose, and throat) specialist.
records.tags_raw: snoring, sleep, airway, uvula, obesity, sleep apnea, otolaryngology, headache, severe headache, migraine, back-of-head pain, nasal congestion, clear nasal discharge, yellow nasal discharge

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Snoring is a sound caused by narrowing of the upper airway during sleep. Muscle tone throughout the body decreases during sleep. This can cause the tongue to fall back, the uvula to sag, or the pharyngeal mucosa (the lining inside the throat) to vibrate, producing sound.

Alcohol use, sedatives, tranquilizers, and physical exhaustion can further reduce muscle tone, causing even people who do not normally snore to snore. In children, snoring can occur due to enlarged tonsils or adenoids (lymphoid tissue in the throat). Nasal congestion from conditions such as rhinitis, a deviated nasal septum, or sinusitis can also cause snoring.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptom of snoring is the sound itself during sleep, which is often first noticed by a spouse or family member.

If the following symptoms are also present, sleep apnea may be occurring alongside snoring.
· Frequent tossing and turning or waking during the night
· Dry mouth or severe headache upon waking
· Daytime sleepiness while reading or driving
· A history of high blood pressure or stroke

Snoring is an important warning sign that can lead to the detection of sleep apnea. If episodes of stopped breathing during sleep occur, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Diagnosing the cause of snoring involves checking the following.

· Whether sleep duration is adequate, and whether factors that disrupt sleep are present, such as alcohol use, sedative use, smoking, or caffeine.
· Measurements related to obesity, including body mass index (weight in kg ÷ height in m²), neck circumference, and waist circumference.
· The presence of nasal congestion, tonsil enlargement, or structural abnormalities.

The most important test is polysomnography, a comprehensive sleep study that measures brain waves, eye movement, breathing, and oxygen saturation during sleep. This allows an objective assessment of the severity of sleep apnea and helps determine the appropriate treatment.

Since July 2018, national health insurance has covered polysomnography and CPAP device rental. Please discuss this with your doctor.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for snoring generally falls into three categories.

■ Behavioral therapy
This includes weight management and changing sleep position to sleeping on one's side. Avoiding alcohol and sedative use also helps.

■ Device-based therapy
· CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure): A mask delivers continuous pressure to the airway to keep it open during sleep. This is mainly used for moderate or more severe sleep apnea (an apnea-hypopnea index of 15 or more events per hour).
· Oral appliance: A device connected to the upper and lower jaw that moves the lower jaw forward to widen the airway.

■ Surgical treatment
Surgery is considered when there is a clear structural cause of airway obstruction, such as enlarged tonsils, or when other treatments are not feasible.

The choice of treatment is determined by the specialist based on polysomnography results and the patient's condition. Please be sure to consult an otolaryngology specialist.

records.title: Eye Health Care for Contact Lens Wearers
records.intro: Because contact lenses sit directly on the cornea, improper use can lead to serious eye conditions such as keratitis and dry eye disease. Proper use and hygiene are important. If any unusual symptoms occur, please see an ophthalmology specialist right away.
records.tags_raw: contact lenses, soft lenses, rigid (hard) lenses, keratitis, lens care, lens cleaning, swimming, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of the hands and feet
keywords: swelling of the hands and feet

sections.heading: Contact Lenses and Eye Health
sections.content: Unlike eyeglasses, contact lenses sit directly on the cornea. Soft lenses fit closely against the cornea and can interfere with tear circulation, reducing the oxygen supply to the eye. This can lead to problems such as keratitis, corneal edema, and corneal neovascularization (the growth of new blood vessels into the cornea). Lenses can also draw moisture from the tear film, contributing to dry eye disease.

sections.heading: Cleaning and Storage
sections.content:
· Use an approved saline solution for rinsing lenses. Homemade saltwater solutions are dangerous.
· Once opened, saline solution carries a risk of contamination, so use it promptly and follow the manufacturer's recommended usage period.
· Saline solution is for rinsing after cleaning only; it does not disinfect.
· Never use tap water to clean soft lenses, due to the risk of infection with organisms that cause keratitis.
· Use a protein remover only if recommended for your lens type by your eye care professional or the manufacturer. Follow the recommended cleaning, disinfection, and lens replacement schedule. Do not reuse daily disposable lenses.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
· As a general rule, it is best not to wear contact lenses while swimming. Pool water may contain Acanthamoeba, a microorganism that can cause serious corneal damage. If wearing lenses while swimming is unavoidable, be sure to wear swimming goggles.
· If any of the following symptoms occur while wearing lenses, remove them immediately and visit an ophthalmologist.
  - Sudden pain or severe irritation
  - Blurred vision or halos around lights
  - Severe or persistent redness
  - Excessive eye discharge
  - Blurred vision even after removing the lens and putting on glasses
  - A lens that sticks to the eye and is difficult to remove

records.title: Cholinergic Urticaria
records.intro: Cholinergic urticaria is a condition in which numerous small hives appear on the skin when body temperature rises, such as from strenuous exercise, mental stress, or a hot bath. Please consult a dermatology specialist.
records.tags_raw: cholinergic urticaria, hives, exercise, sweating, body temperature, allergy, stinging sensation, abdominal pain, stomachache, abdominal discomfort, stomach pain

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Cholinergic urticaria is hives that develop when core body temperature rises by 1°C or more, such as from strenuous exercise, mental stress, or a hot bath. It is a type of physical urticaria.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Numerous small wheals (raised swellings), about 1 to 2 mm in size, appear on the skin, surrounded by 1- to 2-cm areas of redness. They tend to occur mainly on the trunk and are less common on the face, hands, and feet. The affected skin is more often described as stinging rather than itchy. Generalized sweating, abdominal pain, or dizziness may also occur.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content: Characteristic hives can be reproduced by having the patient exercise until sweating occurs, or by having them bathe in water at about 43°C (109°F) for 20 to 30 minutes. An accurate diagnosis is made through evaluation by a dermatology specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: Avoiding triggers such as strenuous exercise, hot baths, and stress is important. Antihistamines are the main treatment. Even if symptoms improve, continue taking medication as directed by your doctor and do not stop on your own.

records.title: Structure and Function of the Kidneys
records.intro: The kidneys are vital organs that filter the blood and remove waste products through urine. Beyond waste removal, the kidneys perform a range of functions, including regulating water and salt balance, controlling blood pressure, and stimulating red blood cell production. Understanding the structure and function of the kidneys can help you protect your kidney health. If a problem with kidney function is suspected, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: kidney, renal, glomerulus, renal tubule, erythropoietin, renin, water balance regulation, salt balance regulation, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of the hands and feet
keywords: swelling of the hands and feet

sections.heading: What Are the Kidneys?
sections.content: The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs, one on each side of the body, located beneath the lower ribs toward the back. Each kidney is roughly the size of an adult fist, and about one-quarter to one-fifth of the blood pumped by the heart passes through the kidneys — reflecting how closely the kidneys are connected to the heart and blood vessels.

sections.heading: Structure of the Kidneys
sections.content:
The kidney can be divided into four main components.

① Blood vessels: Large vessels that supply blood to the kidney. High blood pressure or atherosclerosis (hardening of the blood vessel walls) can affect the vessels supplying the kidney.

② Glomerulus: A cluster of capillaries (very small blood vessels) that filters the blood. Each kidney contains about 1 million glomeruli. When the glomeruli are damaged, protein or blood may leak into the urine.

③ Renal tubule: The channel through which substances filtered at the glomerulus pass. Here, water and electrolytes (minerals the body needs, such as sodium and potassium) are regulated to form the final urine.

④ Interstitium: The tissue surrounding the renal tubules. This is where renin, which regulates blood pressure, and erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell production, are made. It also plays a role in activating vitamin D.

sections.heading: The Kidneys and Water and Salt Regulation
sections.content:
The kidneys filter about 150 liters of fluid each day, but nearly 99% of this is reabsorbed, so the actual amount excreted as urine is about 1 to 2 liters per day.
When the brain detects a change in the body's water balance, it releases antidiuretic hormone, prompting the kidneys to increase water reabsorption and keep the body's fluid level stable.

The kidneys also regulate salt (sodium, the main component of table salt). Too little salt can lead to low blood pressure and dehydration, while too much salt can lead to swelling and high blood pressure. A hormone called aldosterone signals the kidneys to regulate the amount of salt excreted.

sections.heading: Main Functions of the Kidneys
sections.content:
The main functions of the kidneys can be summarized in four areas.

① Waste excretion: The kidneys filter waste products generated by the body's metabolism out of the blood and excrete them in urine, while also regulating water, electrolyte, and acid-base balance.

② Removal of drugs and toxins: Drugs and toxins are eliminated from the body through the renal tubules. When kidney function declines, drug- and toxin-related kidney damage can be compounded, so caution is needed.

③ Hormone production: The kidneys produce renin, which regulates blood pressure; erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell production; and active vitamin D, which is needed for bone health. This is why kidney damage can lead to anemia or bone disease.

④ Maintaining acid-base balance: The kidneys keep body fluids from becoming too acidic or too alkaline, helping cells function normally.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Habits for Kidney Health
sections.content:
The following habits can help keep the kidneys healthy.
· If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, manage them consistently.
· Reduce salty foods such as broths, stews, and salted seafood.
· Drink adequate fluids.
· Avoid taking pain relievers or anti-inflammatory drugs on your own over a long period.
· Consult your doctor before taking health supplements or herbal medicine.
· Get regular urine and blood tests.
If a problem with kidney function is suspected, or if you have risk factors, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Surfer's Myelopathy
records.intro: Surfer's myelopathy is a rare condition in which reduced blood flow to the spinal cord during activities that involve excessive backward bending of the spine — such as surfing, yoga, or Pilates — leads to neurological symptoms. If leg paralysis or loss of bladder or bowel control develops after low back pain, go to the emergency room immediately.
records.tags_raw: surfer's myelopathy, surfing, spinal cord, paralysis, hyperextension, low back pain, urinary dysfunction, back pain, lower back pain, back strain, numbness in the hands and feet, arm numbness, tingling in the legs, weakness in the arms or legs, one-sided weakness
keywords: numbness in the hands and feet
weakness in the arms or legs

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Surfer's myelopathy is a condition in which nerve damage occurs due to reduced or interrupted blood flow to the spinal cord during excessive backward bending (hyperextension) of the spine. It was named after being first reported in novice surfers.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The blood vessels supplying the spinal cord have limited collateral circulation, meaning other vessels cannot easily compensate if one becomes blocked. Excessive backward bending of the spine can stretch these vessels and reduce blood flow, resulting in nerve damage.

Besides surfing, this condition can occur with other activities that involve excessive spinal extension, such as yoga, Pilates, cheerleading, swimming, and acrobatics. It is more common in novice surfers because their limited postural control tends to produce more severe and sudden hyperextension.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The initial symptom is sudden low back pain. The following symptoms may then develop.

· Leg weakness (partial or complete paralysis)
· Numbness or abnormal sensation in the legs
· Bladder dysfunction

If low back pain during exercise is accompanied by leg weakness or sensory changes, stop the activity immediately and go to the emergency room.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
There is currently no specific medication or surgical treatment for this condition.

In the early stage, management may include the following.
· Rest.
· Maintaining adequate blood pressure and giving intravenous fluids to improve blood flow.
· Considering anticoagulant medication (to help dissolve blood clots).
· High-dose steroid treatment may also be used early on in some cases.

When initial symptoms are mild, many patients recover. However, if paralysis persists, rehabilitation and management of bladder function are needed.

Prevention remains the most important approach to this condition.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The following measures can help prevent surfer's myelopathy.

· Before surfing, be fully aware of the risks of spinal hyperextension and receive thorough instruction on proper posture.
· Stretch adequately and stay hydrated before exercise.
· Avoid prolonged sessions and take sufficient rest.
· Wear appropriate thermal clothing when exercising in cold water, since blood vessels constrict in cold conditions and increase the risk.
· Build up tolerance to backward-bending movements gradually and slowly over time.

records.title: Parainfluenza Virus Infection
records.intro: Parainfluenza virus causes acute respiratory illness in infants and young children. It is a major cause of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), which can produce a harsh, barking cough or hoarseness. Most cases recover with supportive care, but please consult a medical specialist if symptoms are severe.
records.tags_raw: parainfluenza, croup, laryngotracheobronchitis, children, infants, barking cough, respiratory infection, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Despite its similar-sounding name, parainfluenza virus is distinct from the influenza virus. It is a common cause of acute respiratory illness in infants and young children, and it can also cause respiratory infection in people with weakened immune systems.

The illness caused often depends on the virus type.
· Types 1 and 2: Mainly cause croup (laryngotracheobronchitis).
· Type 3: Can cause bronchiolitis (inflammation of the small airways) or pneumonia.

sections.heading: What Is Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)?
sections.content:
Croup is inflammation and swelling of the larynx (voice box) and the trachea and bronchi caused by parainfluenza virus infection. It mainly occurs in children between 6 months and 3 years of age.

The main symptoms are as follows.
· A harsh, barking cough resembling a dog's bark
· Hoarseness
· Inspiratory stridor: a wheezing or high-pitched sound when breathing in
· Mild fever

If symptoms worsen to the point of visible breathing difficulty, or if cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the lips, hands, or feet) appears, please go to the emergency room immediately.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content:
Diagnosis can be confirmed with PCR testing (a genetic test).

Recovery generally occurs with supportive care. Adequate rest and fluid intake are helpful. When croup symptoms are severe, medication is given based on the physician's assessment.

There is currently no vaccine to prevent this infection. Good personal hygiene, such as handwashing, helps prevent infection.

If symptoms worsen or breathing difficulty develops, please see a medical specialist immediately.

records.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
records.intro: Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common type of skin cancer. Ultraviolet (UV) exposure is the main risk factor, and it is more likely to recur and metastasize than basal cell carcinoma. If you notice any unusual changes in your skin, please consult a dermatology specialist.
records.tags_raw: squamous cell carcinoma, skin cancer, ultraviolet radiation, actinic keratosis, skin, keratin

sections.heading: Causes and Risk Factors
sections.content: Ultraviolet exposure is the main risk factor; longer periods of sun exposure increase the risk. The condition occurs more often in men in their 60s. Actinic keratosis can progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Actinic keratosis is a precancerous lesion that develops on skin with long-term UV exposure and can resemble an age spot.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant tumor that arises from keratinocytes, the cells that produce keratin in the skin. In Korea, it is the second most common skin cancer after basal cell carcinoma. It is also the most common skin cancer among organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: Use sunscreen regularly and avoid exposure to strong sunlight. If you have actinic keratosis, please seek treatment to help prevent progression to squamous cell carcinoma. Regular skin checkups can help with early detection.

sections.heading: Course and Metastasis
sections.content: Squamous cell carcinoma recurs and metastasizes (spreads to other areas) more often than basal cell carcinoma. The 5-year metastasis rate for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is reported to be about 5%. Careful monitoring for recurrence is needed even after surgical removal.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content: Diagnosis is made through evaluation by a dermatology specialist and a skin biopsy. Complete surgical removal of the lesion is the standard treatment. Appropriately treating precancerous lesions such as actinic keratosis is also important.

records.title: Flat Feet (Pes Planus)
records.intro: Flat feet refers to a condition in which the arch of the foot — the inward curve along the sole — is so low that it touches the ground. The arch normally acts like a spring, absorbing shock to the foot during walking or running. If symptoms persist, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: flat feet, foot arch, foot and ankle, foot fatigue, foot pain, posterior tibial tendon, orthotic insole, low energy, lethargy, persistent tiredness

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The inner sole of the foot has a curved indentation known as the arch. A normal foot maintains this arch even while standing, and the arch helps absorb shock while walking or running.
Flat feet occur when the arch is so low that the sole nearly or completely touches the ground. The opposite condition, in which the arch is too high, is called a 'high arch' (pes cavus). Both conditions can cause the feet to tire easily.
Mild flat feet may cause little to no disruption to daily life.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
With flat feet, the arch cannot properly absorb shock, so the feet tire easily. The calves or soles may ache, and pain can worsen with prolonged walking or running.
In severe cases, viewing the ankle from behind may show the heel angled outward relative to the ankle. The big toe may also tilt toward the second toe in this case.
If symptoms occur, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Using a special orthotic insole that supports the arch can help reduce pain. It is best to have the insole custom-made or selected to fit your foot based on your specialist's recommendation.
Combining insole use with consistent foot-strengthening exercises can be even more effective.

sections.heading: Exercise Methods
sections.content:
A key exercise for flat feet strengthens the posterior tibial tendon, the muscle on the inside of the ankle. This tendon plays an important role in supporting the arch from above and preventing it from collapsing.
· While sitting in a chair, rest one ankle across the opposite knee. Point the foot downward and turn it inward, holding the position for 6 seconds. Alternate between both feet.
Start with this seated exercise, and gradually increase intensity as muscle strength improves.
Please decide on an exercise program after consulting a specialist or physical therapist.

records.title: Lung Cancer
records.intro: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the bronchi or lungs and is the leading cause of cancer death in Korea. It often causes no symptoms in its early stages, so regular screening is important for high-risk groups. Smoking is the leading cause, and quitting smoking is the most effective way to help prevent it.

keywords: weakness in the arms or legs

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Smoking is associated with about 70% of lung cancer cases. Smokers have approximately 20 times the risk of developing lung cancer compared with non-smokers.

Lung cancer also occurs in non-smokers. Contributing factors include secondhand smoke, indoor air pollution from cooking, radon exposure, pre-existing lung disease, occupational exposure to carcinogens, and genetic predisposition.

A family history increases lung cancer risk. Having an immediate family member (parent or sibling) with lung cancer roughly doubles the risk. Risk is further increased when a smoking history and family history occur together.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Lung cancer often causes no specific symptoms in its early stages, or the symptoms that do occur resemble common conditions such as a cold or bronchitis, making them easy to overlook.

■ Symptoms to watch for
- A cough lasting 3 weeks or longer
- Blood-streaked sputum
- Difficulty breathing
- Chest pain
- Hoarseness (from vocal cord paralysis)
- Chronic fatigue, weight loss, reduced appetite

Cough in particular is experienced by more than 75% of lung cancer patients from an early stage. If you have a smoking history or are age 50 or older, please do not dismiss recurring respiratory symptoms lightly, and consult a medical specialist.

When diagnosis occurs after symptoms have already developed, the cancer has often already progressed to a later stage. Early detection through screening, before symptoms appear, is the most important factor.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Lung cancer may be suspected based on chest CT findings, but a tissue biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.

■ Biopsy methods
· Bronchoscopy: Used to access tumors located centrally within the bronchi.
· Percutaneous needle biopsy: Tissue is obtained using a needle inserted from outside the chest. Complications such as pneumothorax (air leak) or hemothorax (blood leak) can occur.
· Electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy: A newer technique that allows precise access to small or hard-to-reach lesions.

■ Staging tests
PET-CT (to check for spread throughout the body), brain MRI, bone scan, abdominal CT, and endobronchial ultrasound (to evaluate mediastinal lymph nodes), among others.

sections.heading: Treatment and Surgery
sections.content:
Lung cancer is broadly divided into two types based on cell size and appearance.
· Small cell lung cancer (about 15% of cases): Tends to metastasize readily and is mainly treated with chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
· Non-small cell lung cancer: Includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. Surgery is possible if caught early.

■ Treatment by stage
· Stage 1 to 2: Surgery is the main treatment.
· Stage 3: Surgery, or combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
· Stage 4: Systemic drug therapy (cytotoxic chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy).

■ Targeted therapy
Used when specific gene mutations, such as EGFR, ALK, ROS1, or BRAF, are present. These are oral medications with fewer side effects than conventional chemotherapy.

■ Immunotherapy
These medications help immune cells attack cancer cells. They cause less hair loss and nausea/vomiting than conventional chemotherapy, but can cause autoimmune-related side effects such as colitis, dermatitis, hepatitis, or pneumonitis.

■ Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)
A technique in which small incisions are made in the chest to remove lung tissue using endoscopic instruments. Compared with open chest surgery, it causes less pain and allows faster recovery.

■ Robot-assisted thoracic surgery (RATS)
Using a three-dimensional view and precision instruments, this approach allows safe surgery even in complex areas. It can also benefit older patients or those with reduced lung function.

■ Extent of resection
- Lobectomy: The traditional method of removing the single lobe (of the lung's five lobes) that contains the cancer.
- Segmentectomy: A method that removes only part of a lobe (a segment), used for small lesions found early through screening. It preserves as much lung function as possible, which is favorable for recovery after surgery.

sections.heading: Screening
sections.content:
■ Low-dose chest CT
Standard chest X-rays often cannot detect lung cancer at an early stage. Low-dose chest CT involves less radiation exposure and provides results within minutes, making it effective for early lung cancer detection.

■ Who is considered high-risk for screening
Regular low-dose CT screening is strongly recommended for people who meet all of the following criteria.
- Age 54 or older
- A smoking history of 30 pack-years or more (for example, 1 pack a day for 30 years, or 2 packs a day for 15 years)
- Currently smoking, or having quit within the past 15 years

■ Non-smokers should also be aware
Because the proportion of lung cancer occurring in non-smokers has recently been increasing in Korea, regular lung cancer screening is worth considering even for those outside the high-risk group.

The 5-year survival rate for stage 1 lung cancer is about 73%, compared with under 30% for stage 3 or higher. Early detection is the key factor in treatment outcomes.

sections.heading: Postoperative Complications and Follow-Up
sections.content:
■ Major complications
Respiratory complications, such as pneumonia, atelectasis (lung collapse), and persistent air leak, are the most common. Active deep-breathing exercises and rehabilitation starting immediately after surgery are important for prevention.

■ Follow-up
- Periodic CT and imaging studies are performed for up to 5 years after surgery to check for recurrence.
- The first 1 to 2 years after surgery carry the highest risk of recurrence, so follow-up during this period is especially important.

■ Lifestyle management
Smoking cessation is essential both before and after surgery. Wearing a mask when going outdoors on days with high levels of fine particulate air pollution can also help.

records.title: Treatment and Chemotherapy for Lung Cancer
records.intro: Treatment for lung cancer — surgery or chemotherapy — is determined by the appearance of the cancer cells and how far the disease has spread. Please do not delay treatment out of fear of side effects; be sure to discuss your options with a pulmonology specialist to find a safe treatment approach suited to you.
records.tags_raw: lung cancer, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy, loose stools, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Targeted Therapy
sections.content: Targeted therapy consists of medications that specifically attack the particular gene mutations driving the cancer. Because they are taken as pills rather than given by injection, they are convenient and tend to cause fewer side effects. However, they can cause dry skin, acne-like breakouts on the face or scalp, or diarrhea.

sections.heading: Immunotherapy
sections.content: Immunotherapy strengthens the body's own immune cells to help them fight cancer cells directly. It does not cause hair loss, but overactivated immune cells can sometimes mistakenly attack the body's own tissues, leading to side effects such as colitis, pneumonitis, or hepatitis.

sections.heading: Types and Stages of Lung Cancer
sections.content: Lung cancer is divided into small cell lung cancer, in which the cancer cells are small, and non-small cell lung cancer, which is not. Based on how far the cancer has spread, it is staged from 1 to 4. Stage 1 to 2 is mainly treated with surgery, while stage 3 or 4 is often treated with systemic drug therapy (chemotherapy).

sections.heading: Conventional Chemotherapy (Cytotoxic Chemotherapy)
sections.content: This is the most basic form of chemotherapy, given by injection to attack and kill cancer cells. However, because normal cells in the body can be affected as well, it can cause hair loss, gastrointestinal side effects such as vomiting and diarrhea, and reduced bone marrow function, which can lead to anemia or a weakened immune system.

sections.heading: Essential Habits During Treatment
sections.content: For lung cancer patients, quitting smoking is not optional — it is essential. Continued smoking reduces the effectiveness of treatment. In addition, because the immune system is weakened during treatment, making infection more likely, it is important to avoid raw foods and eat well-cooked meat and vegetables to help maintain strength.

records.title: Structure and Function of the Lungs
records.intro: The lungs are organs that play a central role in breathing. They are responsible for external respiration — delivering oxygen from the air into the blood and expelling carbon dioxide produced by the body. There is one lung on each side of the heart, and each lung is made up of roughly 500 million alveoli (tiny air sacs).
records.tags_raw: lung, alveoli, bronchus, respiration, oxygen, carbon dioxide, thoracic cavity, external respiration, lung function

sections.heading: Lung Volumes
sections.content:
Here are some representative figures related to the lungs.

· Lung weight: About 1 kg
· Total lung capacity in a normal adult: About 4 to 6 liters
· Tidal volume: The amount of air inhaled and exhaled in one breath at rest, about 500 mL in a healthy adult man. Of this, only about 350 mL reaches the alveoli to take part in actual gas exchange.
· Total lung capacity after maximal inhalation: About 5,800 mL
· Residual volume: The amount of air remaining in the lungs even after maximal exhalation, about 1,200 mL.

Pulmonary function tests (spirometry) are used to check whether lung function is normal. If a problem with lung function is suspected, please consult a pulmonology specialist.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The lungs exist to carry out respiration. The body's cells need oxygen to survive and must eliminate the carbon dioxide produced through metabolism.

· External respiration (pulmonary respiration): The process of taking in oxygen from the air and delivering it to the blood, while releasing carbon dioxide carried by the blood into the air.
· Internal respiration (tissue respiration): The process by which the blood delivers oxygen to individual cells and collects carbon dioxide.

The lungs also play a role in regulating body temperature and maintaining the acid-base balance of the blood.

sections.heading: Structure of the Lungs
sections.content:
■ Location and size
The lungs are located within the thoracic cavity, one on each side of the heart. The right lung is generally larger than the left.

■ Lobes
· Right lung: Made up of three lobes — the upper, middle, and lower lobes.
· Left lung: Made up of two lobes — the upper and lower lobes.

■ Airway and bronchi
Air inhaled through the nose passes through the trachea (windpipe) and divides into the right and left main bronchi. The bronchi continue to branch like tree limbs into progressively smaller airways (bronchi → bronchioles), ending in the alveoli.

■ Alveoli
Alveoli are small, grape-like air sacs surrounded by capillaries, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged. The lungs contain about 500 million alveoli, which together would cover a surface area of about 70 m² (roughly half the size of a tennis court) if spread flat.

records.title: Uveitis
records.intro: Uveitis is inflammation of the uvea — the iris, ciliary body, and choroid — inside the eye. It can cause redness, pain, and reduced vision, and in severe cases can lead to blindness. If symptoms occur, please consult an ophthalmology specialist without delay.
records.tags_raw: uveitis, iritis, choroiditis, eye redness, decreased vision, autoimmune disease, ankylosing spondylitis, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of the hands and feet, weakness in the arms or legs, one-sided weakness, blurred vision, poor vision, hazy vision
keywords: swelling of the hands and feet
weakness in the arms or legs

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The uvea is a thin, highly vascular membrane located between the white of the eye and the nervous tissue of the eye. It regulates the light entering the eye and supplies nutrients through the blood. It forms the middle layer of the eye and consists of three parts.
· Iris: The part visible as a brown or black colored ring at the front of the eye
· Ciliary body: A muscular structure that adjusts the thickness of the lens
· Choroid: The layer at the back of the eye that supplies blood to the retina

Uveitis is inflammation of these structures. Based on its location, it is classified as anterior, intermediate, posterior, or panuveitis (involving the entire uvea).

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms of uveitis vary depending on where the inflammation occurs. Common symptoms include eye pain, marked redness, and reduced vision. Bright light may cause discomfort, and floating spots may be seen in the field of vision. Unlike ordinary conjunctivitis, which produces eye discharge, uveitis causes deep, severe eye pain.

Anterior uveitis (iritis):
· Redness and pain
· Marked sensitivity to bright light
· Tearing
· Reduced vision in severe cases

Intermediate and posterior uveitis:
· Reduced vision
· Floaters (a sensation of small spots or strands drifting in the field of vision)
· Metamorphopsia (objects appearing distorted)

If any of these symptoms occur, please be sure to visit an ophthalmologist for an accurate diagnosis.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Uveitis has many possible causes.
· Infection, including bacterial, viral, or parasitic infection
· Trauma
· Systemic inflammatory conditions such as Behçet's disease or ankylosing spondylitis
· Autoimmune disease (a condition in which the body's immune cells attack its own tissue)

In some cases, no cause is found despite extensive testing; this is known as idiopathic uveitis.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The following tests are used to diagnose uveitis.
· Slit-lamp examination: Checks for inflammation in the front part of the eye.
· Intraocular pressure measurement: Eye pressure can be either lower or higher than normal in uveitis.
· Fundus examination: Checks for inflammation in the back part of the eye.
· Fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography: Check for retinal complications.
· Blood tests and imaging studies: Check for an underlying systemic condition.

If a systemic inflammatory condition is suspected, evaluation by an internal medicine specialist may also be needed.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for uveitis depends on the underlying cause.
· Infectious causes: Antibacterial or antiviral medication targeted to the causative organism.
· Non-infectious causes: Steroid eye drops or oral steroids to control inflammation.
· Pupil-dilating eye drops (cycloplegics): Used to relieve pain and prevent adhesion of the iris.
· Steroid injections around or within the eye when needed.
· Immunosuppressive medication may be needed for chronic or recurrent uveitis.

If an immune-related cause is involved, steroid medication may be taken orally or used as eye drops to control inflammation. Evaluation by other specialists, such as a rheumatology specialist, may also be needed to identify the underlying condition.

Uveitis can lead to various complications, such as macular edema and glaucoma. Because recurrence is common even after treatment, regular ophthalmologic checkups are essential. If the same symptoms recur, please visit an ophthalmologist immediately.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Without early treatment, complications such as glaucoma or cataracts can develop, and vision loss may become complete in some cases. Because treatment can be challenging and recurrence is common, ongoing follow-up care is necessary.

records.title: Heat Waves and Heart Health
records.intro: Extreme heat raises the risk of angina, heart attack, and cardiac arrest by increasing heart rate, promoting blood clotting, and placing added strain on the heart. Older adults age 65 and older, people with cardiovascular disease, and those with chronic conditions such as high blood pressure or diabetes need to be especially careful. On days when a heat wave warning is issued, please stay active indoors for safety.
records.tags_raw: heat wave, sudden cardiac death, heat stroke, heat-related illness, heart attack, angina, cardiac arrest, arrhythmia, hydration, summer health, dizziness, feeling faint, unsteadiness, vision going dark, fainting, loss of consciousness, syncope, breath holding, difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, choking sensation

sections.heading: Effects of Heat Waves on the Heart
sections.content:
When body temperature rises abnormally during a heat wave, the body's homeostasis (its ability to maintain internal balance) can be disrupted.

■ Strain placed on the heart
- High temperatures stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, rapidly increasing heart rate.
- The resulting increase in heart rate can impair oxygen supply to the heart, which can suddenly lead to angina (chest tightness and pain from insufficient blood flow to the heart) or a heart attack (damage to the heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery).
- The blood becomes more prone to clotting, increasing the risk of thrombosis (a blood clot forming within a blood vessel).

■ Higher-risk groups
- Older adults age 65 and older
- People with obstructive coronary artery disease (narrowing of the arteries that supply blood to the heart)
- People with arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat)
- People with chronic conditions such as high blood pressure or diabetes

These higher-risk groups require particular caution, as a rapid rise in body temperature can trigger sudden cardiac arrest.

sections.heading: Symptoms That Require Immediate Medical Attention
sections.content:
If any of the following symptoms occur, please seek medical care immediately or call emergency services without delay.

- Chest pain or a feeling of pressure
- Difficulty breathing
- Dizziness or fainting
- Persistent high fever
- Severe weakness or decreased consciousness

The heart is an organ that can be very difficult to recover once it stops, even briefly. Responding quickly to warning signs is far more important than assuming 'it's probably nothing.'

sections.heading: Lifestyle Guidelines During a Heat Wave
sections.content:
■ Staying hydrated
Drink about 1.5 to 2 liters of water consistently throughout the day. If you are taking a diuretic (a type of blood pressure medication that increases urination and reduces fluid in the body), please discuss dosage adjustments with your doctor during periods of extreme heat.

■ Limiting outdoor activity
Avoid going outdoors between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. When outdoors, wear light clothing and a hat, use a parasol, and avoid direct sun and UV exposure.

■ Managing the indoor environment
Keep indoor temperatures at or below 26°C (79°F) and ventilate frequently.

■ Exercise
On days when a heat wave warning is in effect, choose safe indoor activities. Under normal conditions, it is best to exercise in the early morning or evening, when temperatures are cooler.

sections.heading: Regular Checkups and Medication Management
sections.content:
In summer, cardiovascular events can occur even in people who have not had problems before. Understanding your own health status and avoiding overexertion is most important.

■ Regular checkups
Regular health checkups help monitor cardiovascular health. If you have cardiovascular disease, pay closer attention to any changes in your condition during heat waves, and consult your doctor if needed.

■ Taking medication
Do not stop or adjust your medications on your own; if a change is needed, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: How to Apply Dermatologic Ointments Correctly
records.intro: The way dermatologic ointments should be applied varies by type. Knowing the correct method significantly improves treatment results. Please do not rely on internet information alone — use these medications safely and only according to the evaluation and prescription of a dermatology specialist.
records.tags_raw: dermatology, ointment, corticosteroid, moisturizer, skin biopsy, cryotherapy

sections.heading: Wound Care After a Skin Biopsy
sections.content: After a small piece of skin is removed for biopsy, keep the wound covered with a sealed dressing to prevent water contact, and keep it clean and disinfected until the stitches are removed.

sections.heading: Care After Cryotherapy
sections.content: After treating a wart or similar lesion by freezing it with liquid nitrogen, a scab or blister may form. If a blister becomes large and painful, do not pop it yourself — visit a clinic to have it properly disinfected.

sections.heading: Why Different Ointment Types Are Used
sections.content: This is because absorption into the skin differs depending on the symptom and the area treated. Thicker, greasier ointments are used on dry, thick skin, while thinner lotions are used on larger areas or areas with hair.

sections.heading: Precautions for Topical Corticosteroids
sections.content: Because absorption is greater on the face and groin, a milder-strength preparation should be used in these areas. Even if a product looks like a lotion, it should not be applied liberally over the whole body as a moisturizer — apply only a thin layer to the affected, inflamed areas.

sections.heading: Correct Amount and Frequency of Application
sections.content: Always follow the frequency of application prescribed by your doctor. As a general guide, an amount equal to the length of one fingertip segment (from an adult's index finger) is appropriate for covering an area about the size of two adult palms.

records.title: Skin Aging
records.intro: Skin aging refers to changes that occur in the skin over time, including wrinkles, reduced elasticity, and pigmentation changes. Sun protection and consistent skin care can help slow this process. If any new abnormality appears on the skin, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: skin aging, photoaging, wrinkles, ultraviolet radiation, aged skin, dry skin, hyperpigmentation

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
Skin aging is broadly divided into two types.
· Intrinsic aging: The unavoidable changes that occur with age over time, including fine wrinkles, reduced elasticity, a somewhat paler skin tone, and dryness.
· Extrinsic aging (photoaging): Aging caused by external factors such as UV exposure, heat, and pollutants, with UV exposure being the leading cause. Compared with intrinsic aging, it produces deeper, coarser wrinkles, blotchy pigmentation, and more pronounced roughness.
The visible signs of aging on the skin actually reflect intrinsic aging combined with photoaging.

sections.heading: Prevention and Care
sections.content:
· Use sunscreen, hats, and parasols consistently for thorough UV protection.
· Take care to avoid skin injuries.
· Get adequate vitamin D.
· If a new or changing spot appears on the skin, have it evaluated by a dermatology specialist.
Paying consistent attention to skin health becomes increasingly important with age.

sections.heading: Changes in Aging Skin
sections.content:
· Pigmented conditions such as solar lentigines (brownish spots similar to age spots), as well as seborrheic keratoses, benign tumors, and skin cancer, become more likely to develop.
· Reduced skin regeneration: Wounds heal more slowly with age.
· Reduced immune function: The skin becomes more susceptible to bacterial, viral, and fungal infection.
· Reduced vitamin D synthesis: Less vitamin D is produced in the skin, which can increase the risk of osteoporosis (a condition in which the bones become weak).

records.title: Skin Cancer
records.intro: Skin cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the skin. A malignant tumor is an abnormal mass of cells that harms the body. In its early stages, it may cause no symptoms or may resemble an ordinary mole or age spot. If you notice any unusual changes, please consult a dermatology specialist.
records.tags_raw: skin cancer, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, ultraviolet radiation, skin tumor, early detection, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of the hands and feet
keywords: swelling of the hands and feet

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
The three most common types of skin cancer are as follows.
· Basal cell carcinoma: Occurs mainly on sun-exposed areas such as the face.
· Squamous cell carcinoma: Commonly occurs on sun-exposed areas and can develop from actinic cheilitis (a form of lip inflammation).
· Malignant melanoma: In East Asian populations, including in Korea, this often develops on the extremities, such as the palms and soles.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
In the early stages, there are usually no symptoms, and the lesion can resemble an ordinary mole, age spot, or blemish.
Please consult a dermatology specialist if you notice any of the following changes.
· An existing mole or spot that grows larger or changes shape
· Pain, itching, or bleeding
· A spot that looks noticeably different in shape or color from other spots on the body
· A lesion that recurs in the same location after previous removal, such as by laser

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: · Ultraviolet exposure is a major cause of skin cancer. Both long-term exposure and intermittent, intense exposure carry risk.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· Use sunscreen, hats, and parasols to protect against UV exposure.
· When detected early, skin cancer can often be successfully treated with complete removal of the lesion alone.
· Pay ongoing attention to your skin, and please be sure to see a medical specialist whenever a suspicious lesion appears.

records.title: Lower Extremity Reconstruction
records.intro: Lower extremity reconstruction is surgery that restores a severely injured leg — damaged by trauma or disease — without amputation. Evaluation by a plastic and reconstructive surgery specialist is essential to determine whether the leg can be saved.
records.tags_raw: lower extremity reconstruction, flap surgery, skin grafting, microsurgery, amputation

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Lower extremity reconstruction is surgery that restores the bone, skin, and muscle of a leg that has been severely damaged by major trauma, bone infection (osteomyelitis), a tumor, or similar causes, with the goal of saving the leg.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: The main technique used is flap surgery, in which healthy skin, muscle, or bone is taken from elsewhere on the body, along with its blood supply, and reattached at the injured site. This is a highly technical procedure that involves suturing tiny blood vessels under a microscope. Skin grafting, which transplants a thin layer of skin alone, may also be used alongside flap surgery.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If the reconnected blood vessels become blocked, the transplanted tissue can die, so close monitoring after surgery is very important. Bone infection can recur even after surgery, so ongoing treatment is needed. If the leg's blood vessels are severely blocked, amputation may unfortunately be necessary.

records.title: Lower Extremity Arterial Disease (Peripheral Arterial Disease)
records.intro: Lower extremity arterial disease occurs when the arteries supplying blood to the legs become narrowed or blocked, reducing blood flow and causing symptoms such as pain, numbness, and delayed wound healing. Delayed diagnosis can lead to serious complications, so please be sure to consult a medical specialist if you experience any unusual symptoms in your legs.
records.tags_raw: lower extremity arterial disease, peripheral arterial disease, peripheral vascular disease, leg pain, atherosclerosis, limb ischemia, diabetic foot, numbness in the hands and feet, arm numbness, tingling in the legs
keywords: numbness in the hands and feet

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
■ Major risk factors
· Smoking: Strongly associated with lower extremity arterial disease. Smokers have more than twice the risk of developing the condition compared with non-smokers.
· Diabetes
· High blood pressure
· Dyslipidemia (elevated blood fat levels)
· Older age (risk increases after age 50, rises sharply after 65, and affects about 20% of people by age 80)
· Risk is higher in men.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Lower extremity arterial disease occurs when the arteries running from the abdomen down to the legs become narrowed or blocked due to atherosclerosis (a buildup of fatty deposits that hardens and narrows the blood vessel walls) or thrombosis (a blood clot). This impaired circulation to the legs produces a range of symptoms.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms vary depending on the degree of arterial narrowing.

· Early stage: Leg pain or numbness occurs only with prolonged walking or running, and improves quickly with rest.
· Moderate: Pain, heaviness, or a bursting sensation in the legs occurs even with light walking.
· Severe: Pain persists even at rest.
· Advanced cases: Wound healing slows, and skin ulcers or tissue necrosis (dying of the skin tissue) can develop.

■ Other symptoms that may suggest this condition
· The skin on the legs feels pale or cold.
· Leg hair thins or stops growing.
· The pulse in the ankle feels weak or cannot be felt.

If symptoms worsen with leg activity (such as walking or running) and improve quickly with rest, lower extremity arterial disease is likely.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The main diagnostic test is the ankle-brachial index (ABI), calculated by dividing ankle blood pressure by arm blood pressure; a normal value is 0.9 to 1.4. A lower value raises suspicion of peripheral arterial narrowing.
Testing is recommended for people age 65 or older, or those with diabetes, high blood pressure, dyslipidemia, or a history of smoking.
Vascular ultrasound, CT angiography, or MR angiography may also be performed to directly evaluate the blood vessels.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
① Medication: The most basic treatment, used to control symptoms and help prevent further progression of atherosclerosis.

② Interventional procedures: Used when the artery is significantly narrowed or blocked and medication alone is not sufficient. These include balloon angioplasty (widening the narrowed vessel with a balloon) and stent placement.

③ Surgical treatment: Options include bypass surgery, in which a synthetic or biological graft is connected before and after the narrowed segment, and endarterectomy, which removes the blockage from within the vessel.

The choice between surgery and a less invasive procedure is based on the location and extent of the arterial disease.

sections.heading: Precautions and Prevention
sections.content:
Lower extremity arterial disease often occurs together with other atherosclerotic conditions, such as coronary artery disease and cerebrovascular disease. Left untreated, it increases the risk of cardiovascular death from causes such as heart attack or stroke. If tissue necrosis develops in the leg, it can lead to infection and become life-threatening, and in severe cases, amputation may be required.

■ Lifestyle habits for prevention
· Quit smoking completely.
· Actively manage high blood pressure, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
· Exercise regularly (3 to 5 times a week, at an intensity that causes slight breathlessness).
· If your legs hurt or feel numb while walking, consult a medical specialist promptly.
· People with diabetes should pay particular attention to foot wound care.

records.title: Cold Urticaria
records.intro: Cold urticaria is a condition in which hives develop upon exposure to cold air, cold water, or ice. In severe cases, dangerous symptoms such as difficulty breathing can occur, so please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: cold urticaria, hives, cold exposure, allergy, cold water, winter, headache, severe headache, migraine, back-of-head pain, breath holding, difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, choking sensation, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of the hands and feet
keywords: swelling of the hands and feet

sections.heading: Causes and Symptoms
sections.content:
Cold urticaria accounts for about 1% to 3% of all chronic urticaria cases and is most often acquired rather than present from birth.
· The exact cause is not known, but it is understood to be mediated by IgE, a type of immune substance.
· Hives develop upon exposure to cold air, cold water, or ice, and often appear as the body rewarms.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
· Most cases involve itching and swelling, but severe cases can involve difficulty breathing, a rapid pulse, and headache.
· Swimming or cold-water bathing, which expose the whole body to cold water, can be especially dangerous.
· If you have cold urticaria, avoid sudden exposure to cold water, and please be sure to consult a medical specialist for appropriate treatment and precautions.

records.title: Proper Use of Antibiotics
records.intro: Antibiotics are essential medications for treating bacterial infections, but improper use can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria, making future infections harder to treat. Please take antibiotics correctly and only as prescribed by your doctor.
records.tags_raw: antibiotics, antibiotic misuse, antibiotic resistance, correct dosing, antibiotics for colds, prescription, loose stools, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: What Are Antibiotics?
sections.content:
Antibiotics are medications that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth. They are vital, life-saving medications for bacterial infections such as pneumonia, urinary tract infection, and sepsis (a serious condition in which bacteria spread through the bloodstream).

However, antibiotics are effective only against bacteria. They have no effect on viral illnesses such as the common cold, influenza, or COVID-19. Because more than 90% of common colds are caused by viruses, antibiotics are not needed for them.

sections.heading: What Is Antibiotic Resistance?
sections.content:
Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria, through repeated exposure to antibiotics, undergo mutations that allow them to survive, so that the antibiotic no longer works against them.

The more frequently, unnecessarily, or incompletely antibiotics are taken, the faster resistant bacteria develop. Infection with resistant bacteria leaves fewer effective antibiotic options, making treatment much more difficult.

Antibiotic resistance is not only a personal concern — resistant bacteria can also spread to family members and others nearby.

sections.heading: How to Use Antibiotics Correctly
sections.content:
The key principles for using antibiotics correctly are as follows.

· Take antibiotics only when prescribed by a doctor: They are prescribed only when a bacterial infection is clear or strongly suspected. It is important not to request antibiotics for a cold.
· Complete the full prescribed course: Stopping early just because symptoms have improved can allow surviving bacteria to develop resistance.
· Do not start or stop antibiotics on your own: Antibiotics are prescription-only medications that require a doctor's order.
· Always inform your doctor if you have had side effects or an allergic reaction to antibiotics in the past.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Antibiotics can also cause side effects, ranging from mild symptoms such as diarrhea and nausea to, rarely, serious allergic reactions. If you notice any unusual reaction while taking antibiotics, please consult your doctor immediately.

Antibiotics are also used in livestock and seafood farming, which can be another route through which resistant bacteria spread to humans. Antibiotic resistance is a public health issue that requires a coordinated response from healthcare institutions and society as a whole.

records.title: Preventing Infectious Diseases During Overseas Travel
records.intro: Overseas travel can expose you to infectious diseases that are uncommon domestically. Extra caution is needed when visiting developing countries in tropical regions. Please consult a medical specialist 3 to 4 weeks before departure and arrange any needed vaccinations and preventive medications in advance.
records.tags_raw: overseas travel, travel-related infectious disease, malaria, yellow fever, dengue fever, vaccination, travel medicine, fever, body feels hot, high fever, low-grade fever, loose stools, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Major Infectious Diseases to Watch For
sections.content:
Travel-related infectious diseases refer to bacterial or viral illnesses — such as typhoid fever, malaria, or dengue fever — that are prevalent in the country being visited. Diseases requiring particular caution during overseas travel include the following.

· Waterborne infections (spread through contaminated water or food): Cholera, typhoid fever, bacterial dysentery, and hepatitis A, among others. Main symptoms are fever and diarrhea, and severe dehydration and shock can occur without appropriate treatment.
· Mosquito-borne infections: Malaria, dengue fever, and yellow fever, among others. Particular caution is needed when traveling to sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, and tropical South America.
· Meningococcal meningitis: Risk is elevated in certain regions of central Africa.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: These infections occur when a person is bitten by an infected mosquito or tick in a hot, humid country, or when bacteria and viruses enter the body through contaminated water or undercooked food in areas with poor sanitation.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Before traveling, arrange any needed vaccinations or begin taking malaria prevention medication in advance. While traveling, use insect repellent, drink only boiled or commercially bottled water, and make sure food is thoroughly cooked.

Recommended vaccinations vary depending on the destination country. Major infectious diseases that can be prevented by vaccination include the following.
· Yellow fever, meningococcal meningitis, hepatitis A, cholera, typhoid fever, Japanese encephalitis, and rabies, among others.

Some countries (particularly in Africa and parts of South America) require proof of yellow fever or meningococcal vaccination for entry. Please be sure to check the entry requirements of your destination country before traveling.

Because most vaccines take about 2 weeks after administration to produce adequate antibody protection, consulting a medical specialist 3 to 4 weeks before departure is recommended.

Country-specific infectious disease information and vaccination guidance can be found through the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency's overseas travel health information center.

sections.heading: Malaria Prevention
sections.content:
Malaria is a parasitic infection transmitted by mosquitoes. There is currently no vaccine used for travel-related prevention, but taking preventive medication can help protect against it.

The type of preventive medication needed varies by travel destination, and in some cases it must be started before departure. Please be sure to consult a medical specialist and obtain a prescription before traveling.

Even while taking preventive medication, care should be taken to avoid mosquito bites. Avoid outdoor activity after dusk, wear long sleeves and long pants, and use insect repellent.

If fever or other cold-like symptoms develop within a year after visiting a malaria risk area, please be sure to visit a hospital to check for malaria infection.

sections.heading: Personal Hygiene Guidelines
sections.content:
In addition to vaccination and preventive medication, the following personal hygiene practices are important.
· Eat food that has been thoroughly cooked whenever possible.
· Avoid street food when possible.
· Wash your hands frequently.
· Wear long clothing and use insect repellent to avoid mosquito bites.
· Limit outdoor activity after dusk.

records.title: Forgetfulness and Dementia
records.intro: It can be difficult to tell whether forgetfulness is simple age-related forgetfulness or a sign of dementia. Forgetfulness is a normal experience, but dementia is a brain disease. Rather than judging this on your own, please consult a medical specialist if you notice any concerning symptoms.
records.tags_raw: forgetfulness, dementia, mild cognitive impairment, memory, brain cells, stress, trouble falling asleep, frequent waking, poor sleep quality

sections.heading: Definition and Differences
sections.content:
Forgetfulness occurs when the brain's capacity is temporarily overloaded from trying to remember too much information at once, causing a brief lapse in memory. With a hint, the person quickly remembers, thinking, 'Oh, right!'



Dementia, or its earlier stage known as 'mild cognitive impairment,' involves a disease process in the brain that causes complete loss of a memory. The person forgets that an appointment was ever made in the first place, and even with a hint responds with, 'Did we have plans?' This complete lack of recall is the key difference.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
As people age, the number of neurons in the brain decreases, which can lower cognitive function, including memory.



However, forgetfulness is not caused by age alone — it is also common in middle-aged adults dealing with stress, depression, insomnia, or excessive worry. Constant stress while the brain is encoding and storing information, as well as heavy alcohol use and smoking, can reduce concentration and make forgetfulness considerably worse.

sections.heading: Self-Check and Precautions
sections.content:
If any of the following symptoms are present, they may indicate early dementia rather than simple forgetfulness, and you should see a doctor.



· Completely forgetting something heard just days ago and repeating the same question

· Recent memory noticeably worse than memory of the more distant past

· Getting lost or disoriented on a familiar, frequently traveled route

· Frequent mistakes with simple calculations, such as counting change

· Difficulty making situationally appropriate judgments, such as dressing inappropriately for the season



If you yourself notice that you have forgotten something, it is more likely to be simple forgetfulness. If someone else notices something is wrong before you do, dementia should be suspected.

records.title: Herniated Lumbar Disc (Lumbar Disc Herniation)
records.intro: A herniated lumbar disc (lumbar disc herniation) occurs when a disc between the vertebrae of the spine moves out of its normal position and presses on a nerve. It is characterized by low back pain along with numbness or pain radiating down the leg. With timely treatment, most cases may improve without surgery.
records.tags_raw: herniated lumbar disc, disc herniation, intervertebral disc, radiating leg pain, sciatica, low back pain, spine, low back ache, back pain, lower back strain, numbness in hands and feet, arm numbness, tingling leg, weakness in the arms or legs, difficulty moving one side of the body
keywords: weakness in the arms or legs
difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Definition and Causes
sections.content:
The intervertebral disc (disc) is a structure located between the vertebrae that absorbs shock and allows smooth movement of the spine.



As people age, the disc loses water content and becomes less elastic. When enough pressure is applied, the disc can be pushed backward and press on a nearby nerve — a condition known as disc herniation.



Degenerative changes can begin as early as the late teens, and the condition occurs most often in physically active adults in their 30s and 40s.



Bending only at the waist to lift heavy objects, sitting on the floor for long periods, and sitting with the legs crossed can all place extra strain on the disc.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
When a disc presses on a nerve, the following symptoms may occur.



· Numbness or pain radiating down the leg (varies depending on which nerve is compressed)

· Reduced sensation

· In severe cases, weakness in the leg

· In very severe cases, loss of bladder or bowel control (cauda equina syndrome)



If pain or numbness worsens when the neck is tilted backward, disc disease may be suspected.



Leg numbness or weakness is a more important warning sign than low back pain alone.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
If a spinal condition is suspected, the following tests are performed.



· MRI: An essential test that most accurately shows the disc, nerves, muscles, and other soft tissue.

· X-ray: Checks the basic structure.

· CT: Performed when the bone structure needs to be checked, and used mainly for surgical planning or post-surgical evaluation.



The patient's symptoms are the most important basis for diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Most cases of herniated lumbar disc can be treated without surgery.



· Medication: Anti-inflammatory pain relievers reduce inflammation and pain. It is important to take them consistently for at least 2 to 4 weeks.

· Injection therapy (nerve block): Medication is injected around the nerve if there is no improvement after medication. Caution is needed in patients with diabetes.

· Surgery: Considered when there is leg weakness or paralysis, or when there is no improvement despite adequate conservative treatment. Only about 20-30% of patients require surgery.



If a nerve remains compressed for a long time, recovery may be difficult even after surgery, so it is important to discuss the appropriate timing of treatment with a specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Because this is a degenerative condition, complete prevention is difficult, but the following habits can help.



· Maintain good posture: When sitting in a chair, keep your hips against the backrest and sit at a right angle.

· Avoid crossing your legs.

· When lifting heavy objects, bend your knees rather than bending only at the waist.

· If sitting for long periods, get up and stretch every 50 minutes.

· Stretch right after waking up in the morning.

records.title: Blood Cancer
records.intro: Blood cancer refers to cancer that arises in the bone marrow, the organ responsible for producing blood cells. The bone marrow makes three types of blood cells: white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When the bone marrow malfunctions, abnormalities in the number, shape, or function of these cells can cause a variety of symptoms. Frequent nosebleeds or easy bruising can occur, but these symptoms do not necessarily mean a person has blood cancer. If abnormal results appear on a blood test, please consult a hematology-oncology specialist.
records.tags_raw: blood cancer, leukemia, multiple myeloma, platelets, bone marrow, anemia, chemotherapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for blood cancer varies depending on the type.

· Acute leukemia: Chemotherapy is given during hospitalization, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered afterward.
· Chronic leukemia, multiple myeloma, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia: In some cases, the condition is monitored without immediate treatment; when treatment becomes necessary, a combination of injectable or oral chemotherapy agents is used.
· Chronic myeloid leukemia: Most cases are treated with oral targeted chemotherapy agents.

Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is divided into autologous transplantation, which uses the patient's own stem cells, and allogeneic transplantation, which uses stem cells from a donor. It is performed for conditions such as acute leukemia, multiple myeloma, and lymphoma.

The specific treatment method and plan are determined by a specialist based on the patient's condition and the type of blood cancer.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management During Treatment
sections.content:
· Maintain a balanced diet. Since preserving physical strength is important, avoid excessively restricting specific foods or eating a limited diet, and instead eat a variety of easily digestible foods.
· During periods of significantly reduced immunity, eating mainly cooked foods can help prevent infection.
· Dietary supplements can interact with treatment medications, reducing their effectiveness or worsening side effects. Please consult your doctor before taking any supplement.
· If you have any questions or concerns, the safest approach is to consult your care team.

If you have previously received chemotherapy or radiation therapy to the pelvic area, your risk of developing blood cancer may be increased, so please have regular checkups.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
If blood cancer is suspected, the following tests are performed.

· Blood tests: Check the number and shape of blood cells, protein levels, and other markers.
· Bone marrow test: A sample of bone marrow, usually taken from the pelvic bone, is examined for cancer cells. Cancer-related genetic testing and chromosome analysis of the marrow are often performed together to support an accurate diagnosis.
· Imaging tests: CT, MRI, and other imaging studies are used to check for organ abnormalities or bone lesions.

For an accurate diagnosis, please consult a hematology-oncology specialist.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
When the bone marrow malfunctions, abnormalities in the number, shape, or function of blood cells can cause the following symptoms.

· White blood cell abnormalities: Reduced immunity, making the person more prone to infections such as pneumonia, enteritis, and urinary tract infections.
· Red blood cell deficiency: Anemia, causing paleness, fatigue, shortness of breath, and dizziness.
· Platelet deficiency: Frequent nosebleeds that are slow to stop, and easy bruising. In severe cases, this can lead to serious bleeding, such as bleeding in the brain or gastrointestinal tract.

Frequent nosebleeds or easy bruising do not necessarily mean a person has blood cancer. Low platelet counts can result from a wide range of causes. When a blood test shows an abnormality, the first step is to evaluate the person's overall health.

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
The most common types of blood cancer include the following.

■ Leukemia
Leukemia is a malignant tumor that arises from immature blood cells in the bone marrow. It is classified as acute or chronic leukemia. Acute leukemia often develops quickly with severe symptoms. Chronic leukemia tends to cause mild symptoms and is sometimes found incidentally during a health checkup. In chronic leukemia, enlargement of the spleen (an organ located under the left rib cage) can cause discomfort or bloating on the left side of the abdomen, which may bring patients to seek care.

■ Multiple Myeloma
Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, the cells that produce antibodies. It occurs mainly in older adults. Large amounts of an abnormal protein (a monoclonal antibody) are produced, which weakens immunity and can lead to anemia, kidney failure (reduced kidney function), and high blood calcium levels. It also weakens bone, making fractures — such as spinal compression fractures — more likely, and severe bone pain is a characteristic feature.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Blood cancer is cancer that arises in the bone marrow, the blood-forming organ located inside bone. The bone marrow produces three types of blood cells: white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets.

records.title: Angina (Angina Pectoris)
records.intro: Angina is a cardiovascular condition in which the coronary arteries — the blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients to the heart — become narrowed, causing a dull chest pain. Because heart disease can be a major cause of sudden death, if you feel chest discomfort that is different from what you normally experience, please do not delay in consulting a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: angina, chest pain, myocardial infarction, coronary artery, atherosclerosis, stent, sudden death

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment is divided into medication, procedural treatment, and surgical treatment.

① Medication: Stabilizes atherosclerotic plaque to help prevent myocardial infarction and widens blood vessels to relieve symptoms. When narrowing is not severe, medication alone may be sufficient.

② Stent placement: A procedure in which the narrowed vessel is accessed through the wrist (radial artery) or a leg vessel, widened with a balloon, and then held open with a metal mesh tube (a stent). After stent placement, antiplatelet medications such as aspirin must be taken continuously to prevent blood clots. Stopping these medications without medical guidance increases the risk of myocardial infarction caused by stent thrombosis.

③ Drug-coated balloon angioplasty: A method that widens the vessel using a drug-coated balloon without leaving a stent behind. Because no foreign material remains in the body, it avoids the risk of stent thrombosis, and the required duration of long-term antiplatelet therapy may be shorter.

④ Coronary artery bypass surgery: Considered when multiple vessels are affected or when severe calcification makes procedural treatment difficult. The specific treatment approach is determined by a specialist based on the patient's condition.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To help prevent angina and myocardial infarction, it is important to manage the risk factors for atherosclerosis.
· Smoking cessation: Smoking is a major risk factor for coronary artery disease, with a particularly strong effect in younger people.
· Blood pressure management: High blood pressure damages blood vessels and worsens atherosclerosis.
· Blood sugar management: People with diabetes have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.
· Cholesterol management: Manage cholesterol appropriately according to your doctor's prescription.
· Regular aerobic exercise: Recommended at least three times per week.
· Dietary management: It is best to eat legumes and fish instead of meat high in saturated fat and fried foods.
· Reduce salty food intake.

If you experience chest discomfort or pain, do not dismiss it — please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
For the heart to keep working continuously, it must receive blood and oxygen through vessels called the coronary arteries. Angina is a condition in which these vessels narrow, leaving the heart short of blood supply. When the coronary arteries narrow due to atherosclerosis, blood flow becomes inadequate during situations that increase the heart's demand for blood — such as exercise or emotional excitement — leading to chest pain and other symptoms.

■ Difference from Myocardial Infarction
Myocardial infarction occurs when fatty deposits (atherosclerotic plaque) inside a vessel suddenly rupture, forming a blood clot that blocks the vessel and damages the heart muscle. It can occur suddenly even when the vessel narrowing was not previously severe.
