Both conditions arise from problems in the coronary arteries, but they differ in that angina causes temporary symptoms, whereas myocardial infarction damages the heart muscle.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The most common cause of vessel narrowing is atherosclerosis, a process in which fatty deposits build up on the vessel wall, narrowing and hardening the passage through which blood flows.
Smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol are the leading risk factors. The condition is increasingly seen in younger adults in their 20s and 30s, in whom smoking is considered the biggest contributing factor. It can also occur when severe stress or excessive alcohol use causes sudden constriction of the blood vessels.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The most characteristic symptom of angina is a sense of pressure, tightness, or dull discomfort in the center of the chest.

· Symptoms occur during activity, such as climbing stairs or walking briskly, and improve with rest.
· Symptoms occur over a broad area in the center of the chest and are difficult to point to with a finger.
· May be accompanied by a sensation that spreads from the chest to the shoulder or arm.
· Symptoms usually last 2 to 10 minutes and go away with rest.

The following types of pain are less typical of angina and may have another cause. Because some of these causes can also be serious, please seek medical evaluation promptly, and call 119 (Korea's emergency number) if the pain is severe or comes with difficulty breathing.

· Sharp, needle-like pain
· Pain that can be pinpointed precisely with a fingertip
· Pain that changes with body position or breathing, or that worsens with pressure from the hand

Do not wait for chest pain to last 30 minutes. If chest pain or pressure lasts more than a few minutes, occurs at rest, returns after going away, or is accompanied by shortness of breath, cold sweats, or dizziness, call 119 (Korea's emergency number) immediately. A heart attack can occur even when symptoms are brief or not severe.

records.title: Macular Degeneration
records.intro: Macular degeneration is a condition in which the macula — the central part of the retina — is damaged, leading to decreased vision. In severe cases it can lead to blindness, but early detection and consistent treatment can help slow its progression. If you are 50 or older, please have regular retinal examinations.
records.tags_raw: macular degeneration, macula, retina, decreased vision, eye injection, dry macular degeneration, wet macular degeneration, lutein, blurry vision, difficulty seeing, hazy vision

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
· Fundus examination: Checks the macula for drusen, bleeding, and exudates.

· Optical coherence tomography (OCT): Provides a CT-like, detailed view of fine changes in the retina and is essential for guiding treatment decisions.

· Fluorescein angiography: Checks for abnormal new blood vessels to diagnose wet macular degeneration.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The retina is a thin layer of nerve tissue at the back of the eye, comparable to the film in a camera. The macula is the central part of the retina and is the most important area for sharp, central vision.



Macular degeneration is a condition in which waste deposits build up in the macula with age, or abnormal new blood vessels form and cause bleeding or fluid leakage, resulting in decreased vision.



Macular degeneration is classified into two types.

· Dry macular degeneration: Deposits called drusen accumulate beneath the macula, gradually destroying the light-sensing cells.

· Wet macular degeneration: Abnormal new blood vessels form, causing bleeding and fluid leakage and leading to a rapid decline in vision.



Because treatment and prognosis differ between the two types, accurate differentiation is important.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Decreased vision: The most common symptom.

· Blurred or dark areas in the center of vision

· Objects appearing distorted or warped



If you notice any of these symptoms, please visit an ophthalmologist promptly.



■ Self-Check Method: The Amsler Grid

This method uses a grid pattern resembling graph paper. Cover one eye and look at the center of the grid, checking whether the center appears blocked, whether the lines appear bent, or whether the squares appear unequal in size. If you notice any abnormality, please visit an ophthalmologist immediately.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Dry Macular Degeneration

The goal of treatment is to slow progression. This includes taking macular supplements (containing lutein, zeaxanthin, and similar nutrients), protecting the eyes from UV exposure, and adjusting the diet. Macular supplements do not prevent the condition or cure it, but they may reduce the risk of progressing to late-stage macular degeneration. Healthy individuals with no signs of macular degeneration do not necessarily need to take them.



■ Wet Macular Degeneration

Injections into the eye (anti-VEGF injections) are the most important treatment. The injection is given into the white of the eye and can be performed relatively simply in an outpatient setting. It works by suppressing abnormal blood vessel growth, helping to prevent further vision loss. In rare cases of extensive bleeding, surgical treatment may be needed.



Please discuss your treatment options with your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· Smoking cessation: Smoking is a major risk factor for macular degeneration.

· UV protection: Wear sunglasses when sunlight is strong.

· Diet: Reduce foods high in cholesterol and eat more dark green and yellow vegetables and oily fish.

· Regular checkups: If you are 50 or older, please have regular retinal examinations.

· If you have dry macular degeneration, it is important to watch closely for any progression to the wet form. Self-checking at home with an Amsler grid can also help.

records.title: Drug Treatment for Rheumatoid Arthritis
records.intro: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own joints and causes inflammation. After diagnosis, drug treatment is started to reduce inflammation and slow disease progression. In recent years, in addition to conventional antirheumatic drugs, a variety of targeted therapies have come into use, including biologics and small molecule inhibitors (JAK inhibitors). Because each drug has different characteristics and side effects, please discuss treatment options thoroughly with your doctor before deciding on the approach that is right for you.
records.tags_raw: rheumatoid arthritis, antirheumatic drugs, biologics, JAK inhibitors, small molecule inhibitors, methotrexate, targeted therapy, immunosuppressants

sections.heading: Biologics
sections.content:
Biologics are injectable medications derived from living organisms or made using living organisms, and they work by targeting specific substances or cells that cause inflammation. A 'target' refers to the specific protein or cell that a drug acts on.

■ Main Types
- Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors: Block tumor necrosis factor, a substance that promotes inflammation.
- Interleukin-6 (IL-6) inhibitors: Suppress interleukin-6, which transmits inflammatory signals.
- T-cell inhibitors: Suppress the activation of T cells involved in the inflammatory response.
- B-cell inhibitors: Reduce the number of B cells, which produce antibodies, to help control inflammation.

■ Administration
Depending on the drug, the medication may be self-injected or given by intravenous infusion at the hospital. The injection interval also varies by drug, such as once a week, once every 2 weeks, or once every 4 weeks.

■ Checks Before Treatment and Side Effects
Because these drugs work by suppressing the immune response, they can increase the risk of infection. For this reason, patients are tested for latent tuberculosis (a condition in which tuberculosis bacteria are present in the body without causing symptoms) before starting treatment, and preventive measures or vaccinations may be given depending on the results. Local reactions such as redness and itching at the injection site can occur. If any adverse reaction occurs, please contact your care team immediately.

■ Insurance Coverage Criteria
Because these drugs are costly, there are criteria for National Health Insurance coverage. When conventional antirheumatic drugs have been used adequately but are not effective enough, or cannot be used because of side effects, the decision to use a biologic is made after reviewing whether the patient meets the insurance criteria. After treatment begins, the response is evaluated every 6 months; the drug is continued if it is working, and changed or stopped if it is ineffective or causes side effects.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis is a condition in which the immune system, which normally protects the body, attacks the body itself for unknown reasons and causes inflammation.

Inflammation occurs mainly in the synovium, the thin membrane that lines the inside of the joint around the bones, causing the joints to become stiff, swollen, and painful.

Because the disease results from an abnormality of the immune system, inflammation can also occur throughout the body, including the lungs, eyes, skin, and blood vessels, in addition to the joints.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The goal of treating rheumatoid arthritis is to use medication to reduce inflammation and regulate the immune response so that the disease does not progress further.

■ Drugs That Reduce Inflammation
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; anti-inflammatory pain relievers): Reduce inflammation and pain quickly.
- Steroids: Have a strong anti-inflammatory effect, but long-term use can cause side effects, so they are used for a short period or at a low dose.

■ Order of Treatment
Antirheumatic drugs take several weeks to several months to take effect after starting. For this reason, anti-inflammatory pain relievers or steroids are initially used together with them; once inflammation begins to come under control, the anti-inflammatory drugs and steroids are reduced while the antirheumatic drugs are continued.

sections.heading: Small Molecule Inhibitors (JAK Inhibitors) and Drug Selection
sections.content:
■ About Small Molecule Inhibitors
Small molecule inhibitors are oral targeted therapies that have been developed extensively in recent years. They help control inflammation by blocking a substance called Janus kinase (JAK), which transmits inflammatory signals inside cells. JAK is a protein that helps inflammatory signals spread within the cell.

Their mechanism of action is similar to that of biologics, but the key difference is that they are made as small-molecular-weight chemical compounds rather than biological substances, so they can be taken as pills rather than injections.

■ How a Drug Is Chosen
For targeted therapies such as biologics and small molecule inhibitors, the doctor and patient decide together after considering the following points as a whole.
- The drug's mechanism of action
- Its most common side effects
- The method of administration (oral, self-injection, or intravenous infusion) and the dosing interval
- The patient's health status, coexisting conditions, and medical history
- The patient's preferred method of administration

■ Importance of Self-Management
Self-management by the patient is very important with targeted therapies. For self-injected drugs, please make sure to receive thorough instruction from your care team, before and after the prescription, on the correct injection technique, storage precautions, and keeping a record of doses.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Types of Antirheumatic Drugs
sections.content:
Antirheumatic drugs have immune-regulating effects and form the core of rheumatoid arthritis treatment.

■ Drugs Usually Used First
- Methotrexate: The most representative antirheumatic drug, taken once a week. It is usually taken as a pill, and an injectable form is sometimes used when taking it orally is very difficult.
- Hydroxychloroquine: Originally developed as a malaria treatment, but also effective for rheumatoid arthritis and therefore used for it.
- Sulfasalazine: An antirheumatic drug that suppresses inflammation.

■ Drugs Added or Switched to When Effects Are Insufficient or Side Effects Occur
- Leflunomide: An antirheumatic drug with immunosuppressive effects.
- Tacrolimus: An immunosuppressant that can be used when the condition cannot be controlled with other drugs.

■ Criteria for Choosing a Drug
Because each drug has different precautions and side effects, the drug best suited to the patient's condition is selected after considering the patient's age, coexisting conditions, and kidney, liver, and lung function as a whole.

records.title: Rotator Cuff Tear
records.intro: A rotator cuff tear is a condition in which the rotator cuff — the four muscles and tendons that surround the shoulder — is torn. It is often confused with frozen shoulder, so accurate diagnosis and treatment are important. If shoulder pain persists, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: rotator cuff tear, impingement syndrome, shoulder pain, supraspinatus tendon, acromion, shoulder surgery, tendon rupture

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of a rotator cuff tear are as follows.
· Shoulder pain and muscle weakness
· Pain worsens when the arm is raised in certain directions.
· Nighttime pain may make it hard to sleep.
· The tear can slowly enlarge over several years.
Frozen shoulder is characterized by a reduction in the shoulder's range of motion itself, whereas a rotator cuff tear mainly causes muscle weakness and pain in specific directions. The two conditions must be distinguished by a medical specialist's examination.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Medication for a rotator cuff tear aims to relieve pain and control inflammation; it is not expected to restore the structure of the torn tendon. The treatment approach is determined by the extent of the tear and the patient's condition.
· Conservative (non-surgical) treatment: For older patients or when there is no major functional problem, medication, injection therapy, and physical therapy are used to relieve pain.
· Surgical treatment: For patients under 60 or when the tear is severe, arthroscopic tendon repair is performed. Arthroscopic surgery is done through small openings, with a camera inserted, without a large incision. Improving the flexibility of the rotator cuff through stretching, including exercise, can help with prevention.
Please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions about treatment.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The main mechanism is 'impingement syndrome.' When the rotator cuff tendon repeatedly strikes the acromion (the bone at the top of the shoulder) as the arm is raised, the tendon can tear over time. Symptoms of impingement syndrome can begin as early as the 30s and 40s.
Sports that heavily use the shoulder, such as tennis, swimming, and bodybuilding, and work activities that involve raising the arms also increase the risk. Exercising with improper form raises the risk of a tear.

sections.heading: Definition and Causes
sections.content: The rotator cuff refers to the four muscles that surround the shoulder (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis, and teres minor) and their tendons. A rotator cuff tear is a condition in which these tendons are partially or completely torn.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
A rotator cuff tear is diagnosed using the following tests.
· Physical examination: Shoulder range of motion, muscle strength, and pain provocation tests
· MRI (magnetic resonance imaging): Accurately shows the location and extent of the tear.
· Ultrasound: Allows the condition of the tendon to be checked in real time.
If the problem is assumed to be simple frozen shoulder and treatment is delayed, the tear may enlarge. If shoulder pain lasts for more than a month or keeps recurring, it is advisable to be examined by a medical specialist.

records.title: Rotator Cuff Disorders
records.intro: Rotator cuff disorders are conditions in which the main muscles and tendons that surround the shoulder (the rotator cuff) are affected. Among people with shoulder pain, rotator cuff disorders are far more common than frozen shoulder. If your shoulder hurts, please consult a medical specialist for an accurate diagnosis.
records.tags_raw: rotator cuff, shoulder pain, rotator cuff tear, shoulder muscles, shoulder tendons, shoulder rehabilitation

sections.heading: Differences from Frozen Shoulder
sections.content:
Shoulder pain is often assumed to be frozen shoulder. However, when the cause of shoulder pain is investigated, rotator cuff disorders are found far more often than frozen shoulder.
· Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis): Inflammation of the shoulder joint capsule causes the shoulder itself to stiffen. Movement of the arm is significantly limited in every direction.
· Rotator cuff disorders: Caused by problems in the tendons and muscles, and pain often occurs when the arm is raised in a specific direction.
Because the two conditions are treated differently, an accurate diagnosis is important.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The rotator cuff refers to the four main muscles and tendons that wrap around the shoulder joint through a full 360 degrees. These structures maintain the stability of the shoulder and allow the arm to be raised and rotated.
Rotator cuff disorders are conditions in which these muscles and tendons become inflamed or are partially or completely torn (ruptured). The risk of damage increases with age and with heavy use of the arm.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Most cases of rotator cuff disorders may improve when they are accurately diagnosed and treated early. If treatment is postponed or neglected, surgery may become necessary later.
· Physical therapy and exercise therapy: Exercises are performed in stages within a pain-free range.
· Injection therapy: Performed when necessary, at the judgment of a medical specialist.
· Surgery: Surgical treatment is considered in serious cases, such as a complete tear.
It is important to avoid actions that put sudden strain on the shoulder, such as suddenly lifting a heavy object with one hand.

sections.heading: Exercises
sections.content:
Exercises for the rotator cuff are performed in stages. Each exercise is generally recommended to be repeated 10 to 20 times, twice a day.
■ Stage 1 - Safe Initial Exercises
· Isometric exercise: With the elbow bent, place the arm against a wall and push toward the wall. This strengthens the muscles without moving the shoulder joint itself.
· Stick (wand) exercise: Hold a long stick or towel with both hands and raise and lower the arms or move them to the side, within the range that pain allows.
■ Stage 2 - Strengthening Exercises
· Resistance band exercise: Secure one end of a resistance band to a doorknob and repeatedly pull the arm inward or outward at the shoulder.
Exercises should be performed within a pain-free range, and the method should be decided under the guidance of a medical specialist or therapist.

records.title: Viral Hepatitis
records.intro: Viral hepatitis is a disease in which a harmful virus invades the liver, causing inflammation and destroying liver cells. The route of transmission and the treatment differ depending on the type of virus (hepatitis A, B, or C). Please do not judge your condition on your own; consult a gastroenterology specialist for accurate blood tests and treatment.
records.tags_raw: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, antiviral drugs, hepatitis vaccination

sections.heading: Hepatitis A
sections.content: Hepatitis A is spread by mouth through contaminated water or food. It causes fever, extreme tiredness, vomiting, and jaundice, and adults tend to become much sicker than children. There is no specific treatment drug, and most people recover with plenty of rest. Two doses of the vaccine can provide long-lasting protection.

sections.heading: Hepatitis C
sections.content: Like hepatitis B, hepatitis C is spread through blood, but there is currently no vaccine to prevent it. Infected people often have no symptoms at all, so the disease can progress without being noticed.

sections.heading: Hepatitis B
sections.content: Hepatitis B is spread through blood and body fluids, and it is the leading cause of liver cancer in Korea. If you have chronic hepatitis B and your doctor has prescribed antiviral treatment, it is important to take the antiviral pill every day, without missing doses, so that the virus cannot become active. If a blood test shows that you do not have protective antibodies, you should receive the hepatitis B vaccine in three doses.

records.title: Raynaud's Phenomenon
records.intro: Raynaud's phenomenon is not simply cold hands and feet; it can be a sign of another underlying rheumatic disease. Please do not ignore it — consult a rheumatology specialist for examination and testing.
records.tags_raw: Raynaud's phenomenon, cold hands and feet, rheumatic disease, systemic sclerosis, vasoconstriction, stuffy nose, clear runny nose, yellow runny nose

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: In Raynaud's phenomenon, exposure to cold or stress suddenly cuts off blood flow to the fingers or toes, causing the skin to turn white, blue, or red.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: It is divided into 'primary' Raynaud's, which occurs without a specific cause, most often in young women, and 'secondary' Raynaud's, which is caused by another disease. Secondary Raynaud's is mainly caused by rheumatic diseases such as systemic sclerosis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: The first step is behavioral treatment: keeping the whole body warm and avoiding the cold, for example by wearing gloves. If symptoms are severe or an underlying disease is present, medication that widens blood vessels may be needed.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: It can also occur after prolonged use of vibrating tools, after frostbite, or as a result of certain medications, such as blood pressure medicines or medicines for a runny nose. Please discuss this thoroughly with your doctor.

records.title: Robotic Cholecystectomy
records.intro: Robotic cholecystectomy is a minimally invasive surgery in which a surgeon controls a robotic system to remove the gallbladder. 'Minimally invasive' means the operation is performed through small openings in the body. It may be considered as treatment for gallbladder conditions such as cholecystitis, gallstones (cholelithiasis), and gallbladder polyps. Please discuss the choice of surgical method thoroughly with your treating specialist before making a decision.
records.tags_raw: robotic surgery, cholecystectomy, gallbladder, laparoscopy, single-port surgery, minimally invasive surgery, gallstones, cholecystitis, gallbladder polyp, hand tremor, body tremor

sections.heading: Types of Gallbladder Surgery
sections.content:
Cholecystectomy is broadly divided into three methods.

· Open surgery: An incision of about 15 to 20 cm is made in the right upper abdomen. It is considered when minimally invasive surgery is difficult.

· Laparoscopic surgery: Performed through three to four openings, each 1 to 2 cm in size. This is currently the most commonly performed method.

· Robotic surgery: Performed through a single small opening of about 2 to 3 cm, with a smaller scar and, in general, a quicker recovery.



Compared with open surgery, minimally invasive surgery such as laparoscopic or robotic surgery generally involves less pain and a faster return to daily activities.

sections.heading: What Is Robotic Cholecystectomy?
sections.content:
In robotic surgery, the robot does not move on its own. The operating surgeon sits at a console (control station), directly controls the robot, and performs the entire operation.



· The surgical site can be viewed precisely through a 3D image magnified 10 times.

· The system compensates for the surgeon's hand tremor, allowing precise surgery.

· The robotic arms have joints, allowing the surgeon to work from a variety of angles in a stable surgical setting.



In most cases, cholecystectomy can be performed with a single-port approach, in which only one opening is made inside the navel. 'Single-port' means that only one opening is made. However, when inflammation is severe or the structure of the gallbladder or bile duct is unusual, several openings may be made, and additional incisions may be needed depending on the situation during surgery.

sections.heading: Preparation Before Surgery
sections.content: There is no special additional preparation required for robotic cholecystectomy. Because the surgery is performed under general anesthesia, the usual preparation for general anesthesia, such as fasting, is needed. Please follow the instructions of your care team for specific preparation.

sections.heading: Hospital Stay and Recovery
sections.content:
The length of the hospital stay is similar to that of laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Patients are usually admitted the day before surgery, have surgery the next day, and are discharged the day after surgery, for a stay of 2 nights and 3 days. However, the length of stay may vary depending on the patient's condition, diagnosis, and recovery after surgery.



After discharge, patients usually visit the outpatient clinic 7 to 10 days later to check the biopsy results and the surgical wound. After that, in most cases there is no need for ongoing medication or regular outpatient visits, and in most cases there are no special restrictions on diet or activity.

sections.heading: Postoperative Precautions
sections.content:
Postoperative precautions are not very different from those after open or laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Keep the wound clean and care for it according to your care team's instructions. In recent years, in many cases patients can shower right after surgery and do not need separate wound disinfection visits.



In most cases there are no special restrictions on diet or activity after gallbladder removal, but this can vary from person to person, so please discuss the specifics with your treating specialist.

records.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis of the Shoulder
records.intro: Rheumatoid arthritis of the shoulder is a disease that weakens the tendons surrounding the shoulder joint and damages the bone. If left untreated, the bone can be severely damaged and even surgery may become difficult, so please consult an orthopedic specialist and continue regular management.
records.tags_raw: rheumatoid, shoulder arthritis, shoulder pain, rotator cuff, joint replacement

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Severe shoulder pain develops and movement becomes difficult. If the tendons tear, it becomes hard to raise the arm, and as the disease advances, the bone can erode and the shape of the joint can change. If the pain continues, please do not rely on this Health Encyclopedia; visit a hospital.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Rheumatoid arthritis of the shoulder is a disease in which the body's immune system attacks the shoulder joint and causes chronic inflammation. As a result, the bones of the shoulder wear away, and the rotator cuff, an important set of tendons that move the shoulder, becomes thinner and can eventually tear.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Tests
sections.content: The most important step is to check early on the condition of the shoulder tendons and how much the bone has been damaged. Detailed tests such as X-rays, ultrasound, and MRI should be used to monitor how much the disease is progressing over time.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: The most important treatment is to take medication consistently to help prevent the disease from getting worse. If the condition cannot be controlled with medication and the bones and tendons are severely damaged, surgery is considered. Surgical options include surgery to remove inflamed tissue (debridement) and joint replacement surgery, in which a new joint is implanted.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If surgery is delayed too long and the bone erodes severely, the surgery itself can become very difficult. Because it is important to find the timing and method of surgery that suit the patient, please consult a medical specialist thoroughly before making a decision.

sections.heading: Prevention and Management
sections.content: It is difficult to completely prevent rheumatoid arthritis itself, but early detection and good drug treatment can help prevent bone damage. Regular hospital visits to check the condition of the shoulder are an important part of managing the disease.

records.title: Vaccinations for Patients with Rheumatic Diseases
records.intro: Rheumatic diseases involve dysregulation of the immune system and can make a person more vulnerable to infectious diseases. Immunosuppressive drugs used in treatment also increase the risk of infection. Vaccination is an effective way to help prevent infectious diseases, so please consult your doctor and receive vaccinations at the appropriate time.
records.tags_raw: rheumatic disease, vaccination, vaccine, immunosuppressants, influenza, herpes zoster, pneumonia, rheumatic vaccination clinic

sections.heading: Timing of Vaccination
sections.content:
It is ideal to be vaccinated when you are in good health. If you are being treated for an acute illness, please wait until your symptoms have sufficiently recovered before being vaccinated. However, a mild cold without fever is not a contraindication to vaccination.

Patients with rheumatic diseases should, if possible, complete their vaccinations before starting immunosuppressive treatment.
· Live vaccines: Completing vaccination at least 4 weeks before starting immunosuppressive treatment is recommended.
· Inactivated vaccines (vaccines made with killed organisms): Completing vaccination at least 2 weeks before starting treatment is recommended.

When treatment cannot be delayed, vaccination is given at a time when the degree of immunosuppression is low. Please consult your doctor about the exact timing.

sections.heading: Vaccination: Myths and Facts
sections.content:
■ If I still get the disease after being vaccinated, does that mean the vaccine did not work?
Vaccination does not prevent disease 100% of the time; rather, it boosts immunity so that symptoms are less severe even if infection occurs. Among people aged 65 and older, influenza vaccination is reported to have a disease-prevention effect of about 30 to 40%, while its effect in preventing death is reported to be about 80%. Early COVID-19 vaccines were also less effective at preventing infection with variant strains, but they have been shown to be effective in reducing progression to severe illness and death.

■ Can I receive several vaccines on the same day?
Receiving several vaccines on the same day is known not to reduce their effectiveness or significantly increase the risk of adverse reactions. Whenever possible, vaccines are given in different sites, and if the same site must be used, at least 2.5 cm apart. Vaccination can be carried out safely according to your care team's judgment and instructions.

sections.heading: Contraindications and Precautions for Vaccination
sections.content:
In the following cases, the decision to vaccinate should be made after consulting a medical specialist.
· A serious adverse reaction occurred after a previous vaccination
· Pregnancy
· Taking high-level immunosuppressive drugs or having severely impaired immune function

In particular, 'live vaccines,' which contain a weakened form of the living organism (such as the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine and the yellow fever vaccine), can lead to actual disease if given when immunity is severely reduced. Vaccination may be considered only in limited cases depending on the individual patient's condition, so please consult a medical specialist.

Yellow fever vaccination is required for travel to regions of Africa and Central and South America where yellow fever is endemic, but it is not recommended for patients with rheumatic diseases who are taking immunosuppressive drugs. If travel is unavoidable, a medical letter stating that vaccination is not possible can be issued.

sections.heading: Recommended Vaccines for Patients with Rheumatic Diseases
sections.content:
Among the vaccines recommended for all adults, the following are particularly important for patients with rheumatic diseases.
· Influenza (flu): Annual vaccination
· Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis: According to the adult vaccination schedule
· Hepatitis A and B: Vaccinate when antibodies are absent
· Human papillomavirus (HPV): Recommended for adults aged 26 and younger (including men)
· Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae): Vaccination is recommended for patients with rheumatic diseases
· Herpes zoster (shingles): The existing live vaccine was of limited use in immunocompromised patients, but an inactivated herpes zoster vaccine has recently been released and can now be given to patients with rheumatic diseases.

Family members and other close contacts are also recommended to be vaccinated. However, for at least 2 weeks after receiving a live vaccine, contact with a patient who is receiving immunosuppressive treatment should be minimized.

Please discuss your specific vaccination plan with your doctor.

sections.heading: Why Vaccination Is Important for Patients with Rheumatic Diseases
sections.content: Rheumatic diseases are conditions in which the regulatory function of the immune system is abnormal. As a result, when pathogens (viruses, bacteria, and others) invade, the risk of contracting an infectious disease is higher than in the general population, and once infection occurs, the likelihood of progressing to severe illness is also higher. Immunosuppressive drugs used in treatment, such as steroids and biologics, also increase the risk of infection. Because vaccination is one of the most effective ways to prevent infectious diseases, it is especially emphasized.

records.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
records.intro: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own joints and causes inflammation. Joint stiffness, swelling, and pain usually appear symmetrically on both sides, mainly in the small joints of the hands and feet. Early diagnosis and treatment can help reduce the impact on daily life. If you suspect symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune disease, synovitis, morning stiffness, antirheumatic drugs, biologics, targeted therapy, joint deformity, remission, joint aching, knee pain, shoulder pain, wrist pain, arthralgia, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?
sections.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks its own joint tissue for unknown reasons, causing inflammation.



■ Areas Mainly Affected

Inflammation of the synovium, the membrane that lines the inside of the joint around the bones, causes the joints to become stiff, swollen, and painful.



■ Whole-Body Symptoms

Because the cause is an abnormality of the immune system, inflammation can also occur in the lungs, eyes, skin, blood vessels, and other parts of the body, in addition to the joints.



■ Incidence

It occurs about 3 to 4 times more often in women than in men, and incidence is highest, on average, in people in their 40s and 50s.



■ Causes

The exact cause has not been identified, but in people with a genetic predisposition, the disease is known to develop when triggered by environmental factors such as smoking and periodontitis.

sections.heading: Suspected Symptoms and Diagnosis
sections.content:
■ Main Symptoms

- Morning stiffness (stiff joints in the morning) lasts for more than 1 hour.

- It often starts in the small joints of the hands and feet.

- Symptoms appear in multiple joints on both the left and right sides at the same time.

- Whole-body symptoms such as fatigue, loss of appetite, and general weakness may appear first, followed by joint symptoms.



■ Self-Check List

If many of the items below apply to you, please consult a rheumatology specialist.

- Pain or swelling in the hands or wrists

- Difficulty making a fist

- Joint stiffness in the morning lasting more than 1 hour

- Pain in both joints symmetrically

- A family member has rheumatoid arthritis



Symptoms appear gradually, so diagnosis can be difficult in the early stages. Diagnosis is made by combining blood tests, X-rays, and other findings.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The goals of treating rheumatoid arthritis are to control pain and inflammation, maintain joint function, and help prevent deformity. Rather than a 'cure,' the aim is to achieve and maintain 'remission' (a state without joint pain or swelling).



■ Treatment Steps

① Anti-inflammatory pain relievers (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and steroids are used to quickly reduce initial inflammation.

② Antirheumatic drugs (such as methotrexate) are used to regulate the immune response. It takes several weeks to several months for their effect to appear.

③ If the effect of antirheumatic drugs is insufficient, targeted therapies such as biologics or small molecule inhibitors (JAK inhibitors) are used.



■ Risks of Leaving the Disease Untreated

If the disease is not properly treated and inflammation keeps recurring, the bones can erode, joints can be destroyed, and deformity can develop that is difficult to reverse. Early treatment is very important.

sections.heading: Management During Seasonal Changes
sections.content:
During seasonal changes, when the weather gets colder and barometric pressure drops, changes in pressure inside the joints may worsen pain and lengthen morning stiffness.



■ Exercise

- Regular exercise helps maintain muscle, protect the joints, and reduce bone density loss.

- When joint swelling or pain is severe, focus on light stretching instead of strenuous exercise.

- If a joint becomes swollen or warm after exercise, rest and resume once the inflammation has subsided.



■ Vaccination

Because taking antirheumatic drugs increases the risk of infection, consider getting an annual flu vaccination between October and December. Please consult your doctor for safe vaccination.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Weather
records.intro: People with arthritis may experience worse pain with changes in the weather, particularly when barometric pressure drops or temperatures fall. If joint pain becomes severe or lasts for a long time, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, degenerative arthritis, arthralgia, weather, barometric pressure, low pressure, joint aching, knee pain, shoulder pain, wrist pain

sections.heading: Weather and Joint Pain
sections.content:
Some people with arthritis find that their pain changes with the weather.



One weather factor that can affect joint pain is a change in barometric pressure. Joint pain tends to worsen on days when barometric pressure drops (rainy or overcast days). This can occur in both rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory arthritis) and osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis).



Cold weather is another factor that can make pain feel more sensitive. The same degree of pain can feel more severe when temperatures are low.



However, pain varies greatly from person to person, and even the same person may feel it differently depending on the situation.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
When joint pain worsens because of weather changes, the following methods may help.



· Do appropriate stretching regularly.

· Get enough rest.

· Maintain regular, good-quality sleep.

· Keeping a positive mindset can also help with pain management.



If pain is severe or lasts a long time, please consult your doctor. Arthritis is a condition that requires ongoing management and treatment.

records.title: Rheumatoid Cervical Spine Disease
records.intro: Rheumatoid cervical spine disease is a condition of the neck (cervical spine) that can occur in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Unlike common neck conditions, its main feature is instability of the first and second cervical vertebrae, the uppermost bones of the neck. If symptoms worsen, the spinal cord can be compressed and may lead to paralysis, so please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: rheumatoid, cervical spine, myelopathy, cervical instability, upper cervical spine, cervical myelopathy, weakness in the arms or legs, difficulty moving one side of the body, anxious feeling, nervousness, worrying for no reason
keywords: weakness in the arms or legs
difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The cervical spine refers to the neck bones. It consists of vertebrae and the intervertebral discs (cartilage) between them, and it has a wider range of motion than the rest of the spine.

Rheumatoid cervical spine disease occurs when rheumatoid arthritis affects the neck bones. It is characterized in particular by instability of the first and second cervical vertebrae (the upper cervical spine), the uppermost bones of the neck. The upper cervical spine is the area where much of the rotation involved in turning the head takes place.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The main underlying process in rheumatoid arthritis is synovitis. Synovitis refers to inflammation of the membrane lining the inside of the joint.

This inflammation gradually destroys the joints and loosens the ligaments. As a result, the space between the first and second cervical vertebrae becomes unstable, and when the head is bent forward, the gap between the vertebrae can widen and compress the spinal cord located behind them.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves that runs from the brain to the rest of the body. When the spinal cord is compressed, a condition called cervical myelopathy develops.

When cervical myelopathy develops, the following symptoms may occur.

· Gait abnormality: Weakness when walking, or an unsteady gait.

· Reduced hand function: Fine hand movements such as buttoning clothes, using chopsticks, and writing become clumsy.

· Sensory changes: The hands and feet feel dull or numb.

If treatment is delayed, these symptoms may remain even after treatment. If symptoms appear, please consult a medical specialist promptly.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
When compression of the spinal cord is severe and neurological symptoms (such as paralysis or sensory changes) are present, surgical treatment may be considered.

Rheumatoid cervical spine disease is a condition in which even minor trauma can cause neurological impairment. Please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions about the direction of treatment. If symptoms appear, please take care not to delay treatment.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
If you have rheumatoid arthritis and notice any abnormality in the neck area (such as a dull feeling in the hands or feet, difficulty walking, or clumsy hand movements), please consult a medical specialist immediately.

Delaying treatment based on self-diagnosis or your own judgment may cause symptoms to worsen. This content is provided as health information and does not replace diagnosis or treatment for an individual's symptoms. Please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Chronic Hepatitis B
records.intro: Hepatitis B is an infection caused by the hepatitis B virus. If chronic hepatitis B is not treated, it can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer. People without antibodies should get vaccinated. If you have chronic hepatitis B, please have regular checkups and consult a medical specialist about treatment.
records.tags_raw: hepatitis B, chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis, liver cancer, antiviral drugs, vaccination, vertical transmission, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, loose stools, watery diarrhea, frequent bathroom visits

sections.heading: Definition and Routes of Transmission
sections.content:
Hepatitis B is an infection caused by the hepatitis B virus. Chronic hepatitis B refers to infection that persists for 6 months or longer.



The main routes of transmission are as follows.

· Vertical transmission from an infected mother to her newborn: Infection during the newborn period has a very high likelihood of progressing to chronic hepatitis.

· Contact with the blood or body fluids (such as saliva or semen) of an infected person

· Sexual intercourse

· Unsterilized syringes, tattoo or piercing equipment, and similar items



The prevalence of chronic hepatitis B in Korea has decreased substantially thanks to vaccination programs.

sections.heading: Symptoms and Course
sections.content:
Acute hepatitis B may cause diarrhea, fatigue, loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and muscle pain.



Chronic hepatitis B often causes no symptoms. However, if left untreated, it can progress to cirrhosis or liver cancer.



If you have chronic hepatitis B, you should have a regular checkup at least once every 6 months, even if you have no symptoms. If you are 40 or older, it is also important to have regular liver cancer screening.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The goals of treating chronic hepatitis B are normalizing liver enzyme levels, suppressing the virus, and helping to prevent cirrhosis and liver cancer.



Drug treatment broadly falls into two types.

· Injection (peginterferon): Strengthens immune function to suppress the virus.

· Oral antiviral drugs: Suppress viral replication.



The appropriate treatment depends on each patient's condition, so please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions. Once treatment has started, it is important to take the medication consistently without missing doses.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
People who do not have hepatitis B antibodies should be vaccinated (three doses, given at 0, 1, and 6 months).



Even if a family member has chronic hepatitis B, handshakes, hugs, and sharing meals are not a concern. However, it is best not to share items that may come into contact with blood, such as razors, toothbrushes, and nail clippers.

records.title: Chronic Osteomyelitis
records.intro: Chronic osteomyelitis is a condition in which bone is infected by bacteria and inflammation persists for a long time. It most often occurs after an open fracture (a fracture in which the bone is exposed to the outside). It is difficult to treat and often recurs, so care at a specialized medical institution is important.
records.tags_raw: chronic osteomyelitis, osteomyelitis, open fracture, shinbone, tibia, bone infection, flap surgery, multidisciplinary care, seeing double, overlapping images

sections.heading: Definition and Causes
sections.content:
Osteomyelitis is a condition in which bacteria infect the bone (bone marrow) and cause inflammation. Chronic osteomyelitis refers to a condition in which this infection persists for a long time or recurs repeatedly.

It can occur mainly when a severe accident causes an open fracture, in which the bone is exposed to the outside. In an open fracture, the periosteum that surrounds the bone is torn and the blood supply is cut off, causing tissue death (necrosis) and creating an environment in which bacteria can multiply easily.

It occurs particularly often in the shinbone (tibia). The shinbone has no muscle covering and is covered only by periosteum and skin, so wounds are difficult to close and the bone is vulnerable to bacterial infection.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of chronic osteomyelitis are as follows.

· Persistent pain and swelling at the fracture site or around the bone

· A small opening (fistula, or sinus tract) in the skin that drains pus

· Death (necrosis) of the skin and surrounding tissue

· Repeated recurrence

Osteomyelitis in its early stage is relatively easy to treat, but advanced chronic osteomyelitis is very difficult to treat because the inflammation has spread widely into the surrounding tissue.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment of chronic osteomyelitis varies depending on the stage and the patient's condition.

· Early stage: Dead tissue is removed and appropriate antibiotics are used.

· Advanced cases: The bone and the soft tissue (skin and muscle) must be treated together. For treatment to be successful, orthopedic treatment of the bone generally needs to be combined with plastic surgery flap surgery (an operation that covers the defect with transplanted healthy skin and muscle).

· Flap surgery: Needed when there is a skin defect, in order to help the bone and surrounding tissue heal.

Chronic osteomyelitis is difficult to cure with fracture treatment alone. Treatment through multidisciplinary collaboration among several departments, such as orthopedics, plastic surgery, and radiology, is important.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
· If only the fracture is treated and treatment of the skin and soft tissue is neglected, infection and tissue death may progress.

· If recurrences keep happening, amputation may eventually be needed in some cases, so if you have symptoms, it is important to be seen early at a specialized medical institution.

· If a wound does not heal well after an open fracture, or pain and swelling around the bone persist, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Chronic Renal Failure
records.intro: The kidneys are important organs that filter waste products from the body and remove them in the urine. When a chronic disease has damaged the kidneys completely, a new kidney may need to be transplanted to sustain life. Lifelong careful management is needed even after transplantation, so please do not rely on this Health Encyclopedia alone; receive proper management through consultation with a transplant specialist.
records.tags_raw: kidney transplantation, chronic renal failure, kidney, end-stage renal disease, hemodialysis, immunosuppressants

sections.heading: Lifestyle After Transplantation
sections.content:
For a transplant to succeed, taking medication and managing daily life after surgery are essential.

· Taking immunosuppressants: To keep the body's cells from mistaking the transplanted kidney from another person for a foreign invader (like a virus) and attacking it, you must take a medication called an 'immunosuppressant,' which slightly lowers the body's defenses (immunity), every day for life.
· Preventing infection: Because the body's defenses are lowered, you become very vulnerable to infections such as colds and pneumonia. Make careful personal hygiene a habit, such as washing your hands after going out and eating cooked food.

Kidney transplant outcomes in Korea are comparable to leading international standards, with a 5-year survival rate of 95% or higher in recent years. With good care after surgery, many patients can maintain a relatively healthy life without dialysis.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
When a person has a long-standing illness such as diabetes or high blood pressure, kidney function can gradually decline, resulting in 'chronic renal failure.'

When kidney function declines severely, the condition may be classified as kidney failure. However, a low kidney function level alone does not mean that dialysis must begin immediately. The decision to start dialysis depends on symptoms, laboratory results, fluid balance, and the patient's overall condition. Treatment options include hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and kidney transplantation.

Kidney transplantation may offer better long-term outcomes for suitable patients, but not everyone is eligible. A kidney specialist will help determine the most appropriate treatment based on each patient's medical condition and preferences.

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
Kidney transplantation is broadly divided into two types, depending on who provides the kidney.

· Living donor transplantation: An operation in which one kidney is donated by a healthy living person, such as a family member or relative. Because people are born with two kidneys, the remaining kidney can perform the necessary functions even after one is removed, so in most cases the donor can also carry on daily life in good health.
· Deceased donor (brain-dead donor) transplantation: When there is no donor among family or acquaintances, the patient is registered on the national waiting list and later receives the organ of a person who has been declared brain-dead.

In the past, transplantation was not possible if the blood types of the donor and recipient differed because of rejection. In recent years, however, special treatment techniques that filter antibodies out of the blood and use medication before surgery have been developed, and in many cases transplantation across blood types (ABO-incompatible transplantation) can now be performed.

sections.heading: Precautions After Transplantation
sections.content:
Some patients, after a hard-won successful transplant and return to daily life, let their guard down and start drinking alcohol or smoking again. This is a major risk behavior that can reduce the function of the transplanted kidney.

· Smoking cessation is essential: Harmful substances in tobacco can narrow the blood vessels of the transplanted kidney and significantly shorten its lifespan. Multiple studies have reported that smoking increases the risk of decline in the function of the transplanted kidney.
· Alcohol abstinence is essential: Alcohol can dehydrate the body by drawing out water, or raise cholesterol levels and strain the heart. From before surgery and for life after surgery, quitting smoking and abstaining from alcohol are not optional but essential.

records.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
records.intro: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition in which abnormalities in kidney function or structure persist for 3 months or longer. In the early stages there are often no particular symptoms, so the disease may go unnoticed and be discovered only after it has progressed considerably. People who have diabetes or high blood pressure, or who have a family history of kidney disease, need regular testing. If a health checkup reveals a kidney abnormality, please consult a medical specialist to confirm it.
records.tags_raw: chronic kidney disease, chronic renal failure, kidney, renal, proteinuria, glomerular filtration rate, diabetic nephropathy, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Chronic kidney disease is diagnosed when proteinuria (protein in the urine) on a urine test persists for 3 months or longer, or when reduced kidney function on blood tests continues for 3 months or longer. It can also be diagnosed when imaging tests or a biopsy find a structural abnormality in the kidneys.

Kidney disease often progresses. Early detection and management can help slow its progression to end-stage renal disease, which requires dialysis or a kidney transplant.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The two most common causes are diabetes and high blood pressure.

· Diabetes: Accounts for about 50% of the causes of end-stage renal disease.

· High blood pressure: Accounts for about 20% of the causes of end-stage renal disease.

· Glomerulonephritis: A disease in which the filtering units inside the kidney (glomeruli) become inflamed. It is the third most common cause.

· Others: Polycystic kidney disease (a genetic disorder in which many fluid-filled cysts form in the kidneys), autoimmune diseases, and drug misuse or overuse.



It occurs especially often in older adults. Chronic kidney disease is reported to be present in about 40% of people in their 70s and about 60% or more of people in their 80s.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Chronic kidney disease often causes no obvious symptoms until it has progressed considerably. Symptoms may also appear gradually, so some people do not notice the changes in their body.



If you have any of the following symptoms, please have your kidneys tested.

· Unexplained fatigue, lack of energy, and reduced concentration

· Unexplained loss of appetite

· Sleep disturbance and frequent leg cramps

· Swelling of the eyelids in the morning, or swelling of the feet and ankles

· Frequent urination at night

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content:
As kidney function declines, a variety of complications can occur.

· Edema (swelling): The body cannot remove enough sodium (salt) and water, causing swelling.

· Anemia: A shortage of erythropoietin (a hormone that stimulates the production of red blood cells) leads to anemia.

· Bone disorders: Metabolic acidosis (a condition in which body fluids become acidic) and abnormal phosphorus regulation can weaken the bones.

· Hyperkalemia (high blood potassium): When potassium builds up in the body, arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat) can occur, so caution is needed.

sections.heading: Treatment and Management
sections.content:
The most important step is to keep the underlying diseases, diabetes and high blood pressure, under careful control.

· Some classes of blood pressure medication are beneficial for the kidneys, so choose medication in consultation with your doctor.

· Reducing salty foods such as soups, stews, salted fermented seafood (jeotgal), and salt-cured foods can help prevent swelling.

· If a blood test shows a high potassium level, fruits, vegetables, and raw greens may be restricted according to your care team's instructions.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
It is important to avoid things that can put a burden on the kidneys.

· Anti-inflammatory pain relievers (NSAIDs) can worsen kidney function, so caution is needed.

· The contrast agent used in CT scans can affect the kidneys, so please inform your care team before the test.

· Dietary supplements, traditional herbal medicines (hanyak), and similar products can also cause unexpected problems, so consult your doctor before taking them.

· If a health checkup has shown a kidney abnormality, please consult a medical specialist to confirm it.

· Simple urine tests, blood tests, and blood pressure measurements can reveal abnormalities, so please have regular checkups.

records.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
records.intro: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic lung disease in which the airways (the passages through which air travels) gradually narrow, making breathing difficult. The leading cause is smoking. Airways that have narrowed are mostly not restored, so early detection and smoking cessation are especially important. If cough, sputum, or shortness of breath persists, please consult a pulmonology and allergy specialist.
records.tags_raw: COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, airway obstruction, smoking, pulmonary function test, bronchodilator, smoking cessation, emphysema, dry cough, persistent minor cough, cough that will not stop

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a condition in which the airways gradually narrow because of chronic bronchitis (a state in which chronic inflammation of the bronchi causes persistent sputum and cough) or emphysema (a state in which the air sacs of the lungs become enlarged and destroyed).



Airway obstruction progresses slowly over many years and, in most cases, is not reversible. It rarely occurs before the age of 40, and its incidence is highest between the ages of 55 and 85. COPD is a systemic disease that affects not only the lungs but also the cardiovascular system, muscles, bones, and the rest of the body.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The most important cause of COPD is smoking. Of people with COPD, 80 to 90% are smokers. The more a person smokes, the higher the risk of developing COPD. Quitting smoking can significantly slow the rate of decline in lung function.



Other risk factors are as follows.

· Occupational exposure: Long-term exposure to dust, chemicals, harmful gases, and similar substances

· Air pollution: Fine dust (particulate matter), indoor combustion gases, and similar sources

· Genetic factors: Deficiency of a specific protein (alpha-1 antitrypsin)

· Airway hyperresponsiveness



Only about 15% of smokers develop COPD, and genetic predisposition also plays a role.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Chronic cough and sputum

· Shortness of breath (dyspnea): At first it occurs only during exercise, but as the disease progresses it also occurs during everyday activities.

· Wheezing

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content: COPD can be confirmed only through a pulmonary function test. It is diagnosed when a pulmonary function test (spirometry) shows that the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled is lower than normal and does not recover well even after a bronchodilator is used. It is important to distinguish COPD from conditions with similar symptoms, such as asthma, heart failure, and bronchiectasis.

sections.heading: Treatment and Management
sections.content:
■ The Most Important Treatment: Smoking Cessation

COPD patients who smoke must quit smoking. Quitting smoking alone can significantly slow the rate of decline in lung function.



■ Drug Treatment

· Bronchodilators (inhalers): Widen the narrowed airways to make breathing easier.

· Inhaled steroids: Reduce airway inflammation.

· Antibiotics: Used during acute exacerbations accompanied by bacterial infection.



■ Oxygen Therapy

When the oxygen level in the blood is significantly low, long-term oxygen therapy, in which supplemental oxygen is given for at least 15 hours a day, is used.



■ Rehabilitation

A pulmonary rehabilitation program can help improve exercise capacity and quality of life.



■ Vaccination

Influenza (flu) and pneumococcal vaccinations are recommended. They can help prevent acute exacerbations.



■ Management of Complications

If osteoporosis is found, bisphosphonates, calcium supplements, and vitamin D are taken together. Dietary management and rehabilitation exercise are needed to maintain nutritional status and body weight.



Treatment varies depending on the severity of the disease, so please consult a pulmonology and allergy specialist.

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content:
As COPD progresses, a variety of complications can occur outside the lungs as well.



· Cor pulmonale and pulmonary hypertension: A condition in which the blood vessels of the lungs narrow because of COPD, increasing the strain on the heart (especially the right side of the heart). It can lead to heart failure.

· Lung cancer: Because smoking is a shared cause, people with COPD have a higher risk of developing lung cancer.

· Osteoporosis: The bones weaken because of steroid use, reduced physical activity, poor nutrition, and other factors.

· Muscle weakness: The strength of the arm and leg muscles decreases.

· Weight loss: Energy expenditure for breathing increases and appetite decreases, leading to weight loss.

· Depression



For people with COPD, it is important to detect these complications early through regular checkups.

records.title: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
records.intro: Chronic fatigue syndrome is a condition in which severe fatigue persists for 3 months or longer even with adequate rest. Because there are many hypotheses about its cause, treatment is tailored to each individual. Antidepressants, cognitive behavioral therapy, and graded exercise therapy have been reported to be helpful. Please consult a medical specialist before deciding on the direction of treatment.
records.tags_raw: chronic fatigue syndrome, antidepressants, cognitive behavioral therapy, exercise therapy, chronic fatigue, fatigue, sleep disorder, depression, rehabilitation, headache, splitting headache, migraine, pain at the back of the head, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness
keywords: pain at the back of the head

sections.heading: What Is Chronic Fatigue Syndrome?
sections.content:
Chronic fatigue syndrome is a condition in which severe fatigue that does not recover with adequate rest persists for 3 months or longer, accompanied by a variety of symptoms such as reduced cognitive function, sleep disturbance, headache, and muscle pain.



■ Differences from Spring Fatigue and Ordinary Fatigue

- Spring fatigue (seasonal fatigue): Lasts within a few weeks, recurs with the season, improves with rest

- Chronic fatigue syndrome: Lasts 3 months or longer, unrelated to the season, does not recover with rest, impairs daily functioning



Patients often suffer a double burden: being rejected by people around them who do not understand the symptoms, and not receiving appropriate help. It is important for medical staff to listen carefully to patients' complaints and make an effort to understand them.

sections.heading: Treatments Reported to Be Effective
sections.content:
■ 1. Antidepressants

Depression accompanies chronic fatigue syndrome in a considerable number of patients. In addition to depression, antidepressants can help improve pain and sleep disturbance.



■ 2. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

This treatment addresses the patient's thoughts and beliefs about the illness in order to encourage changes in behavior. It is carried out by adjusting patterns of rest, sleep, and activity while gradually increasing the amount of activity and reducing rest time.



■ 3. Graded Aerobic Exercise Therapy

This method involves gradually increasing aerobic exercise such as walking, cycling, and swimming. It has been reported to be more effective than stretching and relaxation therapy alone.



Example Exercise Prescription

- 5 days per week, for at least 12 weeks

- Start with 5 to 15 minutes per session, increasing by 1 to 2 minutes each week up to a maximum of 30 minutes

- Intensity: Limited to moderate (not too strenuous)

- If fatigue worsens, reduce the intensity, and increase it again once symptoms have stabilized.

sections.heading: Importance of Cool-Down Exercise
sections.content:
Cool-down exercise is especially important for people with chronic fatigue syndrome. It is thought to help fatigue-causing substances be broken down and cleared more quickly after exercise.

· Simple finishing stretches

· Walking in place to gradually bring breathing back to normal

· Applying ice to heavily used muscle areas

· Light massage

sections.heading: Precautions and Management
sections.content:
■ Adjusting Exercise Intensity

Exercising excessively beyond the prescribed limits can make fatigue worse. Even when symptoms have improved, it is important to avoid a vicious cycle in which excessive physical activity causes symptoms to worsen again. It is important to maintain a regular, appropriate activity plan.



■ Other Treatments

Various other methods, such as biofeedback and immunoglobulin therapy, have been introduced, but there is considerable disagreement among experts and the evidence is insufficient. Please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions about treatment.



■ Trusting Relationship with Your Doctor

The most important element in treating chronic fatigue syndrome is an ongoing relationship between patient and doctor built on trust. The understanding and cooperation of family and those around the patient can also be a great help to recovery.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Behavioral Therapy and Prevention
sections.content:
Along with exercise therapy, efforts to promote psychological stability are needed.

· Find and practice your own way of relieving stress.

· Try to maintain a positive way of thinking and an optimistic attitude toward life.

It is important to try to prevent chronic fatigue syndrome before it develops. Please maintain steady exercise and healthy lifestyle habits. If symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Malaria
records.intro: Malaria is a parasitic infectious disease caused by the bite of a mosquito carrying the malaria parasite. It causes cold-like symptoms such as fever and chills, and delayed treatment can lead to serious complications. Before traveling to an area where malaria is a risk, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: malaria, mosquito, parasite, fever, chills, overseas travel, preventive medication, headache, splitting headache, migraine, pain at the back of the head, feeling feverish, body heat, high fever, low-grade fever, body shaking, feeling cold and shivering, cold sensation, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, hand tremor, body tremor
keywords: pain at the back of the head

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Malaria is a disease contracted through the bite of a mosquito carrying the malaria parasite (Plasmodium). When the mosquito bites a person, the parasite enters the bloodstream and causes the disease. The mosquitoes that transmit malaria are active mainly at night.



It is widespread in tropical regions such as Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America. Vivax malaria (Plasmodium vivax) also occurs in Korea, but falciparum malaria (Plasmodium falciparum), which is contracted abroad in places such as Africa, can cause more severe symptoms.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of malaria are as follows.

· Fever (high fever)

· Chills (shivering)

· Fatigue

· Headache and muscle pain



The symptoms resemble those of a cold and can be confused with it. Without treatment, anemia, reduced kidney function, and other problems can develop, and falciparum malaria can be fatal because of serious complications such as brain involvement (cerebral malaria).



If symptoms such as fever appear within 1 year after visiting a malaria-risk area, seek immediate medical attention to check for malaria.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
There are two main ways to prevent malaria.



· Preventive medication: The type of preventive medication needed differs depending on the travel destination, and in some cases it must be started before departure. Some medications cannot be used by pregnant women, children, or people with certain medical conditions. Please consult a medical specialist before your trip and obtain a prescription.

· Avoiding mosquito bites: Even when taking preventive medication, take care to avoid mosquito bites. Reduce outdoor activity after sunset, wear long sleeves and long pants, and use mosquito repellent.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content:
Malaria is diagnosed with a blood test. If you have suspected symptoms, seek immediate medical attention and get tested.



Antimalarial drugs are available, and the type depends on the species of malaria parasite and the region where the infection was acquired. Early detection and appropriate treatment can improve the chances of recovery. Treatment must be carried out under the prescription and guidance of a medical specialist.

records.title: Peripheral Vascular Disease (Leg Vascular Disorders)
records.intro: Peripheral vascular disease is a condition in which the blood vessels in the legs, far from the heart, become narrowed or blocked by blood clots (thrombi), and it can be a medical emergency. In serious cases, tissue in the leg can die and amputation may be necessary, so if your leg is severely swollen and painful, please consult a cardiology or vascular specialist immediately.
records.tags_raw: peripheral arterial disease, deep vein thrombosis, varicose veins, atherosclerosis, edema, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Three Main Leg Vascular Disorders
sections.content: Diseases of the blood vessels in the legs fall broadly into three types: 'lower extremity arterial disease (peripheral arterial disease),' in which a blocked artery causes severe, bursting pain in the leg; 'deep vein thrombosis,' in which a blood clot forms in a deep vein and causes swelling; and 'varicose veins,' in which the veins become twisted and bulge.

sections.heading: Main Symptoms
sections.content: The most common symptom is pain and numbness in the calf after walking only a short distance, which improves with rest. If only one leg becomes markedly swollen, or the skin of the leg turns bluish or pale white, this may indicate a serious blockage of a blood vessel.

sections.heading: Diagnostic Methods
sections.content: At the hospital, the blood pressure at the ankle is compared with the blood pressure in the arm (ankle-brachial index), because ankle blood pressure drops sharply when blood flow is poor. The doctor also checks whether pulses can be felt well in the groin, behind the knee, and on the top of the foot, and examines the inside of the blood vessels in detail with ultrasound or CT imaging.

sections.heading: Treatment Methods
sections.content: In mild cases, drug treatment is used to keep the blood vessels from hardening further. If a vessel is so severely blocked that medication is not enough, a procedure may be performed in which a balloon or mesh tube (stent) attached to the tip of a thin wire is inserted to widen the vessel, or surgery may be needed to connect a new artificial blood vessel (bypass graft).

sections.heading: Prevention and Management
sections.content: Smoking is a major cause of blood vessel damage. Smoking can more than double the risk of leg amputation, so smokers should quit. Taking medication for high blood pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol as prescribed and managing these conditions on a regular basis is an important way to protect the blood vessels.

records.title: Retinal Artery Occlusion
records.intro: Retinal artery occlusion is a condition in which the artery that supplies blood to the retina is suddenly blocked. Like a stroke, in which a blood vessel in the brain is blocked, it damages the nerve cells involved in vision, and it is sometimes called an 'eye stroke.' If sudden vision loss occurs, seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room or ophthalmology department.
records.tags_raw: retinal artery occlusion, retina, decreased vision, eye stroke, central retinal artery occlusion, high blood pressure, diabetes, blurry vision, difficulty seeing, hazy vision

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Retinal artery occlusion most often appears as a sudden loss of vision in one eye without pain. If this symptom occurs, seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room or ophthalmology department. As time passes, retinal cells are irreversibly damaged and it becomes difficult to recover vision.

sections.heading: Causes and Risk Factors
sections.content:
Retinal artery occlusion occurs when an artery is blocked by a thrombus (a blood clot within a blood vessel) or an embolus (a foreign particle that blocks a blood vessel). The risk is higher in people with the following underlying conditions.

· High blood pressure

· Diabetes

· Atherosclerosis

· High cholesterol (hyperlipidemia)

· Heart disease (especially atrial fibrillation)



It occurs more commonly in people in their 50s and older.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
If sudden vision loss occurs, seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room or ophthalmology department. Because photoreceptor cells cannot be restored once damaged, prompt treatment is important.



Retinal artery occlusion is a medical emergency that requires immediate evaluation. At an emergency department, specialists will assess whether any time-sensitive treatment, such as thrombolysis, may be appropriate. Traditional treatments such as eye massage and procedures to lower eye pressure have not been proven effective and may be harmful. These procedures should not be attempted on your own.


When retinal artery occlusion occurs, it may also be necessary to see a neurologist to help prevent a future cerebral infarction (stroke).

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The retina is a thin membrane lining the inside of the eye, comparable to the film in a camera. It receives light and transmits visual signals to the brain. Retinal artery occlusion is a condition in which the artery that supplies blood and oxygen to the retina is blocked, damaging retinal cells.



It is divided into two types depending on the extent of the blocked vessel.

· Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO): Blood is not supplied to the entire retina, so the whole visual field suddenly goes dark.

· Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO): Only some of the vessels are blocked, so either the upper or lower part of the visual field is suddenly lost.



In winter, cold weather causes blood vessels to constrict and blood pressure to rise, which increases the risk of occurrence.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To help prevent retinal artery occlusion, it is important to manage the underlying conditions that are risk factors.

· Check blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol regularly and treat them.

· If you have heart disease, have regular checkups.

· Stop smoking.

· In winter, take care to stay warm and avoid sudden exposure to cold.



People with underlying conditions should have regular eye examinations at an ophthalmology department.

records.title: Syphilis
records.intro: Syphilis is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, which is spread mainly through sexual contact. It can be treated when detected early, but if left untreated, serious complications can develop. If you have suspected symptoms or risk factors, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: syphilis, sexually transmitted infection, Treponema, ulcer, rash, penicillin, sexually transmitted disease, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Syphilis is a chronic, systemic infectious disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
It is spread mainly through sexual contact.



In addition to sexual contact, it can be spread in the following ways.

· Transmission from a pregnant woman to her fetus (congenital syphilis)

· Close contact with active lesions (such as ulcers)



Infectiousness is highest in the early stage (when ulcers are present) and decreases over time.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The symptoms of syphilis differ depending on the stage of the disease.
