· Primary syphilis: About 3 weeks after sexual contact, on average, a painless, firm ulcer forms at the site where the bacteria entered (such as around the genitals). The ulcer goes away on its own after several weeks even without treatment, but this does not mean the infection has resolved.

· Secondary syphilis: The stage in which the bacteria spread throughout the body. Symptoms may include a non-itchy skin rash, low-grade fever, fatigue, muscle pain, and swollen lymph nodes.

· Latent syphilis: A stage with no symptoms. Blood tests are positive.

· Late (tertiary) syphilis: If left untreated, serious complications may develop in some people in important organs such as the heart and the nervous system.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Syphilis is diagnosed with a blood test. Additional tests are performed when there is a skin rash or a genital lesion, or when an abnormal finding is detected during a health checkup.



Even without symptoms, testing is advisable if you have a history of sexual contact or other risk factors. Syphilis blood (serologic) testing is recommended for all pregnant women.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Syphilis is treated with injectable penicillin. Penicillin is an antibiotic that is effective against syphilis. The duration of treatment may vary depending on the stage of the disease and the patient's condition.



Early detection and treatment can improve the chances of recovery. If treatment is delayed, complications may develop, so if you have suspected symptoms, please consult a medical specialist promptly.



If syphilis is diagnosed, it is important for sexual partners to be tested and treated as well. It is also necessary to check whether other sexually transmitted infections, such as HIV/AIDS, are present at the same time.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Ways to help prevent syphilis include the following.

· Use a condom during sexual intercourse.

· Get regular testing for sexually transmitted diseases.

· Take care to avoid contact with the blood or body fluids of a person with syphilis.



If you have suspected symptoms or risk factors, please consult an infectious disease specialist or another relevant medical specialist immediately.

records.title: Meniere's Disease
records.intro: Meniere's disease is a condition in which excess endolymph builds up in the inner ear, raising the pressure and causing repeated episodes of dizziness, hearing loss, tinnitus, and a feeling of fullness in the ear. The inner ear is the innermost part of the ear and consists of the cochlea, which is responsible for hearing, and the vestibular organ, which is responsible for balance. If left untreated, hearing and vestibular function may worsen permanently. Please consult an otolaryngology (ENT) specialist.
records.tags_raw: Meniere's disease, dizziness, hearing loss, tinnitus, inner ear, vestibular organ, endolymph, aural fullness, lightheadedness, spinning sensation, unsteadiness, vision going dark, nausea, feeling about to vomit, vomiting, blurry vision, difficulty seeing, hazy vision, ringing in the ears, noise in the ear, cannot hear, difficulty hearing sounds

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Meniere's disease is a condition of the inner ear, the innermost part of the ear. The inner ear has two parts: the cochlea (responsible for hearing) and the vestibular organ (responsible for balance). Inside the inner ear is a fluid called endolymph, and an abnormal increase in this fluid, which raises the pressure, is known to be the main underlying cause of Meniere's disease. This affects both hearing and the vestibular organ, causing a variety of symptoms.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: The exact cause has not yet been fully identified. Stress, overwork, excessive salt intake, alcohol, and caffeine are known to be associated with triggering and worsening symptoms.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The four main symptoms of Meniere's disease are as follows.



· Dizziness: Unlike benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), dizziness persists regardless of body position. Repeated episodes of spinning dizziness (vertigo) lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours occur.

· Hearing loss: A decline in hearing. It is characterized by hearing loss that affects low-pitched sounds (low frequencies) first.

· Tinnitus: Hearing sounds in the ear.

· Aural fullness: A muffled feeling, as if the ear is full.



Rather than worsening with changes in position as it does in BPPV, the dizziness tends to last for a set period of time. An important difference from BPPV is that hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness occur together with the dizziness.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Meniere's disease is diagnosed mainly on the basis of clinical symptoms. Testing for nystagmus (involuntary, rhythmic movement of the eyes) is used as a supporting test.



The diagnostic criteria are as follows.

· Two or more episodes of dizziness (each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours)

· Changes in ear symptoms that occur together with the dizziness episodes (tinnitus, aural fullness, hearing loss, etc.)

· The symptoms are not explained by another vestibular disorder

→ Diagnosed as 'probable Meniere's disease.'



If a hearing test confirms hearing loss in the low to mid frequencies, it is diagnosed as 'definite Meniere's disease.'



Dizziness can occur not only in BPPV but also in other serious conditions, such as stroke. Please consult a medical specialist for an accurate diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Drug treatment is the main approach for Meniere's disease.



· Diuretics: Help reduce the amount of endolymph.

· Betahistine (a histamine analog): Used to improve blood flow in the inner ear.

· Anti-dizziness medication: Used during an acute attack to reduce dizziness, nausea, and vomiting.

· Steroids: When hearing loss is present, high-dose steroid treatment or intratympanic steroid injection (a method of injecting medication directly into the ear) may be needed.



Depending on the severity of symptoms and how often they recur, additional medication injection procedures or surgical treatment may be considered. Please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions about treatment.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Meniere's disease is a condition that often recurs. In addition to receiving treatment consistently, lifestyle management is very important.



· Follow a low-salt diet. Reducing salt intake can help lower endolymph pressure.

· Avoid or reduce alcohol, smoking, and coffee (caffeine).

· Avoid overexertion and stress, and maintain regular lifestyle habits.

· If left untreated, hearing and vestibular function may be permanently damaged. Please consult a medical specialist whenever symptoms appear.

· It is advisable to obtain a prescription for emergency medication and carry it with you in case of a recurrence.

records.title: Moyamoya Disease
records.intro: Moyamoya disease is a rare cerebrovascular disease in which the major blood vessels leading to the brain gradually become blocked and abnormal blood vessels form. It often presents as cerebral infarction in children and as cerebral hemorrhage in adults. Whether symptoms are present or the condition is found incidentally, please consult a neurosurgery specialist.
records.tags_raw: Moyamoya disease, cerebrovascular, cerebral infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, transient ischemic attack, revascularization surgery, pediatric stroke, headache, splitting headache, migraine, pain at the back of the head, weakness in the arms or legs, difficulty moving one side of the body

weakness in the arms or legs

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Moyamoya disease is a cerebrovascular disease in which the major artery that supplies blood to the brain (the terminal portion of the internal carotid artery) gradually narrows and becomes blocked for unknown reasons. As the vessel becomes blocked, thin abnormal blood vessels form a net-like network deep in the brain to compensate.



On cerebral angiography images, these abnormal vessels look like puffs of cigarette smoke drifting upward, which is why the disease was given the Japanese name 'moyamoya' (meaning hazy, drifting like smoke).



It occurs relatively often in East Asia, including Korea, Japan, and China.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms differ between children and adults.



· Children: Symptoms mainly appear as ischemic symptoms caused by reduced blood flow to the brain. Transient ischemic attacks recur, in which sudden difficulty speaking or paralysis of the arms and legs occurs and then resolves. Symptoms often appear during hyperventilation, such as when crying, exercising, or eating hot food.

· Adults: The disease often first appears as a cerebral hemorrhage or cerebral infarction. Symptoms occur suddenly and persist.



If any of the following symptoms appear suddenly, you should go to the emergency room immediately.

· Sudden difficulty speaking or weakness in the arms and legs

· Severe headache and vomiting

· Decreased level of consciousness

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Diagnosis is made with the following tests.



· MRI and MRA (magnetic resonance angiography): Check the condition of the blood vessels in the brain noninvasively. Recent high-performance MRI allows diagnosis with a high degree of accuracy.

· Cerebral angiography: The most accurate diagnostic method. It is also important for treatment planning.



With the increase in health checkups in recent years, more cases are being found incidentally without symptoms. Because the condition should not be dismissed even when there are no symptoms, it is important to see a neurosurgery specialist and set up a follow-up plan.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment is determined by the type of disease, ischemic (insufficient blood flow) or hemorrhagic (ruptured blood vessel), and the patient's condition.



· Revascularization surgery: Surgery that creates a new blood supply pathway to increase blood flow to the brain. It can help reduce recurrence of cerebral infarction or cerebral hemorrhage.

· Drug treatment and observation: Determined by your doctor based on your condition.



Whether or not symptoms are present, it is important to see a neurosurgery specialist in cerebrovascular disease for regular follow-up testing and to decide on the appropriate timing of treatment.

records.title: Herniated Cervical Disc (Cervical Disc Herniation)
records.intro: A herniated cervical disc (cervical disc herniation) is a condition in which a disc between the vertebrae of the neck presses on a nerve. The main symptoms are arm numbness or arm weakness. Most cases can be treated without surgery, but if there is paralysis or loss of bladder or bowel control, please consult a medical specialist immediately.
records.tags_raw: herniated cervical disc, cervical disc herniation, arm numbness, neck pain, forward head posture, straight neck, cervical spine, sore neck, pain in the back of the neck, stiff neck, numbness in hands and feet, tingling arm, tingling leg, weakness in the arms or legs, difficulty moving one side of the body
keywords: pain in the back of the neck
weakness in the arms or legs
difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Definition and Causes
sections.content:
The cervical spine (the vertebrae of the neck) is a structure of seven bones connected by discs and ligaments. The discs absorb shock and allow smooth movement of the neck.



As people age, the disc loses water content and becomes less elastic. When enough pressure is applied, the disc can be pushed backward and press on a nearby nerve. This is called cervical disc herniation.



When viewed from the side, a normal neck has a C-shaped curve. Looking at a smartphone for long periods or maintaining poor posture can flatten this C-shaped curve, resulting in a straight neck or a reversed C-shaped neck. In this case, strain is concentrated on the discs, which can speed up degenerative changes.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms are as follows.



· Arm numbness or pain: Numbness or pain appears in a specific part of the arm, depending on which nerve is compressed.

· Arm weakness

· In severe cases, paralysis of the hands and feet

· In very severe cases, loss of bladder or bowel control



Arm numbness or weakness is a more important warning sign than neck pain alone. If arm numbness or pain worsens when the neck is tilted backward, a herniated cervical disc may be suspected.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
If a spinal condition is suspected, the following tests are performed.



· MRI: An essential test that most accurately shows soft tissue such as the discs and nerves.

· X-ray: Checks the basic bone structure.

· CT: Used mainly for surgical planning and for evaluation after surgery.



The patient's symptoms are the most important basis for diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Most cases can be treated without surgery.



· Medication: Anti-inflammatory pain relievers reduce inflammation and pain. It is important to take them consistently for at least 2 to 4 weeks.

· Injection therapy (nerve block): Medication is injected around the nerve causing the symptoms. If you have diabetes, dose adjustment is needed, so please be sure to consult your doctor.

· Surgery: Considered when there is arm weakness or paralysis, or when there is no improvement despite adequate conservative treatment.



If a nerve remains compressed for a long time, recovery may be difficult even after surgery, so it is important to discuss the appropriate timing of treatment with a specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Complete prevention is difficult, but the following habits can help.



· Maintain good posture: Do not push your head forward when looking at a smartphone or monitor.

· Get up every 50 minutes and stretch your neck and shoulders.

· Stretch forward, backward, to the left and right, and in rotation, just until you feel a slight pull in the muscles.

· Stretch right after waking up in the morning.

records.title: Athlete's Foot (Tinea)
records.intro:
Athlete's foot is a common fungal skin infection. It is a skin condition caused by a fungus called a dermatophyte infecting the foot. It occurs easily in hot, humid environments such as summer and is contagious.

It can occur not only on the feet but also in many other areas, including the nails, groin, and scalp.
records.tags_raw: athlete's foot, tinea pedis, fungal infection, fungus, antifungal agents, onychomycosis, ringworm

sections.heading: Definition and Symptoms
sections.content:
Athlete's foot is a condition in which a fungus infects the outer layer of the skin (the stratum corneum).
 · Foot (tinea pedis): Scaling and peeling of the skin develop between the toes, blisters form, or the skin thickens like a callus. At first there may be no noticeable symptoms, and the condition is often discovered only when itching or pain develops.
 · Body (tinea corporis): Red, round patches form with raised edges, and the skin peels. It is also called 'ringworm.'
 · Nails (tinea unguium): The nails thicken, lose their shine, and become discolored.
 · Scalp (tinea capitis): Hair loss may accompany the infection.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
It is a skin condition caused by a fungus called a dermatophyte infecting the foot.

· The fungus that causes athlete's foot multiplies easily in hot, humid environments.
 · The infection can spread when skin flakes shed from a patient's skin come into contact with another person's skin.
 · There is a risk of spread if a family member with athlete's foot goes without socks or shares towels or slippers.
 · If the skin is kept dry and clean, infection is less likely to occur even when the fungus comes into contact with it.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
· Wash areas that sweat easily, such as the feet and groin, frequently and keep them dry.
 · Wear breathable clothing.
 · Change out of wet socks or underwear quickly.
 · If the infection recurs often, using an antifungal soap preventively in the summer may also help.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Athlete's foot is treated with antifungal agents (medications that kill fungus).
 · Topical treatments: Available as ointments, creams, gels, and nail lacquers (for the nails), and used when the infection is not severe.
 · Oral medication (oral antifungal agents): Used for severe or widespread infections and for long-standing infections. A liver function test is needed before starting, and regular blood tests are needed during treatment.
Please consult a medical specialist to choose the appropriate treatment.

records.title: Fine Dust (Particulate Matter) and Health
records.intro: Fine dust consists of tiny particles floating in the air. It directly affects the respiratory tract, including the nose, bronchi, and lungs, and can also harm the whole body, including the heart, brain, and blood vessels, through the bloodstream. Long-term exposure increases the risk of asthma, reduced lung function, and cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease. On days when fine dust levels are high, limit outdoor activities, and people at high risk are advised to wear a health protection mask.
records.tags_raw: particulate matter, fine particulate matter (PM2.5), Asian dust (yellow dust), respiratory system, mask, KF80, KF94, asthma, air pollution, dry cough, minor cough, persistent cough

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Fine dust (particulate matter) is an air pollutant made up of very small particles. It is divided by size as follows.



· Particulate matter (PM10): particles 10 μm (micrometers) or less in diameter

· Fine particulate matter (PM2.5): particles 2.5 μm or less in diameter



Because PM2.5 is extremely small, it can penetrate deep into the lungs and be absorbed into the bloodstream, where it may have a greater effect on the whole body.



Fine dust occurs all year round. Levels tend to be higher in winter and spring, and the amount carried in from China by the prevailing westerly winds also increases during this period.



Asian dust (yellow dust) is a phenomenon in which sand and dust from deserts in China and Mongolia are carried by the wind in spring. It is distinct from fine dust.

sections.heading: Health Effects
sections.content:
Fine dust affects the body in the following ways.



■ Effects on the Respiratory System

· It can cause inflammation in the nose, throat, bronchi, and lungs.

· Cough, phlegm, and shortness of breath may occur.

· In people with asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), symptoms may worsen rapidly, increasing the risk of emergency room visits or hospitalization.



■ Effects on the Whole Body

Long-term exposure to fine dust has been linked to the following health problems.

· Reduced lung function and development of asthma

· Cardiovascular disease, such as myocardial infarction and arrhythmia

· Cerebrovascular disease and nervous system disorders

· Diabetes mellitus and osteoporosis

· Preterm birth and skin aging

· Increased risk of death and cancer

sections.heading: Vulnerable High-Risk Groups
sections.content:
The following groups are especially vulnerable to fine dust.



· Children and older adults

· Pregnant women

· People with chronic respiratory diseases, such as asthma and COPD

· People with cardiovascular disease

· People who live near busy roads or work in occupations with high fine dust exposure



When a fine dust warning is issued, people in these groups should avoid going outdoors as much as possible.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
These are guidelines for protecting your health from fine dust.



■ Before Going Outside

· Check fine dust forecasts and warnings often.

· On days when levels are high, limit outdoor activities.

· Avoid busy roadsides, construction sites, and areas near factories.



■ Wearing a Mask

· If you must go outside when fine dust levels are high, wear a health protection mask (KF80 or higher).

· A mask is effective only when it fits snugly against the face with no gaps.

· For people with chronic conditions that reduce lung or heart function, wearing a mask may make breathing more difficult. Please consult your doctor before wearing one.

· People with asthma should always carry their symptom-relief (rescue) medication when going outside.



■ After Returning Home

· Wash your hands and face thoroughly. It is best to wash with soap under running water for at least 30 seconds.



■ Indoor Management

· Ventilate appropriately when outdoor fine dust levels are low.

· Ventilate well when cooking, and use an air purifier.

· Drinking enough fluids and eating vegetables and fruits with antioxidant properties may help.

records.title: Meniscus Tear
records.intro: A meniscus tear is a tear in the crescent-shaped cartilage (the meniscus) located between the thighbone (femur) and the shinbone (tibia) in the knee. When this happens, the meniscus may absorb shock less effectively, which can affect the health of the knee joint. If you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: meniscus, meniscus tear, knee cartilage, knee pain, arthroscopic surgery, sports injury, knee locking

sections.heading: Rehabilitation and Prevention
sections.content:
After surgery, rehabilitation begins with restoring the range of motion of the joint, followed by a gradual progression of muscle-strengthening exercises. Depending on the type of surgery, a return to exercise may be possible between 6 weeks and 6 months.
The following are important for preventing sports injuries.
· Do adequate warm-up and cool-down exercises before and after exercising.
· Choose exercise with an intensity and difficulty level suited to your own fitness.
· If knee pain develops, stop strenuous exercise and consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment methods differ depending on the extent, location, and shape of the tear.
· Conservative treatment: If there is no locking or severe swelling, drug therapy such as anti-inflammatory medication is tried first.
· Surgical treatment (arthroscopic surgery): This is performed when there is no improvement with conservative treatment. A tear in an area with a blood supply is repaired with sutures (meniscal repair), and a tear in an area without a blood supply is treated with partial removal of the meniscus (partial meniscectomy).
If strenuous exercise is continued despite cartilage damage and without surgery, arthritis may progress more quickly. Please consult a medical specialist about the extent of the damage and the treatment plan.

sections.heading: Symptoms and Diagnosis
sections.content:
Symptoms vary depending on the location and extent of the tear.
· Pain along the joint line of the knee
· Swelling of the knee
· A catching sensation in the knee (locking): the knee cannot be fully straightened or bent
· Clicking sounds in the knee
An MRI scan is generally needed to confirm the diagnosis. If you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Causes and Circumstances of Occurrence
sections.content:
A meniscus tear can result from acute trauma (such as a sports injury or a fall) or from repetitive overuse. As people age, the meniscus becomes weaker, and a tear can occur even during everyday movements.
Tears commonly occur in sports that involve a lot of knee movement, such as running, basketball, soccer, and skiing.

sections.heading: Definition and Function
sections.content:
The meniscus (crescent-shaped cartilage) is a crescent-shaped structure located between the femur (thighbone) and the tibia (shinbone). There is one on the inner (medial) side and one on the outer (lateral) side of the knee.
Its main functions are as follows.
· It absorbs shock applied to the knee.
· It helps maintain the stability of the knee joint.

records.title: Foot Health and Choosing the Right Shoes
records.intro: Choosing appropriate shoes and taking good care of your feet can help prevent various foot problems. If you notice any problems with your feet, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: shoe selection, foot health, high heels, proper footwear, foot care, foot, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Effects of High Heels on the Feet
sections.content:
Shoes with a heel higher than 3 cm are called high heels. Wearing high heels shifts body weight toward the front of the foot, which may cause the following problems.

· Pain in the lower back, shoulders, and back of the neck

· Fatigue throughout the body

· Lumbar hyperlordosis (excessive forward curvature of the lumbar spine)

· Hallux valgus, or bunion (the big toe angles toward the second toe)

· Calluses at the base of the toes and on the top of the toes

To protect foot health, it is best to wear high heels less often.

sections.heading: How to Choose the Right Shoes
sections.content:
It is important to choose shoes that fit your own feet.

· Length: Shoes about 1 cm longer than the tip of your longest toe are suitable. The part of the shoe that bends when you walk should line up with the part where your big toe bends.

· Ball of the foot: The ball of the shoe should match the ball of your foot. If the ball of the shoe is too narrow, the toes are squeezed.

· Laces over the instep: Shoes that lace over the instep are better for the feet. Tighten and loosen the laces each time you put the shoes on and take them off.

· Insoles: Using insoles made to fit the shape of your own sole can distribute body weight evenly and may make your feet more comfortable.

If new shoes do not feel comfortable from the start, they may not fit your feet.

sections.heading: Foot Health Care
sections.content:
· After wearing high heels, take your shoes off often and do toe curl-and-stretch exercises and toe-spreading exercises.

· Massaging the soles of the feet can help relieve tired foot muscles.

· Once the feet become deformed, it is very difficult to restore them to their original condition. It is important to wear proper shoes while the feet are still normal.

· If your feet hurt and walking is uncomfortable, please consult a specialist in physical medicine and rehabilitation.

records.title: Bladder Cancer
records.intro: Bladder cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the inner lining of the bladder. In the early stages, treatment that preserves the bladder is often possible, but in advanced cases the bladder may need to be removed. Early detection is very important for treatment outcomes. If you have suspicious symptoms such as blood in the urine, be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: bladder cancer, hematuria, cystoscopy, transurethral resection, radical cystectomy, BCG, cancer immunotherapy, smoking, renal pelvis cancer, ureteral cancer, stomachache, abdominal pain, belly ache, gut pain, fever, feeling hot, high fever, low-grade fever, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet, frequent urination, frequent bathroom visits, blood in urine, red urine, bloody urine

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The bladder is a sac-shaped organ that stores urine made by the kidneys and releases it out of the body. Bladder cancer is a disease in which cancer cells grow as a mass in the inner mucosa or muscle layer of the bladder.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The most common symptom of bladder cancer is painless blood in the urine (hematuria). Hematuria is a condition in which blood is mixed into the urine.



Other symptoms that may occur include the following.

· Irritative bladder symptoms: frequent urges to urinate or discomfort when urinating

· Flank pain (pain in the side of the abdomen)

· Swelling of the lower limbs: swelling of the legs



Hematuria is divided into gross hematuria, which can be seen with the naked eye, and microscopic hematuria, which is found only on testing. Both require appropriate testing. In people who have a history of smoking in particular, painless hematuria may be a sign of bladder cancer and should be evaluated promptly.



Blood mixed into the urine is the most important noticeable symptom of bladder cancer. Hematuria may stop on its own and then recur, and it is often painless. Some people miss the opportunity for timely treatment because they take hematuria lightly.



■ Changes in Symptoms as the Disease Progresses

- Early stage: There are few noticeable symptoms other than hematuria.

- Advanced stage: Irritative bladder symptoms such as frequent and urgent urination, along with pain, become more severe.

- If you are 40 or older and have blood in the urine that is visible to the naked eye, seek immediate medical attention.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The best-known risk factor for bladder cancer is smoking. Smoking is a cause not only of bladder cancer but also of renal pelvis cancer, ureteral cancer, kidney cancer, lung cancer, and others.



Genetic factors also influence the development of bladder cancer. If someone in your family has had bladder cancer, it is advisable to get tested proactively.



Exposure to secondhand smoke may also increase the risk.



■ Major Risk Factors

- Smoking: The best-known risk factor, it substantially increases the risk of bladder cancer.

- Alcohol consumption: May be associated with the development of bladder cancer.

- Long-term use of certain pain medications and some anticancer drugs

- Age: The risk rises sharply from the 60s, but bladder cancer also occurs in people in their 40s and 50s.



■ Increase in Female Patients

Bladder cancer is far more common in men, but the number of female patients has also been increasing steadily in recent years.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The most important test for diagnosing bladder cancer is cystoscopy. In cystoscopy, a thin endoscopic instrument is passed through the urethra into the bladder to directly examine the inside of the bladder. Unlike the rigid cystoscope used in the past (rigid cystoscopy), flexible cystoscopes are now available, and discomfort during the test has decreased considerably.



· Urine cytology: A test in which cells in the urine are examined under a microscope to help assess the grade (degree of malignancy) of a cancer.

· CT scan: Checks how deeply the cancer has invaded the bladder wall and whether it has spread to other areas.



If you smoke or have been exposed to secondhand smoke and have blood in your urine, please do not hesitate to see a medical specialist for tests such as cystoscopy.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment of bladder cancer depends on how deeply the cancer has invaded the bladder wall.



■ Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT)

This is the first surgery performed for all bladder cancers, and it is also a diagnostic method. The tumor is removed with an electrosurgical instrument through a cystoscope, and at the same time it is checked whether the cancer has invaded the muscle layer. If the cancer is limited to the mucosal layer, the bladder may be preserved.



■ Radical Cystectomy

This is performed when the cancer has invaded the muscle layer of the bladder. It is done by open, laparoscopic, or robotic surgery. After the bladder is removed, a passage for urine is created in one of two ways.

· Ileal conduit: A passage for urine is created from a segment of the small intestine and connected to a urine bag outside the skin.

· Orthotopic neobladder: A new bladder is created from the small intestine and sutured in the position of the original bladder.

The choice of method is decided according to the patient's condition and preferences.



■ Metastatic Bladder Cancer

When the cancer has spread to other sites, chemotherapy or immunotherapy is used. Recently, immunotherapy has become covered by insurance as a second-line treatment in Korea, and new anticancer drugs based on genetic analysis are in clinical trials. The 5-year survival rate for invasive bladder cancer is about 40 to 50%, and the prognosis is generally less favorable for metastatic disease. Early detection is very important.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Bladder cancer can recur in up to 50% of cases within 1 year, even after the tumor has been removed successfully. The following are important for managing recurrence.



· Regular cystoscopy: Recurrence should be detected early through regular outpatient follow-up. Even after a certain period has passed since treatment, please do not stop outpatient follow-up on your own.

· Intravesical BCG or chemotherapy instillation: Treatment given directly into the bladder that can lower the recurrence rate (BCG works by stimulating the immune response in the bladder). Bladder irritation symptoms, blood in the urine, fever, and other symptoms may occur after BCG instillation.

· Smoking cessation: Quit smoking right away. Smoking is the strongest risk factor for bladder cancer. Quitting smoking is very important even after the bladder has been removed.

· Maintaining a balanced diet and appropriate exercise can also help.

records.title: Cataract
records.intro: A cataract is a condition in which the lens inside the eye, which acts like a camera lens, becomes cloudy and vision declines. Aging is the most common cause. If your vision is blurry or dim, please consult an eye specialist (ophthalmologist).
records.tags_raw: cataract, lens, vision loss, presbyopia, macular degeneration, phacoemulsification, intraocular lens, multifocal lens, blurry vision, difficulty seeing, cloudy vision, double vision, overlapping images

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The eye has a structure similar to a camera. Just as a camera has a lens, the eye contains a clear lens called the crystalline lens. A cataract is a condition in which this lens becomes cloudy so that light cannot pass through properly. As a result, vision may look hazy or dim, and visual acuity declines.



Age-related (senile) cataract is the most common type. It starts to develop after age 50 and is present in more than half of people in their 60s and older.



Difference from glaucoma: A cataract is clouding of the lens, and vision may be improved with surgery. Glaucoma is a disease in which the optic nerve is damaged, and the damage generally cannot be completely reversed.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Most cataracts are acquired (not present at birth).

· Aging: The lens becomes cloudier with age. This is the most common cause.

· Excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light

· Eye injury

· Inflammatory eye diseases

· Long-term use of steroid medications

· Diabetes mellitus

· Smoking



Less commonly, cataracts can be congenital (present at birth).

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Vision is hazy or dim, as if seen through fog.

· Glare is severe in daylight.

· Some people see better at night or in dark places than during the day.

· Monocular diplopia (seeing double even when one eye is covered) may occur.

· Nearsightedness may develop, so that some people can see near objects without reading glasses.



Difference from presbyopia: The main symptom of presbyopia is difficulty seeing near objects, which can be corrected with reading glasses. With a cataract, vision looks blurry at a distance as well, and even when reading glasses are worn.



Blurry vision and reduced vision can also be caused by conditions other than cataracts, such as macular degeneration and retinal vascular disease. Do not dismiss these symptoms as just part of getting older. Please visit an eye specialist for an accurate diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
There is no medication that can cure cataracts. Some eye drops are used with the aim of slowing progression, but the definitive treatment is surgery.



Surgery is considered when vision has declined enough to interfere with daily life. If a cataract is left untreated for too long, complications such as glaucoma and uveitis may develop, and surgery may become more difficult.



■ Phacoemulsification

This is the most commonly used surgical method. The clouded lens is broken up with ultrasound energy and removed, and an intraocular lens (artificial lens) is inserted in its place.



Types of intraocular lenses:

· Monofocal intraocular lens: Focuses at one distance, either near or far.

· Multifocal intraocular lens: Can focus at both near and far distances, so it may also correct presbyopia.

· Toric (astigmatism-correcting) lens: Used when astigmatism is present.



Surgery is mostly done as day surgery, with admission and discharge on the same day, followed by outpatient visits. Please discuss treatment options thoroughly with your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Age-related cataracts cannot be fundamentally prevented. The following measures may help slow progression.

· Wear sunglasses or a hat when going outside on days with strong ultraviolet light.

· Quit smoking.

· If you have diabetes, keep your blood sugar well controlled.

· Take care to avoid eye injuries.

· If you need to use steroid medications for a long time, consult a medical specialist.

· Have regular eye examinations to check for cataracts, and receive treatment if needed.

records.title: Leukemia
records.intro: Leukemia is a malignant tumor that arises from immature blood cells in the bone marrow. It is classified as acute or chronic, and as myeloid or lymphoid depending on the type of cell involved. Unlike in the past, advances in medicine, including targeted therapy, have expanded the treatment options. Please discuss the diagnosis and treatment plan thoroughly with a hematology-oncology specialist.
records.tags_raw: leukemia, acute leukemia, chronic leukemia, myeloid leukemia, lymphoid leukemia, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, fever, feeling hot, high fever, low-grade fever, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Leukemia is a malignant tumor (cancer) that arises from the immature cells that make blood in the bone marrow. It is classified according to two main criteria.



■ Classification by Speed of Progression

· Acute leukemia: Progresses rapidly and causes severe symptoms. Prompt treatment is needed.

· Chronic leukemia: Progresses slowly, and symptoms are often mild or absent. It is sometimes found by chance during a health checkup.



■ Classification by Cell of Origin

· Myeloid leukemia: Arises from myeloid cells (granulocytes).

· Lymphoid leukemia: Arises from lymphocytes.



Combining these two criteria, leukemia is divided into acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, chronic myeloid leukemia, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and others.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Acute leukemia often causes the following symptoms, which can be severe.



· Fever and repeated infections (weakened immunity)

· Severe fatigue and pallor (anemia)

· Nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and easy bruising (low platelet count)

· Bone pain



Chronic leukemia often causes mild symptoms or none at all. In chronic myeloid leukemia, the condition is sometimes found because the spleen (an organ under the left rib cage) becomes enlarged, causing discomfort in the left side of the abdomen, a palpable mass (a lump that can be felt), or early satiety (feeling full quickly).

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Leukemia is diagnosed with the following tests.



· Blood tests: Check for abnormalities in blood cell counts and cell shape.

· Bone marrow examination: Cells are collected from the bone marrow to check for cancer cells. Cancer gene testing and chromosome testing are performed together and used for an accurate diagnosis and risk group classification.



Risk groups are classified differently depending on the type of genetic and chromosomal abnormality, and the treatment method and treatment results may differ accordingly. Please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with a hematology-oncology specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment for leukemia varies depending on the type and risk group.



■ Acute Leukemia

Treatment basically involves hospital admission for chemotherapy. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered depending on treatment response and risk group. If certain genetic abnormalities are present, molecular targeted therapy (drugs that target specific molecular abnormalities in cancer cells) may be used together with chemotherapy. For older patients, treatment with drugs that have fewer side effects may be used.



■ Chronic Myeloid Leukemia

Treatment has advanced significantly, and targeted therapy alone (oral medication) may make long-term survival possible. Drugs that target the Philadelphia chromosome abnormality (a characteristic chromosomal abnormality of chronic myeloid leukemia) are the main examples. These drugs are also used to treat acute lymphoblastic leukemia with certain genetic abnormalities.



■ Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia

In some cases, treatment is not started right away and the condition is monitored instead. When treatment becomes necessary, various chemotherapy drugs are used in combination.



Please discuss the treatment method and plan thoroughly with a hematology-oncology specialist before making any decisions.

records.title: Burnout and Stress Management
records.intro: Burnout (exhaustion) is not simply a matter of fatigue or lack of willpower. It is a state in which accumulated chronic stress is thought to reduce the brain's ability to regulate itself. Rather than simply 'enduring' it, management aimed at helping the brain recover is needed. It is important to recognize the early signs of burnout and find your own ways to manage stress.
records.tags_raw: burnout, stress, exhaustion, sleep, mindfulness, goal management, workplace, mental health, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Burnout (exhaustion) is a state in which stress has built up over a long period and the brain's ability to regulate itself is thought to be reduced. It does not arise simply from being tired or from weak willpower.



Pay attention if the following early signs appear.

· Feeling emotionally drained

· Feeling that your ability to empathize is decreasing

· Reacting oversensitively to minor stimuli



These signs can be taken as a warning that the brain's energy is running low.

sections.heading: Stress Management
sections.content:
Stress cannot be eliminated completely. It is important to find your own ways of managing it.



The following approaches may help.



· At least once a day, set aside time that is unrelated to work on purpose. Any form is fine, such as exercise, reading, or simply resting quietly.

· Take care of your sleep quality. Not getting enough sleep can speed up emotional exhaustion. Getting sufficient, deep sleep is key to helping the brain recover.

· Practice recognizing and managing your stress response with methods such as breathing-based relaxation and mindfulness.



It is important to find recovery methods that suit you and to practice them consistently.

sections.heading: Goal Setting and Burnout Prevention
sections.content:
A common reason that New Year's resolutions and goals fail is that the energy needed to carry them out is not taken into account.



The following approaches can help you keep your goals while preventing burnout.



· Include your own condition in your criteria, for example, 'as long as fatigue does not become excessive' rather than 'work harder.'

· Break large goals down into monthly and weekly goals.

· Check whether you are recovering, not only whether you have achieved your goals.

· Set goals that focus on the process rather than the outcome.



Adjusting a goal for a while or slowing down is not failure. It is choosing an approach that can be sustained over the long term.



If burnout persists or interferes with daily life, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Constipation
records.intro: Constipation is a condition in which bowel movements are difficult or less frequent. Adequate fluid intake, high-fiber foods, and regular exercise are the basic ways to manage it. If symptoms persist or are severe, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: constipation, dietary fiber, prunes, laxatives, fluid intake, bowel motility, chronic constipation, unable to pass stool, difficulty passing stool, hard stools, blood on stool, bloody stool, bright red stool

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Constipation refers to a condition in which bowel movements become less frequent, stools are hard and dry, or a great deal of straining is needed to pass stool.



There are various causes, including insufficient fluid intake, insufficient dietary fiber, lack of exercise, and abnormal bowel function. If chronic constipation persists, it is advisable to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Dietary Fiber and Fluid Intake
sections.content:
High-fiber foods and adequate fluid intake can help manage constipation.



· High-fiber foods: vegetables, fruits, whole grains (brown rice, barley, etc.), and legumes

· Prune (dried plum) juice: It contains a substance called sorbitol and dietary fiber, which help stimulate bowel movement. Drinking about half a cup to one cup on an empty stomach in the morning may help. It is best to drink plenty of water along with it.



People with diabetes need to be careful about rises in blood sugar. People with chronic kidney disease should consult a medical specialist before taking it. Do not take it if an intestinal obstruction (a blocked bowel) is suspected.

sections.heading: Laxatives (Constipation Medications)
sections.content:
Laxatives are medications that increase the water in the bowel to soften stool or stimulate bowel movement.



· Osmotic laxatives: Draw water into the bowel to soften stool. They are generally considered less likely to cause dependence.

· Stimulant laxatives: Directly stimulate bowel movement. Caution is needed because long-term use may affect the bowel.



Continue to drink enough fluids while using laxatives. If blood is present in the stool, do not use laxatives without a medical specialist's examination.



For chronic constipation, it is important to receive appropriate treatment after a medical specialist's diagnosis rather than deciding on your own to take medication.

records.title: Abdominal Wall Hernia
records.intro: An abdominal wall hernia is a condition in which the abdominal wall around a surgical incision weakens after abdominal surgery, allowing tissue from inside the abdominal cavity to push out. Early detection and surgery may allow a faster recovery. If you feel an unusual lump in the abdomen or develop sudden abdominal pain, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: abdominal wall hernia, hernia, laparoscopy, robotic surgery, minimally invasive surgery, bowel obstruction, abdominal surgery, stomachache, abdominal pain, belly ache, gut pain, dry cough, minor cough, persistent cough, unable to pass stool, difficulty passing stool, hard stools

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A hernia is a condition in which an organ inside the abdominal cavity (mainly the small intestine) pushes out through a weakened part of the abdominal wall. Abdominal wall hernias often develop after abdominal surgery, when the muscles around the surgical incision become weak. The risk increases with age, especially in older adults who have had abdominal surgery.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· A soft lump can be felt near the surgical scar when coughing or straining.

· In the early stages, there is usually no pain.

· If the bowel becomes trapped in the abdominal wall opening, severe abdominal pain and vomiting may occur. This may mean that a bowel obstruction has developed, so seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room.



The longer a hernia is left untreated, the larger it may become, and the greater the risk of complications and the difficulty of surgery. If you suspect any abnormal symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Abdominal wall hernias are treated with surgery. Earlier surgery tends to be associated with fewer complications and faster recovery.



【Robotic/Laparoscopic Surgery (Minimally Invasive Surgery)】

The surgery is performed by inserting robotic arms and a camera through small openings of less than 1 cm. Blood vessels and nerves can be preserved, and because it may cause less pain and fewer complications than open surgery, discharge the day after surgery may be possible. Robotic surgery may also allow repair of abdominal wall hernias that are difficult to reconstruct laparoscopically.



【Open Surgery】

This is performed when the hernia site is large or complex. The recovery period may be longer than with robotic or laparoscopic surgery.



Please discuss the treatment method with a medical specialist, taking into account your condition and the extent of the hernia, before making any decisions.

sections.heading: Postoperative Recovery
sections.content: After robotic or laparoscopic surgery, many patients are discharged on the day of surgery or the next day. Pain may be present for about 1 to 2 days after surgery, but it is usually not severe, and many people can return to daily activities soon afterward. The degree of pain may vary depending on the size of the hernia, but it can usually be controlled with medication.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
It is difficult to prevent hernias fundamentally. Reducing the following risk factors may help lower the chance of recurrence.

· Prevent constipation.

· If you have benign prostatic hyperplasia, receive treatment for it.

· Quit smoking.

· Avoid lifting excessively heavy objects.

records.title: Cerebral Aneurysm
records.intro: A cerebral aneurysm is a condition in which the wall of a blood vessel in the brain becomes abnormally thin and bulges outward. Before it ruptures, it usually causes no symptoms and is sometimes found by chance during a health checkup. Because a rupture can become a life-threatening emergency, people with risk factors are advised to talk with their doctor about regular screening. If a health checkup shows an abnormal finding, please consult a neurosurgery specialist, and if a sudden, severe headache occurs, seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room.
records.tags_raw: cerebral aneurysm, subarachnoid hemorrhage, headache, cerebral blood vessels, coil embolization, surgical clipping, brain hemorrhage, MRA, CTA, head pain, splitting headache, migraine, pain at the back of the head, double vision, overlapping images
keywords: pain at the back of the head

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
A cerebral aneurysm is a condition in which the muscle layer that makes up the wall of a brain blood vessel becomes thin, and part of the vessel bulges out like a balloon. It is known to occur in about 3% or more of the general population.



Cerebral aneurysms are broadly divided into two types depending on whether they have ruptured.

· Unruptured aneurysm: An aneurysm that has not burst. It usually causes no symptoms and is found by chance during a health checkup (MRA, CTA).

· Ruptured aneurysm: An aneurysm that has burst, causing bleeding into the space beneath the arachnoid membrane, which surrounds the brain. This is called subarachnoid hemorrhage and is a life-threatening emergency.



An aneurysm does not resolve with medication or lifestyle changes alone. Surgical treatment is needed to reduce the risk of rupture, although not every aneurysm requires treatment.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
When the vessel is only bulging, there are usually no symptoms. However, if the bulging area bursts, a very severe headache develops suddenly, and in some cases it can lead to death or serious disability.



Before rupture, a cerebral aneurysm usually causes no symptoms. However, if it is large (10 mm or more) or located in certain places, it can press on nearby nerves and cause the following symptoms.

· Drooping of one eyelid

· Double vision (diplopia), seeing two images when looking at one object

· Dizziness

· Pain on one side of the head



When a cerebral aneurysm bursts (ruptures), a very severe headache suddenly develops. It may feel like the worst headache you have ever had. Nausea, vomiting, and a stiff neck may also occur. In severe cases, consciousness may be lost. If these symptoms occur, seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room.



If a headache comes on suddenly, seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room. A ruptured aneurysm can bleed again within a day or two, so prompt treatment is very important.

sections.heading: Risk Factors
sections.content:
If you have any of the following risk factors, consider having your brain blood vessels examined, and please talk with your doctor.

· Uncontrolled high blood pressure

· Smoking

· A parent who has had a cerebral aneurysm (family history)

· Excessive alcohol consumption



Even if you have no risk factors, please talk with your doctor about whether screening for a cerebral aneurysm with MRA or CTA is appropriate for you after age 40 to 45.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
A cerebral aneurysm is often found by chance during a health checkup even when there are no symptoms. The main tests are as follows.

· MRA (magnetic resonance angiography): A test that examines the condition of the brain blood vessels without radiation exposure.

· CTA (CT angiography): A test that uses CT to view the brain blood vessels in detail.

· Cerebral angiography: A test in which a thin tube is inserted into a blood vessel to examine the vessels directly.



If a rupture is suspected, a CT scan is performed first. A sudden severe headache called a 'warning headache' (sentinel headache) may occur before rupture, so if you have this symptom, seek immediate medical attention.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Not every aneurysm is treated right away. Whether to treat is decided by considering the location, shape, and size of the aneurysm and the patient's condition. When the risk of rupture is low, the aneurysm is observed with lifestyle improvement and regular follow-up tests.



There are two main types of treatment for cerebral aneurysms.



· Coil embolization (endovascular surgery): A thin tube is passed through an artery in the thigh or wrist to the brain blood vessel, and the aneurysm is filled with platinum coils to keep blood from entering it. If needed, a stent (a supporting mesh tube) that strengthens the vessel wall may be inserted at the same time. Because the aneurysm may recur over the long term, follow-up tests are needed.



· Surgical clipping (craniotomy): The head is opened, and a metal clip is placed at the neck of the aneurysm to keep blood from entering it.



The two methods are sometimes used together. Which method is suitable is decided by a medical specialist according to the location and size of the aneurysm and the patient's condition. Please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with your treating physician.

sections.heading: Postoperative Precautions and Prevention
sections.content:
【After Coil Embolization】

Antiplatelet medication (such as aspirin or clopidogrel) is often prescribed for several months to help prevent blood clots. During this period, bleeding may not stop easily during other surgeries, procedures, injections, or acupuncture, so be sure to tell your healthcare providers that you are taking it. Take extra care to avoid head injuries.



【After Craniotomy】

Light exercise such as walking is suitable for the first 1 to 2 months after surgery. After 2 to 3 months, strength training, long-distance travel, and air travel may be possible, as advised by your doctor. Avoid headstands and activities that jolt or vibrate the head.



Regular follow-up tests are needed after surgery as well. If any unusual symptoms appear, contact a medical specialist immediately.





To help prevent rupture of a cerebral aneurysm, the following management is important.

· Smoking cessation: Smoking increases the risk of rupture.

· Blood pressure control: If you have high blood pressure, it is important to have it treated appropriately.

· Alcohol moderation: Avoid excessive drinking.

· Regular screening: If you have risk factors such as high blood pressure, smoking, or a family history, it is advisable to talk with your doctor about regular testing.



If symptoms such as headache, changes in vision, or double vision occur, please consult a medical specialist immediately.

records.title: Malocclusion and Orthodontic Treatment
records.intro: Malocclusion is a condition in which the upper and lower teeth do not fit together correctly. When the teeth fit together well, it is easier to chew food effectively, speak clearly, and maintain a natural appearance. Leaving malocclusion untreated may reduce chewing efficiency and make tooth decay and gum disease more likely, so an accurate diagnosis and treatment at an appropriate time are important. Please consult an orthodontic specialist to decide whether and when to begin orthodontic treatment.
records.tags_raw: malocclusion, orthodontics, orthodontic treatment, open bite, deep bite, anterior crossbite, clear aligners, brackets, tooth alignment

sections.heading: Digital Orthodontic Systems
sections.content:
Digital technology is now being actively applied in orthodontic treatment as well.

- AI analysis: The analysis results of artificial intelligence (AI) trained on big data (large sets of past records) are referred to by the orthodontic specialist and used to help make an accurate diagnosis.

- Final bite design: Before treatment, the target final bite (how the teeth fit together) is designed in advance, and brackets are placed at precise positions or clear appliances are made based on this design.

Digital technology is improving the precision of treatment planning, but orthodontic results can vary depending on the individual's condition. Please discuss the direction of treatment thoroughly with an orthodontic specialist before making any decisions.

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
Malocclusion takes many forms. It can be divided into patterns seen from the front and patterns seen from the side.

- Open bite: The upper and lower front teeth do not touch each other.
- Deep bite: The upper teeth cover the lower teeth too deeply.
- Anterior crossbite (reverse bite): The lower front teeth sit in front of the upper front teeth, so the bite is reversed.
- Maxillary protrusion (protruding mouth): The upper teeth stick out too far forward compared with the lower teeth.

These front-tooth bite problems often occur together with bite problems in the back molars.

In addition, crooked teeth and gaps between teeth are common.
- Crowding (crooked teeth): A condition in which the teeth are large or the dental arch (the jawbone) is small, so the teeth overlap or sit crookedly. The 'dental arch' refers to the curved, bow-shaped structure of the jaw along which the teeth are lined up.
- Spacing (gaps between teeth): Gaps form between teeth when the teeth are small or when there are fewer teeth than needed.

sections.heading: Why Orthodontic Treatment Is Needed
sections.content:
Leaving malocclusion untreated may lead to several problems.

- Tooth decay and gum disease: When teeth are crooked or overlapping, food tends to remain between the teeth even with careful brushing, which can make tooth decay and gum disease more likely.

- Damage to the supporting bone: When teeth are displaced from the gum bone (alveolar bone) or tilted, gum disease is more likely to develop. The 'alveolar bone' is the bone that surrounds and supports the tooth roots.

- Tooth wear: Abnormal wearing away of the teeth, including attrition (wear from teeth rubbing against each other) and abrasion, may occur in association with malocclusion.

- Reduced chewing function: Chewing efficiency may decrease, which can also affect digestion.

- Psychological discomfort: Orthodontic treatment may also help when tooth position, such as protruding teeth, makes a person's smile feel awkward or lowers self-confidence.

Orthodontic treatment may help create an oral environment in which the teeth can be kept healthy for a longer time.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Children and Adolescents
The condition of a growing child varies widely, so the time to start treatment cannot be fixed at a single point. However, it is recommended to have a first orthodontic checkup at around age 7.

At age 7, the first permanent molars (first molars) come in and the front teeth are replaced by permanent teeth. At this time, the growth of the upper and lower jaws, the number and development of the teeth, and problems with space can be checked together. If a problem is found, early treatment may prevent a more severe malocclusion and may reduce the likelihood of more complex treatment later.

Even if the first checkup shows that everything is normal, it is recommended to have a checkup with an orthodontic specialist once a year.

The timing of treatment differs depending on the type of malocclusion.
- Around age 7: anterior crossbite, mandibular (lower jaw) overgrowth, etc.
- Around age 9: problems with space for permanent teeth
- Around age 12: problems with tooth alignment

■ Adults and Middle-Aged Adults
Recently, adults and middle-aged patients have also been receiving orthodontic treatment for various reasons. It is advisable to begin treatment after thoroughly discussing the goals and expectations of treatment. In some cases, partial orthodontic treatment that corrects only some of the teeth may be possible, and in other cases full orthodontic treatment is needed.

Adult and middle-aged patients have considerations that differ from those of younger patients. Many people worry about discomfort or pain from the appliances, but thanks to research and technological advances, treatment may now be considerably more comfortable than in the past.

sections.heading: Types of Orthodontic Appliances
sections.content:
Orthodontic appliances are broadly divided into intraoral appliances, which are placed inside the mouth, and extraoral appliances, which are used outside the mouth.

■ Intraoral Appliances
① Fixed Bracket Appliances
This is an orthodontic appliance that has been widely used for a long time. Brackets (small metal or ceramic pieces) are attached to the tooth surfaces and connected with wires (thin metal wires) to move the teeth in the desired direction. The orthodontic specialist checks the tooth movement directly and adjusts the wires and elastic devices (such as power chains and springs).

② Clear Aligners
These appliances have been developed using 3D digital imaging technology. The final result after treatment is simulated first (previewed by computer), and custom-made clear trays are placed over the teeth to move them. They are nearly invisible and can be removed when eating or brushing, which can make hygiene care easier. However, they cannot be used in every case, so consultation with an orthodontic specialist is needed.

③ Removable Appliances
These appliances can be taken out and put back in as needed, and they are used for treatment in growing children or as auxiliary appliances.

■ Extraoral Appliances
These appliances are used outside the mouth to control jaw growth or to help move the teeth. They are mainly used in growing children.

■ Retainers
Retainers are appliances that keep the teeth from returning to their original positions after orthodontic treatment ends. There are removable retainers that can be taken out and put back in, and fixed retainers that are attached to the back surfaces of the teeth. Wearing a retainer is as important a step as orthodontic treatment itself.

records.title: Arrhythmia
records.intro: An arrhythmia is a condition in which the heartbeat is abnormally slow, fast, or irregular. The heart beats about 100,000 times a day to supply blood to the whole body, and when there is a problem with this rhythm, various symptoms may occur. The types and causes of arrhythmia vary, so if you have symptoms, be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: arrhythmia, atrial fibrillation, bradycardia, tachycardia, pacemaker, ventricular fibrillation, stroke, anticoagulants, dizziness, spinning sensation, unsteadiness, vision going dark, collapse, loss of consciousness, fainting, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, rapid heartbeat, pounding heart, fast pulse

sections.heading: Definition and How the Heartbeat Works
sections.content:
In a healthy adult at rest, the heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Inside the heart is an area called the sinoatrial node, which generates electrical signals. These signals travel from the atria through the atrioventricular node to the ventricles, and the heart beats.



An arrhythmia occurs when there is a problem with the generation or conduction of these electrical signals.

· Bradycardia (an arrhythmia with a slow pulse): when electrical signal generation is slow or signals are not conducted well to the ventricles

· Tachycardia (an arrhythmia with a fast pulse): when abnormal electrical signals arise from areas other than the sinoatrial node

sections.heading: Bradycardia
sections.content:
Bradycardia is a condition in which the heartbeat is too slow and the body does not receive enough blood.



■ Main Symptoms

· Shortness of breath during activity

· Sudden fainting (syncope) (a temporary decrease in blood supply to the brain)

· Fatigue



Oral medication is currently of limited use for treating bradycardia. For symptomatic bradycardia, treatment may involve implanting a permanent pacemaker in the heart to help maintain a normal heartbeat.

sections.heading: Tachycardia and Atrial Fibrillation
sections.content:
Symptoms of tachycardia range from palpitations, shortness of breath, and dizziness to, in severe cases, sudden cardiac death.



Tachycardia is classified according to where it originates.

· Supraventricular tachycardia: Originates above the ventricles, and palpitations are the main symptom.

· Ventricular tachycardia: Originates in the ventricles and, in serious cases, can lead to sudden cardiac death.



■ Atrial Fibrillation

Atrial fibrillation is the most common arrhythmia among the supraventricular tachycardias. It is associated with aging. Irregular, rapid electrical signals arise in the atria, making blood flow within the atria irregular. As a result, blood clots may form in the atria, and if a clot travels to a blood vessel in the brain, a stroke may occur.

Atrial fibrillation may cause no symptoms and is sometimes found by chance during a health checkup. If you have risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, advanced age, heart failure, or a previous stroke, treatment with an anticoagulant (a medication that helps prevent blood clots from forming) may be needed to help prevent stroke.

sections.heading: Ventricular Tachycardia and Sudden Cardiac Death
sections.content:
If ventricular tachycardia continues, the ventricles, which are responsible for the heart's main pumping function, may not work properly, and blood pressure may drop sharply and consciousness may be lost. Without treatment, it can be fatal.



For people at high risk of ventricular tachycardia, or who have already had it, treatment may include implanting an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), a device that delivers an electric shock to return the heart to a normal rhythm when ventricular tachycardia occurs.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
If palpitations recur, if you have fainted for no apparent reason, or if you have severe dizziness during exercise, be sure to consult a medical specialist.

If you have been prescribed an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation, do not stop taking the medication on your own. Treatment differs depending on the type of arrhythmia, so please follow the treatment decided by your medical specialist.

records.title: Insomnia
records.intro: Insomnia is not simply fatigue. It is a condition that can harm both physical and mental health. Non-drug treatment that changes lifestyle habits is important before taking sleeping pills, so please consult a specialist in psychiatry.
records.tags_raw: insomnia, sleep hygiene, cognitive behavioral therapy, sleeping pills, mental health, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, unable to fall asleep, frequent awakening, difficulty sleeping deeply

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: When difficulty falling asleep at night, waking repeatedly during sleep, or waking too early in the morning and being unable to fall back asleep continues for 3 months or more, it is considered chronic insomnia.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: Common causes include stress, poor sleep habits, coffee or alcohol consumed before bed, and mental health conditions such as depression.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
'Cognitive behavioral therapy,' which changes habits without medication, is recommended as the first approach. 'Stimulus control' training can be helpful: if you cannot fall asleep within 20 minutes of lying down, get out of bed and do a quiet activity, and return to bed only when you feel sleepy.



When insomnia is treated at an appropriate time, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) alone, without medication, may improve it. Cognitive behavioral therapy is a type of psychological treatment that corrects mistaken thoughts and habits about sleep. Please do not leave insomnia untreated. Talk with a specialist in psychiatry early.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Alcohol consumed before bed may make you sleepy at first, but it ultimately leads to lighter sleep and can make insomnia worse. Rather than fixating on the idea that you must sleep 8 hours, keeping a regular wake-up time is especially important.

records.title: Insomnia (Summer Tropical Nights)
records.intro: Insomnia is a sleep disorder in which difficulty falling asleep or frequent waking during sleep continues and interferes with daily life. Sleep can also be disrupted by environmental factors, such as tropical nights (very hot summer nights). If symptoms persist for 3 weeks or longer, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: insomnia, sleep disorder, tropical night, sleep hygiene, body temperature, cognitive behavioral therapy, sleep, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, unable to fall asleep, frequent awakening, difficulty sleeping deeply, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason

sections.heading: Prevention and Relief Methods
sections.content:
The following methods may help relieve insomnia during tropical nights.

· Sleep environment: Set an air conditioner or fan on a timer to keep the room cool at the start of sleep.

· Showering: Taking a lukewarm shower 1 to 2 hours before bedtime temporarily raises body temperature and then lets it fall naturally, which may help induce sleep.

· Keeping a consistent wake-up time: Even if you slept poorly during the night, get up at your usual time in the morning. Limiting naps to 30 minutes or less may help restore your sleep rhythm.

sections.heading: Definition and Diagnostic Criteria
sections.content:
Insomnia is a sleep disorder in which difficulty falling asleep, frequent waking during sleep, or waking early in the morning and being unable to fall back asleep continues over time.

Insomnia is generally diagnosed when all of the following conditions are met.

· Sleep problems occur 3 or more times a week.

· This continues for 3 weeks or longer (1 month under some criteria).

· The sleep problems cause difficulties in daily life during the day, such as fatigue, reduced concentration, or mood changes.

If poor sleep does not interfere with daily life, it is not necessarily considered insomnia.

sections.heading: The Relationship Between Tropical Nights and Sleep
sections.content:
Sleep is closely related to a gradual fall in body temperature. The brain prepares for sleep when body temperature drops before bedtime.

In Korea, a tropical night is defined as a night when the lowest temperature stays at or above 25 °C. When nighttime temperatures are this high, body temperature does not fall enough, making it harder to enter deep sleep (slow-wave sleep) and causing frequent waking. This is a natural response to the environment, but if pressure to 'get to sleep' and anxiety are added, it can lead to chronic insomnia.

sections.heading: Health Effects of Sleep Deprivation
sections.content:
Even a few days of sleep deprivation may cause the following effects.

· Fatigue and reduced concentration

· Difficulty regulating emotions and increased irritability

Over the long term, it may lead to weakened immunity, an increased risk of high blood pressure, diabetes, and obesity, and depression or anxiety disorders. Rather than dismissing poor sleep as simply caused by the heat, it is important to take care of your sleep quality.

sections.heading: Sleep Hygiene
sections.content:
Sleep hygiene refers to the lifestyle habits and environment to maintain for healthy sleep.

· Keep regular sleep and wake-up times.

· Avoid napping, or limit naps to 30 minutes or less.

· Avoid caffeine (coffee, energy drinks, etc.), alcohol, and smartphone use before bed, as they can interfere with sleep.

· Keep the bedroom dark, quiet, and at a comfortable temperature.

· If you cannot fall asleep, rather than forcing yourself to lie in bed, get up and do a quiet activity, and lie down again when you feel sleepy.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Once the tropical nights pass, sleep often recovers naturally. However, if insomnia lasts for 3 weeks or longer or makes daily life difficult, it is advisable to consult a medical specialist.

When insomnia is treated at an appropriate time, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) alone, without medication, may improve it. Cognitive behavioral therapy is a type of psychological treatment that corrects mistaken thoughts and habits about sleep. Please do not leave insomnia untreated. Talk with a specialist in psychiatry early.

records.title: Blueberries
records.intro: Blueberries are a fruit rich in antioxidants and have been associated with various potential health benefits. With a balance of sweetness and tartness, they taste good and can be enjoyed in many ways.
records.tags_raw: blueberry, antioxidant, anthocyanin, constipation, colon, vision, blood circulation, aging, unable to pass stool, difficulty passing stool, hard stools

sections.heading: Potential Health Benefits
sections.content:
Blueberries are a fruit rich in antioxidants and have been associated with the following potential health benefits.



· Antioxidant activity: May help neutralize free radicals (reactive oxygen species), which are associated with cancer and age-related diseases.

· Gut health: Because they are rich in dietary fiber, they may support bowel movement and help prevent constipation.

· Eye health: They have been suggested to support vision and concentration and to help protect against retinal degeneration and cataracts, although evidence for these effects is limited.

· Blood circulation: May help protect blood vessels and limit unnecessary platelet activity, which may support healthy blood circulation.

· Cognitive function: Some studies suggest they may help slow age-related decline in cognitive function.



Blueberries are a food and are not a substitute for medical treatment. If you have a health concern, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Obesity
records.intro: Obesity is a chronic disease in which excess body fat accumulates, and it can cause various complications, such as high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and arthritis. Under Asia-Pacific criteria, obesity is diagnosed when body mass index (BMI) is 25 kg/m² or higher, and, like high blood pressure and diabetes, it is a condition that needs lifelong management. Please consult a medical specialist before deciding on a treatment method.
records.tags_raw: obesity, body mass index, BMI, abdominal obesity, severe obesity, anti-obesity medication, liraglutide, bariatric (metabolic) surgery, fatty liver, metabolic syndrome

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Obesity is a condition in which too much fat accumulates in the body. It is classified as a chronic disease, not simply a matter of appearance, that tends to recur and may worsen over time.

When obesity persists, the risk of the following conditions increases.
· Diabetes mellitus
· High blood pressure
· Hyperlipidemia (dyslipidemia)
· Cardiovascular disease
· Cancer

In particular, visceral fat (fat stored deep inside the abdomen) increases insulin resistance (a state in which the body responds less well to insulin) more than subcutaneous fat (fat stored under the skin) and therefore has a greater effect on metabolic disease. If the upper abdomen (near the pit of the stomach) protrudes, there may be a larger amount of visceral fat.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
■ Body Mass Index (BMI) Criteria (Asia-Pacific Criteria)
BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²
- Overweight: 23.0 to 24.9 kg/m²
- Class 1 obesity: 25.0 to 29.9 kg/m²
- Class 2 obesity: 30.0 to 34.9 kg/m²
- Class 3 obesity (severe obesity): 35.0 kg/m² or higher

■ Abdominal Obesity Criteria
Waist circumference: 90 cm or more for men, 85 cm or more for women

Compared with Westerners, Asians are known to have an increased risk of diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease starting at the overweight stage, at a BMI of 23 kg/m².

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content:
Conditions associated with obesity are broadly divided into two groups.

■ Conditions Caused by Metabolic Abnormalities
High blood pressure, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, hyperuricemia (a cause of gout), coronary artery disease, stroke, cancer, and others

■ Conditions Caused by Excess Body Weight
Arthritis, low back pain, sleep apnea, and others

As BMI rises, the risk of these complications increases, and obesity is also associated with higher mortality. Obesity is not simply a lack of willpower. It is a chronic disease involving multiple causes, including genetic factors and individual differences in metabolism.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Treatment Goal
The goal is to lose 5 to 10% of body weight within 6 months.

■ Lifestyle Treatment
- Dietary treatment: calorie control and maintaining a balanced diet
- Exercise treatment: a combination of aerobic exercise and strength training
- Behavioral treatment: keeping a food diary and correcting behavior patterns

■ Drug Therapy
This is used when it is difficult to maintain weight with lifestyle changes alone. Anti-obesity medications approved for long-term use in Korea include orlistat, naltrexone/bupropion combination, phentermine/topiramate combination, and liraglutide. Because side effects differ for each medication, they must be prescribed after consultation with a medical specialist.

If medication is stopped after short-term use, rapid weight regain (the yo-yo effect) may occur. What matters more than losing weight is maintaining the lost weight over the long term.
