■ Bariatric (Metabolic) Surgery
This is considered when the following criteria are met and lifestyle and drug treatments have failed.
- BMI of 35 kg/m² or higher
- BMI of 30 kg/m² or higher with obesity-related complications
- For people with diabetes, a BMI of 27.5 kg/m² or higher with difficulty controlling blood sugar
Surgical methods include sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. In Korea, national health insurance has covered these procedures since 2019.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Obesity is a chronic disease that requires lifelong health management, like high blood pressure and diabetes mellitus. Sustained improvement of lifestyle habits and consistent follow-up are more important than weight loss itself.

■ Key Rules for Managing Obesity
- Lose weight gradually, with a long-term perspective.
- Always consult a medical specialist before using unproven diet supplements or psychotropic appetite suppressants.
- Visit the hospital regularly to manage weight, blood pressure, blood sugar, and lipid levels together.
- The bias that people with obesity are lazy is mistaken. Obesity is a condition involving multiple causes and requires individualized treatment.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Habits
sections.content:
The most important parts of obesity management are dietary control and regular exercise.

■ Diet
· Eat regularly, but avoid eating until you are very full.
· Eat home-cooked food whenever possible and reduce instant (processed) foods.
· Avoid foods high in simple sugars, such as added sugar. (Examples: soft drinks and snack foods)
· Avoid excessive protein and phosphorus intake.

■ Exercise
· Do aerobic exercise regularly, at a moderate intensity, and often.
· Increasing muscle mass helps maintain the basal metabolic rate (the energy your body uses at rest), which may help with weight management.

■ Other Lifestyle Habits
· Get an appropriate amount of sleep.
· Manage stress well.

Diets that involve fasting without a plan or eating only one type of food may be harmful to health.

records.title: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)
records.intro: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is a condition in which excess fat builds up in the liver even in people who drink little or no alcohol. If left untreated, it may progress to serious conditions such as cirrhosis or liver cancer. Do not rely on dietary supplements on your own. Please consult a medical specialist and begin healthy weight loss under their guidance.
records.tags_raw: fatty liver, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: It tends to occur in people who have problems with metabolic regulation, such as obesity, overweight, diabetes mellitus, and metabolic syndrome. In particular, frequently eating high-calorie foods or snacks such as sweet soft drinks high in sugar and fruit juice may cause fat to build up in the liver more quickly.

sections.heading: Exercise and Lifestyle Habits
sections.content: Losing even 5 to 10% of your current body weight may noticeably reduce the fat built up in the liver and may improve liver health. In addition to aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or running that leaves you a little short of breath, it is advisable to do strength training, which builds firmer muscle, regularly as well.

sections.heading: Dietary Therapy
sections.content: There is no medication that removes fat from the liver all at once. The most established treatment is to lose weight by adjusting your diet. Reduce foods that contain carbohydrates and sugar, and adopt healthy eating habits that provide a balanced variety of nutrients.

records.title: Tachycardia
records.intro: Tachycardia is a condition in which the heart beats abnormally fast, and it may cause dizziness or fainting. If symptoms occur, please consult a cardiology specialist so that the condition can be managed safely.
records.tags_raw: tachycardia, arrhythmia, palpitations, catheter ablation, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, dizziness, spinning sensation, unsteadiness, vision going dark, collapse, loss of consciousness, fainting, rapid heartbeat, pounding heart, fast pulse, weakness in arms and legs, difficulty moving one side of the body
keywords: difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If your heart pounds even while you are resting, or if palpitations start suddenly and do not settle down, seek immediate medical attention. If your face turns pale, you break out in a cold sweat, and you feel as if you might collapse, this can be a sign of a medical emergency, and prompt treatment is needed.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: An adult's heart usually beats about 60 to 100 times per minute. Tachycardia is a type of arrhythmia in which the heart beats abnormally faster than this, sometimes irregularly.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Symptoms include severe palpitations, dizziness, or shortness of breath. When the heart beats too fast, it cannot pump blood properly to the whole body, so blood pressure may actually drop. In severe cases, a person may lose consciousness and collapse, and the condition can be life-threatening.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: Depending on the type of tachycardia, treatment may involve medication or a procedure in which a thin tube (catheter) is used to locate and destroy the area of the heart that is causing the problem (catheter ablation). In high-risk cases, a small device (an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator) may be placed inside the body to help prevent sudden cardiac death.

records.title: Strabismus
records.intro: Strabismus is an eye movement disorder in which the two eyes cannot look at the same point together. One eye may turn in a different direction, which can reduce the ability to see objects in three dimensions. If you suspect symptoms, please consult an eye specialist (ophthalmologist).
records.tags_raw: strabismus, exotropia, esotropia, intermittent exotropia, amblyopia, stereopsis (3D vision), diplopia, strabismus surgery, head pain, splitting headache, migraine, pain at the back of the head, double vision, overlapping images
keywords: pain at the back of the head

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Strabismus is a condition in which the two eyes cannot look at the same object at the same time. Normally, the two eyes look at one object together, which allows objects to be perceived in three dimensions. This is called 'stereopsis' (3D vision). When strabismus is present, one eye turns in a different direction, and stereopsis may be reduced or lost.



Strabismus is classified by the direction in which the eye turns.

· Exotropia: One eye turns outward.

· Esotropia: One eye turns inward.

· Hypertropia: One eye turns upward.

· Hypotropia: One eye turns downward.



The most common type of strabismus in Korea is 'intermittent exotropia.' In intermittent exotropia, the eye drifts outward when the person is tired or sleepy.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of strabismus are as follows.

· Double vision (diplopia): Objects appear doubled or overlapping.

· Visual confusion: The two eyes look in different directions, causing a confusing visual experience.

· Reduced stereopsis: It is difficult to perceive depth and volume.



When a child has strabismus, 'amblyopia' (lazy eye) may develop, in which the vision of the eye that does not fixate on objects does not develop properly. In adults, the main problems with strabismus are double vision, headache, dizziness, and discomfort in social life. If you suspect any abnormal symptoms, please consult a medical specialist without delay.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: Each eye is moved by 6 muscles (the extraocular muscles) and several cranial nerves. If there is a problem with any one of these muscles or nerves, strabismus can occur. In some cases, an eye may drift temporarily when a person is tired or ill, or after drinking alcohol. As people age, the ability to turn the eyes inward together (convergence) may decline, and strabismus may become more noticeable.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
To diagnose strabismus, an eye specialist performs the following tests.

· Cover–uncover test: Checks for the presence of strabismus (tropia) and phoria (latent strabismus).

· Alternate cover test: Uses prisms to measure the angle of deviation (the angle at which the eye is turned).

· Eye movement (ocular motility) test: Checks for abnormal function of the extraocular muscles.



Additional imaging tests such as CT or MRI may be performed if needed. In children, early detection through regular vision checkups and strabismus examinations is important.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment of strabismus depends on the angle of deviation, the cause, and the patient's age.

· Glasses: If a refractive error (such as nearsightedness or farsightedness) is the cause, it is corrected with glasses.

· Prism glasses: When the angle of deviation is small, special prism glasses may reduce double vision.

· Strabismus surgery: Surgery adjusts the position of the extraocular muscles to align the direction of both eyes. It may be performed under general anesthesia in children and under local anesthesia in adults.



Adult strabismus may also be corrected with surgery. Do not give up thinking that 'there is no treatment.' Please consult an eye specialist for an examination.

records.title: Growth Hormone Therapy
records.intro: Growth hormone is a hormone secreted by the pituitary gland that is responsible for growth and metabolic function. Growth hormone therapy may be considered when short stature is caused by growth hormone deficiency or certain genetic conditions. Treatment continues for a long period, and consultation with an experienced pediatric endocrinology specialist is needed.
records.tags_raw: growth hormone, short stature, growth clinic, pediatric endocrinology, growth, height, Turner syndrome, head pain, splitting headache, migraine, pain at the back of the head, joint pain, knee pain, shoulder pain, wrist pain, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet
keywords: pain at the back of the head

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Growth hormone is a hormone secreted by the pituitary gland (an endocrine organ located at the base of the brain). It is secreted mainly at night and, in addition to promoting growth, is responsible for various metabolic functions, such as strengthening bones, increasing muscle mass, and reducing body fat.



Short stature means being among the shortest 3 of 100 children of the same sex and age (the 3rd percentile or below).



If short stature continues until ages 3 to 4, it is advisable to visit a growth clinic with a pediatric endocrinology specialist.

sections.heading: Indications for Treatment
sections.content:
Growth hormone therapy may be considered in the following cases.



· Short stature caused by growth hormone deficiency

· Children born with low birth weight (small for gestational age)

· Genetic conditions such as Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, and Noonan syndrome

· Idiopathic short stature: short stature with no identifiable cause



Before treatment begins, the appropriate time to start is decided through checks of overall health, nutritional assessment, hormone tests, and bone age assessment.

sections.heading: Treatment Method
sections.content:
Growth hormone is given once a day, at bedtime, as a subcutaneous injection (an injection placed under the skin). After training, it can also be given at home using a simple pen-type injector.



It is not a treatment that produces results in a short time. It is a long-term treatment that generally needs to be continued for 2 years or longer. If you meet the national health insurance coverage criteria in Korea, insurance coverage may be available up to a certain height.



Treatment effects vary from person to person, and the treatment method and goals are decided after thorough consultation with your treating physician.

sections.heading: Side Effects and Precautions
sections.content:
The following side effects may occur during growth hormone therapy, so regular monitoring is needed.



· Swelling of the hands, feet, or face (peripheral edema): the most common side effect

· Headache, joint pain, and muscle pain

· Changes in blood sugar and decreased thyroid hormone levels

· Orthopedic problems such as scoliosis



It has not been confirmed that growth hormone therapy artificially brings on puberty early or interferes with growth after treatment is stopped. Enlargement of only the hands, feet, or jaw rarely occurs at treatment doses.



Please consult a pediatric endocrinology specialist before making any decisions about whether and how to treat.

records.title: Dysphagia (Swallowing Disorders)
records.intro: Dysphagia is a condition in which the ability to swallow food or drink is impaired. If 'aspiration,' in which food enters the airway, occurs, complications such as pneumonia may develop. If you suspect a decline in swallowing function, please consult a medical specialist for examination and testing.
records.tags_raw: swallowing disorder, dysphagia, aspiration, swallowing rehabilitation, diet modification, stroke, swallowing test, fever, feeling hot, high fever, low-grade fever, dry cough, minor cough, persistent cough

sections.heading: Definition and Risks
sections.content:
Dysphagia (swallowing disorder) is a condition in which there is a problem with the ability to swallow food or drink. It can occur for various reasons, including stroke, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease), dementia, and after surgery or radiation therapy for head and neck cancer.

The main risk is 'aspiration.' Aspiration means that food or liquid enters the airway (the passage for breathing) instead of the esophagus. Repeated aspiration may lead to aspiration pneumonia. There is also 'silent aspiration,' in which aspiration occurs without the person noticing.

sections.heading: Dietary Modification
sections.content:
When dysphagia is present, it is important to adjust the texture of food and the thickness of liquids. The appropriate diet texture should be decided based on test results and a medical specialist's prescription.

· Food texture: Stages are set in this order: smooth puréed food → minced food → soft bite-sized food → regular diet.

· Liquid thickness: Viscosity (the degree of thickness) is adjusted from thin liquids like water to thick liquids like honey or pudding. When the risk of aspiration is high, it may be safer to thicken liquids with a thickening agent, as prescribed.

· Foods that require caution: Foods that mix solids and liquids, such as rice soup (gukbap) and seaweed soup (miyeokguk), crumbly foods such as crackers and dried seaweed sheets, and tough meat require caution. Food that has been blended and thinned in a blender may also raise the risk of aspiration.

Do not change the food texture on your own. Please follow the medical specialist's prescription.

sections.heading: How to Eat
sections.content:
· Posture: Sit upright with a straight back at a 90-degree angle while eating.

· Pace and amount: Start with about one teaspoon (about 5 mL) per bite. If food remains in the mouth or throat after a swallow, swallow again (a dry swallow) before trying the next bite.

· Meal time: It is best to finish a meal within 30 minutes. If mealtimes become very long, swallowing function may have changed, so please tell your medical specialist.

· Avoid talking while eating, as it increases the risk of coughing, choking, and aspiration.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation
sections.content:
Rehabilitation for dysphagia involves more than diet modification alone. A variety of treatments carried out together by a rehabilitation medicine physician and therapists are used in combination.

· Orofacial exercises: Exercises that increase the strength and range of motion of the muscles of the lips, tongue, jaw, and pharynx.

· Shaker exercise: Lie flat on your back on the floor, keep your shoulders on the floor, and lift only your head to look at your toes. It strengthens the muscles that lift the larynx (the voice box, a cartilage structure in the neck) when swallowing.

· Electrical stimulation therapy, neuromodulation therapy, and other treatments may be added depending on the patient's condition.

Please carry out all treatments and exercises under the guidance of a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Criteria for Returning to a Regular Diet
sections.content:
To return to a regular diet, all of the following criteria should be met.

· There should be no signs of aspiration on an objective test such as a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS).

· There should be no symptoms such as choking, coughing, fever, or aspiration pneumonia.

· The person should be able to take in the needed calories and fluids safely and maintain body weight.

Switching to a regular diet simply because you feel 'fine' can be risky. Please be sure to follow the decision of your medical specialist.

records.title: Biological Age and Health Age
records.intro: Biological age is an estimate of the degree of aging, expressed as a number, based on health indicators such as blood pressure, blood glucose, and liver function. Health age is an age that reflects health risk factors such as lifestyle habits and family history. Neither measure is a definitive diagnostic tool, but both can be used to motivate people to adopt healthier lifestyle habits.
records.tags_raw: biological age, health age, physiological age, aging, health checkup, lifestyle habits, metabolism, health risk assessment

sections.heading: What Are Biological Age and Health Age?
sections.content:
■ Biological Age
Biological age is not your chronological age (the age on your official records). It is an age that expresses the degree of aging as a number, calculated with a statistical formula from health indicators such as blood pressure, blood glucose, hormones, blood fats (lipids), waist circumference, body mass index, kidney function, and liver function. For example, if your actual age is 52 but your biological age is 55, it may mean that aging is progressing faster than in people of the same age.

■ Health Age
Health age is an age that combines health risk factors (lifestyle habits such as smoking and exercise, measurements such as blood pressure, and medical history including family history) to show 'how old the group of people with the same level of health risk as me is.' It also presents a 'target age' that could be achieved if all correctable risk factors were improved.

■ Differences
- Biological age: Focuses on blood test values → motivates management of values such as blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol
- Health age: Focuses on lifestyle → communicates the effects of lifestyle changes in an easy-to-understand way

sections.heading: Lifestyle Guidelines for Improving Biological Age
sections.content:
■ Diet
- Eat a balanced diet and eat less salt
- Eat more vegetables and fruits and less refined sugar

■ Exercise
- Do a good mix of aerobic exercise, strength training, stretching, and balance exercises.

■ Lifestyle Habits
- Get enough sleep and manage stress
- Quit smoking and drink less alcohol (or abstain)
- Maintain an appropriate weight

■ Drug Therapy
Do not hold on to the mistaken belief that 'once you start taking medication, you have to take it for life.' For blood pressure, blood sugar, and hyperlipidemia, medication at the dose your doctor prescribes should be taken consistently, together with exercise and dietary control. Please do not start, stop, or change medication on your own; consult your doctor.

It is advisable to have regular health checkups at a reliable facility and to do so while consulting a regular doctor.

sections.heading: Limitations and Proper Understanding
sections.content:
Neither biological age nor health age is a definitive diagnostic tool, and both have a margin of error of about 1 to 2 years.

- Do not treat good results in other indicators as a 'free pass' for specific bad habits (smoking, heavy drinking).
- Predictions may differ depending on an individual's genetic predisposition and environmental factors.
- Health age has lower predictive power in very young age groups or when several diseases coexist.
- If you have symptoms or a family history that are not included in the indicators, consulting a doctor is even more important.

In conclusion, rather than fixating on the numbers, it is more important to consult a doctor and start improving right away the areas that need management in your own health status, such as blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol.

records.title: Tongue Cancer
records.intro: Tongue cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the tongue and accounts for about 10 to 15% of all head and neck cancers. Because early symptoms resemble those of stomatitis (mouth sores), it is often left untreated and found late. Treatment outcomes tend to be better when the cancer is detected early, so if you have a sore on the tongue that does not heal or a lump you can feel, please consult a medical specialist without delay.
records.tags_raw: tongue cancer, oral cancer, head and neck cancer, squamous cell carcinoma, smoking, human papillomavirus, HPV, tongue ulcer, glossectomy, flap reconstruction, nausea, feeling like vomiting, vomiting

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Tongue cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the tongue. More than 90% of people with tongue cancer have squamous cell carcinoma (cancer that arises from the flat cell layer), and because the tongue is rich in lymphatic vessels, metastasis (spread of cancer to other sites) can occur early.



■ Major Risk Factors

- Smoking: The biggest risk factor. The risk is even higher when combined with alcohol consumption.

- Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection

- Repeated irritation from old, poorly fitting dentures or sharp teeth

- Radiation exposure, nutritional deficiency, and genetic predisposition

sections.heading: Symptoms and Diagnosis
sections.content:
Tongue cancer causes relatively noticeable symptoms, but they are often dismissed in the early stage. If you have any of the symptoms below, be sure to consult a medical specialist.



■ Main Symptoms

- An ulcer (sore) on the tongue that does not heal for several weeks or longer

- Swelling of the tongue or a lump that can be felt

- Persistent pain or discomfort when swallowing

- Repeated unexplained bleeding in the mouth

- A lump that can be felt in the neck



Tongue cancer mainly develops on the sides and underside of the tongue and is uncommon at the tip.



■ Diagnosis

Diagnosis begins with visual inspection and palpation (examination by touch), and is confirmed with imaging tests such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound and with a biopsy (a test in which a small piece of tissue is removed and examined under a microscope).

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Surgery

For early-stage (stage 1 and 2) lesions, surgery alone may be effective. Advanced (stage 3 and 4) lesions are often treated with a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.



During surgery, the cancer is removed with a sufficient safety margin around it, and partial or complete removal is performed as needed. The lymph nodes of the neck are often removed at the same time.



■ Tongue Reconstruction

When a large part of the tongue has been removed, the tongue is reconstructed with a 'flap reconstruction' using skin and blood vessels from areas such as the thigh, wrist, or back, in order to help preserve speech and swallowing function.



■ Radiation Therapy and Chemotherapy

Radiation therapy or chemotherapy may be given after surgery or instead of surgery.

sections.heading: Postoperative Complications and Rehabilitation
sections.content:
■ Main Complications

- Reduced speech and swallowing function: This is the most common complication. Speech therapy and swallowing exercises can help recovery.

- Scarring at the flap donor site

- Neck and shoulder discomfort

- Side effects of chemotherapy: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, hair loss, mouth sores, and others

- After radiation therapy: The risk of dental caries (cavities) is higher, so careful oral care is needed.



■ Regular Follow-Up

Because lymph node metastasis is common in tongue cancer, regular follow-up is essential even after surgery. Even in the early stage, the cancer may recur, so regular checkups should be continued for at least 5 years after treatment.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
■ Prevention

- Quitting smoking and drinking less alcohol are the most important steps.

- Limit strongly flavored or irritating foods and maintain thorough oral hygiene.

- If dentures do not fit well or repeated sores develop in the mouth, see a dentist early.

- Adults aged 40 or older who smoke or drink are recommended to have a regular oral examination once a year.

records.title: Adult Vaccination
records.intro: As people age, their immune defenses against infectious diseases weaken, so vaccination is important. To get the right vaccines for your own health condition, please consult an infectious disease specialist before being vaccinated.
records.tags_raw: vaccination, influenza, pneumonia, herpes zoster (shingles), immunity

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content: Adults aged 65 and older are advised to receive influenza and pneumonia (pneumococcal) vaccines. Adults aged 50 and older are advised to receive the shingles vaccine, and it is advisable to receive a tetanus booster every 10 years.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: Even if you were vaccinated as a child, the body's ability to fight germs gradually weakens over time. In addition, adults and older people are at a higher risk of serious complications when they catch an infectious disease.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Live attenuated vaccines (vaccines made from weakened live germs) may actually cause illness in people whose immune systems are greatly weakened, such as people with cancer, and they are generally not recommended during pregnancy. Be sure to consult your doctor before receiving one.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A vaccine, usually given as an injection, helps the body build up defenses (immunity) against germs before you become ill. It is important not only for children but also for adults and older people.

records.title: Obesity Treatment in Adults
records.intro: Obesity is a chronic disease caused by multiple factors, including an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure, genetics, environment, and lifestyle habits. Like high blood pressure and diabetes mellitus, it needs ongoing management through education, counseling, diet, exercise, and drug therapy. Please consult a medical specialist before deciding on a treatment method.
records.tags_raw: obesity treatment, diet therapy, exercise therapy, food diary, calories, protein, appetite suppressants, anti-obesity medication, weight loss, yo-yo effect, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason

sections.heading: Principles of Obesity Treatment
sections.content:
Obesity is assessed by BMI (body mass index) = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². In Korea, overweight is defined as a BMI of 23 to 24.9 kg/m² and obesity as a BMI of 25 kg/m² or higher. A waist circumference of 90 cm or more in men or 85 cm or more in women is considered abdominal obesity.



In cases of pregnancy, unstable psychiatric illness, anorexia nervosa, terminal illness, gallstones, or osteoporosis, weight loss should be avoided or approached with caution. Before treatment begins, secondary obesity (obesity caused by another disease or medication) is first ruled out.



One of the most important factors in obesity treatment is the patient's own motivation.

sections.heading: Dietary Therapy
sections.content:
Losing 1 kg of body weight generally requires an energy deficit of roughly 7,000 kcal. Adjusting your diet is generally a faster and easier approach than exercise.



■ Key Principle: Cut Calories Without Feeling Hungry

Reduce calories while maintaining fullness by choosing foods with low energy density (vegetables, fruits, and protein foods).



■ How to Eat

- Eat three meals a day in reduced portions, and use low-calorie snacks between meals.

- Snack examples: cherry tomatoes, cucumbers, milk, eggs, and chicken breast

- Increase protein intake (to maintain fullness and help prevent muscle loss).

- Alcohol is high in calories and weakens self-control, so it is best to avoid it while dieting.



■ Food Diary

Keeping a food diary that records what you eat each day is a method that has been shown to help with weight loss.

sections.heading: Exercise Therapy and Drug Therapy
sections.content:
■ Exercise

For the first month, it is advisable to get used to dietary changes first and then start exercising gradually. Starting to exercise right away may increase appetite and make dietary control more difficult.

- If the goal is weight control, swimming and cycling, which are easier on the joints, are recommended.

- To increase muscle mass, combine strength training with aerobic exercise.

- Exercise at least 3 times a week for at least 20 minutes each time.

- For weight control and prevention of chronic lifestyle-related diseases, increase your activity level steadily every day.



■ Drug Therapy

Medication is used as a supplement to diet and exercise therapy. If weight loss is less than 2 kg after 3 to 4 months of treatment, the medication may not be effective for that person. Medication alone is unlikely to provide long-term effects, and the effects can be maintained only when diet and exercise control are continued together.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Health Effects of Holding Urine and Stool
records.intro: In service jobs and some other occupations, it can be difficult to use the restroom freely because of the nature of the work. Repeatedly holding urine or stool for long periods may cause various problems in bladder, urinary tract, and digestive health. If you often have to hold urine or stool, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: What Problems Can Occur If You Hold Urine for a Long Time?
sections.content: The bladder is a balloon-like organ that stores urine. Holding urine for a long time may overstretch the bladder and weaken its ability to contract. If the bladder is not emptied regularly, bacteria can multiply more easily, which increases the risk of cystitis or a urinary tract infection (an infection in which bacteria enter the passage that urine flows through and cause inflammation). If you have symptoms such as pain during urination, frequent urination, or a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying (the sense that urine remains even after urinating), please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Problems Caused by Reduced Fluid Intake
sections.content: Some people deliberately drink less water to avoid going to the restroom often. Intentionally holding urine so that you urinate only 2 to 3 times a day is called 'delayed voiding syndrome.' Reduced fluid intake may lead to kidney stones (stones that form in the kidney), urinary tract infection, and lower urinary tract symptoms (such as difficulty urinating and a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying). Dehydration may also cause fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and headache. If you have questions about how much fluid is appropriate for you, please talk with a medical specialist.

sections.heading: What Problems Can Occur If You Hold Stool for a Long Time?
sections.content: The habit of frequently holding stool may cause constipation, chronic abdominal pain, and irritable bowel syndrome (a condition in which the bowel becomes sensitive and abdominal pain, diarrhea, and constipation occur repeatedly). Over time, it may become a risk factor for hemorrhoids (a condition in which the blood vessels around the anus become swollen, commonly called piles). In addition, eating quickly may cause indigestion and reflux esophagitis (a condition in which stomach acid flows back into the esophagus, causing heartburn and pain). If abdominal pain, bloody stool, or constipation persists, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention and Precautions
sections.content:
· It is best not to hold urine or stool, and to use the restroom as soon as you need to.

· Maintain an appropriate daily fluid intake.

· It is important for workplaces to provide sufficient break time and access to restrooms.

· If you are concerned about urination habits or digestive symptoms, please talk with a medical specialist.

· If unusual symptoms persist, be sure to consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Childhood Obesity
records.intro: Childhood obesity is a condition in which excess body fat accumulates in children and adolescents. It may continue into adulthood and increases the risk of high blood pressure, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. Early management is important, especially at younger ages. Please talk with a medical specialist and follow a plan that combines dietary changes, exercise, and lifestyle improvements.
records.tags_raw: childhood obesity, adolescent obesity, pediatric metabolic syndrome, growth, weight management, eating habits, exercise, loose stools, watery diarrhea, frequent bathroom visits

sections.heading: Definition and Risks
sections.content:
Childhood obesity is a condition in which a child has excess body fat compared with peers of the same age and sex.



When childhood obesity persists, it often continues into adulthood. The following problems may also occur.

· Final adult height may be shorter than that of peers.

· Metabolic abnormalities, such as increased blood pressure and hyperlipidemia, may develop.

· It may progress to 'pediatric metabolic syndrome,' in which diabetes, high blood pressure, and hyperlipidemia occur together.

· Psychological stress or difficulties in relationships with peers may occur.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The main causes of childhood obesity include the following.



· Irregular eating habits: going to bed late and waking up late, skipping meals, or frequently eating delivery food or fast food

· Lack of exercise: reduced physical activity and more time spent sitting

· Increased use of smart devices: reduced movement while looking at screens for long periods

· Stress: overeating high-calorie foods because of stress

· Genetic factors and endocrine disorders may also be causes.



In addition to eating and lifestyle habits, obesity may be related to endocrine or genetic disorders. It is important to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Management
sections.content:
The basics of childhood obesity management are dietary changes, exercise, and lifestyle improvement.



· Meals: Eat regularly at set times. Reduce carbohydrate intake, eat an appropriate amount of protein, and cut back on delivery food and late-night snacks. During the growing years, a balanced diet is more important than extreme dietary restriction.

· Exercise: Stay as active as possible when not sitting. Do indoor exercise, such as climbing stairs and jumping rope, consistently.

· Sleep: Keep regular bedtimes and wake-up times.

· Family involvement: It is effective when parents set an example and the whole family practices healthy lifestyle habits together.



If needed, drug therapy may be used together with these measures, at the judgment of a medical specialist. It is important to start weight management early in childhood and to maintain it consistently.

sections.heading: Drug Therapy
sections.content:
Medications used to treat obesity must be used according to a medical specialist's prescription.



· Orlistat (brand name: Xenical): A medication that reduces the absorption of fat from food, thereby lowering calorie intake. It is considered relatively safe, but gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea may occur. Long-term use may also reduce the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (such as vitamins D and E), so caution is needed.

· GLP-1 analogs (e.g., liraglutide [brand name: Saxenda]): These medications reduce appetite and are used to treat obesity. Long-term data are not yet sufficient, and the effect lasts only while the medication is being taken.



Please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions about drug therapy.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
The following methods can be used for weight management.



· Adjusting dinner portions: Weigh yourself before dinner, and if your weight is higher than the day before, reduce the amount of rice by half.

· Controlling snacks: Up to 2 snacks a day are allowed, only between breakfast and lunch and between lunch and dinner. Limit snacks to about half a piece of fruit or one cup of low-fat milk (about 50 kilocalories).

· No late-night eating: Do not eat anything other than water after 8 p.m.

· Aerobic exercise: Do at least 30 minutes of aerobic exercise every day, and do not eat a snack after exercise.



Recording daily meals, snacks, late-night eating, and exercise in a weight diary can help build habits.



Some people skip a meal entirely to lose weight, but this can lead to overeating at the next meal. Skipping breakfast may also reduce the glucose supply to the brain, which may lower concentration and function. Eating small portions regularly three times a day is a better approach over the long term.



Low-carbohydrate, high-fat diets are generally not recommended for adolescents. Some studies suggest a short-term weight-loss effect, but there is not yet enough research on long-term effects and side effects. If other dietary approaches have not worked, this diet may be tried only after consulting a medical specialist.



Extreme dieting may lead to serious health problems such as nutritional deficiency, amenorrhea, and decreased muscle strength. Please lose weight only under the guidance of a medical specialist.



The yo-yo effect refers to regaining the original weight after losing weight. Many studies report that the yo-yo effect is difficult to avoid completely.



To reduce the yo-yo effect, it is important to keep up a healthy diet and exercise routine over the long term, even after short-term weight loss.



Obesity can be influenced by genetics, but children also tend to adopt their parents' eating habits and lifestyle, which can be a major contributing factor. One of the most effective approaches to prevention is for the whole family to practice healthy eating habits and an active lifestyle consistently. Forming a new habit can take two months or more. Parents and children are encouraged to make consistent efforts together.

records.title: Temporomandibular Joint Disorders in Children
records.intro: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is the jaw joint located in front of the ear. When this joint has a problem, symptoms such as pain around the jaw or noises when opening the mouth may occur. These disorders can also occur in children and adolescents. If you have symptoms, please consult a dental specialist.
records.tags_raw: temporomandibular joint, jaw joint, bruxism, jaw pain, splint, occlusal stabilization appliance, pediatric dentistry, TMJ disc displacement

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Temporomandibular joint disorders may cause the following symptoms.
· Pain around the jaw or in front of the ear
· Clicking sounds or a catching sensation when opening or closing the mouth
· Difficulty opening the mouth
· Stiffness or tiredness in the muscles around the jaw upon waking in the morning
If you have any of these symptoms, please consult a dental specialist.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Factors that may contribute to temporomandibular joint disorders include the following.
· Bruxism: a habit of grinding or clenching the teeth, mainly during sleep
· Chewing on only one side
· Nail-biting
· Frequently eating hard, tough foods
These habits place excessive force on the jaw joint and surrounding muscles and may contribute to temporomandibular joint disorders.

sections.heading: What Is the Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ)?
sections.content: The temporomandibular joint is the jaw joint used for chewing food and speaking. Inside the joint is a small, cushion-like structure called a disc, which helps the jaw move smoothly. Problems with this disc or with the surrounding muscles may lead to temporomandibular joint disorders.

sections.heading: Treatment and Prevention
sections.content: An occlusal stabilization appliance (splint) is often used to treat temporomandibular joint disorders. A splint is a device worn in the mouth that can help protect the teeth from grinding, relax the jaw muscles, and support proper disc position. It is usually used for about 2 to 3 months. If temporomandibular joint disorders are left untreated for a long time, changes to the jaw joint or disc that are difficult to reverse may occur. For prevention, it is helpful to develop the habit of chewing evenly on both sides and to reduce hard, tough foods. If you grind your teeth, please consult a dental specialist.

records.title: Urinary Tract Infection in Children
records.intro: A young child who has a fever without cough or runny nose may have a urinary tract infection. If treatment is delayed, the kidneys may be damaged, so be sure to consult a pediatric specialist.
records.tags_raw: urinary tract infection, pediatric fever, bacterial infection, antibiotics, emergency room, fever, feeling hot, high fever, low-grade fever, dry cough, minor cough, cough that will not stop, stuffy nose, clear runny nose, yellow runny nose

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A urinary tract infection is a condition in which bacteria enter parts of the urinary tract, such as the kidneys and bladder, where urine is produced and passes out of the body, and cause inflammation.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Adults can tell when urination is painful, but infants and young children who wear diapers often have only a fever, with no other symptoms.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: Bacteria enter the body through the urethra (the opening through which urine leaves the body), travel upward, and cause inflammation.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: After the bacteria are identified through a urine test, treatment is given with an appropriate antibiotic, either taken by mouth or given by injection. Early and appropriate treatment may allow recovery without complications.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If a child with a fever becomes limp and listless, or if the amount of urine decreases throughout the day, it may be a sign of a serious condition such as sepsis. If left untreated, the kidneys may be permanently damaged. Seek immediate medical attention at an emergency room.

records.title: Key Symptoms in Pediatric Emergencies
records.intro: When a child suddenly becomes ill, it can be difficult to decide whether to go to the emergency room right away or to wait and see a local clinic. Unlike adults, children can worsen quickly, so if your child looks or acts differently from usual, do not hesitate to seek medical care.
