sections.heading: Fever
sections.content:
Fever is not a disease in itself but a symptom. How long the fever lasts is more important than how high it is. If a fever lasts a day or two, it can be observed, but if it lasts 3 days or longer, you should visit a pediatrician.



Go to the emergency room right away, even at night or on a holiday, in the following cases:

· Fever with a seizure (convulsion)

· Fever with fussiness or listlessness, or a generally poor condition

· Fever in an infant younger than 3 months: at this age, the likelihood of a bacterial infection such as a urinary tract infection, bloodstream infection, or meningitis is higher.

sections.heading: Vomiting and Diarrhea
sections.content:
When a child suddenly vomits or has diarrhea, acute gastroenteritis is often the cause. The most important thing to watch for is dehydration. Signs of dehydration include weight loss, reduced skin elasticity, dry mouth, decreased urine output, and altered consciousness.



Go to the emergency room in the following cases:

· Signs of dehydration are present

· Vomiting continues and the child cannot eat or drink anything (this can progress quickly to dehydration)

· Severe abdominal pain is present

· Bloody stool (stool mixed with blood) is seen

sections.heading: Falls
sections.content:
It can be hard to tell whether an emergency room visit is needed when a child has fallen from a bed or sofa.



If all of the following apply, the likelihood of an intracranial (inside the head) injury is lower, but please still have the child examined at a nearby hospital:

· The fall was from a height of less than 1 m

· There was no loss of consciousness, vomiting, or severe fussiness

· There is no wound on the head

· The child is behaving as usual



Go to the emergency room immediately in the following cases:

· The fall was from a height of 1 m or more

· There is a large scalp hematoma (bruise) anywhere other than the forehead

· The child fell onto a hard floor

· The fall was not witnessed

· The child has vomited 3 or more times

· There is loss of consciousness, or the child behaves differently from usual

sections.heading: Rash and Hives
sections.content:
For most rashes, a visit to a local pediatrician is sufficient.



However, if hives appear together with any of the following, go to the emergency room immediately. This may be an early sign of anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction), which can lead to difficulty breathing or loss of consciousness.

· Swelling of the face, arms, or legs

· Cough, vomiting, or abdominal pain

· A rash that appears suddenly and progressively worsens

sections.heading: Cough, Chest Pain, and Lethargy
sections.content:
■ Cough

Cough has many possible causes, and in most cases a visit to a pediatrician is appropriate. However, go to the emergency room if the child has difficulty breathing or is breathing faster than usual. These may be signs of conditions such as laryngitis, bronchiolitis, or asthma, which need prompt treatment.



■ Chest Pain

Among children and adolescents with chest pain, the heart is the cause in only about 5% of cases. Growing pains, musculoskeletal pain, and gastrointestinal conditions are more common causes. However, go to the emergency room in the following cases:

· Pain that lasts several minutes or longer

· Sudden, severe pain that wakes the child from sleep

· Chest pain accompanied by fever or palpitations

· Chest pain that occurs during exercise



■ Lethargy (Listlessness)

A child who is unusually listless for no clear reason, or who has a decreased level of consciousness, is showing a very dangerous sign. Possible causes include hypoglycemia, dehydration, seizures, breathing problems caused by a foreign body, and acute myocarditis. Call 119 immediately and go to the emergency room.



■ A Note to Parents

Parents know their child best. Even if medical criteria are not met, please go to the emergency room if your child looks or acts very differently from usual. Whether the child is eating well, playing well, and passing stool and urine normally is an important thing to watch. If any one of these three is different from usual, please seek medical care.

records.title: Otitis Media in Children
records.intro: If a child complains of ear pain or has trouble hearing after a cold, it may be otitis media. Because hearing development can be affected, please be sure to consult an ENT specialist.
records.tags_raw: otitis media, ear pain, hearing loss, common cold, pediatric otitis media, stuffy nose, clear runny nose, yellow runny nose, blurry vision, difficulty seeing, hazy vision, cannot hear, difficulty hearing

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Otitis media is a condition in which bacteria enter the middle ear, the space behind the eardrum, causing inflammation or a buildup of fluid. It commonly occurs in children who have a cold.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: In children, the tube connecting the ear and nose (the Eustachian tube) is short and flat, so cold viruses or bacteria in nasal mucus can easily pass into the ear.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: In acute otitis media, there is fever and severe ear pain. In contrast, otitis media with effusion, in which only fluid has collected, may not cause ear pain but can make sounds seem muffled and difficult to hear.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: When bacteria are the cause, antibiotics are taken to treat the infection. If fluid does not drain for a long time and hearing is affected, surgery to place a small drainage tube (tympanostomy tube) in the eardrum may be performed.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: After tube placement surgery, be careful for about a week not to blow your nose forcefully or let water get into the ear.

records.title: Orthodontic Treatment for Children
records.intro: In childhood, teeth that are misaligned or an upper and lower bite that does not fit together properly can make chewing uncomfortable and cause problems with speech. They can also affect facial growth. If you suspect your child has a dental problem, please consult a dental specialist.
records.tags_raw: orthodontics, pediatric dentistry, anterior crossbite, underbite, maxillary constriction, permanent teeth, primary teeth, mouth breathing, facial asymmetry

sections.heading: When Orthodontic Treatment May Be Needed
sections.content:
Orthodontic treatment may be needed in the following cases:
· Habits such as thumb sucking, mouth breathing, or tongue thrusting (pushing the tongue forward)
· Front teeth that bite in reverse (anterior crossbite): the lower front teeth sit in front of the upper front teeth when the teeth come together. If left untreated, this can lead to the jaw growing into an underbite.
· Chewing on one side only: if the upper jaw is narrow, a child may twist the lower jaw to one side to chew. If this continues for a long time, the face may grow asymmetrically.
· Primary or permanent teeth that do not erupt symmetrically on the left and right: if one side is delayed by 3 months or more, an examination is needed.

sections.heading: Habits to Watch For and Prevention
sections.content:
The following habits can affect the development of the teeth and jaw, so caution is needed:
· Thumb sucking
· Mouth breathing: if rhinitis is severe, an ENT evaluation may also be needed.
· Tongue thrusting
If your child has any of these habits, please consult a dentist. It is advisable to check the growth of the teeth and jaw through regular dental checkups.

sections.heading: Timing and Duration of Orthodontic Treatment
sections.content: Orthodontic treatment can take as little as 6 months or as long as 1 to 2 years, depending on the patient's condition. For anterior crossbite (reverse bite of the front teeth), the ideal time for treatment is in the first or second grade of elementary school (ages 7 to 8). Treatment at this age may help guide jaw growth, establish a normal bite, and improve the shape of the face. For problems such as chewing on one side because of a narrow upper jaw, it is advisable to identify the cause and begin treatment as soon as the problem is noticed. If permanent teeth are missing from birth, a treatment plan for after growth is complete should be made in advance. Please consult a dental specialist about the exact timing and method of treatment.

sections.heading: Problems That May Occur If Left Untreated
sections.content: If misaligned teeth or bite problems are not treated, chewing and speech may be affected. Facial growth can be affected, which may lead to facial asymmetry or growth of an underbite. A child may also lose self-confidence because of the appearance of their teeth. In anterior crossbite, constant strain on the lower front teeth can damage the gums.

records.title: Syncope in Children and Adolescents
records.intro: Syncope is a temporary loss of consciousness that occurs when blood pressure drops suddenly and blood flow to the brain is briefly reduced. It is commonly called fainting. It occurs more often in adolescents and older adults, and caution is needed because injuries can occur when a person falls. Because there are many possible causes, if syncope occurs, please consult a medical specialist to identify the exact cause.
records.tags_raw: syncope, fainting, adolescents, hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, reflex syncope, children, arrhythmia, feverish, having a fever, high fever, low-grade fever, fever, collapsing, loss of consciousness, passing out, racing heart, pounding heart, rapid pulse, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent trips to the bathroom

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness that occurs when blood pressure drops suddenly and blood flow to the brain is temporarily reduced. It is commonly called fainting. In most cases, the person recovers on their own within several seconds to several minutes. However, if the person strikes surrounding objects or hits their head on the floor while falling, injuries such as fractures and bleeding can occur, which is dangerous.



It occurs more often in adolescents and older adults, and it is more common in girls than in boys.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Warning symptoms like the following often occur before syncope:

· Sudden nausea and a feeling of weakness throughout the body

· A feeling of muffled hearing

· Vision turning black or white

· Cold sweats



If these symptoms appear, it is safer to sit or lie down on the floor right away. If loss of consciousness lasts longer than several seconds to several minutes, or if convulsions occur with the fall, call 119 immediately.

sections.heading: Causes and Types
sections.content:
Syncope has many possible causes. In adolescents and young adults, the following causes are common:



· Reflex (neurally mediated) syncope: the most common type. It occurs when the autonomic nervous system reacts by widening blood vessels or slowing the heart rate. The autonomic nervous system is the part of the nervous system that automatically regulates blood pressure and heart rate. It tends to occur after standing or sitting for a long time, taking a long hot bath, or seeing blood or a frightening scene.

· Orthostatic hypotension: a drop in blood pressure when standing up suddenly. It can be caused by fever, diarrhea, dehydration, and other conditions.

· Cardiac syncope: a type caused by a heart abnormality (such as an arrhythmia or congenital heart disease). It is less common but can be life-threatening, so caution is needed.



Because identifying the cause is important, if syncope occurs, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The most important part of diagnosing syncope is taking a detailed medical history of when and under what circumstances it occurred. The following tests may be performed at the hospital:

· Blood tests: to check for anemia, hypoglycemia, electrolyte abnormalities, and other problems

· Electrocardiogram (ECG): a test that checks for abnormalities in the heart rhythm

· Chest X-ray



If syncope recurs or occurs under special circumstances, the following tests may be added:

· Echocardiogram: checks the structure and function of the heart

· Head-up tilt table test: a test that checks changes in blood pressure and pulse with changes in position

· 24-hour ECG monitoring, brain MRI, EEG (electroencephalogram), and others



The specific tests will be determined by your treating physician.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment of syncope depends on the cause.

· When warning symptoms appear, immediately take a safe position (sitting or lying down) to prevent injury.

· If there is a triggering cause such as a cold, diarrhea, or anemia, the underlying condition is treated.

· If syncope occurs in a specific situation, avoid that situation.

· If lifestyle changes do not lead to improvement, or if low blood pressure persists, medication may be considered.



Please discuss treatment options thoroughly with your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention and When to See a Doctor
sections.content:
The following lifestyle habits can help prevent syncope:

· Regular exercise: lower-body strength training and aerobic exercise (cycling, jogging, jumping rope, etc.) are recommended.

· Keep a regular sleep schedule and eat breakfast.

· Get enough fluids and an appropriate amount of salt.

· Avoid taking long hot showers.



Please be sure to visit a hospital in the following cases:

· Sudden collapse without any warning symptoms

· Palpitations or pain accompany the episode

· It occurs during exercise or while lying down

· There is a history of heart or neurological disease

· A family member died suddenly at a young age or was diagnosed with an arrhythmia

records.title: Neurogenic Bladder
records.intro: Neurogenic bladder is a condition in which a problem in the nervous system, such as the brain, spinal cord, or peripheral nerves, prevents the bladder from storing or emptying urine properly. Symptoms are often mild at first and easy to overlook, but without treatment, serious complications such as urinary tract infection and kidney failure can occur. If you have an underlying condition such as stroke or diabetes mellitus, please have your bladder function checked regularly.
records.tags_raw: neurogenic bladder, overactive bladder, urinary incontinence, residual urine, bladder function, stroke, Parkinson's disease, diabetes mellitus, urodynamic study, clean intermittent catheterization

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
- Medication: the most basic treatment. If started early, the condition may be managed without major complications.
- Clean intermittent catheterization: when bladder muscle function is reduced and a large amount of urine remains in the bladder, a thin tube (catheter) is used to empty the bladder at set intervals.
- Botulinum toxin (Botox) injection into the bladder: used when the bladder is very overactive and cannot be controlled with medication. It can help calm the overactive bladder muscle.

If left untreated, serious complications such as recurrent urinary tract infections, urinary stones, and kidney failure can develop. Early detection and treatment are important.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Normal urination requires two processes to work smoothly: the bladder storing urine and the bladder emptying urine. These processes depend on the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, and urethral sphincter working together in coordination.

Neurogenic bladder refers to a condition in which a problem in any part of this nerve pathway makes it difficult to control urination. Just as a stroke (a condition in which a blood vessel in the brain is blocked or ruptures) can affect the nerves that control the bladder, various types of nerve damage can interfere with normal bladder function.

■ Main Causes
- Past: congenital abnormalities of the spinal cord, spinal disc problems, and spinal cord injury from trauma
- Recently increasing causes: age-related brain disorders such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, and dementia, and complications of diabetes mellitus

The incidence increases with age. In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, symptoms can be more severe, and the condition can worsen urinary incontinence in women.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms of neurogenic bladder vary depending on the location and extent of the nerve damage.

■ Overactive Bladder Symptoms (when the bladder contracts excessively)
- Frequent urges to urinate that are hard to hold back
- Frequent waking at night to urinate
- A sudden urge to urinate, sometimes leading to leakage of urine

■ Difficulty Urinating (when bladder function is reduced)
- Difficulty passing urine
- A strong sense of incomplete emptying after urination
- Acute urinary retention, a sudden complete inability to urinate, can occur

In the early stages, symptoms are mild and easy to overlook.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
■ Diagnosis
- A detailed medical history and physical examination
- Urodynamic study: a test that accurately evaluates bladder function by measuring changes in pressure inside the bladder and urination patterns.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
■ Treating the Underlying Condition
Appropriate treatment for the underlying condition, such as stroke, diabetes mellitus, or Parkinson's disease, should be provided at the same time.

■ Lifestyle Guidelines
- Limit caffeine, carbonated drinks, and alcohol.
- Drink an appropriate amount of fluid each day.
- Reduce fluid intake after dinner to help prevent nocturia.

■ Regular Checkups
If you are being treated for a condition that carries a high risk of neurogenic bladder, such as cerebrovascular disease or diabetes mellitus, it is advisable to have your bladder function evaluated regularly by a urologist even if you have no symptoms.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
records.intro: Noise-induced hearing loss is a condition in which hearing is damaged by loud, sustained sound exposure. It once occurred mainly in industrial workplaces, but it is now increasing among teenagers and young adults as the use of personal audio devices such as earphones grows. There is currently no treatment that restores hearing once it has been damaged, so prevention is most important. If your hearing declines or you develop tinnitus, please consult an ENT specialist.
records.tags_raw: noise-induced hearing loss, earphones, tinnitus, cochlea, hearing damage, noise, hearing, headphones, double vision, overlapping images, ringing in the ear, noise in the ear, cannot hear, difficulty hearing

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Noise-induced hearing loss is hearing loss caused by exposure to loud sound. When sound enters the ear, it exerts a physical impact on the cochlea (the organ in the inner ear that detects sound). The stronger and longer this impact, the more the sensory cells that detect sound are damaged. When these sensory cells are damaged, the ability to hear declines.



According to one study conducted in Korea, hearing tests of 2,879 middle and high school students found noise-induced hearing loss in 17.2%. As earphone use has increased, noise-induced hearing loss has also been increasing among adolescents.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Sound loudness is expressed in a unit called the decibel (dB). Typical sound levels around us are as follows:



· Everyday conversation: 50–60 dB

· Subway: 80 dB

· Car horn: 110 dB

· Concert venue: 120 dB



In general, sounds of 75 dB or below do not cause hearing loss. Sounds of 85 dB or above can have a harmful effect on hearing.



Under Korea's Occupational Safety and Health Act, an environment in which noise of 85 dB or higher occurs over an 8-hour workday is defined as "noise work." For every 5 dB increase in noise, the permissible exposure time is cut in half. The louder the noise, the shorter the exposure time should be.



When you use earphones in a noisy environment (such as a subway or an internet café), you tend to raise the volume because of the surrounding noise. This puts greater stress on the cochlea. Earphones with noise-canceling features reduce surrounding noise so that you can listen at a lower volume, which may help prevent noise-induced hearing loss. Bone-conduction earphones, on the other hand, differ only in how sound is delivered; the intensity of sound reaching the cochlea is similar, so they do not offer much preventive benefit.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Noise-induced hearing loss progresses gradually, so it is often overlooked in the early stages. The following symptoms may occur:



· Difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds

· Frequently asking others to repeat themselves

· Particular difficulty following conversation in noisy places

· Tinnitus (a ringing or humming sound in the ear) may develop

· A feeling of muffled hearing may occur



If hearing temporarily declines or tinnitus develops right after exposure to loud sound, this may be an early sign of noise-induced hearing loss.

sections.heading: Treatment and Prevention
sections.content:
Currently, there is no treatment that restores hearing once noise-induced hearing loss has occurred. Prevention is therefore very important.



■ Prevention Guidelines

· Wear earplugs in places where noise is expected (for example, shooting ranges or concerts).

· Reduce use of earphones and headphones in noisy environments, or lower the volume.

· Rest your ears in a quiet place after noise exposure.

· Consult a doctor before using any medication that may affect hearing, such as certain antibiotics.

· Have your hearing checked regularly. Children and adolescents in particular need attention from their guardians.



If you experience a sudden decline in hearing, tinnitus, or a feeling of muffled hearing, please consult an ENT specialist.

records.title: Wrist Fracture
records.intro: A wrist fracture occurs when a person puts a hand out to break a fall and the impact is transmitted to the wrist. It commonly occurs after falls on icy roads in winter, and older adults and women with osteoporosis-weakened bones can fracture even with minor impact. If left untreated, it can lead to wrist deformity, limited joint motion, and arthritis. If you have pain and swelling in the wrist after a fall, please consult an orthopedic specialist.
records.tags_raw: wrist fracture, fall, fracture, winter fracture, icy road, osteoporosis, wrist, cast

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
A wrist fracture can cause the following symptoms:

· Severe wrist pain
· Swelling around the wrist
· Difficulty moving the wrist
· In severe fractures, the wrist may look deformed

Even if the pain is mild or there is no obvious deformity, if you have wrist pain after a fall, please be sure to see a medical specialist and have an X-ray taken. In older patients and those with dementia in particular, when a fracture is minor, it is sometimes discovered only several days after the injury.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The treatment approach is determined by the type and severity of the fracture.

■ Nonsurgical Treatment
If the bones are not significantly displaced, the bones are set and then immobilized in a plaster splint (cast). The wrist is immobilized for about 6 to 8 weeks.

■ Surgical Treatment
Surgery is used to fix the bones when the fracture is severe, when the bones are significantly displaced, or in an open fracture in which the skin is also damaged.

After immobilization ends, rehabilitation exercises are needed to loosen the stiffened joint. It may take roughly 3 months to return to the condition before the injury.

sections.heading: Complications If Left Untreated
sections.content:
If a wrist fracture is left untreated, the following problems can occur:

· Deformity of the wrist
· Reduced range of motion in the joint
· If the fracture extends into the joint surface (the surface where bones meet), arthritis can develop later, causing ongoing pain.
· When the wrist becomes uncomfortable, the elbow and shoulder may be overused to compensate, which can cause pain in the surrounding joints as well.

If you have pain after a fall, please do not leave it untreated; be sure to consult an orthopedic specialist.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
A wrist fracture occurs when a person reflexively puts a hand forward to break a fall and the impact is transmitted to the wrist bones. It is one of the most common fractures after falls on icy or snowy roads in winter.

Older adults and women are more prone to fractures from the same impact because of osteoporosis (a condition in which bone density decreases and bones become weak). In cold weather, the body also tightens up and loses flexibility, which increases the impact force on the bones during a fall.

records.title: Sleep Disorders and Dementia
records.intro: Sleep is an important time for the brain to recover from fatigue and organize memories. Sleep disorders are more than a simple inconvenience; they are associated with cognitive decline and an increased risk of dementia. If sleep problems persist, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: sleep disorders, dementia, insomnia, sleep apnea, REM sleep, restless legs syndrome, Alzheimer's disease, cognitive function, lack of energy, fatigue, feeling tired all the time, cannot fall asleep, waking up often, cannot sleep deeply, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason

sections.heading: Sleep and Brain Health
sections.content:
Sleep is responsible for functions essential to survival, including mental and physical recovery, memory consolidation, maintenance of immune function, and clearance of waste products from the brain.



Sleeping 6 hours or less, or 10 hours or more, per day can have a harmful effect on health. Sleep deprivation is associated with high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, and obesity, and it can reduce concentration and memory, which may raise the risk of dementia.



Alzheimer's disease occurs when a protein called beta-amyloid builds up abnormally in the brain, and this protein is cleared during deep sleep. If a person does not sleep deeply, this protein may accumulate in the brain, which may raise the risk of dementia.

sections.heading: Types of Sleep Disorders Linked to Dementia
sections.content:
The following sleep disorders are associated with cognitive decline and an increased risk of dementia:



· Sleep maintenance disorder: a condition in which a person wakes frequently during sleep or cannot sleep deeply. It is especially common in older age. A lack of deep sleep allows waste products to build up in the brain, which may raise the risk of dementia.

· Sleep apnea (often accompanied by loud snoring): a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep. Reduced oxygen supply to the brain at night can impair concentration, memory, and judgment, and may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline. The biggest risk factor is obesity.

· Restless legs syndrome: a condition in which an unusual sensation in the legs while lying down creates an urge to move them. It makes it hard to fall asleep and causes fatigue and sleepiness during the day. The underlying conditions that can cause this disorder are associated with cognitive decline, so particular caution is needed in older adults.

· REM sleep behavior disorder: a condition in which a person acts out dream content with the body during sleep (kicking, shouting, etc.). It can be an early sign of a degenerative neurological disease such as Parkinson's disease, so evaluation by a medical specialist is essential.

sections.heading: When Sleep Disorders Are Suspected
sections.content:
If any of the following symptoms persist, please consult a medical specialist:



· Difficulty falling asleep or frequent waking during sleep

· Heavy snoring, or being told that breathing seems to stop during sleep

· Excessive sleepiness or fatigue during the day

· Being told that you kick or shout during sleep

· Leg discomfort when lying down that makes it hard to fall asleep



Treatment differs depending on the type and cause of the sleep disorder. A regular daily routine, maintaining an appropriate weight, and limiting alcohol and overwork can support healthy sleep.

records.title: Sleep Apnea
records.intro: Sleep apnea is a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops or becomes markedly reduced for 10 seconds or longer during sleep. If left untreated, it can worsen various systemic conditions such as high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and diabetes mellitus. It is not a simple sleeping habit but a condition that may require treatment. If you snore heavily or feel severe daytime sleepiness, please consult an ENT specialist.
records.tags_raw: sleep apnea, snoring, polysomnography, positive airway pressure device, CPAP, insomnia, daytime sleepiness, high blood pressure, headache, a splitting headache, migraine, back-of-head pain, lack of energy, fatigue, feeling tired all the time

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Sleep apnea is a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops or becomes markedly reduced for 10 seconds or longer during sleep. When apnea recurs, the oxygen level in the blood (oxygen saturation) falls. This puts strain on major organs, including the brain and heart.



Sleep apnea is not a simple sleeping habit. It is closely associated with systemic conditions such as high blood pressure, ischemic heart disease (a condition in which blood flow to the heart is reduced), asthma, stroke, diabetes mellitus, obesity, acid reflux, and nocturia (frequently waking at night to urinate). Treatment may also help in managing these conditions.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The exact cause of sleep apnea is not yet fully understood. It is thought to result from a combination of various factors.



Major risk factors include the following:

· Obesity: strongly associated with sleep apnea. Fatty tissue around the neck narrows the airway.

· Sex and age: it mostly occurs in men after middle age.

· Menopause: in women, the incidence increases after menopause.

· Children: enlarged tonsils and adenoids (lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat) can be a cause.



As snoring worsens, it can progress through upper airway resistance syndrome to sleep apnea.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms of sleep apnea include the following:



■ Symptoms During Sleep

· Loud snoring

· Pauses in breathing during sleep (often noticed by a spouse)

· Frequent tossing and turning or waking



■ Daytime Symptoms

· Severe daytime sleepiness (drowsiness while reading or driving during the day)

· Headache and fatigue

· Difficulty concentrating

· Dry mouth or a heavy-headed feeling on waking in the morning



If you have these symptoms, please do not leave them unaddressed; consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
A polysomnography (sleep study) is needed for an accurate diagnosis of sleep apnea. In this test, brain waves, eye movements, breathing, oxygen saturation, leg movements, and other measures are recorded together while the patient sleeps overnight at the hospital.



Sleep apnea is diagnosed when the apnea-hypopnea index is 5 or more events per hour of sleep. An index of 15 or more is considered moderate or greater.



Since July 2018, national health insurance coverage has applied to polysomnography and CPAP device rental. Please consult your doctor for details.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment of sleep apnea falls into three main categories.



■ Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)

This method applies continuous pressure to the airway through a mask. It helps keep the airway from collapsing during sleep. It is mainly recommended for moderate or greater sleep apnea (an apnea-hypopnea index of 15 or more events per hour). The device must be used consistently to be effective.



■ Oral Appliance

This method connects devices to the upper and lower jaws to move the lower jaw forward and widen the airway. It is used when a patient declines or cannot use CPAP or surgery. It must be worn consistently to be effective.



■ Surgery

Surgery is considered when there is a clear cause of airway obstruction, such as enlarged tonsils, or when the patient wishes to have it.



The treatment approach is determined by a specialist based on the sleep study results and the patient's condition. Please be sure to consult an ENT specialist.

records.title: Fluid Intake and Health
records.intro: The body keeps its fluid balance by triggering thirst when fluid is low and excreting excess fluid in the urine. Rather than following a fixed standard, the basic principle is to drink enough when you feel thirsty. Drinking water on an empty stomach in the morning can replace fluid used up overnight and may help bowel movement.
records.tags_raw: fluid intake, water, empty stomach, bowel movement, dehydration, health drinks, digestion

sections.heading: Drinking Fluids on an Empty Stomach in the Morning
sections.content:
Fluid is lost through breathing even during sleep. This is why you naturally feel thirsty when you wake up in the morning.

Drinking water on an empty stomach in the morning may help in the following ways:
· It replaces fluid used up overnight.
· When food or fluid enters the stomach, it triggers the reflex that moves the bowel (the gastrocolic reflex), which may help bowel movement.
· It may also help with blood circulation and skin health.

An amount that relieves thirst is enough.

sections.heading: Water Temperature
sections.content:
There is no clear medical standard for water temperature.

When you drink cold water, the body has to warm it to body temperature, which uses extra energy. Middle-aged and older adults, or people with a sensitive digestive system, may find lukewarm water more comfortable than cold water. Choose according to your personal preference and health condition.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The body keeps its fluid balance by triggering thirst when fluid is low and increasing urine output to excrete any excess.

Rather than a fixed rule about drinking a specific amount at a specific time, the basic principle is to drink when you are thirsty. It is best to drink an amount that relieves your thirst slowly. If you have a medical condition or any concerns about how much you should drink, please consult your doctor.

records.title: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease
records.intro: Hand, foot, and mouth disease is a viral infection that causes blisters and rashes on the hands, feet, and inside the mouth. It mainly affects infants and young children, and most cases resolve on their own within 7 to 10 days. Personal hygiene, such as handwashing, is the most important form of prevention.
records.tags_raw: hand, foot, and mouth disease, coxsackievirus, enterovirus, stomatitis, children, infants and toddlers, handwashing, sore throat, scratchy throat, pain when swallowing, feverish, having a fever, high fever, low-grade fever, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Hand, foot, and mouth disease is caused by infection with viruses such as coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71. It is common mainly in infants and young children.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The routes of transmission are as follows:

· Direct contact with an infected person's stool, respiratory secretions, blister fluid, or saliva

· Contact with contaminated objects

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Early symptoms include fever, loss of appetite, sore throat, and a feeling of weakness.



One to two days after the fever begins, the following symptoms usually appear:

· Red spots form inside the mouth (on the tongue, gums, roof of the mouth, etc.) and later develop into blisters (vesicles) or ulcers.

· A rash or blisters appear on the hands, feet, buttocks, groin, and other areas.



Most cases are mild and improve within 7 to 10 days. In infants and young children, pain in the mouth can make it hard to eat, which can lead to dehydration.



Although it is rare, when enterovirus 71 is the cause, serious complications such as encephalitis and myocarditis can occur, so caution is needed.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Personal hygiene is the most important way to prevent hand, foot, and mouth disease.



· Wash your hands with soap under running water for at least 30 seconds: after going outside, after using the toilet, before and after meals, and before and after changing diapers

· Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your sleeve when coughing.

· Disinfect children's toys and play equipment frequently.

· Handle the diapers and clothing of a child diagnosed with hand, foot, and mouth disease with great care.



There is currently no vaccine approved in Korea to prevent hand, foot, and mouth disease.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
There is no specific treatment for hand, foot, and mouth disease. Most cases resolve on their own after 7 to 10 days.



· If there is fever or pain, a fever-reducing pain reliever (antipyretic analgesic) can be taken.

· Infants and young children need to drink enough fluids to avoid dehydration.

· Hospitalization may be needed if serious complications are present.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If hand, foot, and mouth disease is suspected, avoid contact with other children and visit a hospital. It is recommended that the child stay home from daycare, kindergarten, or school until the fever has gone down and the blisters in the mouth have healed.

records.title: Statin-Associated Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy
records.intro: In rare cases, people taking a statin (a medication for hyperlipidemia) can develop immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, in which muscle weakness continues even after the medication is stopped. If weakness in both thighs or shoulders continues for a week or longer while taking a statin, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: statin, myopathy, IMNM, hyperlipidemia, muscle weakness, immunosuppression, autoantibody, CK

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare muscle disease in which muscle damage continues even after the medication is stopped in some people who have taken a statin, a drug used to treat hyperlipidemia.

Ordinary muscle pain caused as a side effect of statins generally improves within several weeks to several months after the medication is stopped. In this disease, however, the body's immune system continues to attack the muscles, and the condition does not resolve after the drug is stopped.

This is a very rare condition and does not occur in everyone who takes a statin.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
It usually begins with a feeling of stiffness or heaviness in the muscles of the thighs, hips, and shoulders.

As the disease progresses, muscle weakness becomes more prominent than muscle pain.
· Weakness in the legs when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair
· Difficulty raising the arms above the head (such as when washing hair or getting dressed)

If symptoms become more severe, walking may become difficult, and the urine may turn brown. In rare cases, the breathing muscles can also become weak.

If you are currently taking a statin or have taken one in the past, and weakness in both thighs or shoulders continues for 1 week or longer, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Diagnosis is made with the following tests:

· Blood test (CK level): checks the level of an enzyme that indicates muscle damage. In this disease, the level remains very high even after the drug is stopped.
· Autoantibody test (anti-HMGCR antibody): if this antibody is positive, this disease is strongly suspected.
· Electromyography, muscle MRI, and muscle biopsy may be performed additionally.

Other causes that produce similar symptoms, such as hypothyroidism and vitamin D deficiency, are also ruled out.

sections.heading: Treatment and Prognosis
sections.content:
Unlike simple muscle pain, this disease requires active treatment to suppress the immune response.

· Steroids are given first to reduce inflammation, and immunosuppressants are added later depending on the patient's condition.
· Treatment proceeds in stages over several months to several years.

When the disease is diagnosed and treated early, many patients may be able to return to daily activities. However, stopping treatment too early can lead to relapse, so ongoing follow-up with a medical specialist is needed.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
If you are taking a statin, please keep the following in mind:

· If muscle symptoms appear, do not stop the medication on your own; be sure to consult a medical specialist.
· Have regular blood tests during treatment (muscle enzyme levels, liver function, etc.).
· Strenuous exercise, excessive alcohol consumption, and dehydration can put strain on the muscles, so be careful.
· If you have an underlying condition such as a thyroid disorder, vitamin D deficiency, or diabetes mellitus, treating it in advance can help.

records.title: Esophageal Diseases (Reflux Esophagitis and Esophageal Cancer)
records.intro: The esophagus is a tube about 25 cm long that carries food from the mouth to the stomach. Reflux esophagitis and esophageal cancer are the main esophageal diseases. If you have symptoms such as heartburn, acid regurgitation (a sour taste rising into the throat), or a feeling that food is getting stuck, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: esophagus, reflux esophagitis, esophageal cancer, heartburn, reflux, sphincter, smoking cessation, digestive system, chest ache, pain in the chest, chest tightness, stuffy feeling in the chest, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: Role of the Esophagus
sections.content:
The esophagus is a tube about 25 cm long that connects the throat (pharynx) and the stomach. It serves as the passage that carries food to the stomach.



At the junction between the stomach and esophagus, there is a sphincter (a ring of muscle that works like a valve) that stays closed most of the time and opens only when food passes through. If this sphincter does not work properly, stomach acid or food can flow back up into the esophagus.

sections.heading: Reflux Esophagitis
sections.content:
Reflux esophagitis is a condition in which stomach acid or food flows back into the esophagus and irritates the esophageal mucosa. The number of patients has been increasing in recent years because of a more Westernized diet, rising obesity, smoking and drinking, and irregular eating habits.



The main symptoms are as follows:

· A sensation of acid rising into the throat (acid regurgitation)

· A burning pain in the chest (heartburn)

· A feeling of something stuck in the throat

· Voice changes

· Chronic cough



Reflux esophagitis can worsen in the following situations:

· Smoking and heavy drinking

· Coffee, chocolate, high-fat foods, carbonated drinks, mint, and onions

· Overeating or eating late at night

· Abdominal obesity

· Lying down right after a meal



If you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Esophageal Cancer
sections.content:
Esophageal cancer is not a common cancer, but its mortality rate is high. There are often no symptoms in the early stages, so early detection through regular endoscopy is important.



The main symptoms are as follows:

· A feeling that food is getting stuck (difficulty swallowing)

· Weight loss

· Nausea and vomiting after meals



Smoking and alcohol use are the most important risk factors. Smoking cessation and moderate drinking are the most important steps for lowering the risk of esophageal cancer.



If you have symptoms or risk factors, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To protect the health of your esophagus, practice the following habits:



· Quit smoking: smoking is a leading cause common to both reflux esophagitis and esophageal cancer.

· Drink in moderation: alcohol weakens the function of the lower esophageal sphincter.

· Avoid overeating, and eat small amounts several times a day.

· Cut back on irritating foods (coffee, chocolate, carbonated drinks, high-fat foods, mint).

· Avoid late-night meals, and wait at least 2 hours after eating before lying down.

· Maintain an appropriate weight. Abdominal obesity increases the pressure that pushes stomach contents back up into the esophagus.

· Have regular endoscopy examinations.

records.title: Esophageal Cancer
records.intro: Esophageal cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the esophagus. It can be difficult to detect in the early stages, and the earlier it is found, the better the treatment outcomes tend to be. Reducing risk factors and getting regular screening are important, and if you have any unusual symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: esophageal cancer, esophagus, Barrett's esophagus, esophagectomy, chemotherapy, radiation, alcohol abstinence, smoking cessation, esophageal cancer prevention

sections.heading: Prognosis
sections.content:
The prognosis of esophageal cancer varies greatly depending on when it is found.
· The 5-year survival rate for early esophageal cancer confined to the mucosa has been reported to be as high as 71.2%.
· Localized disease (not spread to other organs): about 35%
· Distant metastasis (spread to other organs): about 10%

Recurrence can occur in about 30% of patients after surgery, most often around the surgical site or in the lymph nodes. However, after 5 years, the recurrence rate falls to about 8%. Because early detection is very important, please have regular screening.
※ The figures above are based on earlier studies, and the latest statistics can be found at the National Cancer Information Center.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
There are three main treatments for esophageal cancer.

■ Surgery (Surgical Resection)
Surgery is performed first when the cancer has not spread to other organs, the lesion can be removed, and the patient's condition is suitable for surgery. Radiation therapy or chemotherapy may be added before or after surgery as needed.

■ Radiation Therapy and Chemotherapy
These are used when surgery is difficult or when the cancer has spread to other areas.

The treatment approach is determined by your treating physician based on your condition and the stage of the cancer. Please be sure to discuss this thoroughly with a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Postoperative Diet Management
sections.content:
After esophageal cancer surgery, please follow these dietary guidelines:
· Eat a balanced diet that includes high-quality protein, minerals, and vegetables and fruits rich in vitamins.
· Choose soft foods that are easy to swallow.
· Eat slowly, in small amounts, and frequently.
· Avoid eating large amounts of sweet foods at once.
· Do not eat for 2 to 3 hours before going to bed. While you sleep, leftover food or digestive fluid can flow back up and cause aspiration pneumonia (pneumonia caused by food entering the lungs).

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To help prevent esophageal cancer, it is important to reduce the following risk factors:
· Alcohol abstinence and smoking cessation: drinking and smoking are major risk factors for esophageal cancer.
· Weight management: obesity is associated with gastroesophageal reflux and Barrett's esophagus (a risk factor for esophageal cancer).
· Improving eating habits: cut back on burnt food, processed ham and sausages, and hot beverages, and eat plenty of vegetables and fruits.
· Regular screening: if esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus has been diagnosed, appropriate treatment and regular examinations are important. Please be sure to have the endoscopy included in the national health checkup, which is offered every 2 years.

records.title: Food Allergy
records.intro: If you develop hives or shortness of breath after eating a certain food, it may be a food allergy, which can be life-threatening. Please do not take it lightly; be sure to see an allergist or pulmonologist for accurate testing. If you have difficulty breathing, throat tightness, or feel faint after eating, call 119 (Korea's emergency number) immediately, and use your epinephrine auto-injector if one has been prescribed.
records.tags_raw: food allergy, allergy, hives, anaphylaxis, allergy and respiratory medicine

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content: To find out which food is the cause, a skin prick test (lightly pricking the skin to check for a reaction) or a blood test is performed. There are also methods that pinpoint the specific substance that triggers the allergy.

sections.heading: Relationship with Fruit and Pollen Allergies
sections.content: People with a pollen allergy, such as to birch trees in spring, may also have an itchy mouth when eating peaches or apples. This happens because the components are similar, and the body reacts to them as if they were the same.

sections.heading: Can It Develop in Adulthood?
sections.content: Even if you had no problems as a child, an allergy can suddenly develop in adulthood. Adults most often have allergic reactions to crustaceans such as shrimp and crab, nuts, and wheat.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: People with a wheat allergy who exercise to the point of sweating right after eating wheat-containing foods may have a sudden, severe allergic reaction, including shortness of breath. Avoid strenuous exercise right after eating.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Eating a food your body does not tolerate can cause itchy skin, swollen lips, or hives. In severe cases, the throat can tighten, making it hard to breathe, and a person may faint. This is a medical emergency called anaphylaxis.

records.title: Anorexia Nervosa
records.intro: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder in which a person restricts food intake because of an intense fear of gaining weight and insists on maintaining a body weight below the normal range. It is a serious condition that can become life-threatening, so please do not try to judge it on your own; be sure to consult a psychiatrist.
records.tags_raw: anorexia nervosa, loss of appetite, eating disorder, underweight, psychiatry, constipation, difficulty passing stool, hard stool

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Behaviors include extreme restriction of food intake, or binge eating followed by vomiting or misuse of laxatives. Some people become preoccupied with excessive exercise out of an obsessive drive to lose weight, and many do not recognize that they are ill even when they are severely underweight.

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content: Severe malnutrition can cause menstruation to stop, body temperature to drop, hair to fall out, and bones to weaken. In severe cases, it can lead to an arrhythmia (an abnormal heart rhythm) or damage to multiple organs, which can be fatal. It is a serious condition with a high mortality rate.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: The most urgent and important part of treatment is restoring a normal body weight to recover from malnutrition. For adolescents, family therapy that involves the parents can be very helpful. If the condition is critical, hospitalization may be needed so that meals can be provided safely, along with ongoing psychotherapy and medication.

records.title: Bulimia Nervosa
records.intro: Bulimia nervosa is a condition in which a person repeatedly eats a large amount of food in a short time without being able to control it, and then tries to prevent weight gain by forcing vomiting or taking medication. Body weight often appears normal on the outside, so please do not keep it hidden; be sure to seek consultation with a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: bulimia nervosa, eating disorder, vomiting, binge eating, psychiatry, constipation, difficulty passing stool, hard stool, feeling depressed, lack of motivation, not wanting to do anything

sections.heading: Key Features
sections.content: A person binge eats without being able to stop when stressed or depressed. After a binge, they fall into intense guilt and depression, and to make up for it they force themselves to vomit or misuse diuretics, laxatives, and similar medications. During a binge, they typically eat in secret so that no one knows.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.content: Repeated self-induced vomiting can cause severe tooth erosion from strong stomach acid and swelling of the salivary glands under the jaw, which can make the face look larger. Inducing vomiting with the fingers can leave scars on the back of the hand (Russell's sign), and the loss of electrolytes can place significant strain on the heart.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps correct distorted thoughts and eating habits, is considered the most effective treatment. Patients practice telling physical hunger apart from emotional hunger and eating at regular times. Taking an antidepressant together may help reduce binge urges and improve mood.

records.title: Kidney Cancer
records.intro: Kidney cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the kidney. There are almost no symptoms in the early stages, so it is difficult to notice on your own, and in most cases it is found incidentally during a health checkup. Even without symptoms, it is important to detect it early through regular health checkups. If an abnormal finding is detected or you have any concerns, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: kidney cancer, renal cancer, hematuria, flank pain, robotic surgery, partial nephrectomy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, health checkup, headache, a splitting headache, migraine, back-of-head pain, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, labored breathing, feeling of suffocation, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop, blood in urine, red urine, bloody urine

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
When a kidney tumor is small, it causes almost no symptoms. Symptoms appear only after the tumor has grown large enough to push against surrounding organs.



The three classic symptoms of kidney cancer are as follows:

· Hematuria: blood mixed in the urine.

· Flank pain: pain felt in the side or back.

· Abdominal mass: a lump that can be felt in the abdomen.



By the time these symptoms appear, kidney cancer has often already progressed considerably. In addition, about 30% of kidney cancer patients are first diagnosed after the cancer has already spread to other organs. Depending on where it has spread, symptoms such as cough, difficulty breathing, or headache may appear first, and they can be mistaken for other conditions.



Even without symptoms, it is important to detect it early through regular health checkups.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
No single clear cause of kidney cancer has been identified. The following factors are known to raise the risk of developing kidney cancer:



· Smoking: tobacco is one of the risk factors for kidney cancer.

· Obesity: being overweight can raise the risk.

· High blood pressure: the risk may increase if blood pressure stays high over time.

· High-calorie diet: especially a continued high-protein, high-fat diet.

· Chronic kidney failure and hemodialysis: when kidney function has been poor for a long time. Hemodialysis is a treatment that filters waste products from the blood using a machine.

· Having many cysts in the kidneys

· Genetic mutations



If you have risk factors, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Kidney cancer is difficult to detect through tumor marker levels in blood or urine tests. It is diagnosed mainly through imaging tests.



The main diagnostic methods are as follows:

· Ultrasound: checks the shape of the kidney and whether a mass is present.

· CT (computed tomography): checks the size and location of the kidney cancer and whether it has spread.

· MRI (magnetic resonance imaging): performed when needed to examine it in more detail.

· Biopsy: a part of the mass is sampled under ultrasound or CT guidance to check for cancer.



If an abnormal finding is detected at a health checkup, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The main treatment for kidney cancer is surgery. Before surgery, the size and extent of the cancer, the patient's overall health, and underlying conditions (other conditions the patient already has) are considered together.



· Partial nephrectomy: for kidney cancer 7 cm or smaller, only the cancerous area is removed rather than the entire kidney. This can preserve kidney function as much as possible.

· Robotic and laparoscopic surgery: surgery using robotic or laparoscopic techniques, in which instruments are inserted through small incisions, is now widely used. It is generally regarded as safe and precise and can shorten recovery time.

· Open surgery: if the cancer is advanced, surgery with a direct abdominal incision may be needed.



Surgery may also be possible for older patients or those with underlying conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, or heart disease, depending on their health. Whether surgery is possible is determined by your treating physician.

sections.heading: Treatment: Non-Surgical Methods
sections.content:
Besides surgery, the following treatment options are available:



· Radiofrequency ablation: a method that destroys cancer cells using heat. It is used when the tumor is small.

· Cryoablation: a method that destroys cancer cells using extreme cold.

· Targeted therapy: treatment with an oral medication that targets specific features of cancer cells.

· Immunotherapy: treatment that uses the body's immune system to attack cancer cells.



Compared with chemotherapy for other cancers, anticancer treatment for kidney cancer (targeted therapy and immunotherapy) tends to be relatively easy to take, even for older patients. However, it can be a burden for some patients, so it is important to discuss it thoroughly with your doctor and choose the medication that suits you.

sections.heading: Postoperative Care
sections.content:
After kidney cancer surgery, the following care is needed to recover health and help prevent recurrence:



· Healthy eating habits: maintaining a balanced diet is important.

· Appropriate exercise: helps with recovery of physical strength and maintaining health.

· Regular follow-up: regular tests are needed to check for recurrence.

· Kidney function management: high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, and other conditions should be kept under steady control to preserve the remaining kidney function.



Before surgery, it helps to consult a medical specialist and manage your physical strength and weight appropriately. Please follow your treating physician's instructions for specific care.

records.title: Kidney Transplantation
records.intro: Kidney transplantation is a surgery that transplants a healthy kidney into a patient with end-stage kidney failure, whose kidneys can no longer function properly. If the transplanted kidney functions normally, the patient may be freed from dialysis (a treatment that filters waste products from the blood using a machine), which can greatly improve quality of life. Ongoing care after surgery is very important, and please be sure to consult a medical specialist about anything related to transplantation.
records.tags_raw: kidney transplantation, kidney transplant, end-stage kidney failure, immunosuppressants, living-donor transplantation, deceased-donor transplantation

sections.heading: Postoperative Care
sections.content:
After a kidney transplant, immunosuppressants are taken for life so that the body's immune system does not attack the transplanted kidney. Immunosuppressants are medications that prevent the body from recognizing the transplanted kidney as a foreign object and rejecting it.

■ Precautions
· Take your immunosuppressants at the scheduled times without missing doses.
· Have regular blood tests to check drug levels.
· Because a weakened immune system makes you vulnerable to infection, maintain thorough hygiene, including handwashing and wearing a mask.
· Be careful with raw or undercooked seafood and meat.
· Always consult your care team before receiving any vaccination.
· Maintain a stable weight with appropriate calorie and protein intake and enough fluids.

Ongoing care after surgery is as important as the surgery itself. Please attend all regular outpatient appointments.

sections.heading: When Kidney Transplantation Is Needed
sections.content:
Kidney transplantation is performed for patients with end-stage kidney failure.
Preparation for transplantation begins to be considered from stage 4 chronic kidney disease (a glomerular filtration rate of 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m², just before end-stage kidney failure). The glomerular filtration rate is a measure of how well the kidneys filter the blood.
Dialysis alone cannot completely replace all of the functions of the kidneys. Even with continued dialysis, various problems such as cardiovascular complications can occur, so unless there are contraindications, kidney transplantation is recommended as the most definitive treatment.

sections.heading: Donor Requirements and Selection Process
sections.content:
A person who donates a kidney is called a donor. There are living-donor transplants, in which a living person donates a kidney, and deceased-donor transplants, in which a kidney is received from a brain-dead donor.

■ Requirements for Living Donors
· Must be a healthy person between the ages of 16 and 65.
· Must wish to donate of their own free will.
· Must not have diabetes mellitus, severe high blood pressure, a malignant tumor, or psychiatric problems.
· In recent years, transplantation is sometimes possible even when blood types differ.
· There must be no rejection reaction on the histocompatibility crossmatch test.

If there is no suitable donor, the patient can register with the Korean Network for Organ Sharing (KONOS) and wait for a deceased-donor transplant.
Whether the transplant proceeds is decided after approval from KONOS.

sections.heading: Donor Health After Living-Donor Kidney Transplantation
sections.content: According to related studies, even after donating one kidney, the function of the remaining kidney recovers over time to about 70% to 80%. The likelihood of progressing to end-stage kidney disease over the long term is low. Life expectancy after donation is also reported not to differ greatly from that of the general population. However, regular follow-up of kidney function and overall health is needed.

sections.heading: Surgical Procedure
sections.content:
After general anesthesia, an oblique incision of about 20 to 25 cm is made near the inguinal area in the lower abdomen (above the groin). The kidney removed from the donor is connected to the recipient's blood vessels and bladder.
· Arteries are connected to arteries, and veins to veins.
· The tube that carries urine from the kidney (the ureter) is connected to the bladder.
The surgery usually takes about 4 hours, and may be shorter or longer depending on the patient's condition. Recently, robot-assisted surgery is also performed when the patient meets the indications.

sections.heading: Prognosis
sections.content:
According to statistics in Korea, the 5-year survival rate is reported to be about 96% for living-donor kidney transplant patients and about 90% for deceased-donor kidney transplants.
The 5-year graft (transplanted kidney) survival rate is about 85%.
Even if the function of the transplanted kidney declines again, life can often be sustained through dialysis or a repeat transplant.
Please be sure to discuss thoroughly with a medical specialist whether to have a kidney transplant, when, and by what method.

records.title: Kidney Transplant Process
records.intro: Kidney transplantation is a surgery that transplants a healthy kidney into the body to replace a kidney that has lost its function. Unlike dialysis, it can restore most of the kidney's various functions (removing waste products, regulating electrolytes, secreting hormones that stimulate blood cell production, and others), which makes it one of the main treatment options for end-stage kidney failure. Whether and how to have a transplant depends on each patient's health condition, so please be sure to decide through consultation with a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: kidney transplantation, kidney transplant, living-donor kidney transplantation, deceased-donor kidney transplantation, immunosuppressants, rejection, end-stage kidney failure, KONOS, organ transplantation, double vision, overlapping images

sections.heading: Types and Procedures
sections.content:
■ Types of Kidney Transplantation

Kidney transplantation is divided into two types, depending on how the kidney is obtained.



① Living-Donor Kidney Transplantation

A kidney is donated by a healthy donor (a living person) and transplanted. Both the donor and the recipient take enough time to decide whether to proceed with the transplant. After that, the donor and recipient each undergo health examinations, and a social worker confirms the voluntary nature of the donation (that the donor is donating willingly and without compensation). After all of these steps, surgery is performed following approval from the Korean Network for Organ Sharing (KONOS).



② Deceased-Donor Kidney Transplantation

A kidney is donated by a person who has been declared brain-dead and transplanted. If there is no suitable donor, the patient starts dialysis and registers with KONOS as a transplant candidate. Serum (the liquid separated from blood) is drawn and stored every year, and when a brain-dead donor becomes available, a crossmatch test (a test to check whether the donor's and recipient's immune responses are compatible) is performed quickly, and then surgery proceeds.



■ First Consultation Process

After a visit with a nephrologist or transplant surgeon, you will be counseled by a specialist nurse at the organ transplant center.

sections.heading: Pre-Transplant Tests
sections.content:
Both the donor and the recipient undergo a variety of tests before transplantation.



■ Immunologic Tests

- Blood type test

- Lymphocyte crossmatch test: checks whether the recipient's immune system attacks the donor's kidney.



■ Recipient Health Evaluation

Medical, surgical, and psychiatric evaluations are performed to check that there is no infection or tumor and that the patient is fit for surgery.



■ Blood and Other Tests

- Blood tests: to check for anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and other conditions

- Urine tests and liver function tests

- Infection screening: hepatitis B and C, cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and others

- Urine culture: to check for bacterial infection in the urine



For deceased-donor kidney transplants, surgery must proceed within a short time once a donor becomes available, so only the essential tests are performed quickly before surgery.



Having diabetes mellitus does not mean that a kidney transplant is not possible. Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of end-stage kidney failure, and patients with diabetes mellitus can also receive a transplant if they have no uncontrolled severe infection, cancer, or mental health problem and their life expectancy is not excessively short. However, a person with diabetes mellitus is generally unable to donate a kidney.

sections.heading: Managing Immunosuppressants After Transplant
sections.content:
After transplantation, immunosuppressants are taken to prevent rejection, in which the body's immune system recognizes the transplanted kidney as a foreign object and attacks it. These medications must be continued for as long as the transplanted kidney is functioning.



■ Main Types of Immunosuppressants

A combination of three drugs with different mechanisms of action is usually taken.

- Calcineurin inhibitors: block a key pathway of the immune response.

  - Tacrolimus-class drugs (e.g., Prograf, Tacrobel)

  - Cyclosporine-class drugs (e.g., Sandimmune, Cipol)

- Antimetabolites: mycophenolate-class drugs that suppress the proliferation of immune cells.

- Steroids: suppress the immune response and inflammation overall.



■ Precautions for Blood Draws

For some immunosuppressants, it is important to keep the blood level of the drug within a set range. Blood must be drawn immediately before taking the medication (when the level is lowest) or a set time after taking it, so it is important to keep the test timing exactly as your care team instructs.

sections.heading: Dietary Precautions After Transplant
sections.content:
■ Grapefruit, Schisandra, and Similar Products

Grapefruit, grapefruit juice, schisandra (omija) extract, and similar products affect the blood levels of immunosuppressants. Because these foods are involved in drug metabolism and raise drug levels, they can cause toxicity. Please take care not to consume them after transplantation.



■ Raw Foods (Raw Fish, Raw Beef, Shellfish, Oysters, etc.)

Taking immunosuppressants weakens immune function, which makes you more vulnerable to parasites and food-poisoning bacteria. Avoid raw or undercooked fish, meat, and shellfish whenever possible, and if you do eat them, be sure to use fresh ingredients and cook them thoroughly.



■ Dietary Supplements and Folk Remedies

Unverified products such as herbal medicines, ginseng concentrate, and various dietary supplements can interact with immunosuppressants or cause unexpected side effects, so please be sure to consult your care team before taking them.

sections.heading: Weight Gain and Hair Loss After Transplant
sections.content:
■ Weight Gain

Some patients gain weight after transplantation. There are two main reasons:

- Taking steroids and immunosuppressants can increase appetite, leading to greater food intake.

- As kidney function recovers after transplantation, appetite generally improves, and food intake may naturally increase.

Excessive weight gain can put strain on the transplanted kidney and overall health, so please keep monitoring your food intake and weight changes.



■ Hair Loss

Hair loss can occur as a side effect of tacrolimus-class drugs among the calcineurin inhibitors. It mostly occurs early after transplantation and generally decreases over time. Conversely, cyclosporine-class drugs can cause excessive hair growth on the body. If side effects of your medication are bothersome, do not stop taking it on your own; be sure to consult your doctor.
