When the air temperature exceeds 35°C, it becomes difficult for the body to release heat through radiation (the spread of heat into the air). At this point, body temperature must be lowered by sweat evaporation alone, and when humidity is high, even that becomes difficult. As a result, the body loses water quickly and dehydration develops.



Outdoor workers, especially laborers at construction sites, are highly exposed to the risk of heat-related illness. According to statistics from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA), heat-related illness tends to increase sharply from mid-July.

sections.heading: Types and Symptoms
sections.content:
Heat-related illness is divided into the following types according to the kind and severity of symptoms.



■ Heat Edema

Swelling of the feet, ankles, hands, and other areas after exposure to a hot environment. Most cases may improve without separate treatment. It helps to rest in a cool place with the swollen area raised above the level of the heart.



■ Heat Rash (Prickly Heat)

A skin inflammation caused by blocked sweat glands. Red spots and itching appear. Wear breathable clothing, and if symptoms worsen, please see a doctor.



■ Heat Cramps

Muscle cramps that occur when the body's electrolytes (salts) run low after heavy sweating. Drinking a sports drink or electrolyte drink in a cool place can help. Eating salt directly is not recommended. If the cramps do not improve, please seek medical attention.



■ Heat Exhaustion (Heat Fatigue)

It results from dehydration and loss of electrolytes. In addition to the symptoms of heat cramps, it can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, and a feeling that you are about to collapse. Rest in a cool place immediately and replace fluids with an electrolyte drink. If there is no improvement after 30 minutes to 1 hour or longer, or if you have lost consciousness even briefly, please seek medical attention.



■ Heat Stroke

The most dangerous type of heat-related illness. Body temperature rises above 40°C, and neurological symptoms such as abnormal behavior, confusion, seizures, and decreased consciousness occur. Unlike other heat-related illnesses, there may be no sweating at all. The affected person often does not realize it. If someone nearby shows these symptoms, call 119 immediately.

sections.heading: First Aid for Heat Stroke
sections.content:
If heat stroke is suspected, take the following steps immediately and call 119.



① Immediately remove the person from the hot environment and move them to a cool place.

② Remove their clothing, spray them with water or place wet towels on the body, and cool them with the wind from a fan.

③ Because the person's level of consciousness is not normal, forcing them to drink water carries a risk of choking. Do not give water.



Unlike other heat-related illnesses, fluid replacement is not the key to treating heat stroke. Rapid cooling of the body and immediate transport to a hospital are what matter.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
These are the basic guidelines for preventing heat-related illness.



· Drink water often. Replace fluids regularly even if you are not thirsty. (If you have a fluid restriction because of kidney disease or another condition, please consult a medical specialist.)

· Stay cool. Wear loose, light-colored clothing, and use a hat or parasol when going out.

· Rest as much as possible during the hottest hours of the day, between 12 p.m. and 5 p.m.



These are additional guidelines for outdoor workers.

· Work in pairs and check on each other's health.

· If you have difficulty breathing, dizziness, muscle cramps, or similar symptoms, move to a cool place and rest immediately.

· In environments where wearing a mask is required, take extra care to guard against heat-related illness.

records.title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
records.intro: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a mental health condition that develops after experiencing or witnessing a serious, shocking event (a traumatic event), such as a life-threatening accident, disaster, or violence. If symptoms persist, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: PTSD, post-traumatic stress, trauma, psychological first aid, PFA, depression, sleep disorder, anxious feeling, nervousness, worrying for no reason, feeling depressed, lack of motivation, not wanting to do anything

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) is a mental health problem that develops after experiencing or witnessing a serious, shocking event.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· Intrusion symptoms: The event comes back vividly (flashbacks), or nightmares occur repeatedly.

· Avoidance symptoms: Avoiding places, people, or thoughts related to the event.

· Hyperarousal symptoms: A constant state of tension, being easily startled, sleep disturbance, and difficulty concentrating.

· Changes in thinking and mood: Guilt, emotional numbness, and a sense of disconnection from other people may occur.

Symptoms do not always appear right after the event. There is also 'delayed-onset PTSD,' in which symptoms fully appear only 6 months or more after the event, and in some cases symptoms worsen after several years.

sections.heading: Relationship Between PTSD and Depression
sections.content:
PTSD and depression often occur together. Insomnia, nightmares, and hyperarousal caused by a traumatic experience tend to be accompanied by depressive symptoms, and conversely, when depressed mood becomes severe, a person can become more vulnerable to traumatic memories.

Chronic sleep deprivation worsens depression and anxiety and makes PTSD symptoms harder to control. When PTSD and depression are present together, the risk of suicide may increase, so early detection and treatment are important.

sections.heading: Warning Signs of Suicide Risk
sections.content:
If a person who has experienced trauma shows the following signs, caution is needed.

· Saying things such as 'I want to die' or 'It would be better if I disappeared'

· Making a specific plan to die by suicide, writing a suicide note, or putting belongings in order

· Worsening sleep problems and increasing use of alcohol or drugs

· Avoiding family and colleagues and becoming isolated

· A sudden change in personality, becoming irritable or, conversely, emotionally numb

If these signs appear, it is important to help the person connect quickly with professional help. If you think it is a crisis situation, contact the Mental Health Crisis Counseling Line (☎1577-0199) or the Suicide Prevention Hotline (☎109) immediately.

sections.heading: Prevention: Psychological First Aid (PFA)
sections.content:
The first month after a traumatic event is an important period for helping to prevent progression to PTSD. During this time, laying the groundwork for recovery through 'psychological first aid (PFA)' can be effective.

PFA is not professional psychotherapy but basic psychological support provided right after an event. It has five key elements.

① Safety: Protect the person physically and psychologically from danger.

② Calming: Help reduce anxiety and restore a sense of stability.

③ Connection: Link the person with family, colleagues, and formal support systems.

④ Providing information: Explain that the reactions the person is having are a normal response in order to reduce anxiety.

⑤ Access to support: When necessary, connect the person to professional treatment or community resources.

Caution: Having people recall the event in detail as a group right after it happens (psychological debriefing) is not recommended. It may actually cause retraumatization.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
With treatment at the appropriate time, PTSD symptoms may improve. The longer PTSD is left untreated, the higher the risk that it becomes chronic.

· Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy: A type of psychotherapy that processes traumatic memories in a safe environment.

· Drug treatment: Used to help control depression or anxiety symptoms, as prescribed by a specialist.

Getting enough sleep, keeping a regular routine, and maintaining social support are also important for recovery. If you suspect symptoms, please consult a psychiatry specialist as soon as possible.

records.title: ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder)
records.intro: ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) is a neurodevelopmental condition whose main symptoms are inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. It mainly appears in childhood and adolescence, but it can continue into adulthood. If you suspect symptoms, please consult a medical specialist for an examination and evaluation.
records.tags_raw: ADHD, inattention, hyperactivity disorder, concentration, impulsivity, children and adolescents, dopamine

sections.heading: The Role of the People Around the Person
sections.content:
When helping a person with ADHD, please keep the following points in mind.
· If symptoms interfere significantly with daily life, it is advisable to encourage evaluation and treatment.
· It is important not to blame the person by assuming that ADHD symptoms are a 'personality problem' or 'laziness.' ADHD is not a matter of willpower but a condition related to neurodevelopment.
An accurate diagnosis is made through an evaluation by a medical specialist, so if you suspect ADHD, please consult a psychiatry specialist.

sections.heading: Differences from Ordinary Difficulty Concentrating
sections.content:
There are many reasons why concentration may drop. It can also be hard to concentrate when you are worried, when the material is too difficult, or when a task is unpleasant and you are not motivated.
ADHD is not diagnosed on the basis of poor concentration alone. All of the following conditions must be met.
· Difficulty concentrating appears not only in studying or work but also in many situations of daily life.
· There must be a record that symptoms have been present consistently since childhood, before the age of 12.
· Symptoms appear in two or more settings (such as school and home).
· The symptoms must cause real impairment in daily life.

sections.heading: Definition and Symptoms
sections.content:
ADHD is short for 'attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.' It is common in childhood and adolescence, and symptoms begin before the age of 12. There are three core symptoms.

■ Inattention
· Often forgets school assignment notices or homework.
· Often loses belongings (such as umbrellas and school supplies).
· Often gets problems wrong, even ones they know how to solve, because of calculation errors or misreading the question.
· Seems not to listen, for example needing to be told several times even for a simple errand.

■ Hyperactivity
· Has difficulty staying seated and fidgets even when seated.
· May turn around or talk to friends during class.

■ Impulsivity
· Has difficulty waiting for a turn.
· Interrupts other people's conversations or play.
· May engage in dangerous behavior, such as suddenly running into the road or climbing to high places.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The exact cause of ADHD has not yet been fully identified. Genetic and environmental factors are known to interact in complex ways.
· Genetics: Heritability is known to be about 76%, so genetic factors play a strong role. Genes related to dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain have been reported to be involved. Dopamine and norepinephrine are neurotransmitters that are involved in concentration and behavior control in the brain.
· Environment: The mother's health during pregnancy, the environment after birth, and other factors are also known to be related.
It cannot be explained by a single cause, and an accurate evaluation by a medical specialist is needed.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
ADHD is a condition that differs in degree rather than being simply present or absent.
· Mild symptoms: Using a planner, practicing making plans, and breaking large tasks into smaller steps can help.
· Symptoms that interfere with daily life: Drug treatment can be effective. Drug treatment is given according to a specialist's diagnosis and prescription.

records.title: Hepatitis A
records.intro: Hepatitis A is an acute infectious disease caused by the hepatitis A virus. It is spread through contaminated food or water, and most people recover. It does not progress to chronic hepatitis, but in rare cases it can take a serious course. People who do not have antibodies should be vaccinated.
records.tags_raw: hepatitis A, hepatitis, acute hepatitis, hepatitis vaccination, contaminated food, jaundice, liver function, feeling feverish, body heat, high fever, low-grade fever, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness

sections.heading: Definition and Routes of Transmission
sections.content:
Hepatitis A is an acute liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus.



It is mainly spread in the following ways.

· Eating or drinking contaminated food, seafood, or drinking water

· Contact with the feces of an infected person



As improved sanitation has reduced the chance of natural infection in childhood, an adult who is exposed without antibodies can develop acute hepatitis A.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Hepatitis A ranges from mild symptoms to a severe course.



The main symptoms are as follows.

· Fever, loss of appetite, and nausea

· Fatigue

· Jaundice (yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes) and dark-colored urine



Most people recover with sufficient rest and nutritional support. It does not progress to chronic hepatitis. In rare cases it can take a serious course (fulminant hepatitis), so if you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
A safe and effective vaccine is available to prevent hepatitis A. People who do not have antibodies are recommended to receive two doses, 6 months apart.



In addition to vaccination, the following habits are important.

· Wash your hands often.

· Cook food thoroughly before eating.

· Avoid seafood or water that may be contaminated.

records.title: Hepatitis B
records.intro: Hepatitis B is a liver inflammation caused by the hepatitis B virus. In Korea, about 30% of cirrhosis cases and 45% of liver cancer cases are associated with hepatitis B. It can be managed with proper care, including vaccination and consistent treatment, and regular checkups are important to help keep it from progressing to cirrhosis or liver cancer.
records.tags_raw: hepatitis B, chronic hepatitis, antiviral drugs, cirrhosis, liver cancer, HBV, vaccination, liver health, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, dry cough, persistent minor cough, cough that will not stop

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Hepatitis B is a condition in which the liver cells infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV) become inflamed. About 350 million people worldwide and about 2 million people in Korea are infected.



Hepatitis B is not spread through everyday contact such as sharing meals, hugging, holding hands, or coughing. It is mainly spread through blood, sexual contact, and mother-to-child (vertical) transmission (spread from a mother to her newborn during pregnancy).



■ Symptoms

Many people have no symptoms, but fatigue, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), dark brown urine, loss of appetite, nausea, and muscle pain may occur.

sections.heading: Vaccination
sections.content:
Vaccination is recommended for all infants and young children and for adults who do not have antibodies. It is especially important for high-risk groups, such as people with chronic liver disease, patients on hemodialysis, and family members of people who carry the hepatitis B virus.



With three doses given at 0, 1, and 6 months, antibodies develop in more than 90% of people. If antibodies develop and then disappear over time, healthy adults do not need an additional dose. However, for high-risk groups such as dialysis patients, people with weakened immunity, and family members of people with hepatitis B, one additional dose is considered.



To prevent infection in newborns (mother-to-child transmission), an immunoglobulin injection and vaccination are given right after birth.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Completely eliminating the hepatitis B virus itself is currently difficult. The goal of treatment is to keep the virus inactive and help prevent progression to cirrhosis or liver cancer.



■ Drug Treatment

Antiviral drugs are used. In most cases, lifelong use is needed. People with cirrhosis must continue taking them.



■ Criteria for Starting Treatment

Your doctor decides after considering the HBV DNA level, liver function test (ALT) level, degree of liver fibrosis, and other factors together. Stopping the medication on your own can make hepatitis worse, so please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions.

sections.heading: Course and Precautions
sections.content:
Hepatitis B accounts for 30% of the causes of cirrhosis and 45% of the causes of liver cancer. If you have hepatitis B, you should regularly have liver function tests, liver ultrasound (or CT), and liver cancer screening.



For pregnant women with a high HBV DNA level, antiviral medication is recommended between weeks 24 and 32 of pregnancy to help prevent mother-to-child transmission to the newborn. Breastfeeding may be restricted while taking antiviral medication; please consult your doctor about specific management.

records.title: Hepatitis C
records.intro: Hepatitis C is an infection caused by the hepatitis C virus. In most people who are infected, it progresses to chronic hepatitis, and the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer increases. If you are at risk of infection, please have a blood test to check.
records.tags_raw: hepatitis C, chronic hepatitis C, antiviral drugs, cirrhosis, liver cancer, bloodborne infection

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
In the past, hepatitis C required injection treatment, but it is now treated with oral antiviral drugs.

· Treatment duration: About 2 to 3 months
· Side effects are few, and treatment is effective in a high proportion of patients.

Even after successful treatment, reinfection can occur if you are exposed again to the blood or body fluids of an infected person, so caution is needed. Please discuss treatment options with your doctor.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
There is currently no vaccine to prevent hepatitis C. Avoiding exposure is the most important measure.

· Do not share items that may come into contact with blood, such as razors, toothbrushes, and nail clippers, with other people.
· Do not use tattoo or piercing equipment that has not been sterilized.
· Take precautions during sexual intercourse.

Early screening is important, and if you are at risk of infection, please have a blood test to check whether you are infected.

sections.heading: Definition and Routes of Transmission
sections.content:
Hepatitis C is an infection caused by the hepatitis C virus. When the infection lasts 6 months or longer, it is called chronic hepatitis C.

It is mainly spread through blood or body fluids.
· Use of unsterilized syringes or equipment (for tattoos, piercings, acupuncture, and similar procedures)
· Sexual intercourse with an infected person
· Misuse of intravenous drugs

When a person is infected with hepatitis C, it progresses to chronic hepatitis in most cases. Korea's national health screening has offered a hepatitis C antibody test only at age 56 since 2025, so if you have risk factors for infection, please have a blood test.

records.title: HPV (Cervical Cancer) Vaccination
records.intro: HPV (human papillomavirus) vaccination is a vaccine that helps prevent cervical cancer. Cervical cancer is a cancer for which a preventive vaccine exists. Vaccination is most effective when given before sexual activity begins, and the Korean government provides free vaccination for girls aged 12.
records.tags_raw: HPV vaccine, cervical cancer prevention, human papillomavirus, vaccination, age 12, bivalent, quadrivalent, 9-valent

sections.heading: Why Vaccination Is Needed
sections.content:
HPV infection is found in more than 99% of people with cervical cancer, showing that cervical cancer and HPV are directly linked. In other words, preventing HPV infection can greatly reduce the occurrence of cervical cancer.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer for which a preventive vaccine exists. The vaccine does not completely block HPV infection, but it is effective in helping to prevent infection with high-risk HPV, the main cause of cervical cancer.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Even after HPV vaccination, protection against all types of HPV is not complete. In addition, if a person is already infected with HPV, the vaccine does not treat the infection with that type.

Therefore, it is important for vaccinated women to also have regular cervical cancer screening (cervical cytology, or Pap test).

If any adverse reaction appears after vaccination, please tell your care team immediately.

sections.heading: Types of Vaccines
sections.content:
There are currently three types of HPV vaccine available in Korea, distinguished by the number of HPV types they contain.

· Bivalent vaccine: Helps prevent infection with high-risk HPV types 16 and 18.
· Quadrivalent vaccine: Helps prevent infection with high-risk types 16 and 18 and with types 6 and 11, which cause genital warts.
· 9-valent vaccine: Helps prevent infection with a wider range of HPV types.

A specialist decides which vaccine is appropriate based on age, health status, and other factors.

sections.heading: Timing of Vaccination
sections.content:
The HPV vaccine is most effective when given before exposure to the virus, that is, before sexual activity begins.

Korea's national free vaccination program targets girls aged 12. When the vaccine is given at age 12, two doses can provide sufficient protection.

Even if this window is missed, depending on the type of vaccine, two doses may still be effective up to age 13 to 14. At older ages, three doses are generally needed. Please consult a medical specialist about the exact number of doses and schedule.

records.title: HPV and Men's Health
records.intro: HPV (human papillomavirus) is well known as the virus that causes cervical cancer. However, HPV can cause head and neck cancer (cancer that develops in the head and neck area), oropharyngeal cancer, tonsil cancer, and anal and genital warts not only in women but also in men. The HPV vaccine can also help protect men. If you have HPV-related symptoms or are considering vaccination, please consult an otolaryngology (ENT) specialist.
records.tags_raw: HPV, human papillomavirus, head and neck cancer, oropharyngeal cancer, tonsil cancer, vaccine, adult vaccination, men's health

sections.heading: HPV-Related Conditions in Men
sections.content:
The main conditions that HPV can cause in men are as follows.

· Head and neck cancer: Cancer that develops in the head and neck area, including oropharyngeal cancer, tonsil cancer, and oral cancer. The occurrence of HPV-related head and neck cancer is gradually increasing in men.
· Anal and genital warts (papillomas): A condition in which warts form around the anus or genitals because of HPV infection.

Men who are infected with HPV often have no symptoms, so it is difficult to know whether they are infected. In addition, men can pass HPV to women, so HPV management in men is important.

Because the sampling yield of HPV testing in men is low, it is difficult to determine accurately whether a man is infected. For this reason, vaccination and prevention guidelines are currently what matter most.

sections.heading: HPV Vaccine
sections.content:
The HPV vaccine has been reported to have a preventive effect in men as well as in women.

· It may help reduce the occurrence of head and neck cancer (oropharyngeal cancer, tonsil cancer, and oral cancer) in men.
· It can reduce the occurrence of warts in the anal and genital area.
· It can lower how often men pass HPV to women.

Recommended age for vaccination: Vaccination is recommended for men aged 26 and younger, and there is a recent view that vaccination can also be considered for men up to age 45.

There are reports that vaccination can be beneficial even when a person is already infected with HPV. It may help prevent infection with other HPV types and help strengthen the immune response to the current infection.

Please consult a medical specialist before deciding whether and when to be vaccinated.

sections.heading: Prevention Guidelines
sections.content:
These are guidelines for preventing HPV infection and related conditions.

· Get the HPV vaccine. (Decide after consulting a medical specialist.)
· Avoid oral-genital contact.
· Using a condom can help reduce the risk of HPV transmission.
· If a high-risk virus is detected on an HPV test, please have regular oral and throat examinations for the prevention of tonsil cancer and oropharyngeal cancer.
· If unusual symptoms appear (such as a lump in the neck, sores in the mouth, or difficulty swallowing), please consult an otolaryngology (ENT) specialist.

sections.heading: What Is HPV?
sections.content:
HPV (human papillomavirus) is a virus that infects the skin and mucous membranes. There are many types of HPV, and some belong to a high-risk group that can cause cancer. HPV is mainly spread through sexual contact, but it can also be spread through oral contact.

HPV is well known as a cause of cervical cancer. However, in men as well as women, it can also cause oropharyngeal cancer (cancer that develops at the back of the throat), tonsil cancer, oral cancer, and warts in the anal and genital area.

records.title: RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) Infection
records.intro: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) is the most common virus that causes bronchiolitis (inflammation of the small airways) and pneumonia in infants and young children. It is highly contagious, and most children are infected at least once before the age of 2. Premature infants, children with congenital heart disease, and people with weakened immunity need to take extra care.
records.tags_raw: RSV, respiratory syncytial virus, bronchiolitis, children, infants, wheezing, premature infants, feeling feverish, body heat, high fever, low-grade fever, dry cough, persistent minor cough, cough that will not stop, stuffy nose, clear runny nose, yellow runny nose

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
RSV stands for respiratory syncytial virus. It is the most common cause of lower respiratory tract infection (infection of the lower airways, that is, the bronchi and lungs) in infants and young children. It can also cause pneumonia in older adults and people with weakened immunity.



It mainly circulates from late autumn through spring and is highly contagious. It is spread through direct contact and through droplets released by coughing and sneezing. Transmission within hospitals is also an important problem.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Symptoms begin 1 to 3 days after infection.



The early symptoms are as follows.

· Runny nose

· Cough



After that, the following symptoms may appear.

· Wheezing (a whistling sound when breathing): The airways narrow, causing a whistling sound when breathing.

· Fever



If symptoms become severe, the oxygen level in the blood may fall, causing cyanosis, in which the lips or the hands and feet turn blue. In this case, please go to the emergency room immediately.



The risk of progressing to severe illness is especially high in the following cases.

· Premature infants (born before 37 weeks of pregnancy)

· Congenital heart disease

· Weakened immunity (such as after organ transplantation or during chemotherapy)

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Treatment
sections.content:
Diagnosis is confirmed with a PCR test (genetic test) on a sample taken from the nose or throat.



Treatment centers on supportive care (treatment of symptoms). Adequate fluid intake and rest are important. When symptoms are severe, patients may be admitted to the hospital for active treatment such as supplemental oxygen.



During hospital treatment, isolation is needed so that the virus does not spread to other patients. Contact precautions such as hand hygiene are important.



Please consult a medical specialist to decide on a treatment method suited to the symptoms and condition.

records.title: Kawasaki Disease
records.intro: Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile vasculitis of unknown cause that occurs mainly in children. If treatment is delayed, cardiac complications can develop, so please be sure to consult a pediatrics specialist promptly for diagnosis and treatment.
records.tags_raw: Kawasaki disease, high fever in children, vasculitis, cardiac complications, immunoglobulin

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Kawasaki disease is a disease in which the blood vessels, the channels through which blood flows throughout the body, become inflamed. It mainly occurs in young children aged 5 and under.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: A high fever continues for several days or longer even after taking fever-reducing medicine. Both eyes become red and bloodshot, and the lips become red, swollen, and cracked. The hands and feet turn red and may swell, and a red rash appears over the whole body.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: The child receives a special injection called 'immunoglobulin,' which reduces inflammation, and takes an appropriate dose of aspirin as prescribed by a specialist. Giving a child fever-reducing medicine (such as aspirin) on your own can cause fatal complications such as Reye syndrome, so the specialist's prescription and dosing instructions must be followed strictly. If treatment is not received in time, a dangerous heart complication can develop in which the coronary arteries of the heart become swollen, so the child must receive hospital treatment from a specialist.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content: The exact cause has not yet been fully identified. It is thought to arise either from genetic factors or when the child's immune system becomes overly reactive after an infectious illness such as a cold or pneumonia.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: After receiving the immunoglobulin injection, live vaccines such as varicella (chickenpox) and measles vaccines must be postponed for 11 months. Also, even after discharge from the hospital, regular, careful echocardiography (heart ultrasound) should be performed to check for vascular complications.

records.title: Early Detection and Management of Liver Disease
records.intro: The liver is a 'silent organ.' Even as damage progresses, there are no obvious symptoms in the early stage, so fatigue, loss of appetite, and weight loss are often dismissed as minor, and the disease is often discovered only after it has progressed to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Regular checkups are the most important way to protect liver health.
records.tags_raw: liver disease, liver cancer, cirrhosis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, fatty liver, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, hepatectomy, minimally invasive surgery, early screening, alcohol abstinence, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness, nausea, feeling about to vomit, vomiting

sections.heading: Causes and Progression of Liver Disease
sections.content:
The liver is an important organ that performs more than 500 functions, including detoxification, nutrient metabolism, and production of bile (a fluid that aids digestion). It has a considerable ability to regenerate, so early damage causes no symptoms. For this reason, however, by the time symptoms appear, the liver has often already been badly damaged.



■ Main Causes

- Hepatitis B and C viruses: Chronic hepatitis causes inflammation of liver cells for a long time, and through repeated cycles of damage and repair, the liver tissue hardens and progresses to cirrhosis.

- Alcohol-related liver disease: Alcohol is a major cause of liver damage.

- Nonalcoholic fatty liver: The number of people with fatty liver is increasing because of Westernized eating habits and rising rates of obesity and diabetes. Simple fatty liver is relatively benign, but when it worsens to steatohepatitis (fatty liver with inflammation), about 3% progress to cirrhosis and it can develop into liver cancer.

sections.heading: Symptoms and Early Detection
sections.content:
The typical early symptoms of liver disease are listed below, but it is difficult to self-diagnose liver disease from these symptoms alone.



- Unexplained fatigue

- Loss of appetite

- Weight loss



■ Symptoms That Appear in Advanced Disease

- Jaundice (yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin)

- Ascites (a buildup of fluid in the abdomen)

- Nausea and vomiting



In fact, many liver cancer patients are found incidentally during other tests. People in the following groups should be sure to have regular checkups.

- People with chronic hepatitis B or C

- People with cirrhosis

- People with fatty liver

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
■ Hepatectomy (Liver Resection)

In the past, open surgery was the norm, but in recent years minimally invasive surgery using a laparoscope or a robot has become widely performed. Minimally invasive surgery reduces the size of the incision, which can lower pain and speed up recovery.



■ Liver Transplantation

It is considered when the cancer has advanced and liver function has also declined considerably. It is a highly complex operation in which a donor's liver is transplanted.



■ Watching for Recurrence

Liver cancer can recur even after it is removed by surgery, because the underlying chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis that caused it remains. After surgery, regular ultrasound and blood tests are essential.

sections.heading: Prevention and Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
■ Regular Checkups

People with chronic hepatitis B or C and people with fatty liver should have regular ultrasound and blood tests.



■ Limiting Alcohol and Alcohol Abstinence

People with liver disease must abstain from alcohol. Drinking is a direct cause of liver damage.



■ Balanced Diet

Maintain a high-protein, low-fat diet. Unproven dietary supplements or concentrated extracts can actually cause liver damage, so please consult your doctor before taking them.



■ Weight Management

Obesity is a risk factor for fatty liver and liver cancer. Regular exercise and weight control are key to liver health.



Even minor symptoms such as fatigue and loss of appetite can be a sign of liver disease. Please protect your liver health through regular checkups.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Liver Cirrhosis
records.intro: Liver cirrhosis refers to a condition in which the liver has been damaged for a long time by various causes and has become hard. It is also called 'gangyeongbyeon' in Korean. When the liver hardens, it cannot perform its functions well. For an accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: liver cirrhosis, cirrhosis, liver disease, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, ascites, jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swollen hands and feet

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The causes of liver cirrhosis are very diverse. In Korea, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and chronic alcohol use account for about 80% of all causes of cirrhosis. Even people who do not drink alcohol can develop cirrhosis if hepatitis B or hepatitis C is not well managed.



Nonalcoholic fatty liver, metabolic-associated fatty liver (a condition in which fat builds up in the liver because of problems with the body's energy metabolism) linked to obesity, diabetes, and high cholesterol (hyperlipidemia), and autoimmune liver disease can also cause cirrhosis. 'Autoimmune' means that the body's immune system attacks its own liver.



Liver health can also decline when diabetes, high cholesterol, thyroid disease, or similar conditions remain poorly controlled for a long time. On the other hand, it is very rare for cirrhosis to develop from long-term use of medication. In most cases, it is the disease itself rather than medication that harms the liver.



If a health checkup has shown abnormal liver enzyme levels for 6 months or longer, please be sure to consult a medical specialist to find out the cause and ways to improve it.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The liver is called the 'silent organ.' Even when the liver is damaged, there are almost no symptoms at first. By the time the symptoms below appear, the disease has often already progressed considerably, so regular checkups are important.



- Jaundice: The whites of the eyes or the skin turn yellow. 'Jaundice' is a condition in which a substance called bilirubin, which the liver cannot process, builds up in the body and turns the skin and eyes yellow.



- Ascites: Fluid collects inside the abdomen and the abdomen swells. Weight gain or swelling of the legs may also occur even though the person is not eating well.



- Variceal bleeding: Blood vessels in the esophagus or stomach cannot withstand the high pressure and rupture, which can cause vomiting of blood, black stools, or bright red blood mixed in the stool. In this case, please go to the emergency room immediately.



- Hepatic encephalopathy: A condition in which the liver cannot properly detoxify substances in the blood and the brain is affected. Symptoms may include a sudden change in personality, a reversed day-night sleep pattern, and difficulty with things the person usually does well (such as remembering the front-door passcode, using a remote control, or getting dressed).

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The key to treating liver cirrhosis is to find the cause and treat that cause.



- When hepatitis B is the cause: Antiviral drugs (medications that suppress viral activity) are used.

- When hepatitis C is the cause: Effective antiviral treatments that can eliminate the virus in most cases have been developed.

- When alcohol is the cause: Alcohol abstinence is essential.



When the cause is well controlled in the early stage of cirrhosis, some patients may improve.



Liver transplantation may be considered when cirrhosis has become very advanced.



Cirrhosis increases the risk of developing liver cancer. For this reason, it is very important to check liver enzyme levels every 3 to 6 months and to consistently have liver cancer screening, such as ultrasound or abdominal CT, every 6 months. Liver cancer that is detected early can be treated with a variety of treatment options that are associated with a better prognosis.



When receiving other care, such as dental treatment or endoscopy, be sure to tell the medical staff that you have cirrhosis, and it is best to avoid anti-inflammatory pain relievers (NSAIDs) whenever possible. Please consult your doctor each time your medication changes.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
■ Eat Enough Protein

It is important for people with cirrhosis to maintain muscle mass. Having more muscle improves basic physical fitness. Maintaining muscle mass requires adequate protein intake and regular exercise. As long as the amount is not excessive, protein is generally not a problem. Even if you do not eat meat, please get protein from tofu, beans, fish, and similar foods.



■ Reduce Salty Foods

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends limiting salt intake to 5 g a day or less. If you have ascites or edema (swelling), you should greatly reduce your sodium intake. It is best to rinse kimchi with water before eating it, and to eat only the solid ingredients of stews and soups.



■ Avoid Unproven Dietary Supplements

Concentrating a particular food or making it into juice or extract and consuming it in excess can put a burden on the liver. If there is a food that is said to be good for you, it is best to eat it as part of a regular meal. Foods or supplements that are highly concentrated in a particular ingredient can actually cause liver toxicity and greatly worsen liver function.

sections.heading: When to Visit the Hospital
sections.content:
■ When to Go to the Emergency Room Immediately

- Stools turn black or have bright red blood mixed in

- Vomiting blood

- A fever of 38°C or higher

- Sudden confusion, unusual behavior, marked sleepiness, or difficulty staying awake (possible hepatic encephalopathy)



■ When to See a Medical Specialist Soon

- The whites of the eyes or the skin turn yellow (jaundice)

- Weight gain or leg swelling even though you are not eating well (suspected ascites)

- Gradual changes in sleep patterns, concentration, or behavior (possible early hepatic encephalopathy)



When a patient who has had ascites develops a fever, it may be accompanied by 'spontaneous bacterial peritonitis' (a condition in which bacteria grow in the ascitic fluid without any particular cause). Because the fatality rate is high, seek medical attention as quickly as possible.



If symptoms come and go, taking photos or videos with your phone can help you communicate with the medical staff during your visit.

records.title: Hepatobiliary and Pancreatic Cancer
records.intro: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic cancer often has no symptoms in the early stage and is frequently found when surgery is already difficult. However, with advances in medical technology, surgery may become possible after chemotherapy in some cases, so please consult a hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery specialist.
records.tags_raw: liver cancer, bile duct cancer, pancreatic cancer, hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery, chemotherapy

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: There are almost no particular symptoms in the early stage. Symptoms such as abdominal pain, jaundice (yellowing of the eyes and skin), and sudden weight loss appear only after the cancer has progressed considerably.

sections.heading: Prevention and Diagnosis
sections.content: Early detection is the most important way to help improve survival. Even without symptoms, people in high-risk groups, such as those with hepatitis, should be sure to have regular health checkups.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content: Treatment of hepatobiliary and pancreatic cancer is decided by considering the location of the cancer, its stage, whether blood vessels are involved, and the patient's overall condition together. When the tumor cannot be removed at the time of diagnosis because it involves major blood vessels or nearby organs, chemotherapy, or combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy, may be given first, and when jaundice or cholangitis (inflammation of the bile duct) is present, symptoms are controlled through procedures such as biliary drainage. Afterward, whether surgery is possible is reassessed according to the response to treatment.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The liver, the bile duct (the passage through which bile flows), and the pancreas are closely connected structurally, so when cancer develops in one of them, it can easily affect the others. Cancers that develop in these areas are grouped together and called hepatobiliary and pancreatic cancer.

records.title: Comparing the Common Cold, Influenza (Flu), and COVID-19
records.intro: The common cold, influenza (flu), and COVID-19 are all respiratory infectious diseases caused by viruses, but the causative viruses and symptoms differ. It is often difficult to tell the three apart from symptoms alone, so if you have any abnormal symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: common cold, flu, COVID-19, influenza, respiratory infection, comparison, mask, handwashing, sore throat, scratchy throat, pain when swallowing, feeling feverish, body heat, high fever, low-grade fever, body shaking, feeling cold and shivering, cold sensation, dry cough, persistent minor cough, cough that will not stop, stuffy nose, clear runny nose, yellow runny nose, hand tremor, body tremor

sections.heading: Comparing Causes
sections.content:
All three diseases are caused by viruses, but each is caused by a different virus.

· Common cold: Caused by a wide variety of viruses, more than 200 types, including rhinoviruses.

· Flu (influenza): Caused by influenza viruses.

· COVID-19: Caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2).



Therefore, getting a flu vaccine does not protect you against the common cold or COVID-19. There are separate prevention methods for each virus.

sections.heading: Comparing Symptoms
sections.content:
The three diseases have similar symptoms and are hard to tell apart. Because it is difficult to distinguish them accurately from symptoms alone, diagnosis through testing is needed.



· Common cold: Respiratory symptoms such as cough, runny nose, and sore throat mainly occur. Most cases resolve on their own within 1 week.

· Flu: Whole-body symptoms such as high fever, chills, and severe muscle pain are prominent. Respiratory symptoms such as cough and runny nose are less pronounced than in the common cold. Symptoms appear after an incubation period of 2 to 3 days following infection.

· COVID-19: Symptoms such as fever, cough, and sore throat occur. Some people have changes in the sense of smell or taste (difficulty smelling or tasting), which can help distinguish it from flu, but the absence of these symptoms does not rule out COVID-19.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
· Common cold: Antibiotics are not effective. The common cold is caused by viruses, and antibiotics are medications that kill bacteria. Supportive treatment is given to relieve symptoms such as fever and cough. In healthy adults, most cases resolve on their own within 1 week.

· Flu: Treated with antiviral drugs (such as Tamiflu, or oseltamivir). Antiviral drugs are different from antibiotics and act on viruses.

· COVID-19: The treatment method is determined by symptoms and severity.



For all three diseases, if symptoms are severe or do not improve, please consult a medical specialist. Older adults, pregnant women, children, and people with chronic conditions need to be especially careful.

sections.heading: Common Prevention Guidelines
sections.content:
These three respiratory infectious diseases are mainly spread through small droplets released by coughing and sneezing. The following prevention guidelines help against all three.

· Wearing a mask: Reduces the spread of droplets outward and their entry into other people's airways.

· Handwashing: Infection can occur when you touch your nose or mouth with contaminated hands, so wash your hands often.

· Cough etiquette: When coughing, cover your mouth and nose with a tissue, a handkerchief, or your sleeve rather than your hand.

· Avoid crowded places whenever possible.

records.title: Liver Cancer
records.intro: Liver cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the liver, which is responsible for detoxification and nutrition in the body. The liver is called the 'silent organ' because there is no particular pain even when the disease becomes advanced. By the time symptoms appear, the disease has often already progressed considerably, so please do not judge on your own; be sure to have regular checkups and consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: liver cancer, hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver cirrhosis, fatty liver, silent organ, liver transplantation, laparoscopy, lack of energy, listlessness, persistent tiredness

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Liver cancer mainly develops in a liver that has been damaged by long-standing disease, rather than suddenly arising in a healthy liver with no disease.



· Chronic hepatitis: The hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses are the most typical. When a virus causes persistent inflammation in the liver, it worsens into cirrhosis (liver cirrhosis), in which the liver hardens like scar tissue, and liver cancer commonly develops there.

· Fatty liver: Nonalcoholic fatty liver, in which excess fat builds up in the liver because of obesity, diabetes, and similar conditions, can also progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer if left untreated.

· Alcohol: A long-term habit of heavy drinking also destroys liver cells and is a major cause of liver cancer.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
There are usually no symptoms of liver cancer in the early stage. Because the liver tries to keep functioning even when cancer develops, the following symptoms appear only after the disease has progressed quite far.



· Fatigue that is much more severe than usual and a sharp drop in appetite.

· Noticeable weight loss even without dieting.

· A dull, heavy pain in the upper right abdomen, or a hard lump that can be felt from outside the abdomen.

· As the disease worsens, jaundice (yellowing of the whites of the eyes and skin) appears, and ascites, in which fluid fills the abdomen and makes it swell, develops.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Liver cancer causes almost no symptoms until it has progressed considerably. By the time symptoms appear, it has often already progressed far, so the mortality rate of liver cancer itself is high.



■ Diagnostic Methods

A biopsy is the most accurate test, but in people at high risk for liver cancer (those with cirrhosis), the diagnosis is made by imaging when CT or MRI shows typical findings.



■ Regular Checkups

If you have cirrhosis, please be sure to have an abdominal ultrasound or CT scan every 6 months. Please continue regular checkups regardless of symptoms and blood test results.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
· Hepatectomy (liver resection): Surgery that removes the tumor together with the diseased liver tissue around it. Laparoscopic and robotic surgery, in which instruments are inserted through small openings in the abdomen, are now widely performed to reduce pain and scarring. Bloodless surgery techniques (surgery performed without blood transfusion) have also advanced, helping to reduce the risk of infection.

· Liver transplantation: A highly complex operation in which a healthy liver from another person or a brain-dead donor is transplanted when the cancer has advanced considerably or the remaining liver is in such poor condition that it is unlikely to recover on its own.



In addition, a specialist decides on the treatment that suits the patient's condition, such as radiofrequency ablation, which destroys the cancer with heat, chemotherapy drugs, or radiation therapy.

sections.heading: Precautions and Prevention
sections.content:
Even when the tumor is successfully removed by surgery, the annual recurrence rate after surgery reaches 25%. This is because the liver that remains after the cancer is removed is also unhealthy because of the virus or fatty liver.



Therefore, prevention and follow-up care are essential.

· Regular checkups: People with hepatitis B or C and people with fatty liver must have regular abdominal ultrasound and blood tests even if they have no symptoms.

· Strict alcohol abstinence: Alcohol is very harmful to a weakened liver, so people with liver disease should not drink even a drop.

· No folk remedies: Taking unproven decoctions, extracts, juices, or dietary supplements carelessly because they are said to be good for health can overwhelm a weakened liver's ability to detoxify and cause serious liver damage. Please be sure to consult your doctor before taking any.

sections.heading: Care After Treatment
sections.content:
· Regular follow-up for at least 5 years is needed.

· If you have hepatitis B or C, you must keep up the treatment for it consistently.

· Alcohol abstinence and appropriate weight management are important.

· Uncertified dietary supplements (such as mushroom decoctions and juices) can cause liver toxicity. Please be sure to consult your doctor before taking them.

records.title: Liver Cancer: Key Questions
records.intro: Liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) is a malignant tumor that develops from the cells that make up the liver. Because there are almost no symptoms in the early stage, it is often found incidentally during health checkups. Regular checkups are especially important for people with chronic liver disease caused by hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or alcohol-related liver disease. The treatment method and prognosis differ depending on each patient's condition, so please consult a medical specialist before making any decisions.
records.tags_raw: liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, hepatectomy, liver transplantation, Milan criteria, ascites, jaundice, transarterial chemoembolization (TACE)

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Liver cancer is characterized by almost no symptoms in the early stage. As the disease progresses, the following symptoms may appear, but by this time the cancer has often already progressed considerably.

- Dull pain in the epigastric area (the pit of the stomach) or the upper right abdomen
- Weight loss
- A lump that can be felt in the abdomen

When liver cancer invades the major blood vessels or bile ducts of the liver, ascites (a buildup of fluid in the abdomen) or jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) can occur. If the diagnosis is made when these symptoms appear, the disease is already very advanced.

Most liver cancers are found at health checkups before any symptoms appear. If you have chronic liver disease (such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or cirrhosis), early detection through regular ultrasound and blood tests is important.

sections.heading: Why the Recurrence Rate Is High
sections.content:
Even when liver cancer is successfully removed, the annual recurrence rate reaches about 25%. Even a small liver cancer 2 to 3 cm in size has a greater than 50% chance of recurring within 3 years after surgery.

■ Why the Recurrence Rate Is High
The main causes of liver cancer are the hepatitis B virus and the hepatitis C virus. Liver cancer mostly develops in a liver in which chronic hepatitis has progressed to cirrhosis (a condition in which the liver hardens and loses function) or in a liver with chronic hepatitis. Even if the cancer is removed by surgery, the remaining liver is still affected by chronic hepatitis, so new liver cancer can develop again.

For this reason, it is very important to detect recurrence early through regular checkups after surgery.

sections.heading: The Importance of Regular Checkups
sections.content:
Regular checkups are the key to early detection of liver cancer.

■ Regular Checkups Recommended for High-Risk Groups
People in the following groups are recommended to have a liver ultrasound and a serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) blood test every 6 months.
- Carriers of the hepatitis B virus
- People with hepatitis C
- People with cirrhosis
- People with alcohol-related liver disease

The earlier liver cancer is found, the wider the range of treatment options, and the prognosis tends to be better. If you have risk factors, please have regular checkups even without symptoms.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Recurrence After Liver Transplantation
sections.content:
Liver transplantation is one of the effective treatment options for liver cancer, but in advanced liver cancer, the cancer can recur even after transplantation. In addition, the immunosuppressants taken after transplantation to prevent rejection can increase the risk of cancer recurrence.

■ Milan Criteria
To minimize recurrence after transplantation, liver transplantation is performed in patients who meet the 'Milan criteria' below.
- A single lesion of 5 cm or less
- Or up to 3 lesions, each 3 cm or less
- No lesions that have spread outside the liver (extrahepatic lesions)
- No vascular invasion

When the Milan criteria are met, the 5-year survival rate after liver transplantation is reported to be 70 to 90%.

■ When the Milan Criteria Are Not Met
If the size and number of tumors are reduced before transplantation through chemoembolization (a method of delivering anticancer drugs directly to the cancer through blood vessels), radiofrequency heat therapy, or liver resection, and transplantation is then performed once the criteria are met, the risk of recurrence may be lowered.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management After Surgery
sections.content:
After liver resection, liver function declines temporarily. Because people with liver cancer often also have hepatitis B or C, fatty liver, or alcohol-related hepatitis, the decline in function may be greater than in patients with a normal liver.

■ The Most Important Thing: Alcohol Abstinence and Smoking Cessation
Balanced nutrition is needed to help restore liver function, and above all, alcohol abstinence and smoking cessation are the most important.

■ Caution with Unproven Foods and Supplements
Some people take decoctions, concentrated extracts, and dietary supplements because they are said to be good for health, but unproven products can cause liver damage. Please be sure to consult your doctor before taking them.

records.title: Liver Transplantation
records.intro: Liver transplantation is an operation that replaces a liver that has lost its function with a healthy liver, and it is one of the treatment options for several serious liver diseases, such as liver failure caused by cirrhosis and liver cancer. Since it was first performed in Korea in 1988, advances in technology and medication have led to more than 1,500 transplants a year at present, and the overall surgical success rate is reported to be about 90 to 95%. Liver transplantation is an important decision for both the recipient and the donor, so please discuss it thoroughly with your treating physician before making a decision.

sections.heading: When Liver Transplantation Is Needed
sections.content:
Liver transplantation is mainly performed in the following cases.



- Liver failure: Cases in which cirrhosis (a condition in which the liver hardens and loses function) has progressed and the liver can no longer function properly. This also includes cases in which liver function suddenly worsens in an acute manner.



- Liver cancer: About 50% of liver transplant patients in Korea receive a transplant to treat liver cancer. However, transplantation is not possible for every patient with liver cancer. Whether to perform a transplant is decided by evaluating the size and number of tumors, whether blood vessels are involved, and other factors together, according to an international standard called the 'Milan criteria.' In recent years, these criteria have also been applied with some adjustments depending on the institution.



- Other: Transplantation is sometimes performed for autoimmune liver disease (a disease in which the immune system attacks the person's own liver) or for rejection after a previous transplant.



Whether transplantation is appropriate differs depending on each patient's condition, so please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
Liver transplantation is broadly divided into two types according to the type of donor.



■ Deceased Donor (Brain-Dead Donor) Liver Transplantation

In this method, the recipient receives the liver of a person who has been legally declared brain-dead. Because the whole liver is usually received, the operation is relatively straightforward. However, there are about 6,000 people on the liver transplant waiting list in Korea, while fewer than 400 deceased donor liver transplants are performed each year, so the waiting time is long and receiving a liver is difficult. Recipients are selected by the Korean Network for Organ Sharing (KONOS) according to the 'MELD score.' The MELD score is a score that indicates the severity of liver disease by combining jaundice, kidney, and blood clotting test values, and the higher the score (the worse the condition), the higher the priority for transplantation.



■ Living Donor Liver Transplantation

In this method, a portion of a living donor's liver (usually 60 to 70%) is removed and transplanted into the recipient. As an alternative to deceased donor liver transplantation, in Korea only blood relatives and immediate family members can be donors. Because a partial liver is used, the surgical technique requires a more delicate process. The remaining liver regrows over time.



■ Comparing Surgical Success Rates

The overall liver transplant success rate in Korea is about 90 to 95%. Deceased donor liver transplantation is sometimes reported at 70 to 80%, because recipients are often relatively more severely ill, and this should be taken into account when interpreting the figure.

sections.heading: Donor Requirements and Safety
sections.content:
■ Deceased Donor (Brain-Dead Donor) Donation

Donation is possible only after a person has been legally declared brain-dead. A liver is difficult to use for transplantation if the donor has liver disease or severe fatty liver, if liver function has been greatly damaged because of the donor's overall condition, or if there is a problem with the blood vessel structure.



■ Requirements for Living Donors

The range of people who can donate is set by the Act on Organ Transplants, etc., and the following conditions must be met.

- No liver disease

- Enough liver must remain after donation (if too little remains, problems can arise in the donor's recovery)

- Age and overall health must be suitable for liver regeneration



In recent years, the scope has been widening, and living donor liver transplantation is now performed even between people with different blood types.



■ Risks to Donors

Donors are selected through strict testing and screening, and ensuring safety is the top priority. Complications such as bleeding, bile leak (a condition in which bile leaks out), and wound infection can occur after surgery, but in most cases donors recover without long-term aftereffects.

Although the probability is very low, there are risks associated with surgery, so please discuss them thoroughly with your care team.

sections.heading: Rejection and Recurrence of Liver Disease After Surgery
sections.content:
■ Rejection

Rejection is when the immune system recognizes the transplanted liver as a foreign object and attacks it after transplantation. In the past, acute rejection within 1 year after transplantation was reported in up to 30 to 50% of patients, but with advances in immunosuppressants, about 90% of patients now recover even when rejection occurs. Treatment methods include adjusting the dose of immunosuppressants, high-dose steroid pulse therapy, and anti-lymphocyte antibody therapy.



■ Recurrence of the Liver Disease That Was Present Before Transplantation

- Hepatitis B and C (viral hepatitis): It can recur after transplantation, but in most cases it can be controlled with medication.

- Liver cancer: Among the treatment options for liver cancer, liver transplantation has a relatively low recurrence rate. However, the likelihood of recurrence after transplantation can differ depending on the stage (degree of progression) before surgery.

- Other liver diseases: In some cases, the underlying disease present before transplantation recurs.



For this reason, continued follow-up after transplantation is the most important thing.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
■ Taking Immunosuppressants

Immunosuppressants must be taken for life to prevent rejection. The most important thing is to take the exact dose at the prescribed time. The dose can be reduced once the transplanted liver has stabilized, 6 months to 1 year after surgery, but it must never be stopped on your own.



■ Regular Follow-Up

Together with your doctor and the transplant coordinator, rejection, infection, side effects of immunosuppressants, recurrence of other diseases, and similar problems should be detected and addressed early through regular tests and outpatient visits.



■ Preventing Infection

Taking immunosuppressants lowers immune function, which makes you more vulnerable to infection. Practice careful hygiene, including handwashing, and contact your care team immediately if symptoms suggestive of infection, such as fever or cough, appear.



■ Multidisciplinary Care

Care before and after surgery is also very important in liver transplantation. Patients are managed safely through multidisciplinary care, in which several departments, such as surgery, anesthesiology and pain medicine, radiology, and gastroenterology, work together with the operating room, intensive care unit, and ward teams.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Secondhand Smoke (Passive Smoking)
records.intro: Secondhand smoke exposure, also called passive smoking, means that a person who does not smoke breathes in smoke from a smoker's cigarette. Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, including carcinogens (substances that can cause cancer), and long exposure in an enclosed space can be harmful even to nonsmokers. If you are concerned about secondhand smoke, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention and Precautions
sections.content:
Avoiding secondhand smoke is the most important form of prevention.

· Avoid spending long periods with a smoker in an enclosed space.

· Creating a smoke-free environment at work and at home is important.

· Smokers should seek help from a medical institution that specializes in smoking cessation.

· If you work in a poorly ventilated environment, have regular health checkups.

· If any unusual symptoms occur, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: What Is Secondhand Smoke?
sections.content: There are two kinds of tobacco smoke. One is smoke exhaled directly by the smoker (mainstream smoke), and the other is smoke that rises on its own from the burning end of the cigarette (sidestream smoke). Secondhand smoke exposure refers to breathing in both kinds of smoke. It is known that about 37% of the world's population is still exposed to secondhand smoke. Repeated exposure over long periods, especially in enclosed spaces, can have a greater effect on health.

sections.heading: Effects on the Heart and Blood Vessels
sections.content: Combined results of several studies have reported that exposure to secondhand smoke may raise the risk of ischemic heart disease. Ischemic heart disease is a condition in which the blood vessels that supply the heart narrow, so the heart does not receive enough blood. The risk of stroke (a condition in which the brain does not receive enough blood, causing abnormalities in brain function) may also rise. If symptoms such as chest pain, difficulty breathing, or a sudden headache or paralysis of the arms and legs occur, please go to the emergency room immediately or consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Link to Diabetes Mellitus
sections.content: There are study results indicating that secondhand smoke may raise the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a condition in which the body cannot use insulin (a substance that lowers blood sugar) properly, causing blood sugar to rise. However, further research on this association is ongoing. If you are concerned about abnormal blood sugar, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Effects on Cancer and Respiratory Disease
sections.content: There are study results indicating that secondhand smoke may raise the risk of lung cancer. It may also raise the risk of asthma (a condition in which the airways narrow, making breathing difficult), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, a chronic respiratory disease in which damage to the airways and lungs causes shortness of breath), and lower respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia and bronchitis. An association with breast cancer is also being studied, but at this point further research is needed. If you have a cough that lasts 2 weeks or longer, difficulty breathing, or hemoptysis (blood coughed up with sputum), please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Thyroid Nodule
records.intro: A thyroid nodule is a lump found in the thyroid gland. It is found very commonly, and most nodules are benign (not cancer). About 5% to 10% are diagnosed as thyroid cancer, so accurate testing and follow-up are important.
records.tags_raw: thyroid nodule, thyroid, thyroid ultrasound, fine-needle aspiration biopsy, Bethesda classification, atypical, thyroid cancer

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A thyroid nodule is a lump (mass) found in the thyroid gland. It is commonly found, and most nodules are benign and unrelated to cancer. However, about 5% to 10% are diagnosed as thyroid cancer. With advances in diagnostic technology and wider use of health screening, the number of thyroid cancer cases diagnosed is rising worldwide.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
If a thyroid nodule is present or suspected, a thyroid ultrasound, including evaluation of the lymph nodes in the neck, is performed.

■ Ultrasound Findings Suggesting a Higher Likelihood of Malignancy (Cancer)
· Irregular borders of the nodule
· Bright dots (calcifications) within the nodule
· Abnormal orientation of the nodule
· A firm, dark-appearing (hypoechoic) nodule

A large size does not automatically mean the nodule is malignant. Changes in size alone cannot distinguish benign from malignant nodules.

■ Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology
Cells are drawn from the nodule with a thin needle and examined. Results are reported using the Bethesda classification system (nondiagnostic, benign, atypia of undetermined significance, suspicious for follicular neoplasm, suspicious for malignancy, malignant). This system is used to predict the likelihood of malignancy and to decide the direction of treatment.

sections.heading: What Does a Biopsy Result of "Atypical" Mean?
sections.content:
"Atypical" means that a nodule falls short of being clearly malignant, but there are abnormalities in the cell structure or nuclear shape. It falls between malignant and benign.

When the result is atypical, a repeat biopsy or molecular marker testing (genetic analysis) is added. A repeat biopsy can establish a diagnosis in most cases, but about 30% come back atypical again. When an atypical nodule is removed surgically, the proportion confirmed as actually malignant is around 15%.

In recent years, approaches such as gene expression testing have been developing to reduce unnecessary surgery. Please discuss the specific testing plan with your doctor.

records.title: Thyroid Nodules and Thyroid Cancer
records.intro: Thyroid cancer is a malignant tumor that develops in the thyroid gland, a butterfly-shaped endocrine organ at the front of the neck that secretes the thyroid hormones that regulate the body's metabolism. Thyroid nodules (lumps) are very common, and a portion of them are found to be cancer, so early detection through ultrasound and cytology is important. If you can feel a lump in your neck or have symptoms such as voice changes, please consult an ENT specialist.
