sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Thyroid nodules (lumps) are tumors that form in the thyroid gland. They are common enough to be found in about 20% to 45% of the general population. As health checkups have become widespread and ultrasound technology has advanced, more nodules are being found incidentally.



Thyroid nodules matter because 5% to 6% of them can be thyroid cancer. Thyroid cancer is more common in women and often appears in the 30s and 40s. Its cause is not yet fully understood. Radiation exposure and genetic factors are known risk factors.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
The following tests are performed to evaluate a thyroid nodule.



■ Thyroid Ultrasound

This is the most effective test for evaluating thyroid nodules. If the ultrasound findings suggest the nodule is benign, it can be followed with regular ultrasound exams without additional tests. If cancer is suspected, fine-needle aspiration cytology is performed.



■ Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology

This is the most important test for diagnosing thyroid nodules. Cells are drawn from the nodule with an ordinary injection needle and examined. It can be done in the outpatient clinic without anesthesia, is inexpensive, and does not place a major burden on the body.



Cancer should be evaluated more carefully in the following situations:

· Age 20 or younger, or 60 or older

· A history of radiation therapy to the head and neck area

· A nodule that suddenly grows larger

· Vocal cord paralysis or enlarged lymph nodes in the neck accompany the nodule

· A single nodule found in a man

records.title: Melasma
records.intro: Melasma is a condition in which brown or gray-brown pigmented patches appear on the skin. It most often appears on the face, especially the cheeks and forehead. If you have symptoms, please consult a dermatologist.
records.tags_raw: melasma, hyperpigmentation, melanin, ultraviolet rays, skin, laser, photoaging

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Melasma has three main causes.
 · Ultraviolet rays: UV rays in sunlight stimulate melanocytes (pigment-producing cells) in the skin. Melanin is the pigment that darkens the skin. This is also why melasma deepens in summer, when UV rays are strong, and fades in winter.
 · Hormones: during pregnancy or when taking oral contraceptives, female hormones can trigger or worsen melasma.
 · Genetic predisposition: if a family member has melasma, you are more likely to develop it.
These three factors act together to cause or worsen melasma.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Because melasma is a chronic inflammatory photoaging condition, it is difficult to clear completely in a short period. Consistent, ongoing management is needed.
 · Laser treatment: a method called "toning" is currently widely used. It involves repeatedly delivering low-energy laser at regular intervals. Depending on the patient's condition, several types of lasers are applied in combination.
 · Precautions: strict sun protection is needed even during treatment. Wash the face gently, and avoid unnecessary self-care. Be sure to check with your treating dermatologist about any products you use or additional care.

sections.heading: Prevention and Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
The most important part of preventing melasma is sun protection.
 · Sunscreen: recent research indicates that not only UVA and UVB but also visible light can contribute to melasma. Using a physical (mineral) sunscreen containing titanium dioxide or zinc oxide can block light more effectively.
 · Contraception: choosing a contraceptive method that does not contain female hormones may help prevent melasma.
 · Cosmetics: ingredients such as vitamin C and retinol may help with pigment management. It is also important to use enough moisturizer to protect the skin barrier.

records.title: Thyroid Cancer
records.intro: Thyroid cancer is cancer that develops in the butterfly-shaped thyroid gland at the front of the neck. Prognosis varies greatly by type; papillary carcinoma, which accounts for more than 90% of thyroid cancers in Korea, grows slowly and responds well to treatment, so its outlook is relatively favorable. However, some rarer types have a poorer prognosis, so please be sure to decide on an accurate diagnosis and treatment through a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: thyroid cancer, papillary carcinoma, thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine therapy, thyroid hormone medication, levothyroxine, hypothyroidism, lymph node metastasis, thyroid ultrasound

sections.heading: Types of Thyroid Cancer
sections.content:
Thyroid cancer is divided into several types according to cell characteristics.

■ Papillary Carcinoma
This accounts for more than 90% of thyroid cancers. It is known to be a cancer type that grows slowly and has a relatively good prognosis (outcome after treatment). Early detection and treatment are important.

■ Follicular Carcinoma
This accounts for about 5% of thyroid cancers. It tends to spread through the bloodstream to places such as the lungs and bones more often than papillary carcinoma.

Papillary and follicular carcinoma together are called "differentiated carcinoma," and it is important to detect and treat them early.

■ Anaplastic Carcinoma
This sometimes arises when a long-standing differentiated carcinoma undergoes dedifferentiation (a change in its characteristics). Its incidence is higher after the 60s, and it is characterized by rapid growth and a poor response to treatment. Early distinction from differentiated carcinoma is needed.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Early thyroid cancer is difficult to find through self-examination or by feeling the neck with the hands. Thyroid ultrasound is the most effective method for early detection.

The size of the cancer is an important prognostic factor.

· 2 cm or larger: the risk of spread to other organs, invasion of surrounding tissue (the airway, blood vessels, etc.), and lymph node metastasis increases.

■ Small Thyroid Cancers Smaller Than 1 cm
· 5 mm or smaller: if there is no sign of spread elsewhere, treatment is not needed, and it is followed with ultrasound.
· Larger than 5 mm up to 1 cm: if it is close to the airway or near the recurrent laryngeal nerve (the nerve responsible for the voice), surgery is needed. Otherwise, for a low-risk papillary microcarcinoma, active surveillance can be chosen instead of immediate surgery. However, exceptions are made if there is a family history or a history of radiation exposure. If follow-up is expected to be needed for 20 years or longer, surgery often ends up being needed.

If there are findings that suggest a high-risk thyroid cancer (lymph nodes suspected of metastasis, invasion of surrounding organs, distant metastasis, or suspected medullary carcinoma), prompt treatment is needed.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Treatment of thyroid cancer consists mainly of surgery, radioactive iodine therapy, and thyroid hormone therapy.

■ Surgery
This is the most important treatment for thyroid cancer. There are two surgical approaches.
- Total thyroidectomy: the entire thyroid gland is removed.
- Lobectomy: only one side is removed, and the other half is left in place.

Which operation is performed is decided based on the size, location, and number of cancers, whether it has spread to lymph nodes, and the patient's condition. In recent years, there has been a trend toward choosing lobectomy when possible, to preserve function as much as possible. During surgery, the lymph nodes around the thyroid are also removed, and if there is spread to the lymph nodes at the side of the neck (lateral neck), those lymph nodes are removed too.

For the surgical incision, the traditional method of making an incision of about 4 cm along a skin crease at the lower neck is common, and endoscopic or robotic surgery is also performed for cosmetic purposes.

■ Radioactive Iodine Therapy
In some patients who have had a total thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine (a radioactive isotope) is taken to destroy any normal thyroid tissue or microscopic cancer cells that may remain after surgery. It is not performed in patients who have had only a lobectomy.

■ Thyroid Hormone Therapy
This is taken to replace the thyroid hormone that is deficient after surgery, and to keep thyroid-stimulating hormone (a hormone secreted by the pituitary gland that stimulates thyroid cells) low, in order to suppress the growth of cancer cells and help prevent recurrence.

sections.heading: Postoperative Care
sections.content:
■ Diet After Surgery
There are no particular foods to avoid after surgery, and you can simply eat a balanced diet.

■ Low-Iodine Diet for 2 Weeks Before Radioactive Iodine Therapy
To improve the effect of radioactive iodine therapy, iodine-containing foods must be restricted starting 2 weeks before treatment. During this period, you should not eat seaweed (sea mustard, laver, kelp, etc.), fish and shellfish, or dairy products. However, after radioactive iodine treatment is finished, these restrictions no longer apply, so you may eat freely afterward.

■ Precautions When Taking Thyroid Hormone Medication (Levothyroxine)
Thyroid hormone medication is sensitive to absorption, so please follow the points below.
- Always take it on an empty stomach (at least 30 minutes to 1 hour before a meal).
- Taking it at the same time as mineral supplements such as calcium, magnesium, and zinc, probiotics, or other medications can interfere with absorption. Do not take them together; take them at separate times.
- Do not stop taking the medication or change the dose on your own, and check through regular blood tests that you are maintaining the appropriate dose.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Most thyroid cancers cause no symptoms in the early stages and are often found incidentally during health checkups.

■ Symptoms That Warrant a Hospital Visit
If you have any of the symptoms below, there may be various causes, including cancer, so please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
- A hard lump can be felt in the neck
- A lump suddenly grows larger
- Difficulty breathing or swallowing
- A sudden change in voice

By the time these symptoms appear, the cancer has often already progressed considerably. That said, these symptoms do not necessarily mean cancer.

sections.heading: Duration of Thyroid Hormone Medication and Prevention
sections.content:
■ How Long Do I Need to Take Thyroid Hormone Medication?
- Total thyroidectomy: you must take it for life to maintain thyroid function.
- Lobectomy (partial removal): if the remaining thyroid maintains normal function, you may be able to go without medication. About 80% of patients do not need to take medication after lobectomy. However, if the remaining thyroid function is not sufficient or there is a risk of recurrence, medication is needed.

Thyroid hormone medication is generally regarded as a safe medication that people with hypothyroidism also take for life. Pregnant women can also take it, and it does not generally have a harmful effect on the liver or kidneys. However, long-term use at high doses may raise the risk of heart disease and osteoporosis, so it is important to maintain an appropriate dose through regular blood tests.

■ Preventing Thyroid Cancer
Radiation exposure and iodine deficiency are known to be associated with onset, but the clear cause of the disease is not yet well established. For this reason, no specific preventive method is known. However, some studies show that obesity raises the incidence of thyroid cancer, so, as with general cancer prevention guidelines, a healthy diet, regular exercise, and maintaining an appropriate weight may help.

records.title: Text Neck Syndrome

It can be prevented with good posture and regular exercise, and if symptoms are severe, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Text neck syndrome is a neck condition caused by holding the head bent forward for a long time while using a smartphone, computer, or similar device.

The human head weighs about 5 to 6 kg. However, when the neck is bent forward 30 degrees, about 20 kg of weight is placed on the neck because of the lever principle. At 60 degrees, it reaches about 30 kg. Because the head is bent about 30 degrees on average when using a smartphone, long periods of use place a heavy load on the neck.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
In the early stages, pain and stiffness around the neck and shoulders are the main symptoms.

As text neck worsens, cervical kyphosis, a forward curve of the neck bones, can develop. Cervical kyphosis can directly compress nerves, or stretch the spinal cord more when the head is bent forward, which can impair blood circulation. As a result, sensory and motor disturbances can occur.

It is also known to be closely associated with cervical myelopathy (a condition in which compression of the spinal cord causes clumsy hands and feet or gait abnormalities).

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Surgical treatment may be needed for cervical kyphosis severe enough to cause neurological symptoms. In most cases, however, the following conservative treatments are used:

· Correcting posture

· Adequate rest

· Exercise therapy

· Medication

Please be sure to decide the treatment approach after consulting a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
Stretching and isometric strengthening exercises can help prevent text neck. Isometric exercise is exercise in which you tense the muscles without moving the joint.



■ Stretching

① Tense the shoulder blade (scapula) on one side and lower that shoulder.

② Pull the side of your head with the opposite hand, and feel the trapezius muscle around the neck and shoulder stretch.

③ Repeat on the other side in the same way.

④ Gently push your chin upward with your thumb.

⑤ With your fingers interlaced, gently press the back of your head forward.



■ Isometric Strengthening Exercises

① Place your palm against the side of your head, and push your hand and head against each other in opposite directions, holding the position.

② Place your palm on your forehead, and push against each other in opposite directions, holding the position.

③ Place your interlaced hands behind your head, and push against each other in opposite directions, holding the position.



It is good to do stretching often during the day and strengthening exercises at least twice a day (morning and evening).



Neck flexor and extensor strengthening exercises can also help.

· Neck flexor exercise: try to bend your head forward while resisting in the opposite direction with your interlaced hands.

· Neck extensor exercise: try to tilt your head back while resisting in the opposite direction with your interlaced hands.

If symptoms persist or worsen, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
· When sitting in a chair, press your lower back firmly against the backrest so that your neck and back do not bend forward.

· When looking at a smartphone, hold it at about eye level, or tilt your gaze down no more than about 10 degrees.

· Choose a pillow height that fits your own cervical curve, and make sure the pillow supports the entire neck.

· If you already have neck pain or numbness in your hands and feet, see a medical specialist rather than relying on your own judgment.

This content is general health information and is not a substitute for diagnosis or treatment of your individual symptoms.

records.title: Psoriasis
records.intro: Psoriasis is a chronic skin condition in which red patches with white scales (flaking skin) form on the skin. It commonly appears on joint areas such as the elbows and knees. It requires treatment and steady management, so please consult a dermatologist.
records.tags_raw: psoriasis, scales, flaking skin, dermatitis, joints, chronic skin disease, immunity

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
· At first, small bright red papules (raised areas of skin) appear.
 · They gradually enlarge and merge, appearing as well-defined plaques (patches) with white scales (flaking skin).
 · They occur mainly on the outer side of joints such as the elbows and knees.
 · Removing the scales may cause pinpoint bleeding (bleeding that appears as tiny dots).
 · The same lesions can appear at sites of skin irritation or injury.
 · Itching is often less severe than in atopic dermatitis.

sections.heading: Management
sections.content:
· Thorough moisturizing in winter and keeping indoor temperature and humidity appropriate are important.
 · Avoid skin irritation and injury.
 · Psoriasis and atopic dermatitis differ in symptoms and treatment, so an accurate diagnosis is essential.
 · Follow the treatment prescribed by a dermatologist.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Psoriasis occurs when genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors act together.
 · It is a condition in which an immune abnormality causes skin cells to be produced abnormally quickly, so that scales build up.
 · Onset in the 20s is most common.
 · Symptoms often worsen in the dry environment of winter.

records.title: Winter Falls and Hip Fractures
records.intro: Fractures caused by falls in winter are a serious health problem for older adults. Hip fractures in particular (fractures of the hip bone) can lead to serious complications if not treated appropriately. Preventing osteoporosis and being careful to avoid falls are important.
records.tags_raw: hip fracture, fall, winter fracture, osteoporosis, hip bone, femur, joint replacement, fracture prevention

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
In cold weather, muscles stiffen and reflex responses decline, and frozen road surfaces make slipping more likely. According to reports, falls in winter are about 3 times more frequent than in other seasons. Walking with your hands in your pockets on a cold day, or walking hunched over, makes it harder to protect yourself when you fall, leading to fractures.
Fractures caused by falls occur most often in the wrist, spine, and hip joint (hip bone).

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
In winter, fractures often occur from falls on icy roads or from injuries while skiing or skating.

■ Common Fracture Sites in Falls
- Wrist (distal radius) fracture: the most common. When you fall and catch yourself with your hand, your body weight is concentrated on the wrist.
- Hip (femoral neck and trochanteric) fracture: common in older adults, requires surgery, and carries a risk of death.
- Back (vertebral compression) fracture: severe back pain persists, and if left untreated, it can progress to kyphosis.

■ Common Fractures While Skiing
Shinbone (tibia) fracture, and injuries to the knee and ankle joints

■ Why It Is Especially Dangerous for Older Adults
Their sense of balance and reflexes decline, and bones weakened by osteoporosis can break into multiple pieces even with a minor impact.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Most hip fractures require surgery.
· Bone fixation surgery (internal fixation): the patient's own bone is realigned and fixed in place. It is advantageous for returning to normal activities, but rest is needed until the bone heals, and a second operation may be needed.
· Joint replacement surgery: the damaged joint is replaced with an artificial joint. Walking is possible early, but the extent of surgery is greater.
The treatment approach is decided by a specialist according to the patient's age, health condition, and type of fracture.

sections.heading: First Aid for Fractures
sections.content:
If a fracture occurs, respond as follows:

- Do not move the fractured area carelessly. Moving it increases damage to surrounding tissue and makes treatment more difficult.
- Use nearby items such as an umbrella or a board to make a splint and immobilize the area.
- Call 119 or go to a hospital immediately.
- Carry a mobile phone and a backup battery so you can call for help in an emergency.

■ Be Careful Even If Symptoms Seem Mild
Some people mistake a fracture for a bruise and come to the hospital late. In older adults especially, even if symptoms are not severe, leaving a fracture untreated can worsen it to a condition that requires surgery, so please be sure to visit a nearby orthopedic clinic to have it checked.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.content:
Hip fractures are especially dangerous for older adults.
· At first the pain may not be severe and there may be little swelling, so a fracture can be overlooked.
· Even a hairline fracture can later separate completely and worsen over time.
· The hip joint bears about 3 times body weight when walking. If the blood supply is cut off, the bone can die (necrosis) or the fracture site may fail to heal.
· In older adults with dementia or limited mobility, fractures are often detected late.
If you find it hard to stand up or the pain persists after landing on your buttocks in a fall, please be sure to consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To prevent fractures in winter, it is important to follow these points:
· When going out on days with snow or ice, wear non-slip shoes, and take your hands out of your pockets while walking to keep your balance.
· Wear gloves or a scarf so that you do not hunch your body.
· Preventing osteoporosis is important. People with osteoporosis, whose bones are weak, can fracture easily even in a minor fall. Please have bone density tested regularly to diagnose osteoporosis early and receive appropriate treatment.
· Regular exercise (brisk walking, going up and down stairs, etc.) to maintain muscle strength and bone strength can help prevent falls and fractures. Exercise at least 3 times a week for about 1 hour each time is generally recommended, but exercise intensity should be decided after consulting a professional according to your individual health condition.

records.title: Atlantoaxial Instability (Cervical Instability)
records.intro: Cervical instability (atlantoaxial instability) is a condition in which the connection between the first and second neck bones (cervical vertebrae) becomes loose and allows excessive movement. Mild cases may cause no symptoms, but as it progresses it can compress the spinal cord and lead to serious nerve damage. It is relatively common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Please be sure to decide on an accurate diagnosis and treatment approach through a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: cervical instability, first cervical vertebra (C1), second cervical vertebra (C2), cervical disc herniation, cervical spine surgery, rheumatoid arthritis, cervical fusion, spinal cord, numbness in hands and feet, arm numbness, tingling leg, weakness in arms and legs, difficulty moving one side of the body, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason
keywords: difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
The neck bones (cervical vertebrae) consist of 7 bones in total. Among them, the first cervical vertebra (the atlas) is ring-shaped, and the second cervical vertebra (the axis) has a bolt-shaped projection pointing upward, which the first vertebra encircles. The two bones are connected by thin ligaments.



Cervical instability is a condition in which these ligaments weaken or are damaged, so that the gap between the first and second cervical vertebrae widens abnormally and allows excessive movement.



- Normal: gap between C1 and C2 of less than about 3 mm

- Instability: the gap begins to widen to 5 mm or more

- Severe cases: the gap widens to 10 mm or more and can compress the spinal cord (an important bundle of nerves connected to the brain)



Cervical instability has little chance of improving on its own, so early detection and appropriate treatment are important.

sections.heading: Symptoms and How It Differs from a Cervical Disc Herniation
sections.content:
■ Main Symptoms of Cervical Instability

- Neck pain (cervicalgia)

- Pain radiating up toward the back of the head

- Pain when turning the head



■ How It Differs from a Cervical Disc Herniation

A cervical disc herniation (a herniated disc in the neck) mainly causes numbness and pain in the arms or hands because the disc is compressing a nerve. In contrast, the nerves at the level of C1–C2 are not structures that cause arm numbness, so cervical instability is distinguished by neck pain and pain at the back of the head being the main symptoms rather than arm numbness.



■ Symptoms That Can Occur If Left Untreated

When the spinal cord begins to be compressed, pain and numbness of the hands and feet may appear at first. As compression worsens, weakness of the arms and legs, and eventually serious paralysis, can occur. In addition, because the ligaments are loose, the risk of spinal cord injury from even a minor impact increases. If compression of the spinal cord continues for too long, it can reach a state that is difficult to recover from, so prompt evaluation is needed when symptoms appear.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
■ X-ray (Flexion and Extension Views)

X-rays taken while bending the head forward and tilting it back are used to diagnose instability by checking whether the first cervical vertebra slides forward and returns.



■ MRI

This is needed to check the condition of the spinal cord and the degree to which it is being compressed.



■ CT (Including Vascular Imaging)

This is always performed when planning surgery. It is needed to accurately determine the size of the space for inserting screws, the location of blood vessels, and other details. Even if an MRI has already been taken, CT is a separate test that is still required.



For patients with rheumatoid arthritis, checking for cervical instability with flexion and extension X-rays when treatment begins, followed by follow-up testing every 6 to 12 months, can allow early detection.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Cervical instability is a problem of the ligament structure, so it is not resolved by medication or rehabilitation exercise alone. The standard treatment is surgery.



■ When Surgery May Not Be Needed

If the degree of instability is mild and there are no symptoms, stretching and active treatment of the underlying condition (such as rheumatoid arthritis) may be recommended.



■ Surgical Treatment

The first and second cervical vertebrae are fixed with screws and rods, and surgery is performed to encourage bone tissue to grow between the two bones and fuse them (bone fusion). With advances in surgical technique, the range of cases in which surgery can be applied has broadened compared with the past.



■ Surgical Complications

The space for inserting screws is very narrow, so complications such as the following can occur.

- Vascular injury: if a screw strays to the side, the blood vessels going to the head can be damaged and a cerebral infarction can occur. In studies in Korea, the incidence of vascular injury has been reported at about 2% to 3%.

- Nerve injury: if a screw strays inward, the spinal cord can be injured.

- Others: pain at the surgical site, hematoma (a collection of blood), infection, and screw loosening or displacement can occur.



Because there are risks of complications, please be sure to decide whether to have surgery after thorough consultation with a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
■ Chuna Manual Therapy and Spinal Manipulation

Chuna manual therapy (a Korean manual therapy technique) and cervical manipulation are conservative treatments for reversible conditions. If performed forcefully on a patient with cervical instability whose ligaments are already weakened, they risk causing nerve injury. They are not recommended when cervical instability at C1–C2 caused by a rheumatic disease has been diagnosed.



■ Pillow Height

The cervical spine should maintain its normal slight curve (lordosis) so that enough space for the nerves is secured. If a pillow is too high, this curve collapses, the neck bends forward, and the risk of nerve compression increases. In particular, in people with cervical instability, using a high pillow can push the first cervical vertebra further forward and worsen symptoms. Please use a pillow at the height that is most comfortable for you.



■ Precautions for Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammation in the ligaments connecting C1 and C2, and some medications used for treatment can weaken ligaments. During treatment for rheumatoid arthritis, it is important to monitor the condition of the cervical spine with regular X-rays.

records.title: Seasonal Affective Disorder (Seasonal Depression)
records.intro: Seasonal depression is a condition in which depression appears repeatedly and is closely tied to a particular season, such as fall or winter. The accurate diagnostic name is "major depressive disorder, with seasonal pattern." Changes in the amount of sunlight and disruption of the body's circadian rhythm are presumed to be among the causes. If low mood is serious enough to interfere with daily life, please consult a psychiatrist.
records.tags_raw: seasonal affective disorder, depression, major depressive disorder, fall depression, winter depression, amount of sunlight, circadian rhythm, mood disorder, lack of energy, fatigue, feeling tired all the time

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Seasonal depression is a form of depression that appears repeatedly in a particular season (mainly fall and winter). In the diagnostic criteria for mental disorders (DSM-5), it is diagnosed as "major depressive disorder, with seasonal pattern." That is, it is a case in which seasonality appears together with major depressive disorder (a condition in which severe depressive symptoms last 2 weeks or longer).



Major depressive disorder is diagnosed when 5 or more of the following symptoms are present nearly every day for 2 weeks or longer and seriously interfere with daily life.

① Depressed mood

② Loss of interest or pleasure

③ Decreased or increased appetite (change in weight)

④ Insomnia or excessive sleeping

⑤ Marked restlessness (agitation) or noticeably slowed movement

⑥ Fatigue or loss of energy

⑦ Severe feelings of worthlessness or guilt

⑧ Difficulty concentrating or indecisiveness

⑨ Recurrent thoughts of death



A slight dip in mood with the change of seasons can be within the normal range. However, if these symptoms go beyond the normal range and interfere with daily life, evaluation by a medical specialist is needed.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
The cause of seasonal depression is not yet fully understood. As with general depression, it is known that multiple factors act together.



· Genetic factors

· Neurobiochemical factors: an imbalance of neurotransmitters in the brain (serotonin, melatonin, etc.)

· Psychosocial factors: stress and personality traits

· Changes in sunlight: as days become shorter toward fall and winter and exposure to sunlight decreases, the resulting disruption of the body's circadian rhythm is presumed to have a greater effect on seasonal depression.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
When mood changes go beyond the normal range, appropriate treatment is needed. Depression that appears in a previously healthy person often responds to antidepressant medication or psychotherapy, and improvement may come relatively quickly.



The treatment approach depends on the severity and cause of symptoms. Antidepressants, light therapy, psychotherapy, and other treatments may be used. Please decide on the specific treatment approach after consulting a psychiatrist.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
These are ways you can practice in daily life to help prevent seasonal depression and manage symptoms.



■ Regular Exercise

Light aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking for 30 minutes or more to the point of sweating, can help reduce depressed mood. Do not neglect exercise just because the weather has turned chilly or the days have become shorter.



■ Regular Sleep

Sleeping too long or waking up late just because the nights have become longer is not advisable. Keep your bedtime and wake-up time consistent.



■ Managing Emotional Well-Being

It is important to recognize low mood as an unhealthy state and to take an active approach to improving it. If negative feelings continue without a reason or for an excessively long time, please seek help from a professional.

records.title: Preconception Care (Planning a Pregnancy)
records.intro: Preparing before pregnancy is important for a healthy pregnancy and birth. It is recommended to consult an OB/GYN specialist and to have the necessary tests and vaccinations starting 6 months before pregnancy. Planning a pregnancy can help protect the health of both the mother and the baby.
records.tags_raw: planned pregnancy, preconception testing, folic acid, vaccination, pregnancy preparation, couples, prenatal care

sections.heading: Preparation 3 Months Before Pregnancy
sections.content:
Starting 3 months before trying to conceive, practice the following:

· Quit smoking: smoking and secondhand smoke are harmful to pregnancy and the baby's health.
· Drink less alcohol: drinking lowers sperm quality and can also affect fetal development.
· Reduce caffeine intake
· Folic acid: both partners start taking essential nutrients such as folic acid. Folic acid can help prevent birth defects such as neural tube defects.
· Eat a balanced diet and maintain an appropriate weight
· If a genetic disease runs in your family, get genetic counseling.

Because it takes about 100 days for sperm to be produced, it is important for men as well to maintain healthy habits starting 3 months before pregnancy.

sections.heading: Vaccinations Before Pregnancy
sections.content:
Some vaccines cannot be given during pregnancy, so it is important to complete them before pregnancy.

The following vaccinations are recommended before pregnancy:
· MMR vaccine (prevents measles, mumps, and rubella): rubella infection during pregnancy can have a serious effect on the baby.
· Varicella (chickenpox) vaccine
· Tetanus and diphtheria vaccine (Td)
· HPV vaccine (prevents cervical cancer)
· Hepatitis B and hepatitis A vaccines
· Influenza vaccine

Some live vaccines (vaccines made from weakened live viruses) are not permitted during pregnancy. Depending on the vaccine, it can take several months to complete the series, so please make a plan 6 months before pregnancy.

sections.heading: Final Check Right Before Pregnancy
sections.content:
Right before trying to conceive, check the following:

· Medications: some medications must not be taken during pregnancy, so if you are taking any medication, consult a medical specialist.
· Treat infectious conditions such as vaginitis and dental disease in advance.
· If you smoke, quit immediately, and it is advisable to wait until at least 3 months after quitting before trying to conceive.
· Avoid exposure to harmful environments (hazardous substances, radiation, etc.).

Planning a pregnancy is more than simple preparation; it is an important first step for the long-term health of both mother and child. Please consult a medical specialist thoroughly.

sections.heading: Preconception Tests
sections.content:
If you are planning a pregnancy, it is advisable to consult an OB/GYN specialist at least 6 months before.

Basic preconception tests include the following:
· Blood tests: to check for anemia, blood type, blood sugar, thyroid function, and more
· Urine test
· Infection tests: syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and immune status for rubella, varicella, and others
· Gynecologic tests: cervical cancer screening, ultrasound, and others

Men are also advised to have basic tests such as blood tests, urine tests, and infection tests. If you are concerned about infertility, a semen and testicular examination can also be done.

records.title: Hip Fracture
records.intro: A hip fracture is the most serious type of fracture that occurs after a fall. The hip joint is the joint where the pelvic bone and the thigh bone (femur) connect. After a fracture, a person cannot bear weight or stand, which makes walking independently difficult, and in older patients it can lead to complications such as pneumonia, pressure sores, and sepsis, so mortality is high. If you have pain in the hip or upper thigh after a fall, please consult an orthopedic specialist right away.
records.tags_raw: hip fracture, fall, femur, hip bone fracture, joint replacement, fracture fixation, osteoporosis, fracture in older adults

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content:
A hip fracture is especially dangerous for older adults.

· Because the person cannot bear weight and stand after the fracture, they end up lying down for a long time.
· During prolonged bed rest, complications such as pneumonia, pressure sores (skin breakdown from lying down for a long time), and sepsis (a serious infection in which bacteria spread through the blood) can occur.
· For this reason, mortality after a hip fracture is high.

To prevent complications, it is important to have surgery as soon as possible and to start rehabilitation early. Delayed surgery can have a negative effect on the patient's health and on surgical results.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
When a hip fracture occurs, the following symptoms appear:

· Severe pain in the hip or upper thigh
· Being unable to move the leg or bear weight and stand because of the pain
· Swelling and bruising of the area may develop over time
· The legs may look different in length, or the foot may appear turned outward

Most patients notice a problem right after the injury, but in older patients, those with dementia, or when the fracture is minor, it is sometimes found only after several days. If you have pain in the hip or thigh after a fall, please be sure to visit a hospital.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
At the hospital, a physical examination is performed along with the following imaging tests:

· X-ray: can identify most fractures.
· CT (computed tomography): checks the detailed shape and severity of the fracture and whether the joint surface is involved.
· MRI: performed when the fracture is unclear or damage to surrounding soft tissue (muscles, ligaments, etc.) is suspected.

Because older patients often also have osteoporosis, a bone density test is sometimes performed as well.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To prevent a hip fracture, preventing falls is the most important thing.

■ Everyday Guidelines for Preventing Falls
· Avoid going out, if possible, on days with icy roads or heavy snowfall.
· Wear low-heeled, non-slip shoes when you go out.
· Even if shaded areas look free of snow, there may be ice. Be careful when walking.
· Always hold the handrail when going up or down stairs.
· Do not put your hands in your pockets when walking.
· For older adults, use a cane or walker if needed.

■ Osteoporosis Management
· Hip fractures are very closely linked to osteoporosis.
· Have a bone density test every 1 to 2 years. For women, regular testing after menopause is especially important.
· If you are diagnosed with osteoporosis or have a history of an osteoporotic fracture (such as a wrist or hip fracture), take osteoporosis medication as prescribed by a specialist.
· Regular strength training and stretching can help strengthen bones and reduce the risk of falls.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Most hip fractures require surgery. Without surgery, the fracture site often does not heal well and walking can become impossible.

■ Fracture Fixation
This is a method in which the broken bone fragments are realigned and then fixed with a metal plate or other metal fixation device. There is little bleeding, the surgery is relatively simple, and the patient's own joint is preserved. However, care with activity is needed until the bone has fully healed, and if the bone does not heal, another operation may be needed.

■ Hip Replacement Surgery
This is surgery in which the broken bone is removed and replaced with an artificial joint implant. Rehabilitation and walking are possible early after surgery, and if there are no complications, treatment can be completed with a single operation. However, the extent of surgery is large and the risk of infection is relatively higher.

The surgical method is decided by your treating physician according to the location of the fracture, the patient's overall health, and the degree of osteoporosis. Tests are performed before surgery to check for medical problems, and the final decision on whether to operate is made taking into account the opinions of doctors in related fields.

sections.heading: What Is a Hip Fracture?
sections.content:
The hip joint is the joint at the hip formed where the pelvic bone and the thigh bone (femur) meet. It is a large, stable ball-and-socket joint that can move in many directions and connects the trunk to the legs. When there is a problem with the hip joint, basic daily activities such as walking and sitting are immediately and significantly limited.

Hip fractures mainly occur when a person falls toward one side of the hip. The fracture usually occurs at the area where the pelvic bone and femur connect (the proximal femur). They occur in various forms, from simple line (linear) fractures to comminuted fractures in which the bone breaks into multiple pieces.

According to research, the number of fracture patients in the emergency room more than doubles after snowfall, and hip fractures account for a significant share of them.

records.title: Hip Pain and Rheumatic Diseases
records.intro: Hip (hip joint) pain can occur in various rheumatic diseases. Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, lupus, and osteoarthritis are typical examples. When hip symptoms are present, an accurate diagnosis that takes systemic symptoms and blood tests into account is needed, so please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: hip pain, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, lupus, osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, arthritis, multidisciplinary consultation, joint pain, knee pain, shoulder pain, wrist pain
keywords: avascular necrosis of the femoral head

sections.heading: Rheumatic Diseases That Cause Hip Pain
sections.content:
Among patients who visit a hospital complaining of pain in the hip joint (the joint where the thigh bone meets the pelvis), a rheumatic disease is diagnosed in a considerable number. Hip symptoms are often accompanied by involvement of joints throughout the body or other systemic symptoms, so a detailed medical history and blood tests are important.



■ Rheumatoid Arthritis

It usually begins in the small joints of the hands, wrists, and feet, but it can also cause inflammation in the hip joint.



■ Ankylosing Spondylitis

This disease mainly involves the sacroiliac joints (the joints at the back of the pelvis) and the spine, and about 25% to 33% of patients complain of hip pain.



■ Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Arthritis sometimes occurs along with various systemic symptoms. When a lupus patient has hip pain, avascular necrosis of the femoral head (a condition in which the blood supply to the bone is cut off and bone tissue dies) must be distinguished from hip arthritis. Taking steroids, excessive drinking, and smoking are risk factors, and the lupus disease itself can also be a risk factor.



■ Osteoarthritis

This is a condition in which cartilage wears down and is damaged with age, causing joint pain and loss of function, and it often occurs in the hip joint, which bears body weight.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
To determine the exact cause of hip pain, the following tests are performed.



- Examination and medical history: symptoms in joints throughout the body, systemic symptoms, and medication history are checked.

- Blood tests: inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANA are checked.

- Imaging tests: X-ray, MRI, ultrasound, and other tests are used to check for joint damage and avascular necrosis.



When there is hip pain, local imaging alone may not be enough, and it is important to evaluate the condition of the whole body as well.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The goals of treating rheumatic disease in the hip joint are controlling pain and preventing joint dysfunction.



- Medication to control the underlying rheumatic disease is used alongside other treatment.

- Medications that reduce joint pain and inflammation (anti-inflammatory pain relievers, steroids, etc.) are used.

- Depending on the condition, physical therapy or surgical treatment may be needed.



It is important to make the treatment plan in cooperation with orthopedic surgery and rehabilitation medicine.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Severe Obesity
records.intro: Severe obesity goes beyond simple overweight; it is a condition in which excessive fat accumulates in the body and causes serious complications. It is not a short-term cosmetic diet but a condition directly tied to life and health, so rather than judging on your own, you should see a specialist for safe, long-term treatment.
records.tags_raw: severe obesity, diet, weight loss, diabetes mellitus, bariatric surgery

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: Diet herbal medicines and fat-dissolving injections that circulate on the market may have a temporary cosmetic effect, but they are unlikely to treat severe obesity in a long-term, fundamental way. Do not rely on unverified information or procedures; be sure to see a specialist in obesity and make a safe plan.

sections.heading: Surgical Treatment
sections.content: Surgical treatment may be considered for patients who find it hard to lose weight and keep it off with diet and exercise alone. Surgery that reduces the size of the stomach or makes digestion less complete can help considerably in treating the various conditions caused by severe obesity and in maintaining weight healthily over a long period.

sections.heading: Effects on Health
sections.content: Severe obesity can lead to other diseases throughout the body. It can cause heart and blood vessel disease and is a major cause of type 2 diabetes mellitus. In women, it can cause irregular menstrual periods, including amenorrhea, and endometrial cancer, and it also raises the risk of infertility and gestational diabetes mellitus.

sections.heading: Purpose and Methods of Treatment
sections.content: The purpose of severe obesity treatment is not "cosmetic," to become slim, but "therapeutic," to treat the diseases of the body. Diet and exercise are adjusted to each patient's characteristics. Reducing even 1% of current body weight and maintaining that loss steadily over a long time is the key to treatment.

sections.heading: Prevention and Management
sections.content: Managing obesity is a long-term process. Making an unrealistic plan on your own makes it easy to give up. It is important to keep consulting a specialist, build healthy lifestyle habits suited to your own body, and also treat related complications such as sleep apnea (snoring).

sections.heading: Definition and Causes
sections.content: Severe obesity refers to a condition in which fat accumulates in the body far beyond the normal range and threatens health. It most commonly arises when modern, more convenient lifestyles reduce physical activity while people eat more high-calorie foods.

records.title: High-Risk Pregnancy
records.intro: A high-risk pregnancy is a pregnancy with a higher chance than usual of adversely affecting the mother and the fetus. Advanced maternal age (35 or older) is one risk factor for a high-risk pregnancy. Recognizing your own risk factors and following your medical team's guidance can help lead to a good outcome.
records.tags_raw: high-risk pregnancy, advanced maternal age pregnancy, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, preterm birth, preterm labor, obstetrics and gynecology, anxious feeling in the chest, restlessness, worrying for no reason

sections.heading: Definition and Risk Factors
sections.content:
■ Definition

A high-risk pregnancy is a pregnancy with factors that adversely affect maintaining the pregnancy and delivery. Maternal age is one of those factors, and high-risk pregnancy is the broader concept.



■ Criterion for Advanced Maternal Age: Age 35

From age 35, the probability of having a fetus with a chromosomal abnormality increases in a statistically significant way, and the likelihood of difficulties during pregnancy and delivery rises.



■ Major Risk Factors

· Advanced age (35 or older)

· Underlying conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, and uterine malformations

· A history of preterm birth or pregnancy complications in a previous pregnancy

· Multiple pregnancy (twins or more)

· Lifestyle factors such as obesity and smoking

sections.heading: Gestational Hypertension and Diabetes Mellitus
sections.content:
■ Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia

Preeclampsia is a serious complication in which blood pressure becomes very high and proteinuria (protein in the urine) develops. Damage to the mother's blood vessels can become life-threatening, or preterm delivery can become unavoidable. It can also put the fetus at risk through placental abruption (early separation of the placenta).



If systolic blood pressure reaches 140 mmHg or higher, or diastolic blood pressure reaches 90 mmHg or higher, treatment at the hospital may need to begin. Blood pressure can rise suddenly during pregnancy, so it is important to measure it often.



■ Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

All pregnant women have a screening test for gestational diabetes mellitus at around 26 weeks of pregnancy. If you already have diabetes mellitus or had gestational diabetes mellitus in a previous pregnancy, testing is done early in pregnancy. Diabetes mellitus can adversely affect the mother's health and the growth and maturation of the fetus.



Taking medication after a diagnosis of gestational hypertension or diabetes mellitus may be worrying, but the benefits of treatment outweigh the risks, and in some cases the condition can be controlled with lifestyle changes alone. Please be sure to consult your doctor thoroughly.

sections.heading: Preterm Labor and Preterm Birth
sections.content:
It is difficult to predict accurately the risk of preterm birth (delivery before full term). Please visit a hospital promptly in the following situations:

· A history of preterm birth in a previous pregnancy

· A short cervical length measured on examination

· A uterine infection

· Uterine contractions are felt



If a risk of preterm birth is identified, treatment to suppress uterine contractions and steroid treatment to help the fetal lungs mature are given. The closer to full term a baby is born, the fewer the aftereffects, so delaying delivery is advantageous for the fetus as long as it does not harm the mother's health.

sections.heading: Delivery Method
sections.content:
Not every high-risk pregnancy ends in a cesarean section. It is performed only when indications for cesarean delivery (conditions that make it necessary) are present. The delivery method is decided by your treating specialist according to the condition of the mother and the fetus.



A high-risk pregnancy can be a difficult and anxious situation, but recognizing your own risk factors and following your medical team's guidance can help lead to a good outcome. If you have questions or concerns, please be sure to consult your treating specialist.

records.title: Acute Upper Respiratory Infection (Common Cold)
records.intro: An acute upper respiratory infection is a condition in which a viral or bacterial infection causes inflammation in the upper airway, including the nose, tonsils, pharynx (throat), and larynx (voice box). It includes what is commonly called the "common cold." The main symptoms are runny nose, nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and fever. Adequate fluids and rest are the basic treatment, but if you have a high fever or severe symptoms, please consult an ENT specialist.

sections.heading: What Is an Acute Upper Respiratory Infection?
sections.content:
The upper airway is the upper part of the airway (breathing passage), including the nose, tonsils, pharynx (throat), larynx (voice box), and trachea. It is the part that breath passes through before reaching the lower airway, which includes the lungs and bronchi.



An acute upper respiratory infection is inflammation caused by infection in this area. It is a broad diagnostic term that includes rhinitis (inflammation of the nose), tonsillitis (inflammation of the tonsils), pharyngitis (inflammation of the pharynx), laryngitis (inflammation of the larynx), and sore throat. This includes what are commonly called a "nose cold" and a "throat cold."



More than 90% of cases are caused by viruses, and fewer than 10% are caused by bacteria.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
The main symptoms are as follows.



■ Nasal Symptoms

· Runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing



■ Throat Symptoms

· Sore throat, cough, phlegm



■ Systemic Symptoms

· Muscle aches: toxic substances produced by viruses or bacteria can make the whole body ache as if it had been beaten.

· Fever: a fever occurs as the body fights the virus or bacteria. Ordinary viral infections often cause a low-grade fever, while bacterial infections or influenza virus infection often cause a high fever.



Symptoms can be similar to those of allergic rhinitis. If there is a fever or systemic symptoms, a cold (upper respiratory infection) is more likely to be suspected.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.content:
Diagnosis is based on symptoms and a physical examination. Blood tests or X-rays are added if needed.



· On physical examination, the lining of the nose may be swollen, or cloudy discharge may be seen in the sinuses (the spaces around the nose).

· The tonsils may be swollen, and the back wall of the pharynx (the back of the throat) may be red or bumpy.

· If there is a high fever, it may not be a mild cold. Blood tests may show elevated white blood cell counts and inflammatory markers (CRP).

· If a lower airway (bronchi, lungs) infection is suspected, a chest X-ray is taken to check for bronchitis or pneumonia.



If you have a high fever or severe symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The basic treatment of an acute upper respiratory infection is adequate fluids and adequate rest. In many cases, symptoms improve with this alone.



Medication treatment is needed in the following cases:

· A high fever

· A sore throat so severe that eating is difficult

· Nasal congestion that makes it hard to breathe

· A cough so severe that it interferes with sleep



■ Medication

· Antihistamines and nasal decongestants: relieve runny nose and nasal congestion

· Pain relievers/anti-inflammatory medication and gargles: relieve sore throat

· Expectorants and cough suppressants: relieve cough and phlegm

· Antibiotics: prescribed by a doctor when a bacterial infection is suspected or when prevention of secondary bacterial infection is needed. Antibiotics cannot be purchased without a prescription.



There is no need to decide on your own to take antibiotics. Your doctor decides whether they are needed.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
These are guidelines for preventing acute upper respiratory infections.



· Drink enough fluids. This helps keep the mucous membranes from drying out.

· Wash your hands often. It is best to wash with soap under running water for at least 30 seconds.

· Cover your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, so that you do not spread the infection to others.

· If symptoms are severe or you may be contagious, it is best not to push yourself to go to work or school.

· Maintain your immunity with enough sleep and a balanced diet.

records.title: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure)
records.intro: Hypertension is a condition in which blood pressure, the force exerted on the walls of the blood vessels when the heart pumps out blood, stays persistently high; it is classified as a systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or higher or a diastolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or higher. Hypertension often causes no symptoms, so it is called the "silent killer." If left untreated, it can lead to serious complications such as stroke, heart disease, and kidney disease, so evaluation by a medical specialist and steady management are needed.
records.tags_raw: hypertension, blood pressure, blood pressure medication, sodium, arteriosclerosis, antihypertensive drugs, essential hypertension, headache, a splitting headache, migraine, back-of-head pain

sections.heading: Complications
sections.content:
If hypertension is left untreated, the following complications can occur:

· Stroke (a condition in which a blood vessel in the brain is blocked or ruptures)

· Heart attack (myocardial infarction)

· Heart failure (a condition in which heart function weakens)

· Decreased kidney function

· Retinal abnormalities (affecting vision)



Hypertension is one of the most important risk factors for these conditions.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.content:
Hypertension is broadly divided into essential hypertension and secondary hypertension.



· Essential hypertension: high blood pressure that occurs without a specific underlying cause. About 95% of patients with hypertension have this type. It is difficult to identify the exact cause, but diet, lack of exercise, obesity, drinking, smoking, stress, and genetics are associated with it.



· Secondary hypertension: high blood pressure caused by a specific condition, such as kidney inflammation (nephritis), endocrine abnormalities, or preeclampsia (pregnancy toxemia). It accounts for about 5% of patients with hypertension, and blood pressure may return to normal once the underlying condition is treated.



■ Lifestyle Factors That Worsen Hypertension

· Salty food: average sodium intake in Korea is known to far exceed the level recommended by the World Health Organization.

· Heavy drinking: excessive alcohol intake raises blood pressure.

· Smoking: it raises blood pressure temporarily, and excessive smoking can cause a sustained rise in blood pressure.

· Obesity: blood pressure can rise as weight increases. Abdominal obesity in particular is closely related to arteriosclerosis.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Hypertension generally has no characteristic symptoms. Many people think that a headache or a stiff back of the neck is due to high blood pressure, but a direct relationship between such symptoms and blood pressure is not clear.

The most important way to know your blood pressure status is to measure your blood pressure regularly.



About 30% of adults aged 30 and older in Korea, and about half of those aged 60 and older, are known to have hypertension. Many people live without knowing that they have hypertension.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
Lifestyle modification and medication are used together.



In some cases blood pressure comes down with lifestyle modification alone, but when blood pressure is very high or lifestyle modification alone is not enough, medication is needed.

There are many types of blood pressure medication, and if side effects occur, it can be switched to another. It is important to take it steadily as your doctor prescribes. If you stop your medication on your own because your symptoms have gone away, your blood pressure can rise again and dangerous complications can occur, so please be sure to consult a medical specialist.



People with hypertension need to be careful, because some cold medicines for relieving nasal congestion can reduce the effect of blood pressure medication or put a strain on the heart. Before taking cold medicine, please tell your doctor or pharmacist.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Management
sections.content:
To manage blood pressure, it is a good idea to follow these lifestyle guidelines:

· Eat low-salt food. Cut back on salty foods such as soups, stews, and salted seafood.

· Maintain a standard weight. Losing 1 kg can help lower blood pressure.

· Walk briskly or exercise regularly for at least 30 minutes a day.

· Quit smoking and cut down on alcohol.

· Reduce stress and get enough sleep.

· Measure your blood pressure regularly and see a medical specialist.

· Measuring your own blood pressure at home can help with blood pressure management. In the morning, after getting up and using the bathroom, sit at a table, measure twice in a row, and record the results.

sections.heading: Complications and Related Conditions
sections.content:
When you have hypertension, other conditions can occur together with it.

· Hyperlipidemia: it is known to accompany high blood pressure in 60% to 70% of people. Hyperlipidemia is a condition in which there are excessive fat components in the blood.

· Diabetes mellitus: it can occur together with high blood pressure in 30% to 40% of people.

When hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus all occur together, the risk of heart and blood vessel complications increases. Maintaining healthy lifestyle habits also helps prevent hyperlipidemia and diabetes mellitus. Please see a medical specialist regularly.

records.title: Hypertension and Diet Management
records.intro: Hypertension is a condition in which blood pressure stays persistently high. Blood pressure is the force exerted on the walls of the blood vessels when the heart pumps out blood. Hypertension often causes no symptoms, so it is also called the "silent killer." If left untreated, it can lead to complications in the heart, brain, and kidneys, so evaluation by a medical specialist and steady management are needed.
records.tags_raw: hypertension, blood pressure, blood pressure medication, sodium, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, heart

sections.heading: Helpful Foods and Nutrients
sections.content:
The following foods and nutrients can help with blood pressure management:
· Colorful vegetables: vegetables rich in pigment compounds may help lower blood pressure.
· Nuts and legumes: they contain magnesium and can help with blood pressure management.
· Whole grains: they are high in dietary fiber and can help.
· Fish: they contain components that can help with blood pressure management.
If you are overweight, eating less (smaller portions) comes first. Please consult your treating specialist or a dietitian about a specific meal plan.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
In managing hypertension, food matters more than supplements. Be careful with the following foods:
· Salty food: foods high in sodium raise blood pressure. Bamboo salt (jukyeom, roasted salt) does not differ from ordinary salt in sodium content, so please be careful.
· High-calorie foods and overeating: blood pressure can rise as weight increases.
If you feel like drinking a lot of water all at once, you may be very thirsty because you ate salty food. Eat low-salt food, and it is better to drink water in smaller amounts, often.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
To manage hypertension, it is good to maintain the following lifestyle habits:
· Low-salt diet: reduce sodium intake. A habit of eating low-salt food is important.
· Regular exercise: steady exercise can help with blood pressure management.
· Maintain an appropriate weight: being overweight or obese can raise blood pressure.
· Quit smoking and drink less: smoking and heavy drinking have a negative effect on blood pressure.
· Stress management: even in a busy, stressful life, steady and balanced self-care is important.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
If you have hypertension, you may need to take blood pressure medication. Blood pressure tends to rise with age. Unless your lifestyle habits are kept very healthy, it is difficult to stop blood pressure medication once you have started it. Rather, steady management is needed so that the number of types of medication does not increase.
Rather than thinking that taking blood pressure medication alone is enough, it is important to maintain healthy lifestyle habits as well. Please take your medication as prescribed by your treating specialist, and do not stop it on your own.

records.title: Osteoporosis
records.intro: Osteoporosis is a condition in which bones become weaker and can break easily even from a minor impact. There are often no symptoms, and it is frequently discovered only after a fracture occurs. The risk is higher in postmenopausal women and older adults, so regular bone density testing and preventive lifestyle habits are important. Please be sure to discuss treatment options with a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: osteoporosis, bone density, compression fracture, menopause, calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates, fall prevention, vertebral fracture, femoral fracture, dry cough, persistent cough, cough that won't stop

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Osteoporosis is a condition in which bone becomes less dense and weaker, so that it can break easily even from a minor impact. Bone maintains its strength through a continuous cycle of being broken down and rebuilt, and bone weakens with age or when the stimulus for new bone formation decreases.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content:
Osteoporosis itself causes no symptoms. Symptoms occur when a fracture occurs.

- Wrist and hip fractures: these are easily noticed.

- Vertebral compression fracture: a vertebra can be crushed even by a cough or a light fall onto the buttocks. There may be severe back pain, only mild pain, or only a stooping of the back with no pain.

sections.heading: High-Risk Groups
sections.content:
- Postmenopausal women (bone density falls rapidly because of declining estrogen)

- Older adults (risk increases with age in both men and women)

- A family history of osteoporotic fracture, a past fracture, or low body weight

- Insufficient calcium and vitamin D, drinking, smoking, and lack of exercise

- Long-term steroid use, hyperthyroidism, and similar conditions (in this case, secondary osteoporosis)

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.content:
The main goal of osteoporosis treatment is to prevent fractures.



Osteoporosis treatment is divided into treatment of the underlying condition and treatment of osteoporosis itself.



· Treating the underlying condition: if you have a thyroid or parathyroid disease, treating that disease is effective for preventing bone density loss.

· Osteoporosis medication: medications that reduce bone loss or strengthen bone are used. The treatment approach and medication are decided by your treating specialist according to the patient's condition.



Osteoporosis is often discovered only after a fracture occurs, with no symptoms beforehand. If you have risk factors, early detection through a bone density test is important. If you have any abnormalities, please consult a medical specialist.



■ Medication

This is decided by a specialist taking into account the level of bone density and other risk factors.



- Bisphosphonates: the most widely used. There are medications taken daily, once a week, or once a month. Take them on an empty stomach, and do not lie down for 30 minutes to 1 hour after taking them. If taking them is inconvenient or the effect is insufficient, there are also medications given by intravenous injection once every 3 months or once a year.

- Postmenopausal women: a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) or female hormone therapy can be used.

- Newer medications such as parathyroid hormone medication, denosumab, and romosozumab are also available, and are given by injection (daily, once every 6 months, once a month, etc.).



Please consult a medical specialist thoroughly about the choice and order of medications.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.content:
■ Calcium and Vitamin D Intake

- Recommended calcium intake for adults: 800 to 1,000 mg per day

- Average calcium intake in the Korean diet is about 500 mg, which is insufficient.

- Make up the difference with milk and dairy products, fish and seaweed, legumes, green and yellow vegetables, and nuts, or take a calcium supplement.

- Getting some sun exposure each day can help with vitamin D synthesis.



■ Exercise

Weight-bearing activities such as walking, jogging, and hiking are recommended at least 3 times a week for 30 minutes at a time. Adding strength training and balance exercises is also effective for preventing falls.



■ What to Avoid

Heavy drinking, smoking, soft drinks, and excessive caffeine intake can worsen osteoporosis.



■ Secondary Osteoporosis

Correcting the medication or condition that caused it can substantially reduce fracture risk, so identifying it early is important.



※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Coexisting Conditions and Reduced Bone Density
sections.content:
The following conditions are associated with reduced bone density.



· Hyperthyroidism: when there is too much thyroid hormone, bone is broken down faster.

· Hyperparathyroidism: parathyroid hormone increases and calcium leaves the bones.

· Diabetes mellitus: in type 1 diabetes mellitus, a lack of insulin reduces the function of the cells that build bone. In type 2 diabetes mellitus, fracture risk can increase even when bone density measurements are normal or high.

· Rheumatoid arthritis: inflammatory substances throughout the body activate the cells that destroy bone.

· Chronic kidney disease: as kidney function declines, phosphate builds up in the blood and calcium levels fall, drawing calcium out of the bones.

· Prostate cancer and breast cancer treatment: treatments that block male or female hormones cause bone loss.

· Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): loss of body weight and muscle mass can lead to osteoporosis.



If you have any of these conditions, please consult a medical specialist about how to manage bone density.

records.title: Panic Disorder
records.intro: Panic disorder is a mental illness characterized by sudden, recurrent, intense attacks of anxiety (panic attacks), in which a person feels a pounding heart, difficulty breathing, and a fear of dying even though there is no real danger. Repeated attacks are often accompanied by constant worry about having another attack (anticipatory anxiety), which can greatly reduce quality of life. Symptoms can be managed with medication and cognitive behavioral therapy, and if you suspect panic disorder, please consult a psychiatrist.
