sections.content: In the past, donating part of the liver to a family member left a large scar on the abdomen. With robotic surgery, only a few small openings for the robotic arms and a lower incision hidden by underwear remain, so the wounds are much smaller and concerns about scarring may be greatly reduced.

sections.heading: Advantages of Robotic Surgery
sections.content: In robotic surgery, the surgeon operates while viewing the inside of the abdomen on a 3D screen magnified up to 10 times, with clear detail. Robotic arms that bend freely like a human hand allow precise surgery without tremor even deep inside the abdomen, which can help protect important nerves and blood vessels.

records.title: Microsurgical Reconstruction (Free Flap and Perforator Flap Surgery)
records.intro: Microsurgical reconstruction is surgery in which tissue taken from another part of the patient's own body is transplanted to repair a large defect in the skin or tissue caused by conditions such as trauma, cancer, or diabetes. It is a highly complex operation in which blood vessels 1–2 mm in diameter are connected under a microscope, and it is used for legs at risk of amputation and for repairing defects after head and neck cancer surgery.
records.tags_raw: microsurgical reconstruction, free flap, perforator flap, lower limb reconstruction, head and neck reconstruction, microvascular surgery

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content:
Microsurgical reconstruction is a highly complex operation and is performed at medical institutions with experienced reconstructive surgeons.

Before surgery, the condition of the blood vessels is checked with tests such as CT angiography. If the blood vessels are severely blocked, blood flow must first be restored with a vascular procedure or surgery.

Advances in surgical techniques and equipment in recent years have increased the surgical success rate and shortened recovery time. If reconstruction may be possible, please consult a medical specialist thoroughly.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
Microsurgical reconstruction is surgery in which tissue that includes blood vessels is taken from the patient's own body and transplanted to a large defect in order to restore it. For the transplanted tissue to survive, its blood vessels must be connected; to do this, thin blood vessels 1–2 mm in diameter are sutured precisely under a surgical microscope.

Because the patient's own tissue is used, immunosuppressive drugs are not needed, unlike in organ transplantation.

It is used to reconstruct various areas, including the legs (lower limbs), the head and neck (face and neck), and the breast.

sections.heading: Free Flap and Perforator Flap Surgery
sections.content:
A flap is a mass of tissue that includes blood vessels.

· Free flap: A method in which skin, muscle, or other tissue is harvested together with its blood vessels and moved completely to the defect site for transplantation. The blood vessels of the transplanted tissue are connected to blood vessels near the defect under a surgical microscope.
· Perforator flap: A method in which only the skin and the thin blood vessels that pass up through the muscle (perforators, 0.8 mm or less in diameter) are transplanted, without including the muscle. Because a thinner and more natural reconstruction is possible, functionally and aesthetically favorable results may be achieved. Success rates of 92–99% have been reported.

In recent years, perforator flap surgery, which does not sacrifice muscle, has increasingly become a standard method.

sections.heading: Areas of Application
sections.content:
Microsurgical reconstruction is used in the following situations.

· Legs (lower limbs): When a large defect has occurred in the foot or leg because of trauma, diabetic foot, a tumor, or other causes. When bone, ligaments, or other structures are exposed, a simple skin graft is not possible, and flap surgery is needed.
· Head and neck: Repair of defects after surgery for head and neck cancers such as tongue cancer and oral cancer.
· Breast: Reconstruction after breast cancer surgery.

The tissue harvest sites (donor sites) most commonly used are the thigh, flank, and lower abdomen. A specialist decides which site is suitable, taking into account the location and size of the defect, skin color match, and other factors.

records.title: Robotic Surgery for Colon and Rectal Cancer
records.intro: Robotic surgery can offer several advantages when operating on cancers of the colon and rectum. However, robotic surgery is not the right choice for every patient. Do not rely on information from the internet to choose a surgical method; choose it based on an accurate diagnosis by a surgical specialist.
records.tags_raw: colorectal cancer, rectal cancer, robotic surgery, minimally invasive surgery, general surgery

sections.heading: Potential Advantage for Preserving Anal Function
sections.content: Because rectal cancer is located close to the anus, the surgery is very demanding. With robotic surgery, the surgeon can see fine nerves and blood vessels clearly on a high-definition screen, which may help reduce side effects of anal dysfunction, such as difficulty controlling stool after surgery.

sections.heading: Smaller Wounds and Less Pain
sections.content: Unlike open surgery, which involves a large abdominal incision, robotic surgery requires only a few small openings, so pain after surgery may be less and scars may be smaller. As a result, patients may recover more quickly and return to daily life sooner.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Surgical Method
sections.content: The latest robotic surgery does not necessarily lower the cancer recurrence rate. If the cancer has spread extensively or is high-risk, open surgery, in which the abdomen is opened and the cancer is removed carefully by hand, may be safer, so please discuss this thoroughly with your doctor.

sections.heading: Advantages of Robotic Surgery for Colon Cancer
sections.content: Conventional laparoscopic instruments are straight and rod-shaped, which limits their movement. Robotic instruments, however, bend and rotate freely like a human wrist, which may allow the cancer to be removed more precisely even in the narrow, deep space inside the pelvis.

records.title: Novalis Radiosurgery
records.intro: Novalis radiosurgery is a method that precisely treats brain tumors and cerebral vascular malformations without opening the skull. Because the safest treatment differs for each patient, be sure to consult a neurosurgeon thoroughly.
records.tags_raw: Novalis, radiosurgery, brain tumor, cerebral arteriovenous malformation, brain surgery, weakness in arms and legs, difficulty moving one side of the body
keywords: difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: It is often called 'surgery without a knife.' Instead of opening the skull for direct surgery, this method delivers high-dose radiation precisely, in three dimensions, only to the diseased area in the brain (a tumor or abnormal blood vessels), much as a magnifying glass focuses sunlight.

sections.heading: Indications
sections.content: It is mainly used to treat benign brain tumors located deep in the brain where surgery is risky, metastatic brain tumors that have spread to several sites, and cerebral vascular malformations in which blood flows abnormally fast.

sections.heading: Advantages
sections.content: Because general anesthesia and an incision are not required, recovery may be faster and the procedure may be safer. The risk of nerve injury after treatment leading to facial paralysis or hearing loss may also be lower than with conventional surgery.

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: If the lesion is too large, or in an emergency in which the brain is compressed and paralysis may develop immediately, surgery may be needed first. Because the effects of radiation appear slowly, follow-up MRI scans should be continued regularly after treatment.

records.title: Skin Care and Sun Protection After Laser Treatment
records.intro: After laser procedures, proper wound care and thorough protection from ultraviolet (UV) rays can help prevent scarring and pigmentation. If you suspect a side effect, do not try to handle it alone; please consult a dermatologist.
records.tags_raw: sunscreen, sunblock, laser procedure, skin regeneration, scab

sections.heading: Care After Pigmentation and Fractional Laser Treatment
sections.content: Even if a scab forms, forcibly removing it may leave a scar, so wait several days until it falls off on its own. Apply moisturizer often so that the skin does not dry out.

sections.heading: Sun Protection After the Procedure
sections.content: Even after the skin has fully healed following laser treatment, apply sunscreen carefully, even indoors, for at least one month to help prevent pigmentation from darkening again.

sections.heading: Proper Sunscreen Application
sections.content: Apply sunscreen 15–30 minutes before going outdoors so that it absorbs into the skin well. Do not squeeze out an amount about the size of a 500-won coin (about 26.5 mm in diameter) and apply it all at once; instead, divide it into small amounts and pat it over the entire face.

sections.heading: Reapplying Sunscreen
sections.content: If you are outdoors or sweating heavily, reapply every 2 hours to keep your skin protected. If you are wearing makeup, try a sunscreen stick, which is easy to reapply.

sections.heading: Care After Mole Removal (Ablative Laser)
sections.content: Fluid that oozes after a mole is removed is a natural part of the wound-healing process. For 5–7 days, before a scab forms, apply skin regeneration tape and take care to keep the area from getting wet.

records.title: Strength Training and Nutrition
records.intro: Effective strength training requires an understanding of proper nutrition and safe exercise methods. It is advisable to seek help from a qualified professional for your exercise method and meal plan.
records.tags_raw: strength training, bulking, protein, muscle growth, nutrient intake, exercise beginners, resistance exercise, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Additional Energy Intake (Bulking)
sections.content:
When training volume increases during strength training, more energy is needed. Taking in additional energy (increasing food intake or calories) is necessary, but increasing it excessively may cause body fat to increase first.

According to what is currently known, it is recommended to add only a small amount of extra energy (for example, within about 1,500–2,000 kJ per day) and to adjust it to your physical condition and exercise intensity. Because energy absorption and muscle growth vary widely by individual factors such as age, sex, usual activity level, and genetics, it is difficult to set a standard answer.

sections.heading: Protein Intake
sections.content:
Protein intake is important during strength training. Studies indicate that muscle mass increases effectively at a protein intake of about 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day. Protein intake above this level has little additional benefit and may place a burden on the kidneys.

Among types of protein, those containing leucine are known to be favorable for muscle protein synthesis.

Muscle protein synthesis is elevated for 1–2 days after resistance exercise, so it is advisable to replenish protein appropriately after exercise.

sections.heading: Fat Intake
sections.content:
Moderate fat intake is also needed during strength training. An excessively low-fat diet centered on protein may cause side effects such as hormonal imbalance.

The American College of Sports Medicine recommends that 20–35% of total energy come from fat, with saturated fat (such as animal fat) limited to no more than 10% of the total and plenty of unsaturated fat (such as olive oil and omega-3 fatty acids).

sections.heading: Precautions When Using Massage Tools
sections.content:
Myofascial release using tools such as foam rollers or massage balls may help relieve muscle fatigue. However, when using them on the gluteal muscles, it is advisable to take care not to press too hard. It is important to use appropriate pressure for your body size.

If muscle pain or discomfort persists, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Low-Sodium Salt Substitutes
records.intro: Reducing sodium intake is beneficial, but people with poor kidney function who use salt substitutes that provide a salty taste without medical guidance may face life-threatening risks, such as cardiac arrest. Be sure to consult a nephrologist before using them.
records.tags_raw: kidney disease, kidney, low-sodium diet, salt substitute, hyperkalemia, weakness in arms and legs, difficulty moving one side of the body
keywords: difficulty moving one side of the body

sections.heading: Precautions
sections.content: For healthy people, salt substitutes may help reduce the risk of high blood pressure and stroke. However, patients with kidney disease and reduced kidney function have difficulty excreting potassium from the body. If potassium builds up in the body after using salt substitutes, serious complications such as arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat) or cardiac arrest may occur, so extra caution is required.

sections.heading: Recommended Practices
sections.content: Rather than cutting out salt abruptly, avoid processed foods and use natural seasonings such as garlic, onion, and pepper instead of salt when cooking. This is a safer way to help protect kidney health.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Low-sodium salt substitutes reduce sodium, which is harmful in excess, and use potassium in its place to maintain a salty taste.

records.title: Proper Eating Habits and Digestive Health
records.intro: The most basic way to protect digestive health is to maintain proper eating habits. Daily lifestyle changes, such as eating regularly, eating less salty food, and reducing overeating and excessive drinking, can help prevent and manage various digestive conditions, including gastritis and reflux esophagitis.
records.tags_raw: eating habits, digestive health, reflux esophagitis, overeating, low-salt eating, regular meals, indigestion, upset stomach, bloating, poor digestion

sections.heading: Eating Habits That Harm Digestive Health
sections.content:
The following eating habits may have a negative effect on digestive health.



· Late-night meals: Gastric emptying may slow, which can cause indigestion and worsen reflux esophagitis.

· Irregular meals: Overeating after a long period without food may damage the gastric mucosa or cause indigestion.

· Eating too fast: This can contribute to indigestion, belching, and abdominal bloating. It is important to chew food thoroughly and eat slowly.

· Drinking large amounts of water or carbonated drinks during meals: This may dilute stomach acid or distend the stomach, which may not be beneficial.

· Vigorous exercise right after a meal: This may reduce stomach function.

· Stress: An unpleasant mealtime atmosphere can also reduce digestive function.

sections.heading: Practicing Healthy Eating Habits
sections.content:
The following eating habits can help support digestive health.



· Eat a variety of foods.

· Eat an appropriate amount to maintain a normal weight.

· Eat low-salt foods.

· Eat meals regularly and in a pleasant atmosphere.

· Choose fresh, natural foods instead of processed and instant foods.

· Reduce sugar and fat intake.

· Reduce caffeine and carbonated drinks.

· Avoid excessive drinking.

· Increase dietary fiber from vegetables, fruits, and whole grains.



Avoiding harmful foods and habits may be more important for digestive health than seeking out beneficial ones.

sections.heading: Reflux Esophagitis
sections.content:
Reflux esophagitis is a condition in which the valve between the esophagus and the stomach (lower esophageal sphincter) loosens, allowing stomach acid to flow back into the esophagus. Chest pain can be severe and is sometimes mistaken for heart disease.



The main risk factors include the following.

· Abdominal obesity

· Excessive drinking and smoking

· Caffeinated and carbonated drinks such as coffee and cola

· Late-night meals



Lifestyle modification is a key part of treatment. If you have symptoms, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Finding the Right Exercise for You
records.intro: Exercise can help maintain health and prevent disease, but exercise that does not suit your health status and goals can do more harm than good. Choose the type, intensity, and frequency of exercise to suit your condition, and if you have a medical condition, it is advisable to obtain an exercise prescription from a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: exercise prescription, aerobic exercise, strength training, osteoporosis, exercise for diabetes, exercise for weight loss, overweight, swimming, walking, exercise stress test

sections.heading: How to Exercise Consistently
sections.content:
■ Choose Enjoyable Exercise
You can stay consistent only if you enjoy it. Choose exercise you have enjoyed in the past or exercise you can do with others. Group activities such as badminton, table tennis, and hiking may be easier to keep up than exercising alone.

■ Start Light
Overdoing it at the beginning can lead to injury or exhaustion and cause you to stop. It is advisable to plan to reach your target level gradually over 3–6 months.

■ Basic Principles
- At least 3 times a week, at least 20 minutes each time
- Stretch for 10 minutes before and after exercise
- Walking is the easiest exercise. Brisk walking alone may be enough to help maintain health.

If you have a medical condition and need an exercise prescription, it is advisable to have your doctor prescribe the type, intensity, and frequency of exercise.

※ The information in this Health Encyclopedia is for reference purposes only. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, please consult a medical specialist.

sections.heading: Why You Should Choose Exercise That Suits You
sections.content:
Like a medication, exercise works only when it suits your body. Exercise that does not match your goals can harm your health.

■ Examples of Choosing Exercise by Purpose
- Osteoporosis prevention and treatment: Brisk walking and hiking, which directly stimulate the bones, are more suitable than swimming, in which the body is supported by buoyancy.
- Weight loss: Jogging puts considerable stress on the joints, so swimming or cycling may be more suitable. Exercising at an intensity at which you feel slightly challenged may be more favorable for using fat as fuel than running hard. If you want to increase muscle mass, add strength training.
- If you are overweight: Start with swimming or cycling, which put less stress on the joints.

■ Risks of Excessive Exercise
Excessive aerobic exercise with inadequate nutrition may lead to muscle loss, menstrual irregularities, and decreased bone density. A balanced diet that adequately replaces the calories burned is essential.

sections.heading: Exercise Precautions by Condition
sections.content:
■ People With Diabetes
- When exercising for more than 1 hour, replenish fluids and glucose every 30 minutes.
- Carry candy or chocolate in case of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).
- Foot care is essential. Check carefully for blisters and wounds after exercise. Diabetes can reduce sensation, making it easy to overlook an injury.
- Wear cotton socks that absorb sweat well and roomy shoes.
- Rather than focusing on a single activity, combine walking, cycling, yoga, and stretching, and keep exercise to within 1 hour a day.

■ People With Hypertension or Suspected Cardiovascular Disease
Before starting high-intensity exercise, it is advisable to have an exercise stress test to check whether it is safe.

■ Older Adults
Start aerobic and strength exercise at an intensity about 10% lower than that for younger people.

records.title: Oral Hygiene Care During Orthodontic Treatment
records.intro: During orthodontic treatment, appliances attached to the teeth make brushing difficult, and food debris can easily remain. If left unaddressed, this may lead to cavities or gum inflammation, so more careful care is needed. Learn proper brushing techniques and how to use supplementary oral hygiene products to help maintain healthy teeth during orthodontic treatment.
records.tags_raw: orthodontic treatment, oral hygiene, toothbrushing, interdental brush, oral irrigator, dental floss, orthodontic appliance, mouthwash, clear aligners

sections.heading: Precautions During Orthodontic Treatment
sections.content:
■ Foods to Avoid
· Sticky foods (gum, caramel, etc.): They stick to the appliance and may pull it off, or remain around it and become difficult to remove.
· Hard foods (such as bones): Strong force on the appliance may cause it to come off.

■ If the Appliance Comes Off or a Wire Pokes You
Please visit your treating dental clinic as soon as possible. If you cannot visit right away, tear off an appropriate amount of orthodontic wax, roll it into a small ball, and cover the area that is poking you. Remove the wax when eating or brushing.

■ Care of Removable Appliances (Clear Aligners and Removable Active Appliances)
Brush your teeth as described above. Gently clean the appliance at least once a day under running water with a toothbrush without toothpaste.

Orthodontic treatment by itself does not cause cavities or gum problems. Maintaining thorough oral hygiene can help keep your teeth healthy during orthodontic treatment.

sections.heading: Supplementary Oral Hygiene Products
sections.content:
During orthodontic treatment, it may be difficult to clean every area with brushing alone. Using the following supplementary products together can help.

■ Interdental Brushes
They can effectively clean the spaces between teeth and the areas under the appliance that a toothbrush cannot reach. They are easy to buy at pharmacies and supermarkets.

■ Oral Irrigator (Water Flosser)
A strong stream of water cleans food debris from between the teeth, along the gums, and around the appliance. Position the nozzle toward the teeth and press the button.

■ Dental Floss
Helps remove food debris between the teeth. However, during treatment with fixed wire appliances, it is difficult to pass floss between the teeth, so use an interdental brush or an oral irrigator instead.

■ Mouthwash
Mouthwashes may contain ingredients that support oral hygiene, such as antimicrobial agents and fluoride. However, they cannot replace a toothbrush, interdental brush, or oral irrigator. Use mouthwash as a final step after physically removing food debris. Mouthwashes that contain alcohol can cause dry mouth, so it is best not to use them often.

sections.heading: Toothbrushing Method
sections.content:
■ General Toothbrushing
1. Chewing surfaces: Brush the upper and lower molars on both sides without missing any area, and hold the tip of the toothbrush upright to clean the back surface of the last molars.
2. Inner surfaces of the teeth: Brush with a sweeping motion from the gums toward the teeth. For the inner surfaces of the front teeth, hold the brush upright and clean one tooth at a time.
3. Outer surfaces of the teeth: Brush with a sweeping motion from the gums toward the teeth. Move sideways, overlapping each area slightly, so that no area is missed.

■ Toothbrushing While Wearing Orthodontic Appliances
Brush the chewing surfaces and inner surfaces in the same way as in general brushing. Brush the outer surfaces, where the appliance is attached, as follows.
· Tooth surfaces near the gums: Place the brush lightly against the teeth and brush with short vibrating motions.
· Around the appliance: Place the brush lightly against the appliance and brush back and forth from side to side. Then tilt the brush 45 degrees upward to clean above the appliance, and 45 degrees downward to clean below the appliance, using vibrating motions.
If it is difficult to clean with a regular toothbrush, you may use an orthodontic toothbrush with a groove in the center.
The basic brushing method is the same when using an electric toothbrush.

It is important to brush carefully three times a day after meals.

records.title: Postoperative Precautions for Patients With Solid Tumors
records.intro: A solid tumor is a cancer that forms a mass, as opposed to 'liquid' cancers such as blood cancers (hematologic malignancies). Most cancers are solid tumors. Postoperative precautions are as follows.
records.tags_raw: solid tumor, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of hands and feet

sections.heading: Pain Management
sections.content:
Pain after surgery is part of the normal healing process, so take the pain medication prescribed by your healthcare team (for example, acetaminophen, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs], or opioid analgesics) at regular intervals.

If pain suddenly becomes severe or remains uncontrolled, notify your healthcare team immediately.

sections.heading: Wound Care
sections.content:
Keep the surgical site clean and dry at all times.

Change dressings as instructed by your healthcare team, and seek immediate medical attention if there are signs of infection (redness, swelling, warmth, or pus).

When cleaning the wound, use only sterile saline or a method recommended by your healthcare team.

sections.heading: Activity and Exercise
sections.content:
Avoid excessive movement in the early period. For 2–4 weeks after surgery, walking within a comfortable range is recommended.

Exercise restrictions differ depending on the surgical site, so pace your activity according to your healthcare team's instructions. For example, after abdominal surgery, avoid lifting heavy objects for at least 6 weeks.

sections.heading: Nutritional Management
sections.content:
High-protein diet: Eat a high-protein, high-calorie diet to support tissue repair and recovery.

If you have digestive problems, start with a low-residue diet (foods low in fiber) and gradually return to a regular diet.

To avoid dehydration, maintain a fluid intake of at least 1.5–2 L per day.

sections.heading: Smoking Cessation and Alcohol Abstinence
sections.content:
Smoking interferes with wound recovery and tissue healing and increases the risk of postoperative infection and complications.

Excessive alcohol consumption weakens the immune system and interferes with the recovery process, so abstaining from alcohol is recommended.

records.title: Management Strategies for Preventing Complications of Solid Tumors
records.intro: A solid tumor is a cancer that forms a mass, as opposed to 'liquid' cancers such as blood cancers (hematologic malignancies). Most cancers are solid tumors. Management strategies for preventing complications are as follows.
records.tags_raw: solid tumor, fever, feeling feverish, high fever, low-grade fever, body shaking, shivering with cold, chills, unable to pass stool, difficulty passing stool, hard stool, hand tremor

sections.heading: Preventing Blood Clots (Deep Vein Thrombosis, DVT)
sections.content:
Patients with solid tumors have a higher risk of blood clots (deep vein thrombosis, DVT) and pulmonary embolism after surgery, so if you have been prescribed an anticoagulant, take it regularly as prescribed.

Promote blood circulation by walking early after surgery and doing leg stretching exercises.

Ask your healthcare team whether you should wear compression stockings.

sections.heading: Infection Control
sections.content:
If you have a fever (38°C or higher), chills, or purulent discharge from the surgical site, notify the hospital immediately.

If you have a surgical drain, take care of it properly to help prevent infection, and talk with your healthcare team if the color or amount of drainage changes.

sections.heading: Preventing Pneumonia and Respiratory Complications
sections.content:
Do slow, deep breathing exercises several times a day.

If needed, an incentive spirometer can be used.

Avoid lying flat for long periods; simply lying with the upper body slightly raised (30–45 degrees) can help prevent respiratory complications.

sections.heading: Constipation and Recovery of Bowel Function
sections.content:
Anesthesia can slow bowel movement and cause constipation, so use medications that promote peristalsis or eat a small amount of dietary fiber, as directed by your doctor.

Regular walking can help bowel function recover.

records.title: Emotional and Psychological Care After Cancer Surgery
records.intro: Emotional and psychological management strategies after cancer surgery are as follows.
records.tags_raw: solid tumor, cancer surgery, anticancer therapy, cancer treatment, feeling anxious, restlessness, unexplained worry, depressed mood, loss of motivation, loss of interest in activities

sections.heading: Managing Mental Stress
sections.content:
Depression or anxiety may occur after cancer surgery, so manage stress by talking with family or through psychological counseling.

It is recommended to see a psychiatrist (mental health specialist) or a professional counselor regularly to receive psychological support.

sections.heading: Self-Care
sections.content: Try to keep a positive attitude toward the surgery and your recovery, and combine physical activity with mental health care.

records.title: Recurrence Prevention and Additional Treatment Management for Cancer Patients
records.intro: Recurrence prevention and additional treatment management after surgery for cancer patients are as follows.
records.tags_raw: solid tumor, cancer patients, cancer treatment

sections.heading: Regular Follow-Up
sections.content:
Regular checkups after surgery are essential for monitoring for cancer recurrence and for early detection.

In the first 2–3 years, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and blood tests are typically performed every 3–6 months, and annual checkups are generally recommended after that.

sections.heading: Maintaining Immune Function
sections.content:
Get adequate sleep (7–8 hours a day)

Balanced nutrition can help support immune function.

If you are considering immune-related supplements, talk with your healthcare team before taking them.

records.title: Precautions by Time Since Cancer Surgery
records.intro: Precautions depending on the time since cancer surgery are described below.
records.tags_raw: solid tumor, cancer surgery, cancer treatment

sections.heading: Immediately After Surgery (Weeks 1–2)
sections.content:
Focus on pain and wound management, and limit activity to light activity (walking indoors).

Watch carefully for signs of infection.

sections.heading: 2–6 Weeks After Surgery
sections.content:
Begin limited exercise. If you have had abdominal or chest surgery, strictly avoid lifting heavy objects.

Gradually return to a regular diet, and watch for changes in digestion and bowel movements.

sections.heading: More Than 6 Weeks After Surgery
sections.content:
Return to daily life, and begin physical conditioning with aerobic exercise (such as walking or swimming).

Chemotherapy or radiation therapy may be started as additional treatment, so visit the hospital regularly.

records.title: Daily Life Management for Patients Receiving Chemotherapy
records.intro: Daily life management strategies for patients receiving chemotherapy are as follows.
records.tags_raw: anticancer therapy, chemotherapy, fever, feeling feverish, high fever, low-grade fever, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements, unable to pass stool, difficulty passing stool, hard stool, numbness in hands and feet, arm numbness, tingling in legs

sections.heading: Nutritional Management
sections.content:
Balanced Meals

- Eat an appropriate amount of high-protein, high-calorie foods to help with physical recovery and maintaining immune function.

- Recommended foods include lean meat, fish, eggs, tofu, dairy products, and fresh vegetables and fruits.



Eating Small Amounts Frequently

- To minimize nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy side effects, divide meals into small portions eaten several times a day (4–6 meals).



Fluid Intake

- To prevent dehydration, drink at least 1.5–2 liters of water a day, and use clean water to prevent stomach upset.



Foods to Avoid

- Avoid foods with a high risk of bacterial infection, such as raw meat, raw seafood, and raw eggs. In particular, consume only pasteurized dairy products.

sections.heading: Infection Prevention
sections.content:
Strict Hand Hygiene

- Chemotherapy lowers immune function, so wash your hands often and use hand sanitizer when you go out.



Avoiding Public Places

- To avoid the risk of infection when immune function is low, avoid crowded places whenever possible.



Checking for Fever

- Take your temperature every morning and evening, and contact the hospital immediately if you develop a fever (38°C or higher).



Vaccination to Prevent Infection

- Receive inactivated vaccines (for example, the influenza vaccine) after discussing with your healthcare team.

sections.heading: Oral and Dental Care
sections.content:
Maintaining Oral Hygiene

- Use a soft toothbrush and brush in the morning, in the evening, and after meals, and avoid toothpastes that contain strongly acidic ingredients.

- Rinse the mouth with a mild mouthwash that causes little irritation.



Preventing Mouth Pain and Inflammation

- Avoid hot, spicy, and hard foods so that you do not irritate the mouth.

- If you have symptoms of stomatitis (oral mucositis), get a topical anesthetic or pain reliever prescribed at the hospital.

sections.heading: Fatigue Management
sections.content:
Appropriate Rest

- Fatigue is a common side effect of chemotherapy, so combine regular rest with activity rather than overdoing activity.

- Maintain 7–9 hours of sufficient sleep.



Regular Exercise

- Do light exercise (such as walking, yoga, and stretching) 3–5 times a week within a comfortable range to help restore physical strength and mental health.



Managing Work and Daily Life

- Avoid excessive stress, and if needed, apply for sick leave or get help from family and friends.

sections.heading: Skin, Hand, and Foot Care
sections.content:
Protecting the Skin

- Apply moisturizer daily to protect dry or sensitive skin.

- Minimize sun exposure and use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher).



Managing Nail Changes

- Weakening of the fingernails and toenails often occurs during chemotherapy, so do not cut your nails too short and wear gloves to protect your hands.

sections.heading: Psychological Health Management
sections.content:
Maintaining a Positive Attitude

- Negative emotions during cancer treatment can affect a patient's emotional well-being, so try to maintain a positive outlook through practices such as keeping a gratitude journal or meditation.



Professional Support

- If needed, seek professional help from a psychiatrist, a psychological counselor, or a cancer patient support organization.



Communicating With Family and Friends

- Share your feelings with the people around you and receive emotional support.

records.title: Situations Requiring an Emergency Room Visit During Chemotherapy
records.intro: Typical situations during chemotherapy that require an emergency room visit are listed below. Other emergency situations may also occur, so do not judge on your own based on the information below; please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
