sections.heading: Febrile Neutropenia (Most Important)
sections.content:
- Main symptoms: Body temperature of 38.0°C or higher, or 37.5°C or higher lasting 1 hour or longer (chills may accompany)

- Possible causes: Risk of sepsis due to severely reduced immune function (neutrophils).

sections.heading: Severe Bleeding
sections.content:
- Main symptoms: Nosebleeds or gum bleeding that does not stop; red or black bloody stools or blood in the urine; severe headache suggestive of brain hemorrhage.

- Possible causes: Thrombocytopenia, coagulation factor disorders.

sections.heading: Severe Difficulty Breathing
sections.content:
- Main symptoms: Sudden difficulty breathing, chest pain, wheezing when breathing, cyanosis.

- Possible causes: Pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, hypersensitivity reaction (anaphylaxis), cardiotoxicity.

sections.heading: Persistent Severe Vomiting/Dehydration
sections.content:
- Main symptoms: Uncontrolled vomiting 4–5 or more times a day, inability to drink fluids, severe dizziness, decreased urine output, dry mouth.

- Possible causes: Failure to control severe nausea/vomiting, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance.

sections.heading: Diarrhea and Enteritis
sections.content:
- Main symptoms: Watery diarrhea 6 or more times a day, abdominal pain, bloody stools, pain around the anus.

- Possible causes: Chemotherapy-induced diarrhea/enteritis, Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) infection, etc.

sections.heading: Hypersensitivity Reaction (Allergic Reaction)
sections.content:
- Main symptoms: Generalized hives, itching, swelling of the face/tongue/throat, and difficulty breathing during or immediately after administration of chemotherapy.

- Possible causes: Immediate allergic reaction to components of the chemotherapy drug (anaphylaxis).

records.title: Radiation Therapy
records.intro: Radiation therapy is a treatment that uses high-energy radiation to damage the DNA of cancer cells, which stops their growth and ultimately destroys them. Some normal cells are also damaged, but they usually recover more quickly than cancer cells and may return to normal function after treatment ends.
records.tags_raw: radiation therapy, anticancer therapy, cancer treatment, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, dry cough, frequent mild cough, persistent cough, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose 1: Curative treatment. Aims to eliminate the cancer completely.



Purpose 2: Palliative treatment. Relieves symptoms, such as pain.



Purpose 3: Adjuvant (supplementary) treatment. Given before or after surgery to help reduce the risk of cancer recurrence.

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT)

- Uses a machine (linear accelerator) to deliver high-energy radiation precisely to the cancer site from outside the body.

- Advanced techniques: IMRT (Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy), IGRT (Image-Guided Radiation Therapy), SBRT (Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy)



Internal Radiation Therapy (Brachytherapy)

- Radioactive material in capsule form is placed inside or near the cancer for treatment.

- Mainly used for prostate cancer, cervical cancer, and breast cancer.



Systemic Radiation Therapy

- Radioactive substances are given by mouth or into a blood vessel to attack cancer cells throughout the body.

- Example: Radioactive iodine therapy for thyroid cancer

sections.heading: Process
sections.content:
1. Diagnosis and Treatment Planning Stage

Simulation: Imaging such as CT and MRI is used to plan treatment so that the radiation reaches the cancer site accurately.

Treatment planning: The intensity, direction, and dose of radiation are determined according to the type, location, and stage of the cancer.



2. Treatment Preparation

Markings are made on specific areas before treatment, or immobilization devices (custom masks, cushions) are used to limit body movement.



3. Delivery of Radiation Therapy

A session usually takes about 10–15 minutes. During treatment, patients can usually breathe normally and lie comfortably. Treatment is usually painless, and the radiation itself cannot be felt.



4. Treatment Schedule

Treatment is generally given 5 days a week (Monday to Friday) for 3–8 weeks, depending on the type and condition of the cancer.

sections.heading: Possible Side Effects
sections.content:
1. Acute Side Effects (occurring during or immediately after treatment)

Skin reactions

- Skin exposed to radiation may become red, dry, and itchy.

- In severe cases, radiation dermatitis with skin peeling (desquamation) may occur.



Fatigue

- Fatigue may develop as treatment progresses and the body adapts to radiation.



Localized symptoms

- Head and neck radiation therapy: Mouth sores (oral ulcers), dry mouth (xerostomia), difficulty swallowing.

- Chest radiation therapy: Cough, shortness of breath, esophagitis.

- Abdominal radiation therapy: Diarrhea, vomiting.

- Pelvic radiation therapy: Urinary problems, rectal irritation.



2. Chronic (Late) Side Effects (may occur months to years later)

- Tissue fibrosis: Tissue in the irradiated area becomes stiff and less flexible.

- Late organ dysfunction: Decreased lung, liver, kidney, or heart function caused by radiation.

- Increased risk of second cancers: Radiation exposure may increase the risk of developing a second cancer after a long period.



Please discuss treatment options thoroughly with your doctor.

records.title: Care for Patients Receiving Radiation Therapy
records.intro: Care guidelines for patients who have received radiation therapy are as follows. Individual needs may vary, so please be sure to consult a medical specialist.
records.tags_raw: radiation therapy, anticancer therapy, cancer treatment, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Skin Care
sections.content:
- To minimize irritation, treat the irradiated area gently and do not rub it.

- Do not use moisturizers, lotions, cosmetics, or similar products without your doctor's permission.

- Avoid sun exposure and use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher).

sections.heading: Fatigue Management
sections.content:
- Get enough sleep (7–9 hours), and if you feel fatigued, take short, frequent rests.

- Use light exercise (such as walking or yoga) to help manage your energy levels.

sections.heading: Nutritional Management
sections.content: - Soft foods and plenty of fluids are important. Patients receiving head and neck radiation therapy in particular may have difficulty eating because of mouth sores. Plan a personalized diet in consultation with a dietitian.

sections.heading: Oral Care (for Head and Neck Radiation Therapy Patients)
sections.content:
- Clean the mouth with a soft toothbrush after every meal.

- To protect the sensitive mouth, use a non-irritating mouth rinse or an oral spray recommended by your healthcare team.

sections.heading: Monitoring for Side Effects
sections.content:
- If moderate or severe pain, severe skin symptoms, or a persistent feeling of heat occur, notify the hospital immediately.

- If there are changes such as urinary or bowel problems, persistent diarrhea, or severe fatigue, consult your healthcare team.

records.title: Additional Care During and After Radiation Therapy
records.intro: Additional management strategies during and after radiation therapy are described below.
records.tags_raw: radiation therapy, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Regular Hospital Visits
sections.content:
Regular checkups (such as PET-CT and MRI) are used, both during treatment and after it ends, to evaluate the effect of treatment and check for side effects.

Tissue response is monitored at intervals of 1–2 months, and the intervals are gradually extended afterward.

sections.heading: Psychological Support
sections.content: Stress related to radiation therapy can be significant. If needed, seek help from a professional counselor or a patient support organization.

sections.heading: Relief of Discomfort
sections.content:
Fatigue, sleep disturbances, and similar symptoms are managed in collaboration with a palliative care team.

If symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Care Before and After Radiation Therapy
records.tags_raw: radiation therapy, anticancer therapy, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Adequate Nutrition
sections.content: It is very important to eat balanced meals to maintain physical strength during treatment.

sections.heading: Smoking Cessation and Alcohol Abstinence
sections.content: Smoking and alcohol use can reduce the effectiveness of radiation therapy and worsen side effects, so they should be avoided.

sections.heading: Skin Care
sections.content:
The skin in the treatment area tends to become sensitive. Care for it as follows.



Use a mild cleanser: Use a gentle, low-irritant soap, and after showering, pat the skin gently with a towel to remove moisture.

Moisturize: Apply a moisturizing cream or lotion recommended by your healthcare team regularly, 2–3 times a day.

Avoid irritation: Avoid tight clothing and clothing that does not absorb sweat, and take care not to scratch or rub the area.

Sun protection: During treatment and for up to 1 year after treatment, wear a hat or long-sleeved clothing to avoid sun exposure.



If symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Daily Life Management During Radiation Therapy
records.tags_raw: radiation therapy, anticancer therapy, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, feeling anxious, restlessness, unexplained worry

sections.heading: Regular Rest
sections.content: Fatigue can become severe during radiation therapy, so get enough rest.

sections.heading: Light Exercise
sections.content: Light walking or stretching within a comfortable range can help reduce fatigue and maintain physical strength.

sections.heading: Fluid Intake
sections.content: Drink enough water to help prevent dehydration and support metabolism.

sections.heading: Mental Health Care
sections.content: Feelings of anxiety or depression are common. It is important to talk with family or friends and, if needed, to consult your healthcare team to receive psychological support.

sections.heading: Regular Outpatient Visits
sections.content: Even after treatment ends, it is important to visit the hospital regularly as instructed by your treating doctor to check for recurrence.

sections.heading: Maintaining Healthy Lifestyle Habits
sections.content: A healthy diet, regular exercise, smoking cessation, and limiting alcohol are essential for maintaining long-term health.

records.title: Common Side Effects of Radiation Therapy and How to Manage Them
records.tags_raw: radiation therapy, anticancer therapy, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Skin Reactions
sections.content:
The skin may become red or peel.

Apply ointment as directed by your healthcare team and minimize irritation.

sections.heading: Fatigue
sections.content:
This is the most common side effect during treatment.

Avoid overexertion and keep a balance between rest and light activity.

sections.heading: Stomatitis (Oral Mucositis)
sections.content:
In patients with head and neck cancer, the oral mucosa may be damaged, causing pain.

Use a soft toothbrush, avoid spicy and salty foods, and use a mouth rinse.

sections.heading: Nausea/Vomiting
sections.content:
Depending on the treatment area, digestive side effects may occur.

Eat small amounts frequently and, if needed, take medication after consulting your healthcare team.

records.title: The Need for Exercise in Cancer Rehabilitation
records.tags_raw: anticancer therapy, cancer surgery, cancer treatment, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of hands and feet

sections.heading: Physical Recovery and Overall Health Improvement
sections.content:
Cancer treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, etc.) can cause fatigue, muscle loss, and reduced physical fitness.

Exercise can help strengthen muscles and improve physical fitness, which may improve treatment tolerance and physical function.

sections.heading: Reducing Side Effects
sections.content:
Exercise can be effective in reducing side effects of cancer treatment, such as fatigue, pain, lymphedema, and joint stiffness.

In particular, exercise has been shown to help relieve the fatigue that occurs after chemotherapy.

sections.heading: Psychological Benefits
sections.content:
Exercise can help relieve stress and symptoms of depression and improve quality of life.

It may promote the release of endorphins, which may contribute to a more positive mood.

sections.heading: Reduced Risk of Recurrence/Death
sections.content:
In patients with breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and prostate cancer, exercise has been associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence and death.

Please consult a medical specialist before starting or changing any exercise program.

records.title: Basic Principles of Cancer Rehabilitation Exercise
records.tags_raw: anticancer therapy, cancer surgery, cancer treatment, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Designing an Individualized Exercise Program
sections.content:
Different exercises are required depending on the patient's cancer type, treatment course, and physical fitness.

Be sure to talk with a doctor, physical therapist, or exercise professional before starting exercise.

sections.heading: Gradual Progression
sections.content:
Increase exercise intensity, duration, and frequency gradually.

Start with light walking, stretching, and similar activities, and gradually progress to higher-intensity exercise.

sections.heading: Balanced Exercise Plan
sections.content:
Include aerobic, strength, and flexibility exercises to maintain or restore overall physical function.

Balance rest and exercise appropriately.

sections.heading: Avoiding Excessive Exercise
sections.content: Overexertion or excessively intense exercise can increase fatigue and physical stress, so caution is needed.

records.title: Recommended Types of Cancer Rehabilitation Exercise
records.tags_raw: anticancer therapy, cancer surgery, cancer treatment, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of hands and feet, feeling anxious, restlessness, unexplained worry

sections.heading: Aerobic Exercise: Strengthening Cardiorespiratory Function and Fitness
sections.content:
Examples: Walking, light jogging, cycling, swimming

Intensity: Moderate (able to talk but difficult to sing)

Frequency and duration: 3–5 times a week, 20–30 minutes. At the beginning, exercise can be divided into 10-minute sessions.

Possible benefits: Improved lung function and cardiovascular health, relief of fatigue, and decreased body fat.

sections.heading: Strength Training: Maintaining Muscle Mass and Strengthening Muscles
sections.content:
Examples: Simple resistance exercises using dumbbells or elastic bands, squats, stair climbing

Intensity: Start at low intensity and gradually increase to moderate intensity.

Frequency: 2–3 times a week, 2–3 sets of 10–15 repetitions each.

Possible benefits: Physical recovery, prevention of sarcopenia (muscle loss), and relief of disease-related functional decline.

sections.heading: Flexibility Exercise: Maintaining Joint Range of Motion and Managing Lymphedema
sections.content:
Examples: Stretching, yoga, tai chi

Intensity: Perform at low intensity, taking sufficient time.

Duration: Daily, or 10–15 minutes after exercise.

Possible benefits: Reduced joint stiffness, less lymphedema, and relief of stress and anxiety.



Please consult a medical specialist before starting or changing any exercise program.

records.title: Exercise Management by Major Cancer Type
records.tags_raw: anticancer therapy, cancer surgery, cancer treatment, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of hands and feet

sections.heading: Breast Cancer
sections.content:
Flexibility exercises for the arms and shoulders are recommended and may help reduce the risk of lymphedema.

Strengthen the upper body through resistance exercise, and consult your healthcare team if arm swelling is severe.

sections.heading: Colorectal Cancer
sections.content:
Lower-body exercises to strengthen the pelvic muscles (for example, Kegel exercises) are recommended.

Combine walking and breathing exercises to help improve bowel function.

sections.heading: Prostate Cancer
sections.content:
Combine moderate-weight exercise (resistance exercise) with aerobic exercise to help prevent loss of bone density.

Pelvic floor muscle strengthening exercises may help improve urinary function.

sections.heading: Lung Cancer
sections.content: Cardiopulmonary exercise (walking, swimming, light cycling) and breathing exercises are recommended to help restore lung function.

records.title: Precautions for Safe Cancer Rehabilitation Exercise
records.tags_raw: lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Before Exercise
sections.content:
Consult your healthcare team: Get approval from your healthcare team before starting exercise.

Check your condition: Check for fatigue, dizziness, and changes in body temperature, and do not overexert yourself.



Consulting Your Healthcare Team

Before starting exercise, be sure to consult your treating doctor or a rehabilitation medicine specialist (physiatrist) and create an exercise plan suited to your physical condition.



Pain

If you feel pain during exercise, stop immediately and rest. If the pain persists, tell your healthcare team.



Fluid Intake

Drink enough water before, during, and after exercise to prevent dehydration.



Appropriate Clothing

Wear comfortable, sweat-absorbing clothing and non-slip athletic shoes.

sections.heading: During Exercise
sections.content:
If you experience severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or dizziness, stop exercising immediately and rest.

Prevent dehydration by drinking enough fluids.

Manage body temperature (wear appropriate clothing in hot or cold weather).

sections.heading: After Exercise
sections.content:
Allow sufficient rest time and adjust your activity to avoid excessive fatigue.

If muscle soreness lasts longer than 24 hours after exercise or if unusual symptoms occur, consult your healthcare team.

records.title: Stage-Based Cancer Rehabilitation Exercise Program
records.intro: It is important to adjust exercise intensity according to the stage of cancer treatment and the patient's physical fitness.
records.tags_raw: anticancer therapy, cancer surgery, cancer treatment, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer, lack of energy, lethargy, persistent fatigue

sections.heading: Stage 1: Immediately After Treatment – Recovery-Phase Exercise
sections.content:
Goal: Support recovery of the surgical site and improve blood circulation to help prevent complications.

Types of exercise

Bedside ankle pumps: While lying down, move your ankles up and down to help prevent blood clots.

Deep breathing exercises: Repeatedly breathe in deeply and out to help restore lung function and prevent pneumonia.

Lying leg raises: Slowly raise a leg while keeping the knee bent, which helps strengthen the lower body.

sections.heading: Stage 2: After the Recovery Phase – Strength and Aerobic Exercise
sections.content:
Goal: Strengthen full-body muscles and improve physical fitness to prepare for a return to daily life.

Types of exercise

Walking: One of the best aerobic exercises. Start with 10–15 minutes and gradually increase the time.

Light strength exercise: Strengthen full-body muscles with arm exercises using dumbbells (a water bottle can be substituted) or wall squats (leaning against a wall).

Stretching: Improves flexibility and relaxes muscle tension. Gently stretching the muscles around the surgical site is especially important.

sections.heading: Stage 3: After Returning to Daily Life – Maintenance-Phase Exercise
sections.content:
Goal: Build regular exercise habits and maintain health over the long term.

Types of exercise

3–5 times a week, at least 30 minutes: Choose an exercise you enjoy, such as walking, jogging, cycling, or swimming, and do it consistently.

Add strength training: Include strength exercise 2–3 times a week to help prevent loss of muscle mass.



Please consult a medical specialist before starting or changing any exercise program.

records.title: Nutritional Management After Gastrectomy (1–6 Months After Surgery)
records.tags_raw: gastrectomy, cancer surgery, gastric cancer

sections.heading: High-Protein Balanced Diet
sections.content:
Eat 1–2 types of meat, fish, eggs, or tofu at every meal

- Meal composition: porridge, rice, noodles, or bread + protein + vegetables

Eat a balanced variety of fruit and milk/dairy products as snacks

sections.heading: Adjusting Meals According to Digestive Capacity
sections.content:
1. If you have discomfort after eating

Eat small amounts frequently, chew thoroughly, and eat slowly

- (Be careful not to return to your previous eating habits.)

Eat soft, easily digestible foods (allowed foods)

- Caution: Limit mixed grains/beans, tough meat and fish, greasy foods, and tough vegetables/fruit



2. If you have no discomfort after eating

Eat small amounts frequently, chew thoroughly, and eat slowly

- (Be careful not to return to your previous eating habits.)

Gradually increase the amount eaten at each meal (do not overeat)

Carefully try restricted foods

- Try one food at a time and observe how your digestion responds

- Start with a small amount, and increase the amount if there is no discomfort

- If you have discomfort, stop eating the food and try again another time

- Gradually try a wider variety of foods to expand the range of your diet

sections.heading: Guide to Allowed and Restricted Foods
sections.content:
Limit foods and drinks high in added sugar, particularly if they trigger dumping syndrome. How long dietary restrictions are needed depends on symptoms, nutritional needs, and your care team's guidance.


1. Grains

- Allowed: White rice (polished rice, glutinous rice), white noodles, white bread (loaf bread, dinner rolls), sweet potatoes, potatoes, chestnuts, crackers

- Restricted: Mixed grains, beans, corn, very sticky rice cakes, cereal with added sugar



2. Meat and Fish

- Allowed: Soft lean meat, fish, eggs, tofu

- Restricted: Dried meat and fish (dried anchovies, dried pollock, dried yellow pollock [hwangtae], dried whitebait sheets, beef jerky, etc.), fried/smoked meat



3. Vegetables

- Allowed: Soft cooked vegetables

- Restricted: Tough vegetables high in fiber (bellflower root, lotus root, burdock root, bracken fern, deodeok, etc.), dried vegetables, seaweed (gim/laver, miyeok/wakame)



4. Fruit

- Allowed: Soft fruit with skin and seeds removed, unsweetened juice

- Restricted: Persimmons, bananas, jujubes, pineapple, dried fruit, canned fruit



5. Milk/Dairy Products

- Allowed: Unsweetened milk/dairy products

- Restricted: Milk/dairy products with added sugar



6. Other

- Restricted: Nuts, sweet snacks, alcohol, carbonated drinks, caffeinated drinks

sections.heading: Precautions While Eating
sections.content:
Be careful with foods that are too cold, too hot, or irritating

Avoid foods and beverages that are strongly sweet or salty

- Limit candy, sugar, honey, syrup, jam, sweet drinks (such as sikhye, sujeonggwa, and maesil tea), sweet snacks, salted fermented seafood (jeotgal), pickled vegetables (jangajji), and heavily seasoned soups

- Small amounts of seasonings (sugar, honey, salt, jeotgal) are acceptable

Use an appropriate amount of fat (oil) when cooking

sections.heading: Preventing Anemia
sections.content:
Eat meals that provide a balanced supply of the nutrients needed for blood production

- Lean meat, seafood, eggs, beans, dark green and yellow vegetables, fruit, milk/dairy products, peanuts, etc.

Do not have caffeine within 1 hour after meals

sections.heading: Preventing Osteoporosis
sections.content:
Eat foods that contain calcium and vitamin D

- Milk/dairy products, tofu, fish eaten with the bones

- Mackerel, salmon, Pacific saury, egg yolks, shiitake mushrooms

Eat low-salt foods whenever possible

Reduce intake of caffeinated drinks and carbonated drinks



Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.

records.title: Nutritional Management by Stage After Colostomy: 6–8 Weeks After Surgery
records.tags_raw: intestinal stoma, colostomy, colorectal cancer

sections.heading: Characteristics of Each Stage After Colostomy
sections.content:
The condition of the bowel and the degree of recovery differ depending on the time since colostomy surgery. The period from 6 to 8 weeks after surgery is when stoma function gradually stabilizes.



4–6 weeks after surgery: The bowel is swollen and very sensitive

6–8 weeks after surgery (current stage): Stoma function begins to stabilize

  - The bowel begins to adapt

  - Weight recovery begins

More than 8 weeks after surgery: Stoma function stabilizes

sections.heading: Diet Therapy According to Stage Characteristics
sections.content:
① The Bowel Begins to Adapt

Transition to a regular diet: Try restricted foods a little at a time and gradually move to a regular diet.

Food diary: Record everything you eat each day to identify foods that cause problems for you.

Response to symptoms: If you have bowel discomfort, reduce foods that trigger discomfort and try symptom-relieving foods.



② Weight Recovery Begins

Adjusting food intake: If you have lost a lot of weight after surgery, increase the number of meals and snacks.

  - (Example 1): 3 meals a day + 2–3 snacks

  - (Example 2): 5–6 meals a day

Frequent eating: Eat foods that are easy to prepare throughout the day to supplement calories.

sections.heading: Diet Therapy to Follow at All Times
sections.content:
To support stable bowel health after colostomy surgery, follow these basic dietary principles at all times.



1. Eat slowly and chew thoroughly

2. Eat balanced meals that include protein

3. Eat meals and snacks at regular times

4. Drink enough water between meals

  - Drink at least 8–10 cups a day.

  - However, limit fluid intake for 30 minutes before and after meals.

5. Avoid foods that are excessively sweet, spicy, or greasy

6. Be careful with foods that trigger discomfort

7. Use oral nutritional supplements if food intake is insufficient



Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.

records.title: Nutritional Management After Gallbladder Surgery
records.tags_raw: gallbladder cancer, gallbladder, unable to pass stool, difficulty passing stool, hard stool

sections.heading: Dietary Principles After Gallbladder Surgery
sections.content:
Eat mainly easily digestible foods, include meat or fish at every meal, and eat hygienically in sufficient amounts

Eat small amounts frequently, chew thoroughly, and eat slowly

Eat a low-fat, low-fiber diet

  - Avoid fried and greasy foods

  - Avoid mixed grains and tough meat, fish, vegetables, and fruit

  - (Items to avoid: mixed grains/beans, tough meat and fish, greasy foods, tough vegetables/fruit)

Avoid irritating foods

  - Limit alcohol, coffee, carbonated drinks, and spices

sections.heading: Balanced Diet
sections.content:
Eat a balanced variety of grains, meat and fish, and vegetables at every meal

- Grains: porridge, soft-cooked rice, soft noodles/bread → supply energy (if insufficient: reduced strength and weight)

- Meat and fish: (low-fat) → lean meat, fish, seafood, egg whites, etc. → supply protein (if insufficient: reduced immunity and strength)

- Vegetables: soft vegetables (cooked seasoned vegetable dishes, namul) → supply vitamins, minerals, and fiber (if insufficient: reduced metabolic regulation, constipation)



Eat a balanced variety of fruit and milk/dairy products as snacks





- Fruit: soft fruit, juice, etc. → supply vitamins, minerals, and fiber (if insufficient: reduced metabolic regulation, constipation)

- Milk and dairy products: low-fat/fat-free milk and dairy products → supply energy, protein, and calcium (if insufficient: reduced immunity and strength, reduced metabolic regulation)



* If you are lactose intolerant, limit milk and dairy products

* Gradually increase the amount of food and the range of foods according to how well your digestion adapts

sections.heading: Hygienic Eating
sections.content:
Cook meat, fish, seafood, and eggs thoroughly all the way through before eating

Limit raw meat and fish (such as raw fish [hoe] and raw beef [yukhoe])

Be especially careful with shellfish and other seafood in summer (to prevent food poisoning)

Avoid unhygienic foods (such as street food)

sections.heading: Allowed and Restricted Foods
sections.content:
Meat and fish

 - (Allowed) Thoroughly cooked meat, processed meat, fish, seafood, eggs, tofu

 - (Restricted) Undercooked meat and fish (raw fish, raw beef, soft-boiled eggs, undercooked ham/sausage)

Other

 - (Allowed) Foods prepared hygienically at home or in restaurants

 - (Restricted) Unhygienic foods such as street food



Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.

records.title: Dietary Management of Chemotherapy Side Effects (When Weight Changes)
records.intro: Dietary strategies for side effects of chemotherapy are as follows.
records.tags_raw: anticancer drugs, cancer treatment, body swelling, facial swelling, leg swelling, swelling of hands and feet, weight loss, unintentional weight loss

sections.heading: Weight Loss
sections.content:
Precautions

 - Do not base your meals mainly on low-calorie vegetables.

 - Do not take health supplements, black goat extract, or herbal medicines.



Management

 - Add extra ingredients to rice and porridge

 - Use plenty of vegetable oil



Recommended foods

 - Gimbap (Korean rice rolls), beef fried rice, tuna porridge, hotteok (Korean filled pancake), egg toast

sections.heading: Weight Gain
sections.content:
Precautions

 - Avoid foods, beverages, and sauces high in sugar and fat.

 - Eat even healthy fats, such as olive oil and nuts, only in appropriate amounts.



Management

 - Choose steamed or boiled foods instead of fried foods

 - Remove visible fat and skin, and eat mainly lean meat



Recommended foods

 - Dak baeksuk (boiled whole chicken soup), plain bread, unsweetened low-fat latte

sections.heading: Edema and Ascites
sections.content:
Precautions

 - If your intake decreases, eat small amounts frequently.

 - Eat mainly a low-salt diet, and avoid drinking fluids during meals.



Management

 - Avoid salty foods (such as soup broth and kimchi)

 - Check the nutrition facts label and choose foods with low sodium content



Recommended foods

 - Low-sodium rice cakes, low-sodium bread



If symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Managing Side Effects After Gallbladder Surgery
records.tags_raw: gallbladder cancer, cancer surgery, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: When You Have Diarrhea
sections.content:
Drink plenty of fluids (water, electrolyte drinks, clear juice)

- Eat soft, bland foods (thin rice gruel, rice porridge, bananas, mashed potatoes, etc.)

- Avoid milk/dairy products, high-fat foods, high-fiber foods, and irritating foods (fried foods, greasy foods, nuts, mixed grains, tough vegetables, raw fruit, raw vegetables, etc.)

sections.heading: When Fat Is Difficult to Digest
sections.content:
- Limit cooking oil, perilla oil, and sesame oil when cooking

- Use MCT (medium-chain triglyceride) oil instead of cooking oil

- Trim fat from meat and remove the skin from poultry before eating

- Eat mainly steamed, braised, or boiled dishes, and limit jeon (pan-fried battered dishes), buchimgae (Korean pancakes), and fried foods

sections.heading: Food Choices When Fat Is Difficult to Digest
sections.content:
■ Allowed Foods (Low-Fat)

Steamed rice, multigrain rice, glutinous rice, noodles, white bread, rice cakes, misutgaru (roasted grain powder)

Lean meat, skinless chicken, fish, eggs, tofu, legumes

Low-fat milk, nonfat dry milk, low-fat yogurt

Seasoned vegetable dishes (muchim), namul, and raw vegetables prepared without added sesame oil or perilla oil

All fruits except avocado, unsweetened fruit juice

MCT oil, small amounts of cooking oil

Vinegar, soy sauce, soybean paste (doenjang), red pepper paste (gochujang), mustard, pepper, ketchup, malt (yeotgireum)



■ Restricted Foods (High-Fat)

Fried rice, instant noodles (ramyeon), sponge cake (castella), doughnuts, pastries, cakes, hot dogs, snack foods (cookies, chips)

Galbi (ribs), pork belly, beef brisket, oxtail, organ meats, canned fish, oily (blue-backed) fish, eel, egg yolks, ham, cheese

Milk, cheese, ice cream, pudding, yogurt made with whole milk

Stir-fried or fried vegetables

Avocado

Butter, margarine, mayonnaise, nuts

Sesame salt, dressings, mayonnaise, excess simple sugars



If symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Nutritional Management After Gastrectomy (Immediately After Surgery to 1 Month)
records.intro: Applicable period: From immediately after gastrectomy to 1 month after surgery
records.tags_raw: gastric cancer, cancer surgery

sections.heading: Eat Small Amounts Frequently + Chew Thoroughly
sections.content: After gastrectomy, the volume of the stomach is sharply reduced and digestive function is weakened, so changing the way you eat is the most important adjustment.

sections.heading: Eat Small Amounts Frequently, 6–9 Times a Day
sections.content: Eating a large amount at once places great strain on the stomach. Divide your daily food into several meals and eat small amounts frequently.

sections.heading: Do Not Swallow Food Whole—Chew Thoroughly
sections.content: Chewing each mouthful at least 30 times, so that saliva and food mix well, can help prevent digestive problems.

sections.heading: Eat Slowly
sections.content: It is recommended to take your time and allow at least 20–30 minutes to finish a meal.

sections.heading: Stepwise Meals According to Digestive Capacity
sections.content:
Gradually advance the form of food according to the patient's adaptation and recovery rate.

Thin rice gruel (mieum) > Porridge (juk) > Soft-cooked rice (jinbap)

sections.heading: Expanding the Range of Foods as You Adapt
sections.content:
Begin with thin rice gruel (mieum), a soft and easily digestible food (an allowed food). Then progress to porridge in sequence, and move on to soft-cooked rice as digestion improves. As your condition gradually recovers, gradually try a wider variety of foods and cooking methods.

Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.

records.title: Diet Therapy for Stoma-Related Symptoms
records.intro:
When stool odor is strong

• Stool odor can change greatly depending on the foods eaten

• Among the foods you have eaten recently, avoid odor-causing foods and try odor-reducing foods
records.tags_raw: intestinal stoma, cancer surgery, colorectal cancer

sections.heading: Foods That May Cause Odor
sections.content:
Onions, green onions, garlic, radish

Legumes, mushrooms

Broccoli, cauliflower

Asparagus

Cabbage, Brussels sprouts

Eggs, fish

Greasy foods

Smoked foods (such as smoked meats)

Peanut butter, cheese

Beer

sections.heading: Foods That May Help Reduce Odor
sections.content:
Cranberry juice

Tomato juice

Orange juice

Yogurt

Peppermint tea

Fresh parsley



If symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a medical specialist.

records.title: Nutritional Management by Stage After Ileostomy (4–12 Months After Surgery)
records.intro: The condition of the bowel and the degree of recovery differ depending on the time since ileostomy surgery. The period from 4 to 12 months after surgery is an important time during which the bowel gradually recovers and adapts.
records.tags_raw: ileostomy, intestinal stoma, bowel surgery, colorectal cancer, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Characteristics of Each Stage After Ileostomy
sections.content:
• 1–3 months after surgery: The bowel is swollen and very sensitive

• 4–12 months after surgery (current stage): Bowel recovery begins

• More than 12 months after surgery: Bowel recovery reaches its maximum

sections.heading: Major Changes 4–12 Months After Surgery
sections.content:
Diarrhea decreases and the bowel begins to adapt

Weight recovery begins

sections.heading: Diet Therapy According to Stage Characteristics
sections.content:
① Diarrhea Decreases and the Bowel Begins to Adapt

• Food diary: Record everything you eat each day to identify foods that cause problems for you.

• Response to symptoms: If you have bowel discomfort, reduce your intake of foods that trigger discomfort and try foods that may relieve it.



② Weight Recovery Begins

• Adjusting food intake: If you have lost a lot of weight after surgery, increase the number of meals and snacks.

(Example 1): 3 meals a day + 2–3 snacks

(Example 2): 5–6 small meals a day

• Frequent eating: Eat foods that are easy to prepare throughout the day to supplement calories.

sections.heading: Diet Therapy to Follow at All Times
sections.content:
To support stable bowel health after stoma surgery, follow these basic dietary principles at all times.

Eat slowly and chew thoroughly: This aids digestion and reduces the burden on the bowel.

Eat balanced meals that include protein: Get a balanced supply of the nutrients essential for bowel recovery and immune function.

Eat meals and snacks at regular times: This helps keep the bowel's movement cycle regular.

Drink enough water between meals:

Drink at least 8–10 cups a day.

However, limit fluid intake for 30 minutes before and after meals to avoid diluting digestive juices.

Avoid foods that are excessively sweet, spicy, or greasy: These can irritate the lining of the bowel, so caution is needed.

Eat meals that contain a moderate amount of salt: An appropriate amount of salt is needed to replace fluid and electrolyte losses through the stoma.

Be careful with foods that trigger discomfort (see also: the content 'Diet Therapy for Stoma-Related Symptoms' for details.)

Use oral nutritional supplements: If your overall food intake is insufficient, take oral nutritional supplements as a meal replacement or supplement.



Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.

records.title: Nutritional Management by Stage After Ileostomy (1–3 Months After Surgery)
records.intro: The period from 1 to 3 months after surgery is a time when the bowel is swollen and very sensitive. Severe diarrhea may occur, and the bowel needs rest.
records.tags_raw: intestinal stoma, ileostomy, bowel surgery, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Diet Therapy for the Possibility of Severe Diarrhea
sections.content:
• Eat foods that help relieve loose stool/diarrhea

Peeled potatoes, crackers, plain white bread, white rice, porridge, thin wheat noodles (somyeon)

Smooth peanut butter without peanut chunks

Slightly unripe bananas, marshmallows

• Replace potassium and sodium through food

Bananas, potatoes, electrolyte drinks, soups, etc.

sections.heading: Diet Therapy for Bowel Rest
sections.content:
Eat small amounts frequently

From 6–8 weeks after surgery, try restricted foods according to how well you adapt

sections.heading: Diet Therapy to Follow at All Times
sections.content:
Eat slowly and chew thoroughly

Eat balanced meals that include protein

Eat meals and snacks at regular times

Drink enough water between meals

At least 8–10 cups a day

Limit fluid intake for 30 minutes before and after meals

Avoid foods that are excessively sweet, spicy, or greasy

Eat meals that contain a moderate amount of salt

Be careful with foods that trigger discomfort

Use oral nutritional supplements if food intake is insufficient



Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.

records.title: Nutritional Management by Stage After Ileostomy (More Than 12 Months After Surgery)
records.intro:
As time passes after ileostomy surgery, the condition of the bowel and the degree of recovery change, and systematic dietary management suited to each stage is needed.



[1–3 months after surgery]: The bowel is swollen and very sensitive

[4–12 months after surgery]: Bowel recovery begins

[More than 12 months after surgery]: Bowel recovery reaches its maximum, and adequate food intake may be possible

[Characteristics of the period more than 12 months after surgery]: This is the period in which bowel recovery reaches its maximum. Overall digestive function improves, and adequate food intake may become possible.
records.tags_raw: ileostomy, intestinal stoma, colorectal cancer, loose stool, watery diarrhea, frequent bowel movements

sections.heading: Diet Therapy to Follow at All Times
sections.content:
Even after 12 months have passed and the bowel has recovered considerably, continue to practice the following key dietary principles for the health of the stoma and a smooth daily life.



① Forming Proper Eating Habits

• Eat slowly and chew thoroughly

Chew food well before swallowing so that it is absorbed well in the bowel and to help prevent blockage.

• Maintain a regular eating pattern

Eat meals and snacks at set times to keep bowel activity regular.

• Eat balanced meals that include protein

For physical recovery and maintenance of muscle, plan a balanced diet that includes a protein dish at every meal.



② Fluid Intake Guide

• Drink enough water between meals

Drink at least 8–10 cups of fluid a day.

However, it is advisable to limit fluid intake for 30 minutes before and after meals to avoid diluting digestive enzymes and to support smooth digestion.



③ Foods to Avoid and Precautions

• Avoid irritating foods

Avoid foods that are excessively sweet, spicy, or greasy, as they can irritate the bowel and cause diarrhea or abdominal pain.

• Eat meals that contain a moderate amount of salt

To help prevent fluid loss and electrolyte imbalance, meals with a moderate amount of salt are recommended rather than excessively bland food.

• Be careful with foods that trigger discomfort

Foods that cause gas, odor, diarrhea, or bowel obstruction differ from person to person, so caution is needed.

• Use oral nutritional supplements

If your usual food intake is insufficient and you are losing weight or becoming undernourished, supplement with oral nutritional supplements such as balanced nutrition drinks.

sections.heading: Individualized Management According to Stage Characteristics
sections.content:
At this stage, when adequate food intake may be possible, periodic self-checks and communication with your healthcare team are important.



• Regular status checks (monitoring)

Diet check: Check whether you are getting enough fluids and a balanced variety of foods, and whether you are following your stoma diet therapy well.

Symptom check: Watch for digestive symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, gas, and skin problems around the stoma.

Weight check: Regularly record and review changes in body weight, which is an indicator of nutritional status.



• Caution with nutritional supplements

If needed, do not take supplements on your own; always choose and take them safely in consultation with your healthcare team.

records.title: Nutritional Management After Bowel Surgery (Immediately After Surgery to 4–6 Weeks)
records.intro: Meals should be advanced in stages according to digestive capacity.
records.tags_raw: bowel, colorectal cancer, intestinal stoma

sections.heading: Expanding the Range of Foods as You Adapt
sections.content:
• Meal progression: thin rice gruel > porridge > soft-cooked rice > regular cooked rice > multigrain rice

• Allowed foods: Eat soft, easily digestible foods

• Restricted foods: Try small amounts, and gradually expand the types and cooking methods

sections.heading: Dietary Principles
sections.content: • Eat small amounts frequently, and gradually increase the amount of food.

sections.heading: Classification Table of Allowed and Restricted Foods
sections.content:
To avoid placing a burden on the digestive tract during the recovery period after bowel surgery (weeks 4–6), choose the foods you eat carefully.



Grains

· Allowed foods (foods you can eat): White rice (polished rice, glutinous rice), white noodles, white bread (loaf bread, dinner rolls), peeled potatoes, muk (starch jelly)

· Restricted foods (foods to be careful with): Mixed grains, beans, red beans, biji (soybean pulp), whole wheat bread, very sticky rice cakes, sweet potatoes, corn, gangnaengi (puffed corn snack), misutgaru (roasted grain powder)



Nuts and Seeds

· Allowed foods: -

· Restricted foods: Ginkgo nuts, pine nuts, sesame seeds, perilla seeds, walnuts, chestnuts, peanuts, almonds



Meat and Fish

· Allowed foods (foods you can eat): Soft lean meat, fish, eggs, tofu

· Restricted foods (foods to be careful with): Tough meat and fish (meat with a lot of tendon, shellfish, squid, etc.)



Vegetables

· Allowed foods (foods you can eat): Well-cooked vegetables with stems and skins removed (soft namul), vegetable juice

· Restricted foods (foods to be careful with): High-fiber, tough vegetables (lotus root, deodeok, bellflower root, burdock root, bracken fern, cabbage), dried vegetables (dried radish strips, dried namul), seaweed (miyeok/wakame, gim/laver)



Fruit

· Allowed foods (foods you can eat): Soft fruit with skin and seeds removed, fruit juice (※ except prune juice)

· Restricted foods (foods to be careful with): Raw fruit with skin and seeds not removed, persimmons, dried fruit (dried persimmons, dried jujubes, etc.)



Milk and Dairy Products

· Allowed foods (foods you can eat): Nonfat/low-fat milk, lactose-free milk (1 cup a day or less)

· Restricted foods (foods to be careful with): Cream soup, cheese, yogurt, milk (2 cups a day or more)

Other

· Allowed foods: -

· Restricted foods: Irritating foods, gas-producing foods, foods that loosen stool

sections.heading: Tips for Trying Restricted Foods
sections.content:
• Do not try several restricted foods at once; try only one at a time and observe how your body responds.

• If you have discomfort after eating, stop eating the food immediately, and try again in a small amount after the symptoms have resolved.

sections.heading: Foods and Behaviors to Avoid (Irritating, Gas-Producing, Stool-Loosening)
sections.content:
Irritating foods

• Foods that contain strong spices and seasonings

• Foods that are excessively cold or hot

• Greasy foods, fried foods



Gas-producing foods and behaviors

• Foods: Legumes, onions, cabbage, cucumbers, broccoli, cauliflower, carbonated drinks

• Behaviors: Using a straw, smoking, chewing gum, etc. (behaviors that cause you to swallow a lot of air)



Foods that loosen stool

• Prune juice, heavily seasoned foods

sections.heading: High-Protein Balanced Diet
sections.content:
Include a protein dish at every meal

• Be sure to eat 1–2 types of meat, fish, eggs, or tofu at every meal.

• Formula for a balanced meal:

[ Porridge/rice/noodles/bread ] + [ Protein (meat/fish/eggs/tofu) ] + [ Vegetables ]



Eat nutritious snacks

• Eat a balanced variety of fruit and milk as snacks.

• Be sure to choose mainly allowed foods. (Example: nonfat/low-fat milk or lactose-free milk, 1 cup or less recommended)



Please consult a medical specialist or a registered dietitian before making any changes to your diet.
